qs.s: Subtract \(8\) to write the inequality as \(3x^2 - 10x - 8 > 0\), then factor as \((3x + 2)(x - 4) > 0\). Testing values outside the boundary points \(x = -\frac{2}{3}\) and \(x = 4\) yields \(x < -\frac{2}{3}\text{ or }x > 4\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x + 1)(3x - 2) > x^2 + 2x + 13\).
qs.s: Expanding the left side and moving all terms to one side gives \(2x^2 - x - 15 > 0\), which factors into \((2x + 5)(x - 3) > 0\). Testing points shows the inequality is satisfied outside the boundary points, giving \(x < -\frac{5}{2}\text{ or }x > 3\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(3x + 7) \ge 0\).
qs.s: The boundary points from \(x(3x + 7) = 0\) are \(x = -\frac{7}{3}\) and \(x = 0\). Since the parabola opens upward, the product is greater than or equal to zero outside the roots: \(x \le -\frac{7}{3}\text{ or }x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(2x - 9) > 0\).
qs.s: Solving \(x(2x - 9) = 0\) gives boundary points \(x = 0\) and \(x = \frac{9}{2}\). The expression is positive outside this interval, yielding \(x < 0\text{ or }x > \frac{9}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(4x - 3) < 0\).
qs.s: Setting \(x(4x - 3) = 0\) yields boundary points \(x = 0\) and \(x = \frac{3}{4}\). Testing values reveals the inequality is strictly satisfied between the roots, so \(0 < x < \frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(2x - 5) \le 0\).
qs.s: Set \(x(2x - 5) = 0\) to find boundary points at \(x = 0\) and \(x = \frac{5}{2}\). Testing values within each interval shows the expression is non-positive between the roots, giving \(0 \le x \le \frac{5}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(5x + 6) \le 0\).
qs.s: Setting \(x(5x + 6) = 0\) gives boundary points \(x = -\frac{6}{5}\) and \(x = 0\). Testing an interior value like \(x = -1\) satisfies the inequality, giving \(-\frac{6}{5} \le x \le 0\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x(x - 3) \le x + 4\).
qs.s: Expand and collect terms to obtain \(2x^2 - 7x - 4 \le 0\), which factors as \((2x + 1)(x - 4) \le 0\). Testing values between the boundary points \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) and \(x = 4\) yields \(-\frac{1}{2} \le x \le 4\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 3)^2 > 5x - 9\).
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging gives \(x^2 - 11x + 18 > 0\), which factors as \((x - 2)(x - 9) > 0\). Testing intervals outside boundary points \(2\) and \(9\) gives \(x < 2\text{ or }x > 9\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(4 - x(3x - 1) > 0\).
qs.s: Expanding gives \(-3x^2 + x + 4 > 0\), which can be rewritten as \(3x^2 - x - 4 < 0\) or \((3x - 4)(x + 1) < 0\). Testing values between the roots \(-1\) and \(\frac{4}{3}\) confirms the solution \(-1 < x < \frac{4}{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x^2 - 7x \le 15\).
qs.s: Rearrange to \(2x^2 - 7x - 15 \le 0\) and factor as \((2x + 3)(x - 5) \le 0\). Testing points shows the expression is non-positive on the closed interval between the boundary points \(-\frac{3}{2}\) and \(5\), so \(-\frac{3}{2} \le x \le 5\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(x + 5) \ge 2(x + 9)\).
qs.s: Expand and collect terms on one side to get \(x^2 + 3x - 18 \ge 0\), which factors into \((x + 6)(x - 3) \ge 0\). The boundary points are \(-6\) and \(3\), and testing intervals gives \(x \le -6\text{ or }x \ge 3\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 4x - 12 \le 0\)
qs.s: Write the inequality as \((x - 6)(x + 2) \le 0\). The boundary points are \(-2\) and \(6\), and testing values shows the solution set is \(-2 \le x \le 6\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 5x + 6 > 0\)
qs.s: Factoring yields \((x + 2)(x + 3) > 0\). Testing values across the boundary points \(-3\) and \(-2\) shows the expression is positive when \(x < -3 \text{ or } x > -2\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 3x - 10 \le 0\)
qs.s: Factoring the inequality gives \((x - 5)(x + 2) \le 0\). Testing intervals between and outside the boundary points \(x = -2\) and \(x = 5\) shows that the inequality holds for \(-2 \le x \le 5\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 7x + 12 \ge 0\)
qs.s: Factor the expression to get \((x - 3)(x - 4) \ge 0\). The boundary points are \(3\) and \(4\), and the inequality is satisfied outside of them, giving \(x \le 3 \text{ or } x \ge 4\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 2x - 8 < 0\)
qs.s: Factor the quadratic to obtain \((x + 4)(x - 2) < 0\). The roots of the boundary equation are \(-4\) and \(2\), and testing a point in each interval confirms the solution is \(-4 < x < 2\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x^2 - 5x - 3 \le 0\)
qs.s: Factor the quadratic into \((2x + 1)(x - 3) \le 0\). The boundary points are \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\) and \(x = 3\), so testing intervals gives \(-\frac{1}{2} \le x \le 3\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 4x \le 1\)
qs.s: Rewrite as \(x^2 - 4x - 1 \le 0\) and use the quadratic formula to find roots \(x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4(1)(-1)}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{5}\). Since the parabola opens upward, the inequality holds between the roots: \(2 - \sqrt{5} \le x \le 2 + \sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x + 2)^2 \ge 5x + 16\)
qs.s: Expand to get \(x^2 + 4x + 4 \ge 5x + 16\), then subtract \(5x + 16\) to get \(x^2 - x - 12 \ge 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 4)(x + 3) \ge 0\), which is satisfied for \(x \le -3 \text{ or } x \ge 4\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 1)(x + 4) < 6\)
qs.s: Expanding gives \(x^2 + 3x - 4 < 6\), which simplifies to \(x^2 + 3x - 10 < 0\). Factoring yields \((x + 5)(x - 2) < 0\), giving the solution \(-5 < x < 2\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(-2x^2 + 7x - 3 > 0\)
qs.s: Multiply through by \(-1\) and reverse the inequality sign to obtain \(2x^2 - 7x + 3 < 0\), which factors as \((2x - 1)(x - 3) < 0\). The boundary points are \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(3\), giving the solution \(\frac{1}{2} < x < 3\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 2x - 2 \ge 0\)
qs.s: The boundary points from \(x^2 + 2x - 2 = 0\) are \(x = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2} = -1 \pm \sqrt{3}\). Since the inequality is \(\ge 0\), the solution includes the outer intervals: \(x \le -1 - \sqrt{3} \text{ or } x \ge -1 + \sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 2x - 1 \le 0\)
qs.s: Solve \(x^2 - 2x - 1 = 0\) using the quadratic formula to find the boundary points \(x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4(1)(-1)}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}\). Since the parabola opens upward and the inequality is \(\le 0\), the solution is the closed interval between the roots: \(1 - \sqrt{2} \le x \le 1 + \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 4x - 2 > 0\)
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 + 4x - 2 = 0\) yields boundary points \(x = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2} = -2 \pm \sqrt{6}\). Testing \(x = 0\) gives \(-2 > 0\) (false), which means the outer regions satisfy the inequality: \(x < -2 - \sqrt{6} \text{ or } x > -2 + \sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 4x + 1 < 0\)
qs.s: Solve \(x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0\) to get boundary points \(x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}\). Testing \(x = 2\) gives \(2^2 - 4(2) + 1 = -3 < 0\), which is true, so the solution is \(2 - \sqrt{3} < x < 2 + \sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 6x + 7 \le 0\)
qs.s: Setting \(x^2 - 6x + 7 = 0\) gives \(x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 28}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{2}\). Testing \(x = 3\) yields \(3^2 - 6(3) + 7 = -2 \le 0\) (true), so the solution is \(3 - \sqrt{2} \le x \le 3 + \sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 2)^2 \le 3x + 1\)
qs.s: Expanding yields \(x^2 - 4x + 4 \le 3x + 1\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 7x + 3 \le 0\). The boundary roots are \(x = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 - 12}}{2} = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{37}}{2}\), giving the solution \(\frac{7 - \sqrt{37}}{2} \le x \le \frac{7 + \sqrt{37}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x(x - 3) \le 1\)
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging gives \(2x^2 - 6x - 1 \le 0\). The roots of \(2x^2 - 6x - 1 = 0\) are \(x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 4(2)(-1)}}{4} = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{11}}{2}\), and since the parabola opens upward, the inequality holds between the roots: \(\frac{3 - \sqrt{11}}{2} \le x \le \frac{3 + \sqrt{11}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3 - x^2 > 4x\)
qs.s: Rearranging gives \(-x^2 - 4x + 3 > 0\), or \(x^2 + 4x - 3 < 0\) after multiplying by \(-1\) and reversing the inequality sign. Solving \(x^2 + 4x - 3 = 0\) gives \(x = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4(1)(-3)}}{2} = -2 \pm \sqrt{7}\), so the solution is \(-2 - \sqrt{7} < x < -2 + \sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x^2 + 2 < 8x\)
qs.s: Rewrite as \(3x^2 - 8x + 2 < 0\). Using the quadratic formula, \(x = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 - 24}}{6} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{10}}{3}\), and since the inequality is \(< 0\) for an upward-opening parabola, the solution is \(\frac{4 - \sqrt{10}}{3} < x < \frac{4 + \sqrt{10}}{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 1)(x - 5) \ge 2x + 1\)
qs.s: Expanding gives \(x^2 - 6x + 5 \ge 2x + 1\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 8x + 4 \ge 0\). The roots are \(x = \frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 - 16}}{2} = 4 \pm 2\sqrt{3}\), so the solution is the outer intervals \(x \le 4 - 2\sqrt{3} \text{ or } x \ge 4 + 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x^2 - \sqrt{3}x - 2 < 0\)
qs.s: The equation \(3x^2 - \sqrt{3}x - 2 = 0\) has roots \(x = \frac{\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{3 - 4(3)(-2)}}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3} \pm 3\sqrt{3}}{6}\), which gives \(x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\) and \(x = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Since the parabola opens upward, the inequality is satisfied between the roots: \(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} < x < \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - \sqrt{5}x - 10 > 0\)
qs.s: The roots of \(x^2 - \sqrt{5}x - 10 = 0\) are \(x = \frac{\sqrt{5} \pm \sqrt{5 - 4(1)(-10)}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{5} \pm 3\sqrt{5}}{2}\), giving \(x = -\sqrt{5}\) and \(x = 2\sqrt{5}\). For \(> 0\), the solution is strictly outside the roots: \(x < -\sqrt{5} \text{ or } x > 2\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x^2 + 3\sqrt{2}x - 4 > 0\)
qs.s: The boundary points are found from \(2x^2 + 3\sqrt{2}x - 4 = 0\), giving \(x = \frac{-3\sqrt{2} \pm \sqrt{18 - 4(2)(-4)}}{4} = \frac{-3\sqrt{2} \pm 5\sqrt{2}}{4}\), so \(x = -2\sqrt{2}\) and \(x = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). For \(> 0\), the solution consists of the values outside the roots: \(x < -2\sqrt{2} \text{ or } x > \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + \sqrt{3}x - 6 \le 0\)
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 + \sqrt{3}x - 6 = 0\) yields \(x = \frac{-\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{3 - 4(1)(-6)}}{2} = \frac{-\sqrt{3} \pm 3\sqrt{3}}{2}\), which simplifies to \(x = -2\sqrt{3}\) and \(x = \sqrt{3}\). Because the parabola opens upward, the inequality \(\le 0\) holds on the closed interval between the roots: \(-2\sqrt{3} \le x \le \sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - \sqrt{2}x - 4 \ge 0\)
qs.s: Solving \(x^2 - \sqrt{2}x - 4 = 0\) gives \(x = \frac{\sqrt{2} \pm \sqrt{2 - 4(1)(-4)}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{2} \pm 3\sqrt{2}}{2}\), giving boundary points \(x = -\sqrt{2}\) and \(x = 2\sqrt{2}\). Since the inequality is \(\ge 0\), the solution includes the boundary points and the regions outside: \(x \le -\sqrt{2} \text{ or } x \ge 2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x(x + \sqrt{2}) + 5 > 9 - 2\sqrt{2}x\)
qs.s: Expanding and combining like terms yields \(3x^2 + 5\sqrt{2}x - 4 > 0\). The roots of the boundary equation are \(x = \frac{-5\sqrt{2} \pm \sqrt{50 - 4(3)(-4)}}{6} = \frac{-5\sqrt{2} \pm 7\sqrt{2}}{6}\), which are \(-2\sqrt{2}\) and \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\), so the solution is \(x < -2\sqrt{2} \text{ or } x > \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 2\sqrt{3})^2 \ge \sqrt{3}x + 30\)
qs.s: Expanding the square gives \(x^2 - 4\sqrt{3}x + 12 \ge \sqrt{3}x + 30\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 5\sqrt{3}x - 18 \ge 0\). The roots are \(x = \frac{5\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{75 - 4(1)(-18)}}{2} = \frac{5\sqrt{3} \pm 7\sqrt{3}}{2}\), giving \(-\sqrt{3}\) and \(6\sqrt{3}\), so the solution is \(x \le -\sqrt{3} \text{ or } x \ge 6\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(2x + \sqrt{3}) \le 6 - 2\sqrt{3}x\)
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging gives \(2x^2 + 3\sqrt{3}x - 6 \le 0\). The roots are \(x = \frac{-3\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{27 - 4(2)(-6)}}{4} = \frac{-3\sqrt{3} \pm 5\sqrt{3}}{4}\), giving \(-2\sqrt{3}\) and \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so the solution is \(-2\sqrt{3} \le x \le \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(10 - 2x^2 > x(x - \sqrt{5})\)
qs.s: Expanding and collecting all terms on the right yields \(3x^2 - \sqrt{5}x - 10 < 0\). The roots are \(x = \frac{\sqrt{5} \pm \sqrt{5 - 4(3)(-10)}}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{5} \pm 5\sqrt{5}}{6}\), which are \(-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}\) and \(\sqrt{5}\), giving \(-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3} < x < \sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(\frac{x^2 - 5}{3} \le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}x\)
qs.s: Multiplying both sides by \(6\) gives \(2x^2 - 10 \le 3\sqrt{2}x\), or \(2x^2 - 3\sqrt{2}x - 10 \le 0\). Its roots are \(x = \frac{3\sqrt{2} \pm \sqrt{18 - 4(2)(-10)}}{4} = \frac{3\sqrt{2} \pm 7\sqrt{2}}{4}\), which gives \(-\sqrt{2}\) and \(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\), so the solution is \(-\sqrt{2} \le x \le \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 3x + 10 > 0\)
qs.s: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = (-3)^2 - 4(1)(10) = -31 < 0\). Since \(a = 1 > 0\), the parabola lies entirely above the x-axis, making the inequality true for all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x^2 - x + 4 < 0\)
qs.s: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = (-1)^2 - 4(3)(4) = -47 < 0\). Since \(a = 3 > 0\), the graph never dips below the x-axis, so there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x^2 - 3x + 9 \ge 0\)
qs.s: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = (-3)^2 - 4(2)(9) = -63 < 0\). Since \(a = 2 > 0\), the parabola is always above the x-axis, so the solution is all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2x^2 + x + 3 < 0\)
qs.s: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = 1^2 - 4(2)(3) = -23 < 0\). Since \(a = 2 > 0\), the parabola opens upward and is always positive, so the inequality has no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x^2 + 2x + 5 \le 0\)
qs.s: The discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = 2^2 - 4(3)(5) = -56 < 0\). Because \(a = 3 > 0\), the quadratic expression is strictly positive for all real \(x\), so there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2(x - 1)^2 + 8 < x^2 + 2x\)
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging gives \(2x^2 - 4x + 10 < x^2 + 2x\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 6x + 10 < 0\). Because the discriminant is \(b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 40 = -4 < 0\) and \(a > 0\), the expression is always positive, yielding no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x + 1)^2 < 6x - 7\)
qs.s: Expanding gives \(x^2 + 2x + 1 < 6x - 7\), which rearranges to \(x^2 - 4x + 8 < 0\). With discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac = 16 - 32 = -16 < 0\) and \(a = 1 > 0\), the parabola is always positive, resulting in no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(2(x - 1)^2 \ge 2x - 3\)
qs.s: Expanding gives \(2x^2 - 4x + 2 \ge 2x - 3\), which simplifies to \(2x^2 - 6x + 5 \ge 0\). Because \(b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 40 = -4 < 0\) and \(a = 2 > 0\), the parabola never crosses below the x-axis, so the solution is all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x + 3)^2 - 4 > 4x\)
qs.s: Expanding and collecting like terms yields \(x^2 + 6x + 5 > 4x\), or \(x^2 + 2x + 5 > 0\). Since the discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0\) and \(a = 1 > 0\), the inequality is satisfied for all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 3)^2 \le 2x - 16\)
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging terms gives \(x^2 - 6x + 9 \le 2x - 16\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 8x + 25 \le 0\). Since \(b^2 - 4ac = 64 - 100 = -36 < 0\) and \(a = 1 > 0\), the expression is strictly positive, meaning there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 6x + 11 \le 0\).
qs.s: Rewriting the inequality as \((x + 3)^2 + 2 \le 0\), the left side has a minimum value of \(2\) and is never less than or equal to \(0\), so there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 4x + 5 > 0\).
qs.s: Completing the square gives \((x - 2)^2 + 1 > 0\), which is always true for all real numbers since \((x - 2)^2 \ge 0\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 + 2x + 3 < 0\).
qs.s: Since \(x^2 + 2x + 3 = (x + 1)^2 + 2\), the expression is always at least \(2\) and can never be negative, so there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 8x + 17 \ge 0\).
qs.s: Completing the square yields \((x - 4)^2 + 1 \ge 0\), which is satisfied by every real number because \((x - 4)^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0\).
qs.s: Completing the square gives \((x - 3)^2 + 1 > 0\), which is true for all real numbers because \((x - 3)^2 \ge 0\) for all \(x\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(3x^2 + 5 \ge 2(3x - 1)\).
qs.s: Expanding and rearranging gives \(3x^2 - 6x + 7 \ge 0\), which can be written as \(3(x - 1)^2 + 4 \ge 0\); because \(3(x - 1)^2 \ge 0\), this is true for all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(1 - 2x^2 \ge 4x + 5\).
qs.s: Rearranging gives \(-2x^2 - 4x - 4 \ge 0\), and dividing by \(-2\) reverses the inequality to \(x^2 + 2x + 2 \le 0\), which can be written as \((x + 1)^2 + 1 \le 0\); since \((x + 1)^2 + 1 \ge 1\), there is no solution.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(\frac{1}{2}x^2 - 3x + 5 > -1\).
qs.s: Adding \(1\) to both sides and multiplying by \(2\) yields \(x^2 - 6x + 12 > 0\), which completes to \((x - 3)^2 + 3 > 0\) and is satisfied for all real numbers.

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \((x - 2)(x - 4) \le 2x - 10\).
qs.s: Expanding and collecting all terms on the left gives \(x^2 - 8x + 18 \le 0\), or \((x - 4)^2 + 2 \le 0\), which is never true since the minimum value is \(2\).

qs.q: Solve the inequality: \(x(x - 6) + 12 > 2(x - 3)\).
qs.s: Expanding and moving all terms to the left gives \(x^2 - 8x + 18 > 0\), or \((x - 4)^2 + 2 > 0\), which holds for all real numbers.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for a manufacturer producing \(x\) hundred gadgets. Use the graph to determine the maximum profit the company can achieve.
qs.s: The maximum profit is the y-coordinate of the vertex of the parabola. The vertex is at \((4, 2)\), which corresponds to a maximum profit of 2 thousand dollars, or $2,000.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) of a company versus the number of units sold \(x\) (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the initial business expenses (fixed costs).
qs.s: Initial business expenses correspond to the loss incurred when zero units are sold (\(x = 0\)). Reading the graph at \(x = 0\) gives \(P(0) = -5\), which represents a loss of $5,000 dollars, so the expenses are $5,000.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for an apparel company as a function of the number of jackets sold \(x\) (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the company's initial business expenses.
qs.s: Initial business expenses equal the magnitude of the profit when no units are sold (\(x = 0\)). The vertical intercept is at \((0, -10)\), so the initial business expenses are $10,000.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) of a bakery as a function of the number of specialty cakes sold \(x\) (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the bakery's business expenses before any cakes are sold.
qs.s: Before any cakes are sold (\(x = 0\)), the profit is given by the vertical intercept at \((0, -3)\). This loss of $3,000 represents initial business expenses of $3,000.

qs.q: The graph displays the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for an electronics company, where \(x\) represents the number of devices sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the minimum number of devices the company must sell to break even.
qs.s: A business breaks even when its profit equals zero (\(P(x) = 0\)). The first x-intercept occurs at \(x = 2\), which represents \(2 \times 100 = 200\) devices.

qs.q: The graph displays the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for a business, where \(x\) is the number of units sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the interval of sales (in hundreds of units) over which the company's profit is strictly increasing.
qs.s: The profit graph is a downward-opening parabola with its vertex at \((4, 1)\). The function rises from the initial production level \(x = 0\) up to the vertex at \(x = 4\), so the interval of increase is \(0 \le x \le 4\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for a company, where \(x\) represents hundreds of units sold. If fixed business expenses increase by $3,000, shifting the entire profit graph downward by 3 units, use the graph to determine the new maximum profit.
qs.s: The vertex of the current profit curve is at \((4, 9)\), giving a maximum profit of $9,000. Shifting the curve downward by 3 units lowers the maximum profit to $9,000 - $3,000 = $6,000.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) for a startup company, where each unit on the vertical axis represents $2,000 and \(x\) represents sales (in hundreds of units). Use the graph to determine the total dollar increase in profit from zero sales (business expenses) to the point of maximum profit.
qs.s: At zero sales, the graph has a vertical intercept at \(y = -8\), and the vertex is at \(y = 1\). The vertical change is \(1 - (-8) = 9\) units, which corresponds to $9 \times $2,000 = $18,000.

qs.q: The graph displays the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) of a manufacturing firm, where \(x\) represents the number of units produced and sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the interval of units sold over which the firm operates with a positive profit (\(P(x) > 0\)).
qs.s: The profit is positive where the graph lies strictly above the x-axis, between the two break-even points at \(x = 3\) and \(x = 9\). Since \(x\) is in hundreds of units, this corresponds to \(300 < x < 900\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) of a manufacturing business, where \(x\) represents the number of items sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the range of items that must be sold for the company to achieve a profit of at least $5,000.
qs.s: A profit of at least $5,000 corresponds to \(y \ge 5\). The horizontal dashed line at \(y = 5\) intersects the parabola at \(x = 4\) and \(x = 12\), which corresponds to \(400\) to \(1,200\) items.

qs.q: A manufacturer graphs its profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) versus the production level \(x\) (in thousands of units). Use the graph to determine the profit interval.
qs.s: The business operates at a profit where \(P(x) > 0\). From the graph, the curve lies above the horizontal axis between the break-even points \(x = 3\) and \(x = 7\), so the profit interval is \(3 < x < 7\).

qs.q: The graph displays the monthly profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for an electronics retailer, where \(x\) is the number of devices sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to find the profit interval.
qs.s: The retailer operates at a profit when \(P(x) > 0\), which corresponds to the section of the parabola lying above the horizontal axis. Since the break-even points are at \(x = 4\) and \(x = 10\), the profit interval is \(4 < x < 10\).

qs.q: The graph shows a company's profit function, \(P(x)\), in thousands of dollars, where \(x\) is the number of items sold (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the profit interval (the interval of sales for which the company makes a profit, \(P(x) > 0\)).
qs.s: A company makes a profit when \(P(x) > 0\), meaning the graph lies strictly above the horizontal axis. Looking at the graph, the \(x\)-intercepts are at \(x = 2\) and \(x = 8\), so the profit interval is \(2 < x < 8\).

qs.q: The graph represents the profit \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) of an artisanal bakery selling \(x\) hundred specialty cakes per month. Use the graph to determine the profit interval.
qs.s: The profit interval consists of all production levels \(x\) for which \(P(x) > 0\). The curve lies strictly above the horizontal axis between \(x = 2\) and \(x = 10\), yielding the interval \(2 < x < 10\).

qs.q: The graph models a small business's profit, \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars), based on the quantity \(x\) of goods produced (in thousands of units). Use the graph to determine the profit interval.
qs.s: The profit interval is the set of \(x\)-values where \(P(x) > 0\). The graph crosses the horizontal axis at the break-even points \(x = 1\) and \(x = 5\) and is above the axis between them, giving \(1 < x < 5\).

qs.q: The graph shows a company's profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for producing \(x\) hundred units. Use the graph to determine the interval of production where the company makes a profit (\(P(x) > 0\)), but the profit is decreasing as production increases.
qs.s: The company makes a profit for \(2 < x < 8\), where the curve is above the horizontal axis. The profit reaches its peak at the vertex \(x = 5\) and decreases thereafter. Therefore, the profit is positive and decreasing on the interval \(5 < x < 8\).

qs.q: A company's profit \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) is graphed against the number of units sold \(x\) (in hundreds). The dashed horizontal line indicates a target profit of \(12,000 (\)y = 12$). Use the graph to determine the interval of units sold for which the profit meets or exceeds this target.
qs.s: The profit meets or exceeds $12,000 when \(P(x) \ge 12\), which corresponds to the portion of the curve on or above the dashed line \(y = 12\). The graph intersects the line at \(x = 8\) and \(x = 12\), so the interval is \(8 \le x \le 12\).

qs.q: The graph shows a company's profit \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) as a function of production \(x\) (in hundreds of units). The dashed line represents a target profit of \(6,000 (\)y = 6$). Use the graph to determine the interval of production for which the company meets or exceeds this target profit.
qs.s: The company meets or exceeds the target profit where \(P(x) \ge 6\), which is where the parabola lies on or above the dashed line \(y = 6\). Reading the points of intersection on the grid gives \(x = 3\) and \(x = 7\), so the required interval is \(3 \le x \le 7\).

qs.q: The graph shows a firm's profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for selling \(x\) hundred units. Use the graph to determine the interval of sales where the firm is profitable (\(P(x) > 0\)) and its profit is increasing.
qs.s: The firm is profitable where \(P(x) > 0\), which is between the break-even points \(x = 1\) and \(x = 7\). Profit increases up to the vertex at \(x = 4\). Thus, the interval where profit is both positive and increasing is \(1 < x < 4\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for a manufacturing company, where \(x\) represents hundreds of units produced. Use the graph to determine the profit interval (\(P(x) > 0\)) and the production level \(x\) that yields the maximum profit.
qs.s: The graph lies strictly above the horizontal axis between the break-even points \(x = 4\) and \(x = 12\), so the profit interval is \(4 < x < 12\). The vertex of the parabola is located at \((8, 8)\), so the profit is maximized at a production level of \(x = 8\) hundred units.

qs.q: The graph shows a company's profit \(P(x)\), in thousands of dollars, as a function of the number of items sold \(x\) (in hundreds). Use the graph to determine the maximum profit.
qs.s: The vertex of the parabola is located at \((4, 16)\), which gives the peak profit. Since \(P(x)\) is measured in thousands of dollars, the maximum profit is \(16 \times \$1\,000 = \$16\,000\).

qs.q: A student council sells tickets to a school event. The graph displays the profit \(P(x)\), in hundreds of dollars, based on the ticket price \(x\) in dollars. Use the graph to determine the maximum profit.
qs.s: The maximum occurs at the vertex \((3, 9)\). Since the profit axis is scaled in hundreds of dollars, the maximum profit is \(9 \times \$100 = \$900\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit \(P(x)\), in thousands of dollars, as a function of the production level \(x\) (in hundreds of units). Determine the maximum profit.
qs.s: The maximum value of the function occurs at the vertex \((4, 8)\). Since \(P(x)\) is in thousands of dollars, the maximum profit is \(8 \times \$1\,000 = \$8\,000\).

qs.q: The graph represents the daily profit \(P(x)\), in tens of dollars, of a bakery selling \(x\) custom cakes. Use the graph to determine the maximum profit.
qs.s: The vertex of the quadratic curve is at \((6, 9)\). Because \(P(x)\) is given in tens of dollars, the maximum profit is \(9 \times \$10 = \$90\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\), in dollars, for selling \(x\) handcrafted items. Use the graph to determine the maximum profit.
qs.s: The highest point on the graph is the vertex at \((5, 25)\). The \(y\)-value represents the profit, so the maximum profit is $25.

qs.q: The graph shows the weekly profit \(P(x)\), in hundreds of dollars, for a company producing \(x\) machines. By how much does the maximum profit exceed the profit achieved when producing 2 machines?
qs.s: The maximum profit at the vertex \((5, 25)\) is \(25\) hundred dollars ($2 500), while producing \(2\) machines yields \(16\) hundred dollars ($1 600) at \((2, 16)\). The difference is $2 500 - 1 600 = $900.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) as a function of the unit price \(x\) (in dollars). What unit price maximizes the profit, and what is that maximum profit?
qs.s: The vertex is at \((6, 18)\), where the \(x\)-coordinate represents the optimal price of $6 and the \(y\)-coordinate represents the maximum profit of \(18 \times \$1\,000 = \$18\,000\).

qs.q: The graph shows the profit \(P(x)\), in thousands of dollars, from selling \(x\) thousand units of a product. For what range of production \(x\) is the profit at least $12 000?
qs.s: Locating \(P(x) = 12\) on the vertical axis shows that the graph reaches or exceeds \(12\) between \(x = 4\) and \(x = 8\). Therefore, the profit is at least $12 000 for \(4 \le x \le 8\) thousand units.

qs.q: The graph models a company's profit \(P(x)\), in thousands of dollars, for producing \(x\) hundred items. The initial fixed cost is represented by the loss when production is zero. What is the total gain in profit from this initial fixed cost to the maximum profit?
qs.s: At \(x = 0\), the profit is \(-7\) thousand dollars (a $7 000 loss), and the maximum profit at the vertex \((4, 9)\) is $9 thousand dollars ($9 000). The total increase is \(9 - (-7) = 16\) thousand dollars, or $16 000.

qs.q: The graph shows the profit function \(P(x)\) (in thousands of dollars) for manufacturing \(x\) thousand units. Determine the range of units for which the company operates at a profit (where \(P(x) > 0\)), and state the maximum profit.
qs.s: The company earns a positive profit between the horizontal intercepts at \(x = 2\) and \(x = 14\). The maximum profit is given by the \(y\)-value at the vertex \((8, 18)\), which is \(18 \times \$1\,000 = \$18\,000\).

qs.q: In a table tennis tournament where each player plays every other player once, the total number of matches played by \(n\) players is given by \(M = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\), where \(n \ge 2\). For what values of \(n\) will the tournament have at least 66 matches?
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \ge 66\) gives \(n^2 - n - 132 \ge 0\), which factors as \((n - 12)(n + 11) \ge 0\). Since \(n \ge 2\), the inequality is satisfied when \(n \ge 12\).

qs.q: The length of a rectangular garden is 5 metres greater than its width, \(w\). The area of the garden is given by \(A = w(w + 5)\), where \(w > 0\). For what values of \(w\) will the area be greater than or equal to 84 square metres?
qs.s: Setting \(w(w + 5) \ge 84\) yields \(w^2 + 5w - 84 \ge 0\), which factors as \((w - 7)(w + 12) \ge 0\). Because width must be positive, the solution is \(w \ge 7\).

qs.q: If \(n\) is positive, then \(1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\). For what values of \(n\) will the sum \(1 + 2 + \cdots + n\) be greater than or equal to 105?
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2} \ge 105\) gives \(n^2 + n - 210 \ge 0\), which factors as \((n - 14)(n + 15) \ge 0\). Since \(n\) must be positive, the solution is \(n \ge 14\).

qs.q: The number of diagonals, \(D\), in an \(n\)-sided polygon is given by the formula \(D = \frac{n(n - 3)}{2}\), where \(n \ge 3\). For what values of \(n\) will a polygon have at least 90 diagonals?
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{n(n-3)}{2} \ge 90\) yields \(n^2 - 3n - 180 \ge 0\), which factors into \((n - 15)(n + 12) \ge 0\). Because \(n \ge 3\), the valid values are \(n \ge 15\).

qs.q: If \(n\) is positive, the sum of the first \(n\) positive even integers is given by \(2 + 4 + \cdots + 2n = n(n + 1)\). For what values of \(n\) will this sum be greater than or equal to 132?
qs.s: Setting \(n(n + 1) \ge 132\) gives \(n^2 + n - 132 \ge 0\), which factors into \((n - 11)(n + 12) \ge 0\). Since \(n > 0\), the inequality holds for \(n \ge 11\).

qs.q: The height \(h\), in metres, of a flare launched from the deck of a boat is given by \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 35t\), where \(t \ge 0\) is time in seconds. For what time interval is the flare at or above a height of 50 metres?
qs.s: Setting \(-5t^2 + 35t \ge 50\) and dividing by \(-5\) reverses the inequality to \(t^2 - 7t + 10 \le 0\). Factoring gives \((t - 2)(t - 5) \le 0\), which holds for \(2 \le t \le 5\).

qs.q: A rectangular swimming pool has dimensions 10 metres by 6 metres. A concrete walkway of uniform width \(x\) metres surrounds the pool, so that the total area is given by \(A = (2x + 10)(2x + 6)\), where \(x > 0\). For what values of \(x\) will the total area be greater than or equal to 140 square metres?
qs.s: Expanding the area gives \(4x^2 + 32x + 60 \ge 140\), which simplifies to \(4x^2 + 32x - 80 \ge 0\). Dividing by 4 yields \(x^2 + 8x - 20 \ge 0\), or \((x - 2)(x + 10) \ge 0\), so \(x \ge 2\) since \(x > 0\).

qs.q: A company models its daily revenue and cost functions in dollars as \(R(x) = 140x - x^2\) and \(C(x) = 20x + 1500\), where \(x\) is the number of units produced. For what values of \(x\) will the daily profit, \(P(x) = R(x) - C(x)\), be at least $1700?
qs.s: The profit inequality \((140x - x^2) - (20x + 1500) \ge 1700\) simplifies to \(-x^2 + 120x - 3200 \ge 0\). Multiplying by \(-1\) yields \(x^2 - 120x + 3200 \le 0\), which factors as \((x - 40)(x - 80) \le 0\), giving \(40 \le x \le 80\).

qs.q: If \(n\) is positive, then \(1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\). For what values of \(n\) will the sum \(1 + 2 + \cdots + n\) be at least 210 and at most 300?
qs.s: Setting \(210 \le \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \le 300\) gives \(n^2 + n - 420 \ge 0\) (yielding \(n \ge 20\)) and \(n^2 + n - 600 \le 0\) (yielding \(n \le 24\) for \(n > 0\)). Taking the intersection of both intervals yields \(20 \le n \le 24\).

qs.q: If \(n\) is a positive integer, the sum of the first \(n\) terms of an arithmetic sequence is given by \(S = \frac{n(3n + 1)}{2}\). For what values of \(n\) will this sum be greater than or equal to 155?
qs.s: Multiplying by 2 and rearranging gives \(3n^2 + n - 310 \ge 0\), which factors as \((3n + 31)(n - 10) \ge 0\). Since \(n\) must be positive, the solution is \(n \ge 10\).

exercises.name: Write a system of linear inequalities

qs.q: A bike shop stocks mountain bikes and road bikes. Let \(x\) be the number of mountain bikes and \(y\) be the number of road bikes. The owner decides to stock at least three times as many mountain bikes as road bikes. The shop must have at least 6 road bikes, and the floor space allows for no more than 40 bikes in total. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The floor limit of no more than 40 bikes gives \(x + y \le 40\). Stocking at least three times as many mountain bikes as road bikes gives \(x \ge 3y\), and having at least 6 road bikes gives \(y \ge 6\).

qs.q: A bakery bakes loaves of sourdough bread and rye bread each morning. Let \(x\) be the number of sourdough loaves and \(y\) be the number of rye loaves. The baker bakes at least twice as many loaves of sourdough as rye. The bakery must produce at least 15 loaves of rye bread, and the ovens can fit at most 75 loaves in total. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The oven capacity of at most 75 loaves gives \(x + y \le 75\). Baking at least twice as many sourdough as rye loaves gives \(x \ge 2y\), and requiring at least 15 rye loaves gives \(y \ge 15\).

qs.q: A parking lot provides spaces for standard vehicles and compact vehicles. Let \(x\) represent the number of standard spaces and \(y\) represent the number of compact spaces. The lot must have at least 10 compact spaces, and there are at least 4 times as many standard spaces as compact spaces. The entire lot can hold no more than 80 vehicles. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The lot capacity of no more than 80 vehicles gives \(x + y \le 80\). Having at least 4 times as many standard spaces as compact spaces gives \(x \ge 4y\), and having at least 10 compact spaces gives \(y \ge 10\).

qs.q: A florist creates bouquets containing roses and carnations. Let \(x\) be the number of roses and \(y\) be the number of carnations. The florist uses at least twice as many roses as carnations. The bouquet must contain at least 12 carnations, and the vase can hold at most 45 flowers in total. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The vase capacity of at most 45 flowers gives \(x + y \le 45\). Using at least twice as many roses as carnations gives \(x \ge 2y\), and including at least 12 carnations gives \(y \ge 12\).

qs.q: An electronics store sells laptops and desktop computers. Let \(x\) represent the number of laptops and \(y\) represent the number of desktop computers. The store stocks at least three times as many laptops as desktop computers. It must carry at least 8 desktop computers, and the display area has room for no more than 50 computers in total. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The display capacity of no more than 50 computers gives \(x + y \le 50\). Stocking at least three times as many laptops as desktops gives \(x \ge 3y\), and having at least 8 desktops gives \(y \ge 8\).

qs.q: An event coordinator is renting standard tables and deluxe tables. Let \(x\) be the number of standard tables and \(y\) be the number of deluxe tables. Standard tables cost $15 each and deluxe tables cost $25 each, with a total rental budget of at most $600. The banquet hall can hold no more than 32 tables in total. The coordinator needs at least twice as many standard tables as deluxe tables, and must have at least 5 deluxe tables. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The budget limit gives \(15x + 25y \le 600\) and the space limit gives \(x + y \le 32\). Needing at least twice as many standard as deluxe tables gives \(x \ge 2y\), and having at least 5 deluxe tables gives \(y \ge 5\).

qs.q: A farmer allocates land to plant corn (\(x\) acres) and soybeans (\(y\) acres). The farmer has at most 180 acres of land available. Seed and fertilizer cost $120 per acre for corn and $80 per acre for soybeans, and the total budget is at most $18\,000. The farmer plans to plant at least 20 acres more corn than soybeans, and must plant at least 30 acres of soybeans. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The land limit gives \(x + y \le 180\) and the budget limit gives \(120x + 80y \le 18000\). Planting at least 20 acres more corn than soybeans gives \(x \ge y + 20\), and the soybean minimum gives \(y \ge 30\).

qs.q: A freight truck is being loaded with small crates and large crates. Let \(x\) represent the number of small crates and \(y\) represent the number of large crates. Each small crate weighs 40 kg and each large crate weighs 90 kg, with a maximum weight capacity of 3600 kg. The truck can carry no more than 60 crates in total. The number of small crates must be at least 10 more than twice the number of large crates, and there must be at least 8 large crates. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The weight limit gives \(40x + 90y \le 3600\) and the total crate limit gives \(x + y \le 60\). The condition that small crates must be at least 10 more than twice the large crates gives \(x \ge 2y + 10\), and having at least 8 large crates gives \(y \ge 8\).

qs.q: A college student works two part-time jobs: tutoring for \(x\) hours per week and lifeguarding for \(y\) hours per week. She can work no more than 25 hours per week in total. Tutoring pays $20 per hour and lifeguarding pays $14 per hour, and she must earn at least $380 per week. Furthermore, she must tutor for at least 12 hours per week and wants to work at least as many hours tutoring as lifeguarding. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The total hours restriction is \(x + y \le 25\), while the minimum earnings requirement is \(20x + 14y \ge 380\). Tutoring for at least 12 hours is \(x \ge 12\), and working at least as many hours tutoring as lifeguarding is \(x \ge y\).

qs.q: A factory produces two scooter models: Model A (\(x\) units) and Model B (\(y\) units). Producing one Model A takes 3 hours of assembly and 2 hours of painting, while producing one Model B takes 5 hours of assembly and 2 hours of painting. There are at most 240 assembly hours and at most 120 painting hours available each week. The factory must produce at least 15 units of Model A and at least twice as many units of Model A as Model B. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The assembly constraint is \(3x + 5y \le 240\) and the painting constraint is \(2x + 2y \le 120\). Producing at least twice as many Model A as Model B gives \(x \ge 2y\), and producing at least 15 Model A units gives \(x \ge 15\).

exercises.name: Write a system of linear inequalities

qs.q: A farmer has at most 180 acres of farmland to plant with corn (\(x\)) and soybeans (\(y\)). The farmer decides to plant at least 30 acres of corn, and at least three times as many acres of soybeans as corn. Which system of linear inequalities describes the possible acreages?
qs.s: The total area cannot exceed 180 acres, so \(x + y \le 180\). Planting at least 30 acres of corn gives \(x \ge 30\), and planting at least three times that area in soybeans gives \(y \ge 3x\).

qs.q: A community center has up to $9000 to allocate between after-school tutoring (\(x\)) and sports programs (\(y\)). They must allocate at least $1500 to tutoring, and at least four times as much to sports programs as to tutoring. Which system of inequalities models the funding distribution?
qs.s: Total funding is at most $9000, so \(x + y \le 9000\). Tutoring needs at least $1500, meaning \(x \ge 1500\), and sports programs require at least four times that amount, so \(y \ge 4x\).

qs.q: An athlete trains for a triathlon by running (\(x\) hours) and swimming (\(y\) hours). She can train for at most 18 hours per week, plans to run for at least 4 hours, and wants the swimming time to be at least twice the running time. Which system of inequalities represents her weekly training hours?
qs.s: Total weekly training time is at most 18 hours, giving \(x + y \le 18\). Running at least 4 hours gives \(x \ge 4\), and swimming at least twice as much as running gives \(y \ge 2x\).

qs.q: A store manager has a budget of at most $12 000 to purchase standard laptops (\(x\)) and premium laptops (\(y\)). The store must spend at least $2500 on standard laptops, and at least twice the amount spent on standard laptops must be spent on premium laptops. Which system of inequalities represents the amounts that can be spent?
qs.s: The budget restricts total spending to \(x + y \le 12\,000\). Spending at least $2500 on standard laptops gives \(x \ge 2500\), and spending at least twice that on premium laptops gives \(y \ge 2x\).

qs.q: An investor has up to $25 000 to invest in government bonds (\(x\)) and mutual funds (\(y\)). She wants to invest at least $5000 in government bonds, and at least twice as much in mutual funds as in government bonds. Which system of linear inequalities models this investment plan?
qs.s: The total investment cannot exceed $25 000, giving \(x + y \le 25\,000\). Investing at least $5000 in bonds requires \(x \ge 5000\), and investing at least twice that amount in mutual funds gives \(y \ge 2x\).

qs.q: A community theater sells student tickets for $5 each (\(x\)) and general admission tickets for $12 each (\(y\)). The auditorium seats a maximum of 450 people. The organizers want to bring in at least $3000 in total revenue, and they require that the number of student tickets sold is at least 50 more than the number of general admission tickets sold. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: Auditorium capacity limits total tickets to \(x + y \le 450\), and the revenue goal requires \(5x + 12y \ge 3000\). Requiring at least 50 more student tickets than general admission tickets gives \(x \ge y + 50\).

qs.q: A small manufacturer produces two models of chairs: standard (\(x\)) and ergonomic (\(y\)). Each standard chair takes 2 hours of assembly time and each ergonomic chair takes 5 hours. The factory has at most 300 hours of assembly time available this month. The manager requires at least 10 standard chairs to be produced, and the number of ergonomic chairs must be at least 5 more than twice the number of standard chairs. Which system of linear inequalities models this production schedule?
qs.s: Assembly time is limited by \(2x + 5y \le 300\). Producing at least 10 standard chairs gives \(x \ge 10\), and producing at least 5 more ergonomic chairs than twice the standard chairs translates to \(y \ge 2x + 5\).

qs.q: An investor has up to $50 000 to divide between a municipal bond fund (\(x\)) and a high-yield corporate fund (\(y\)). She wants to invest at least $8000 in municipal bonds. The amount in the high-yield fund must be at least $4000 more than three times the amount in municipal bonds, but cannot exceed $36 000. Which system of linear inequalities models this investment?
qs.s: The total investment cannot exceed \(50 000 (\)x + y \le 50\,000$), with at least $8000 in bonds (\(x \ge 8000\)). The high-yield fund requires \(y \ge 3x + 4000\) and has an upper limit of \(y \le 36\,000\).

qs.q: A caterer prepares vegetarian meals (\(x\)) and chicken meals (\(y\)) for an event. Preparing each vegetarian meal costs $6 and each chicken meal costs $9, with a total budget of at most $1800. The client requires a minimum of 150 meals in total, and the number of chicken meals must be at least twice the number of vegetarian meals. Which system of linear inequalities represents these requirements?
qs.s: The budget restriction is \(6x + 9y \le 1800\), while the requirement of at least 150 total meals gives \(x + y \ge 150\). Having at least twice as many chicken meals as vegetarian meals gives \(y \ge 2x\).

qs.q: A clothing manufacturer produces jackets and pairs of trousers. Making a jacket takes 8 hours of sewing, and making a pair of trousers takes 3 hours. There are 5 tailors, each working a maximum of 36 hours per week. If the manufacturer produces 15 jackets, what is the maximum number of pairs of trousers that can be produced?
qs.s: The total hours available are \(5 \times 36 = 180\), so \(8x + 3y \le 180\). For \(x = 15\), \(8(15) + 3y \le 180 \implies 3y \le 60\), which allows a maximum of \(y = 20\) pairs of trousers.

qs.q: A bakery produces custom cakes and trays of pastries. A custom cake takes 6 hours to decorate, and a tray of pastries takes 2 hours. The bakery employs 4 decorators, each working at most 30 hours per week. If the bakery decorates 11 custom cakes this week, what is the maximum number of pastry trays they can produce?
qs.s: The total labour is \(4 \times 30 = 120\) hours, giving the inequality \(6x + 2y \le 120\). For \(x = 11\), \(6(11) + 2y \le 120 \implies 2y \le 54\), which gives a maximum of \(y = 27\) pastry trays.

qs.q: An electronics repair shop repairs laptops and smartphones. Each laptop repair requires 3 hours of labour, and each smartphone repair requires 1 hour. The shop has 3 technicians who each work up to 40 hours per week. If the shop must repair at least 45 smartphones, what is the maximum number of laptops they can repair?
qs.s: The total labour available is \(3 \times 40 = 120\) hours, with constraint \(3x + y \le 120\). Setting \(y = 45\), we have \(3x + 45 \le 120 \implies 3x \le 75\), giving a maximum of \(x = 25\) laptops.

qs.q: A pottery studio makes large ceramic planters and small bowls. A planter takes 12 hours of labour to make and a bowl takes 3 hours. The studio employs 3 potters, each working a maximum of 40 hours per week. If the studio makes 6 planters this week, what is the maximum number of bowls they can produce?
qs.s: The total available labour is \(3 \times 40 = 120\) hours, so \(12x + 3y \le 120\). Substituting \(x = 6\) gives \(72 + 3y \le 120 \implies 3y \le 48\), giving a maximum of \(y = 16\) bowls.

qs.q: A bicycle workshop makes road bikes and mountain bikes. A road bike takes 8 hours of labour to assemble and a mountain bike takes 5 hours. The shop employs 6 mechanics, each working a maximum of 35 hours per week. If the workshop produces 15 road bikes in a week, what is the maximum number of mountain bikes they can produce?
qs.s: The total available labour is \(6 \times 35 = 210\) hours, so \(8x + 5y \le 210\). Substituting \(x = 15\) gives \(8(15) + 5y \le 210 \implies 5y \le 90\), so \(y \le 18\) mountain bikes.

qs.q: A fabrication shop produces standard gates and decorative grilles. The shop has 4 senior welders working 40 hours each per week, and 2 apprentices working 30 hours each per week. Before production begins, 28 hours of total shop labour are used for maintenance. Each gate requires 12 hours of welding and each grille requires 8 hours. If the shop must produce at least 7 gates, what is the maximum number of grilles that can be completed?
qs.s: Net welding hours available are \((4 \times 40 + 2 \times 30) - 28 = 192\) hours. With \(x = 7\) gates, \(12(7) + 8y \le 192 \implies 84 + 8y \le 192 \implies 8y \le 108 \implies y \le 13.5\), so the maximum integer is 13.

qs.q: A commercial printer produces full-colour brochures and spiral-bound manuals in batches. A batch of brochures requires 4 hours on the printing press and 1 hour on the binding machine. A batch of manuals requires 6 hours on the press and 5 hours on the binding machine. The press is available for at most 240 hours and the binding machine for at most 110 hours. If the printer must produce at least 12 batches of manuals, what is the maximum number of batches of brochures that can be produced?
qs.s: The press constraint gives \(4b + 6(12) \le 240 \implies 4b \le 168 \implies b \le 42\), and the binding constraint gives \(b + 5(12) \le 110 \implies b \le 50\). The tighter constraint limits the output to a maximum of 42 batches of brochures.

qs.q: A workshop produces dining tables and benches. Each table requires 6 hours of cutting and 4 hours of assembly. Each bench requires 3 hours of cutting and 5 hours of assembly. The cutting department has at most 180 hours available per week, and the assembly department has at most 190 hours available per week. If the shop produces 15 tables this week, what is the maximum number of benches that can be produced?
qs.s: Cutting requires \(6(15) + 3y \le 180 \implies 3y \le 90 \implies y \le 30\), while assembly requires \(4(15) + 5y \le 190 \implies 5y \le 130 \implies y \le 26\). Satisfying both constraints limits the production to a maximum of 26 benches.

qs.q: A watercraft company makes kayaks and canoes. Each kayak requires 6 hours of molding and 3 hours of finishing. Each canoe requires 9 hours of molding and 2 hours of finishing. The factory has a maximum of 180 hours of molding time and 72 hours of finishing time available this month. If the company must produce at least 15 canoes, what is the maximum number of kayaks they can produce?
qs.s: Molding gives \(6x + 9(15) \le 180 \implies 6x \le 45 \implies x \le 7.5\), while finishing gives \(3x + 2(15) \le 72 \implies 3x \le 42 \implies x \le 14\). Both are satisfied when \(x \le 7\) kayaks.

qs.q: A leather goods company manufactures backpacks and messenger bags. Each backpack requires 5 hours of labour and 14 square feet of leather. Each messenger bag requires 3 hours of labour and 8 square feet of leather. The company has 8 workers, each working 35 hours per week, and a supply of 650 square feet of leather. If the company makes 25 backpacks, what is the maximum number of messenger bags it can produce?
qs.s: Total labour is \(8 \times 35 = 280\) hours, so \(5(25) + 3y \le 280 \implies y \le 51.67\). Leather available gives \(14(25) + 8y \le 650 \implies 8y \le 300 \implies y \le 37.5\). The maximum whole number of bags satisfying both is 37.

qs.q: A landscaper has a maximum budget of $150 to spend on materials. A bag of mulch costs $15 and a bag of decorative stone costs $25. If the landscaper must buy at least two bags of mulch and at least two bags of stone, how many different combinations can be purchased?
qs.s: The inequality is \(15m + 25s \le 150\), which simplifies to \(3m + 5s \le 30\) with integers \(m \ge 2\) and \(s \ge 2\). For \(s = 2\), \(m \in \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) (5 choices); for \(s = 3\), \(m \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}\) (4 choices); for \(s = 4\), \(m \in \{2, 3\}\) (2 choices), yielding \(5 + 4 + 2 = 11\) combinations.

qs.q: A community centre has at most $360 to spend on folding chairs and tables. Chairs cost $20 each and tables cost $60 each. If they must purchase at least two chairs and at least two tables, how many different combinations of chairs and tables can they buy?
qs.s: The constraint is \(20c + 60t \le 360\), or \(c + 3t \le 18\) with integers \(c \ge 2\) and \(t \ge 2\). For \(t = 2\), \(c \in [2, 12]\) (11 options); for \(t = 3\), \(c \in [2, 9]\) (8 options); for \(t = 4\), \(c \in [2, 6]\) (5 options); for \(t = 5\), \(c \in [2, 3]\) (2 options), giving \(11 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 26\) combinations.

qs.q: A school has a maximum budget of $1200 to purchase new technology. Laptops cost $200 each and tablets cost $150 each. If the school must purchase at least one laptop and at least two tablets, how many different combinations of laptops and tablets can they buy?
qs.s: The inequality is \(200L + 150T \le 1200\), which simplifies to \(4L + 3T \le 24\) with integers \(L \ge 1\) and \(T \ge 2\). Testing possible values of \(T\) gives 4 choices for \(T = 2\), 3 choices each for \(T = 3\) and \(T = 4\), 2 choices for \(T = 5\), and 1 choice for \(T = 6\), for a total of \(4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 13\) combinations.

qs.q: A bakery has a budget of at most $160 for ingredients. A sack of flour costs $12 and a sack of sugar costs $20. If the baker must purchase at least two sacks of flour and at least two sacks of sugar, how many different combinations of sacks can be purchased?
qs.s: The inequality is \(12f + 20s \le 160\), which simplifies to \(3f + 5s \le 40\) with integers \(f \ge 2\) and \(s \ge 2\). For \(s = 2\), there are 9 values of \(f\); for \(s = 3\), 7 values; for \(s = 4\), 5 values; for \(s = 5\), 4 values; and for \(s = 6\), 2 values, totaling \(9 + 7 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 27\) combinations.

qs.q: A sports club has a maximum of $200 to spend on balls. Soccer balls cost $20 each and basketballs cost $30 each. If the club must purchase at least two soccer balls and at least two basketballs, how many different combinations of balls can they buy?
qs.s: The inequality is \(20s + 30b \le 200\), or \(2s + 3b \le 20\) with integers \(s \ge 2\) and \(b \ge 2\). Testing values of \(b\) gives 6 options for \(b = 2\), 4 for \(b = 3\), 3 for \(b = 4\), and 1 for \(b = 5\), giving a total of \(6 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 14\) combinations.

qs.q: An art teacher has a budget of at most $90 to buy packs of paintbrushes for $6 each and sketchbooks for $8 each. The teacher must buy at least 11 items in total, including at least 3 packs of paintbrushes and at least 4 sketchbooks. How many different combinations can the teacher buy?
qs.s: The constraints are \(3p + 4s \le 45\), \(p + s \ge 11\), \(p \ge 3\), and \(s \ge 4\). Testing values of \(s\) from 4 to 9 yields 3 options each for \(s = 4, 5, 6\), 2 options each for \(s = 7, 8\), and 1 option for \(s = 9\) (\(p = 3\)), for a total of \(3 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 14\) combinations.

qs.q: A print shop charges a flat setup fee of $50 plus $10 per T-shirt and $25 per hoodie. A club has a maximum budget of $260 and must order at least 5 T-shirts and at least 4 hoodies. How many different combinations of T-shirts and hoodies can the club order?
qs.s: Subtracting the setup fee gives \(10t + 25h \le 210\), or \(2t + 5h \le 42\) with \(t \ge 5\) and \(h \ge 4\). For \(h = 4\), \(t \in [5, 11]\) (7 options); for \(h = 5\), \(t \in [5, 8]\) (4 options); and for \(h = 6\), \(t \in [5, 6]\) (2 options), giving \(7 + 4 + 2 = 13\) combinations.

qs.q: A gym has a rack with a maximum weight capacity of 180 kg. The gym wants to store 10 kg plates and 25 kg plates on it. They must place at least two 25 kg plates on the rack, and the number of 10 kg plates must be at least twice the number of 25 kg plates. How many different combinations of plates can be stored?
qs.s: The constraints are \(10x + 25y \le 180\) (or \(2x + 5y \le 36\)), \(x \ge 2y\), and \(y \ge 2\). For \(y = 2\), \(x \in [4, 13]\) (10 options); for \(y = 3\), \(x \in [6, 10]\) (5 options); and for \(y = 4\), \(x = 8\) (1 option), giving a total of \(10 + 5 + 1 = 16\) combinations.

qs.q: A company has at most $4800 to buy desktop computers and laptops. Desktops cost $400 each and laptops cost $600 each. The company must purchase a total of at least 9 computers, with at least 2 desktops and at least 2 laptops. How many different combinations of desktops and laptops can they purchase?
qs.s: The system of inequalities is \(2d + 3L \le 24\), \(d + L \ge 9\), \(d \ge 2\), and \(L \ge 2\). Evaluating integer values gives 3 combinations for \(L = 2\) (\(d \in \{7, 8, 9\}\)), 2 for \(L = 3\) (\(d \in \{6, 7\}\)), 2 for \(L = 4\) (\(d \in \{5, 6\}\)), 1 for \(L = 5\) (\(d = 4\)), and 1 for \(L = 6\) (\(d = 3\)), for a total of \(3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9\) combinations.

qs.q: A drama department has a maximum budget of $350 for costumes. Adult costumes cost $40 each and child costumes cost $25 each. The department must purchase at least 2 child costumes and at least as many adult costumes as child costumes. How many different combinations of costumes can they buy?
qs.s: The constraints are \(8a + 5c \le 70\), \(a \ge c\), and \(c \ge 2\). For \(c = 2\), \(a \in [2, 7]\) (6 options); for \(c = 3\), \(a \in [3, 6]\) (4 options); for \(c = 4\), \(a \in [4, 6]\) (3 options); and for \(c = 5\), \(a = 5\) (1 option), yielding \(6 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 14\) combinations.

exercises.name: Write a system of linear inequalities

qs.q: A delivery van can carry a maximum of 80 parcels. Small parcels (\(x\)) weigh 4 kg each, and large parcels (\(y\)) weigh 15 kg each. By safety regulations, the total cargo weight cannot exceed 600 kg. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: The van can hold no more than 80 parcels, so \(x + y \le 80\). The weight limit restricts total weight to \(4x + 15y \le 600\), with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: An event organizer is selling tickets for a concert in a hall that holds a maximum of 500 people. General admission tickets (\(x\)) cost $30 each and VIP tickets (\(y\)) cost $75 each. The organizers must raise at least $21 000 in ticket sales to cover production costs. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: The maximum capacity of the hall limits total attendees to \(x + y \le 500\). Raising at least $21 000 from ticket sales requires \(30x + 75y \ge 21\,000\), with non-negativity constraints \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A bookstore has shelf space for no more than 120 new books. It costs the store $8 to purchase each paperback book (\(x\)) and $20 to purchase each hardcover book (\(y\)). The store has a budget of at most $1600 to purchase these books. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: Shelf capacity restricts total books to \(x + y \le 120\). At $8 per paperback and $20 per hardcover, the total cost cannot exceed $1600, giving \(8x + 20y \le 1600\), along with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A farmer has up to 150 hectares of land to plant wheat and barley. It costs $120 per hectare to plant wheat (\(x\)) and $90 per hectare to plant barley (\(y\)). The farmer can spend no more than $15 300 on planting. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: The total land planted cannot exceed 150 hectares, so \(x + y \le 150\). At $120 per hectare for wheat and $90 per hectare for barley, the total cost cannot exceed $15 300, which gives \(120x + 90y \le 15\,300\) along with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A carpenter builds wooden chairs (\(x\)) and wooden tables (\(y\)). The carpenter can build at most 40 pieces of furniture this month. Each chair requires 5 board feet of oak and each table requires 18 board feet of oak. The carpenter has a stock of at most 360 board feet of oak available. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: The total number of furniture items cannot exceed 40, giving \(x + y \le 40\). The total lumber used cannot exceed 360 board feet, yielding \(5x + 18y \le 360\), with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A workshop manufactures standard skateboards (\(x\)) and pro skateboards (\(y\)). Materials cost $25 per standard board and $45 per pro board, with a daily budget of at most $1200. Assembly takes 40 minutes per standard board and 75 minutes per pro board, with at most 25 hours of labor available each day. In addition, the workshop must produce at least 20 total skateboards daily. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: Converting 25 hours to minutes gives \(25 \times 60 = 1500\) minutes, producing \(40x + 75y \le 1500\). Combining this with the minimum production \(x + y \ge 20\), budget \(25x + 45y \le 1200\), and \(x \ge 0, y \ge 0\) models the situation.

qs.q: A manufacturer blends Grain (\(x\) kilograms) and Meat (\(y\) kilograms) to produce a batch of pet food that cannot exceed 500 kg in total mass. Grain provides 2 units of protein and 5 units of carbohydrates per kilogram. Meat provides 8 units of protein and 1 unit of carbohydrates per kilogram. The batch must provide at least 1600 units of protein and at least 1000 units of carbohydrates. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: Total mass cannot exceed 500 kg, giving \(x + y \le 500\). Summing protein yields \(2x + 8y \ge 1600\) and summing carbohydrates yields \(5x + y \ge 1000\), with non-negativity conditions \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A school club prepares two types of gift baskets: fruit baskets (\(x\)) and snack baskets (\(y\)). Each fruit basket costs $12 for the container plus $18 for the contents, and sells for $45. Each snack basket costs $8 for the container plus $14 for the contents, and sells for $35. The club has at most $1500 to spend on making baskets, needs to generate at least $3150 in sales revenue, and can store no more than 80 baskets in total. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: The total cost per fruit basket is \(12 + 18 = 30\) and per snack basket is \(8 + 14 = 22\), giving \(30x + 22y \le 1500\). Together with the storage limit \(x + y \le 80\) and revenue goal \(45x + 35y \ge 3150\) (with \(x \ge 0, y \ge 0\)), this completely models the constraints.

qs.q: A landscaper has a total budget of $3800 to install \(x\) flowerbeds and \(y\) vegetable patches, which includes a fixed equipment rental fee of $200. It costs $150 to install each flowerbed and $240 to install each vegetable patch. The customer requires at least 12 total garden plots, and the number of flowerbeds must be at least three times the number of vegetable patches. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation, where \(y \ge 0\)?
qs.s: Subtracting the $200 equipment rental leaves \(3800 - 200 = 3600\), yielding \(150x + 240y \le 3600\). The requirement of at least 12 plots is \(x + y \ge 12\), and having at least three times as many flowerbeds as vegetable patches gives \(x \ge 3y\) with \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A fruit grower has 120 acres of land available to plant apple trees (\(x\) acres) and peach trees (\(y\) acres). It costs $600 per acre to plant apple trees and $450 per acre to plant peach trees, with a budget of no more than $63 000. To fulfill existing contracts, the grower must plant at least 30 acres of apple trees, and the acreage of peach trees cannot exceed twice the acreage of apple trees. Which system of linear inequalities models this situation?
qs.s: The total land gives \(x + y \le 120\), the budget gives \(600x + 450y \le 63\,000\), the apple quota gives \(x \ge 30\), and peach acreage cannot exceed twice apple acreage gives \(y \le 2x\), with \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: A rancher constructs a rectangular corral along a straight riverbank, requiring no fencing along the water. Using 100 ft of fencing for the other three sides, for what values of the width (perpendicular to the riverbank) will the enclosed area be at most 800 sq ft?
qs.a: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 10\text{ ft}\) or \(40\text{ ft} \le w < 50\text{ ft}\)
d: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 20\text{ ft}\) or \(30\text{ ft} \le w < 50\text{ ft}\)
qs.s: The length is \(100 - 2w\), so the area inequality is \(w(100 - 2w) \le 800\), which simplifies to \(w^2 - 50w + 400 \ge 0\), or \((w - 10)(w - 40) \ge 0\). Combining this with the physical bounds \(0 < w < 50\) yields \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 10\text{ ft}\) or \(40\text{ ft} \le w < 50\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rectangular outdoor play area at a daycare is bounded on one side by the school building and enclosed on the other three sides by 70 m of fencing. For what values of the width (perpendicular to the building) is the enclosed area strictly less than 500 m\(^2\)?
qs.a: \(0\text{ m} < w < 10\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} < w < 35\text{ m}\)
d: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} \le w < 35\text{ m}\)
qs.s: With length \(l = 70 - 2w\), the inequality is \(w(70 - 2w) < 500\), which rearranges to \(w^2 - 35w + 250 > 0\), factoring into \((w - 10)(w - 25) > 0\). Taking the physical domain \(0 < w < 35\) gives \(0\text{ m} < w < 10\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} < w < 35\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular storage yard is to be built against the side of a warehouse using 160 ft of fencing for the remaining three sides. If the width is perpendicular to the warehouse, for what values of the width will the enclosed area be at least 3000 sq ft?
d: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 30\text{ ft}\) or \(50\text{ ft} \le w < 80\text{ ft}\)
qs.s: The length is \(160 - 2w\), giving \(w(160 - 2w) \ge 3000\), which simplifies to \(w^2 - 80w + 1500 \le 0\). Factoring gives \((w - 30)(w - 50) \le 0\), so \(30\text{ ft} \le w \le 50\text{ ft}\), which naturally lies within the domain \(0 < w < 80\).

qs.q: A rectangular vegetable garden is to be fenced along the side of a house, so no fencing is needed on that side. Using 80 m of fencing for the remaining three sides, for what values of the width (the side perpendicular to the house) will the enclosed area be less than or equal to 750 m\(^2\)?
qs.a: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 15\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} \le w < 40\text{ m}\)
d: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(30\text{ m} \le w < 40\text{ m}\)
qs.s: The length is \(80 - 2w\), so \(w(80 - 2w) \le 750\), which simplifies to \(w^2 - 40w + 375 \ge 0\) and factors as \((w - 15)(w - 25) \ge 0\). Since \(w > 0\) and \(80 - 2w > 0\) gives \(w < 40\), the solution is \(0\text{ m} < w \le 15\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} \le w < 40\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular chicken pen is built along the side of a barn using 60 m of wire mesh for the other three sides. If the width is perpendicular to the barn, for what values of the width will the enclosed area be at most 250 m\(^2\)?
qs.a: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 5\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} \le w < 30\text{ m}\)
d: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(20\text{ m} \le w < 30\text{ m}\)
qs.s: The length is \(60 - 2w\), so \(w(60 - 2w) \le 250\), which simplifies to \(w^2 - 30w + 125 \ge 0\) and factors as \((w - 5)(w - 25) \ge 0\). Incorporating the physical conditions \(0 < w < 30\) gives \(0\text{ m} < w \le 5\text{ m}\) or \(25\text{ m} \le w < 30\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A free-standing rectangular storage yard is to be enclosed on all four sides with a total budget of $1200. Fencing costs $15 per meter for the two widths and $20 per meter for the two lengths. For what values of the width will the total enclosed area be at most 225 m\(^2\)?
qs.a: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(30\text{ m} \le w < 40\text{ m}\)
d: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(30\text{ m} \le w < 60\text{ m}\)
qs.s: The budget is \(2(15)w + 2(20)l = 1200\), giving \(l = 30 - \frac{3}{4}w\) and domain \(0 < w < 40\). The area inequality \(w\left(30 - \frac{3}{4}w\right) \le 225\) simplifies to \(w^2 - 40w + 300 \ge 0\), or \((w - 10)(w - 30) \ge 0\), yielding \(0\text{ m} < w \le 10\text{ m}\) or \(30\text{ m} \le w < 40\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A free-standing rectangular animal enclosure is to be built in an open field using 240 m of fencing on all four sides. An interior dividing fence parallel to the width splits the enclosure into two identical pens. For what values of the width will the total enclosed area be less than or equal to 1800 m\(^2\)?
qs.a: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 20\text{ m}\) or \(60\text{ m} \le w < 80\text{ m}\)
d: \(0\text{ m} < w \le 20\text{ m}\) or \(60\text{ m} \le w < 120\text{ m}\)
qs.s: With three widths and two lengths, \(3w + 2l = 240\), so \(l = 120 - \frac{3}{2}w\) and domain \(0 < w < 80\). The inequality \(w\left(120 - \frac{3}{2}w\right) \le 1800\) simplifies to \(w^2 - 80w + 1200 \ge 0\), factoring as \((w - 20)(w - 60) \ge 0\), which gives \(0\text{ m} < w \le 20\text{ m}\) or \(60\text{ m} \le w < 80\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular lot is bounded on one side by a warehouse wall and fenced on the remaining three sides with a budget of $2400. Fencing for the two sides perpendicular to the wall (the width) costs $12 per foot, while fencing for the side parallel to the wall costs $20 per foot. For what values of the width will the enclosed area be less than or equal to 2880 sq ft?
qs.a: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 40\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 100\text{ ft}\)
d: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 40\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 120\text{ ft}\)
qs.s: The budget equation \(2(12)w + 20l = 2400\) gives \(l = 120 - \frac{6}{5}w\) and domain \(0 < w < 100\). The inequality \(w\left(120 - \frac{6}{5}w\right) \le 2880\) simplifies to \(w^2 - 100w + 2400 \ge 0\), factoring into \((w - 40)(w - 60) \ge 0\), so \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 40\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 100\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rectangular garden is built along a 100-foot brick wall using 200 ft of fencing for the other three sides, so the length along the wall cannot exceed 100 ft. If the width is perpendicular to the wall, for what values of the width will the enclosed area be at least 4200 sq ft?
d: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 30\text{ ft}\) or \(70\text{ ft} \le w < 100\text{ ft}\)
qs.s: The length is \(l = 200 - 2w\), and the wall constraint \(l \le 100\) requires \(200 - 2w \le 100 \implies w \ge 50\). The area inequality \(w(200 - 2w) \ge 4200\) simplifies to \(w^2 - 100w + 2100 \le 0\) or \((w - 30)(w - 70) \le 0\), which intersects with \(w \ge 50\) to give \(50\text{ ft} \le w \le 70\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rancher uses 360 ft of fencing to build a rectangular corral alongside a barn, using the barn wall as one side. Two interior dividing fences parallel to the width divide the corral into three equal pens. If the width represents each of the four parallel fence sections perpendicular to the barn, for what values of the width will the total enclosed area be less than or equal to 7200 sq ft?
qs.a: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 30\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 90\text{ ft}\)
d: \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 30\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 180\text{ ft}\)
qs.s: The fencing satisfies \(4w + l = 360\), giving \(l = 360 - 4w\) and domain \(0 < w < 90\). Setting \(w(360 - 4w) \le 7200\) yields \(w^2 - 90w + 1800 \ge 0\), or \((w - 30)(w - 60) \ge 0\), resulting in \(0\text{ ft} < w \le 30\text{ ft}\) or \(60\text{ ft} \le w < 90\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: The power output \(P\) (in watts) of an electrical component depends on the current \(I\) (in amperes) according to \(P = 40I - 2I^2\). For what range of current does the power output exceed \(150\text{ W}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(40I - 2I^2 > 150\) gives \(2I^2 - 40I + 150 < 0\), which simplifies to \(I^2 - 20I + 75 < 0\). Factoring as \((I - 5)(I - 15) < 0\) yields \(5 < I < 15\).

qs.q: The concentration \(C\) (in \(\text{mg/L}\)) of a chemical compound in a solution over time \(t\) (in minutes) is given by \(C = 30t - t^2\). For what time interval will the concentration exceed \(200\text{ mg/L}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(30t - t^2 > 200\) leads to \(t^2 - 30t + 200 < 0\). Factoring as \((t - 10)(t - 20) < 0\) yields \(10 < t < 20\).

qs.q: The yield \(Y\) (in bushels per acre) of a crop depends on the amount of fertilizer \(n\) (in \(\text{kg/ha}\)) applied, modeled by \(Y = 80n - n^2\). For what amounts of fertilizer will the yield exceed \(1200\text{ bushels/acre}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(80n - n^2 > 1200\) rearranges to \(n^2 - 80n + 1200 < 0\). Factoring as \((n - 20)(n - 60) < 0\) gives \(20 < n < 60\).

qs.q: The daily profit \(P\), in dollars, from selling \(x\) handcrafted items is given by \(P = 70x - x^2\). For what number of items sold will the daily profit exceed \(\$1000\)?
qs.s: Setting \(70x - x^2 > 1000\) rearranges to \(x^2 - 70x + 1000 < 0\). Factoring as \((x - 20)(x - 50) < 0\) gives \(20 < x < 50\).

qs.q: The height \(h\) in metres of a projectile launched into the air is given by \(h = 50t - 5t^2\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds. During what time interval is the projectile strictly higher than \(80\text{ m}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(50t - 5t^2 > 80\) gives \(5t^2 - 50t + 80 < 0\), which simplifies to \(t^2 - 10t + 16 < 0\). Factoring as \((t - 2)(t - 8) < 0\) yields \(2 < t < 8\).

qs.q: The length of a rectangular playground is \(3\text{ m}\) less than twice its width \(x\). For what values of the width \(x\) will the area of the playground exceed \(54\text{ m}^2\)?
qs.s: The inequality is \(x(2x - 3) > 54\), which rearranges to \(2x^2 - 3x - 54 > 0\) or \((2x + 9)(x - 6) > 0\). Since width must be positive, the negative region is rejected, leaving \(x > 6\).

qs.q: A company's daily profit \(P\) (in hundreds of dollars) from producing \(x\) hundred units is given by \(P(x) = -2x^2 + 25x - 42\). For what range of production \(x\) will the profit exceed \(21\) hundred dollars?

A manufacturer sells lamps at a price of \(p = 150 - x\) dollars each, where \(x\) is the daily production. The daily cost to produce \(x\) lamps is \(C = 30x + 2000\) dollars. For what range of daily production \(x\) does the manufacturer make a profit?

A flare is launched vertically such that its height is \(h_1 = -5t^2 + 60t\) metres after \(t\) seconds. At the same instant, a drone ascends vertically with height given by \(h_2 = 15t + 70\) metres. During what time interval is the flare strictly higher than the drone?
qs.s: Setting \(h_1 > h_2\) gives \(-5t^2 + 60t > 15t + 70\), which simplifies to \(t^2 - 9t + 14 < 0\). Factoring as \((t - 2)(t - 7) < 0\) gives \(2 < t < 7\).

qs.q: The height \(h\) in metres of a ball thrown upward from a platform is given by \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 28t + 12\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds. During what time interval is the ball at a height greater than \(44\text{ m}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(-5t^2 + 28t + 12 > 44\) simplifies to \(5t^2 - 28t + 32 < 0\). Factoring as \((5t - 8)(t - 4) < 0\) yields \(\frac{8}{5} < t < 4\).

qs.q: A bakery estimates that its weekly profit in dollars from selling \(x\) specialty cakes is given by \(P(x) = -x^2 + 28x - 160\). How many specialty cakes per week must the bakery sell to make a profit?
qs.s: Setting \(P(x) > 0\) gives \(-x^2 + 28x - 160 > 0\), or \(x^2 - 28x + 160 < 0\). Factoring as \((x - 8)(x - 20) < 0\), the profit is positive when \(8 < x < 20\).

qs.q: A carpenter determines that the monthly profit in dollars from building and selling \(x\) wooden chairs is \(P(x) = -x^2 + 40x - 300\). How many chairs per month must be sold to make a profit?
qs.s: A profit requires \(P(x) > 0\), so \(-x^2 + 40x - 300 > 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 40x + 300 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 10)(x - 30) < 0\), which is satisfied for \(10 < x < 30\).

qs.q: A pottery studio models its weekly profit in dollars from producing and selling \(x\) ceramic vases as \(P(x) = -x^2 + 35x - 250\). How many vases per week must be sold to make a profit?
qs.s: To make a profit, \(P(x) > 0\), so \(-x^2 + 35x - 250 > 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 35x + 250 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 10)(x - 25) < 0\), yielding \(10 < x < 25\).

qs.q: A small workshop models its daily profit in dollars from producing and selling \(x\) custom skateboards as \(P(x) = -x^2 + 24x - 80\). How many skateboards per day must be sold to make a profit?
qs.s: A profit is made when \(P(x) > 0\), so \(-x^2 + 24x - 80 > 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 24x + 80 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 4)(x - 20) < 0\), so \(4 < x < 20\).

qs.q: An artisan projects that the weekly profit in dollars from crafting and selling \(x\) leather bags is \(P(x) = -x^2 + 30x - 125\). How many bags per week must be sold to make a profit?
qs.s: Setting \(P(x) > 0\) yields \(-x^2 + 30x - 125 > 0\), which rearranges to \(x^2 - 30x + 125 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 5)(x - 25) < 0\), resulting in \(5 < x < 25\).

qs.q: A factory's daily cost in dollars to manufacture \(x\) bicycles is \(C(x) = 50x + 4000\), and the daily revenue from selling them is \(R(x) = 250x - 2x^2\). How many bicycles per day must be produced and sold to achieve a profit of more than 800 dollars?

An object is launched vertically upward from a platform. Its height \(h\) in metres after \(t\) seconds is given by \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 45t + 50\). During what time interval is the object at a height of at least 140 metres?
qs.s: Setting \(h(t) \ge 140\) gives \(-5t^2 + 45t + 50 \ge 140\), which simplifies to \(-5t^2 + 45t - 90 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-5\) yields \(t^2 - 9t + 18 \le 0\), or \((t - 3)(t - 6) \le 0\), resulting in \(3 \le t \le 6\).

qs.q: A manufacturer sells drones at a price of \(p(x) = 300 - 2x\) dollars per drone, where \(x\) is the number of drones produced each week. The weekly cost of production is \(C(x) = 60x + 3600\) dollars. How many drones must be produced each week to earn a profit of at least 1800 dollars?
qs.s: Weekly profit is \(P(x) = x(300 - 2x) - (60x + 3600) = -2x^2 + 240x - 3600\). Setting \(P(x) \ge 1800\) gives \(-2x^2 + 240x - 5400 \ge 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 120x + 2700 \le 0\), factoring as \((x - 30)(x - 90) \le 0\), so \(30 \le x \le 90\).

qs.q: A manufacturer of electric scooters models its weekly profit in dollars as \(P(x) = -2x^2 + 180x - 1500\), where \(x\) is the number of scooters produced and sold per week. For what range of \(x\) will the weekly profit exceed 1300 dollars?
