qs.s: Setting \(P(x) > 1300\) gives \(-2x^2 + 180x - 1500 > 1300\), or \(-2x^2 + 180x - 2800 > 0\). Dividing by \(-2\) reverses the inequality to \(x^2 - 90x + 1400 < 0\), which factors as \((x - 20)(x - 70) < 0\), yielding \(20 < x < 70\).

qs.q: The average cost in dollars of manufacturing \(x\) backpacks is given by \(x^2 - 20x + 150\). Determine the number of backpacks to manufacture to keep the average cost below $59 per backpack.
qs.s: Set up \(x^2 - 20x + 150 < 59\), leading to \(x^2 - 20x + 91 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 7)(x - 13) < 0\), which yields the interval \(7 < x < 13\).

qs.q: The average cost in dollars of producing \(x\) bicycle helmets is modeled by \(x^2 - 16x + 95\). Determine the number of helmets to produce to keep the average cost below $35 per helmet.
qs.s: Set up \(x^2 - 16x + 95 < 35\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 16x + 60 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 6)(x - 10) < 0\), so the cost is below $35 when \(6 < x < 10\).

qs.q: The cost per unit in dollars to produce \(x\) custom phone cases is given by \(x^2 - 15x + 90\). Determine the number of phone cases to produce to keep the cost per unit below $54.
qs.s: Set up \(x^2 - 15x + 90 < 54\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 15x + 36 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 3)(x - 12) < 0\), meaning \(3 < x < 12\) units keep the cost below $54.

qs.q: The average cost in dollars of producing \(x\) skateboards is given by \(x^2 - 14x + 85\). Determine the number of skateboards to produce to keep the average cost below $40 per skateboard.
qs.s: Set up the inequality \(x^2 - 14x + 85 < 40\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 14x + 45 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 5)(x - 9) < 0\), which holds when \(5 < x < 9\).

qs.q: The average cost in dollars of assembling \(x\) office chairs is modeled by \(x^2 - 22x + 150\). Determine the number of chairs to assemble to keep the average cost below $54 per chair.
qs.s: Subtracting 54 from both sides gives \(x^2 - 22x + 96 < 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 6)(x - 16) < 0\), which is satisfied for \(6 < x < 16\).

qs.q: A manufacturer finds that the daily cost to produce \(x\) lawnmowers is \(C(x) = 120x + 4500\) dollars, while daily revenue is \(R(x) = 360x - 3x^2\) dollars. Find the range of lawnmowers produced each day for which the company generates a net profit (revenue exceeds cost).

The effective resistance \(R_{\text{eff}}\) in ohms of a circuit network is given by \(2R^2 - 13R + 21\), where \(R > 0\) is a variable resistance. For what values of \(R\) is the effective resistance strictly less than \(15\text{ ohms}\)?
qs.s: Set \(2R^2 - 13R + 21 < 15\), giving \(2R^2 - 13R + 6 < 0\). Factoring gives \((2R - 1)(R - 6) < 0\), which results in \(\frac{1}{2} < R < 6\).

qs.q: A company sells portable speakers at a price of \(p(x) = 150 - 2x\) dollars per speaker, where \(x\) is the daily production volume. The total daily production cost is \(C(x) = 30x + 600\) dollars. Determine the range of speakers produced daily to ensure a daily profit greater than $1000.

The average cost in dollars per unit to manufacture \(x\) thousand electronic components is modeled by \(C(x) = 2x^2 - 21x + 95\). For what range of \(x\) (in thousands of components) is the average unit cost strictly less than $55?
qs.s: Set \(2x^2 - 21x + 95 < 55\), giving \(2x^2 - 21x + 40 < 0\). Factoring the quadratic gives \((2x - 5)(x - 8) < 0\), which yields \(\frac{5}{2} < x < 8\).

qs.q: A projectile is launched vertically from a platform. Its height in metres after \(t\) seconds is \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 38t + 12\). During what time interval is the projectile at a height strictly greater than \(60\text{ m}\)?
qs.s: Set \(-5t^2 + 38t + 12 > 60\), which simplifies to \(-5t^2 + 38t - 48 > 0\), or \(5t^2 - 38t + 48 < 0\). Factoring gives \((5t - 8)(t - 6) < 0\), so \(\frac{8}{5} < t < 6\) seconds.

qs.q: A bakery's weekly profit (in dollars) from producing \(x\) specialty cakes is modeled by \(P(x) = -0.2x^2 + 80x - 6000\). What number of cakes, \(x\), will produce a profit for the bakery?
A landscaping business models its daily profit (in dollars) from mowing \(x\) lawns as \(P(x) = -0.5x^2 + 70x - 1200\). What number of lawns mowed, \(x\), will yield a profit for the business?

A catering company determines that its profit (in dollars) for serving \(x\) guests at a banquet is given by \(P(x) = -0.25x^2 + 50x - 1600\). For what number of guests, \(x\), will the banquet generate a profit?

A small electronics firm estimates its monthly profit (in dollars) from manufacturing \(x\) pairs of wireless earbuds as \(P(x) = -0.1x^2 + 30x - 1760\). For what range of units, \(x\), will the firm make a profit?
The weekly profit (in dollars) of a print shop from producing \(x\) promotional banners is given by \(P(x) = -0.1x^2 + 35x - 1500\). For what number of banners, \(x\), will the shop earn a profit?

A boutique bicycle manufacturer sells \(x\) custom bicycles per month at a price of \(p(x) = 750 - 2x\) dollars per bicycle. The monthly cost of operating the workshop is \(C(x) = 150x + 25000\) dollars. For what number of bicycles sold, \(x\), will the manufacturer earn a profit?

A solar panel installation company models its monthly profit (in thousands of dollars) as \(P(x) = -0.05x^2 + 6x - 95\), where \(x\) is the number of installations completed. The company's board requires a monthly profit of at least $65 thousand dollars. What range of installations completed, \(x\), satisfies this requirement?
qs.s: Set \(P(x) \ge 65\), which gives \(-0.05x^2 + 6x - 95 \ge 65\), or \(-0.05x^2 + 6x - 160 \ge 0\). Multiplying by \(-20\) gives \(x^2 - 120x + 3200 \le 0\), which factors as \((x - 40)(x - 80) \le 0\), resulting in \(40 \le x \le 80\).

qs.q: A model rocket is launched vertically from a platform. Its height in meters above the ground after \(t\) seconds is given by \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 50t + 15\). During what time interval, in seconds, is the rocket strictly higher than 95 meters above the ground?
qs.s: Set \(h(t) > 95\), giving \(-5t^2 + 50t + 15 > 95\), which simplifies to \(-5t^2 + 50t - 80 > 0\). Dividing by \(-5\) yields \(t^2 - 10t + 16 < 0\), which factors as \((t - 2)(t - 8) < 0\), so \(2 < t < 8\).

qs.q: A company manufactures portable power stations. When \(x\) units are produced and sold each week, the selling price per unit is \(p(x) = 500 - 2x\) dollars, and the weekly production cost is \(C(x) = 60x + 7200\) dollars. For what range of units sold, \(x\), will the weekly profit be at least $12,000 dollars?
qs.s: Profit is \(P(x) = x(500 - 2x) - (60x + 7200) = -2x^2 + 440x - 7200 \ge 12000\), which simplifies to \(-2x^2 + 440x - 19200 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-2\) gives \(x^2 - 220x + 9600 \le 0\), which factors as \((x - 60)(x - 160) \le 0\), so \(60 \le x \le 160\).

qs.q: An equipment manufacturer determines that the daily revenue from selling \(x\) exercise bikes is \(R(x) = -0.15x^2 + 260x\) dollars, and the daily production cost is \(C(x) = 0.25x^2 + 60x + 9000\) dollars. For what range of bikes produced and sold, \(x\), does the company earn a profit?
The height in feet of a baseball hit upward is given by \(h(t) = -16t^2 + 96t + 22\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds. During what time interval is the baseball above \(150\text{ feet}\)?
qs.s: The inequality \(-16t^2 + 96t + 22 > 150\) simplifies to \(-16t^2 + 96t - 128 > 0\). Dividing by \(-16\) yields \(t^2 - 6t + 8 < 0\), which factors into \((t - 2)(t - 4) < 0\), so \(2\text{ s} < t < 4\text{ s}\).

qs.q: The height in metres of an arrow shot upward from an elevated stand is given by \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 35t + 20\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds. During what time interval is the arrow above \(50\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: Subtracting \(50\) from both sides gives \(-5t^2 + 35t - 30 > 0\). Dividing by \(-5\) reverses the inequality to \(t^2 - 7t + 6 < 0\), which factors as \((t - 1)(t - 6) < 0\), giving \(1\text{ s} < t < 6\text{ s}\).

qs.q: The height in feet of a flare launched from a platform is modeled by \(h(t) = -16t^2 + 80t + 32\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds after launch. During what time interval is the flare above \(96\text{ feet}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(-16t^2 + 80t + 32 > 96\) gives \(-16t^2 + 80t - 64 > 0\). Dividing by \(-16\) reverses the inequality to \(t^2 - 5t + 4 < 0\), which factors as \((t - 1)(t - 4) < 0\), yielding \(1\text{ s} < t < 4\text{ s}\).

qs.q: The height in metres of a tennis ball hit upward from a balcony is given by \(h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 19.6t + 10.3\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds after it is hit. During what time interval is the ball above \(25\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(-4.9t^2 + 19.6t + 10.3 > 25\) gives \(-4.9t^2 + 19.6t - 14.7 > 0\), and dividing by \(-4.9\) yields \(t^2 - 4t + 3 < 0\). Factoring gives \((t - 1)(t - 3) < 0\), which means the ball is above \(25\text{ metres}\) when \(1\text{ s} < t < 3\text{ s}\).

qs.q: A toy rocket is launched upward from an \(11\text{-metre}\) platform. Its height in metres after \(t\) seconds is given by \(h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 34.3t + 11\). During what time interval will the rocket be above \(60\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: The inequality \(-4.9t^2 + 34.3t + 11 > 60\) simplifies to \(-4.9t^2 + 34.3t - 49 > 0\). Dividing by \(-4.9\) gives \(t^2 - 7t + 10 < 0\), or \((t - 2)(t - 5) < 0\), so the solution is \(2\text{ s} < t < 5\text{ s}\).

qs.q: A research rocket is launched vertically, and its altitude in metres after \(t\) seconds is \(h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 147t + 137.6\). During what time interval is the rocket at an altitude greater than \(1000\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: The condition \(-4.9t^2 + 147t + 137.6 > 1000\) simplifies to \(-4.9t^2 + 147t - 862.4 > 0\). Dividing by \(-4.9\) yields \(t^2 - 30t + 176 < 0\), which factors into \((t - 8)(t - 22) < 0\), so the interval is \(8\text{ s} < t < 22\text{ s}\).

qs.q: A flare is launched from a rooftop with height in feet given by \(h_1(t) = -16t^2 + 80t + 96\), where \(t\) is time in seconds. At the same instant, a drone ascends along the path \(h_2(t) = 8t + 152\). During what time interval is the flare higher than the drone?
qs.s: Setting \(h_1(t) > h_2(t)\) gives \(-16t^2 + 80t + 96 > 8t + 152\), which simplifies to \(-16t^2 + 72t - 56 > 0\). Dividing by \(-8\) yields \(2t^2 - 9t + 7 < 0\), factoring as \((2t - 7)(t - 1) < 0\), so \(1\text{ s} < t < 3.5\text{ s}\).

qs.q: A company models the selling price in dollars of a gadget as \(p(x) = 150 - 0.5x\), where \(x\) is the number of units produced and sold daily. The total daily cost to produce \(x\) units is \(C(x) = 30x + 4000\) dollars. During what interval of daily production \(x\) will the company earn a profit?

A ball is thrown from the roof of a building with an initial height given by \(h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 14.7t + 39.2\), where \(h(t)\) is in metres and \(t\) is time in seconds. During what time interval is the ball above \(19.6\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(-4.9t^2 + 14.7t + 39.2 > 19.6\) gives \(-4.9t^2 + 14.7t + 19.6 > 0\), or \(t^2 - 3t - 4 < 0\), which factors as \((t - 4)(t + 1) < 0\). Because time cannot be negative (\(t \ge 0\)) and \(h(0) = 39.2\text{ m} > 19.6\text{ m}\), the physical interval is \(0\text{ s} \le t < 4\text{ s}\).

qs.q: A decorative water jet shoots water into the air such that the height in metres of a droplet is \(h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 1\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds after it leaves the nozzle. During what time interval is the droplet above \(11\text{ metres}\)?
qs.s: Setting \(-5t^2 + 20t + 1 > 11\) gives \(-5t^2 + 20t - 10 > 0\), which simplifies to \(t^2 - 4t + 2 < 0\). Applying the quadratic formula gives roots \(t = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{8}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{2}\), resulting in the interval \(2 - \sqrt{2}\text{ s} < t < 2 + \sqrt{2}\text{ s}\).

qs.q: The height \(h\) in meters of a water jet from a fountain is modeled by \(h = -\frac{1}{5}x^2 + \frac{14}{5}x\) for \(0 < x < 14\), where \(x\) is the horizontal distance in meters from the nozzle. For what horizontal distances is the height of the water jet at least 8 meters?
qs.s: Setting \(-\frac{1}{5}x^2 + \frac{14}{5}x \ge 8\) and multiplying by \(-5\) yields \(x^2 - 14x + 40 \le 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 4)(x - 10) \le 0\), which means \(4 \le x \le 10\) meters.

qs.q: A truck's fuel economy \(E\) in miles per gallon is modeled by \(E = -\frac{1}{25}v^2 + \frac{18}{5}v\) for \(0 < v < 90\), where \(v\) is the speed in mph. For what speeds will the fuel economy be at least 56 mpg?
qs.s: Set \(-\frac{1}{25}v^2 + \frac{18}{5}v \ge 56\) and multiply by \(-25\) to obtain \(v^2 - 90v + 1400 \le 0\). Factoring gives \((v - 20)(v - 70) \le 0\), so the required speeds are \(20 \le v \le 70\) mph.

qs.q: The fuel economy \(F\) in miles per gallon of a delivery van is modeled by \(F = -\frac{1}{10}v^2 + \frac{7}{2}v\) for \(0 < v < 35\), where \(v\) is the speed in mph. For what speeds will the fuel economy be at least 30 mpg?
qs.s: Setting \(-\frac{1}{10}v^2 + \frac{7}{2}v \ge 30\) and multiplying by \(-10\) gives \(v^2 - 35v + 300 \le 0\), which factors as \((v - 15)(v - 20) \le 0\). Therefore, the fuel economy is at least 30 mpg for \(15 \le v \le 20\) mph.

qs.q: The yield \(Y\) in bushels per acre of an apple orchard depends on the planting density \(x\) in trees per acre, modeled by \(Y = -\frac{1}{50}x^2 + \frac{13}{5}x\) for \(0 < x < 130\). For what planting densities will the yield be at least 60 bushels per acre?
qs.s: Setting \(-\frac{1}{50}x^2 + \frac{13}{5}x \ge 60\) and multiplying by \(-50\) gives \(x^2 - 130x + 3000 \le 0\). Factoring yields \((x - 30)(x - 100) \le 0\), so the planting density must be \(30 \le x \le 100\) trees per acre.

qs.q: The electrical power \(P\) in watts dissipated by a variable resistor is given by \(P = -\frac{1}{8}R^2 + \frac{15}{4}R\) for \(0 < R < 30\), where \(R\) is the resistance in ohms. For what resistances will the power dissipated be at least 18 watts?
qs.s: Set \(-\frac{1}{8}R^2 + \frac{15}{4}R \ge 18\) and multiply by \(-8\) to obtain \(R^2 - 30R + 144 \le 0\). Factoring gives \((R - 6)(R - 24) \le 0\), resulting in \(6 \le R \le 24\) ohms.

qs.q: A flare is launched from an elevated platform such that its height in feet after \(t\) seconds is given by \(h(t) = -16t^2 + 80t + 16\). For what time interval is the flare at or above a height of 100 feet?
qs.s: Set \(-16t^2 + 80t + 16 \ge 100\), which simplifies to \(-16t^2 + 80t - 84 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-4\) yields \(4t^2 - 20t + 21 \le 0\), which factors as \((2t - 3)(2t - 7) \le 0\), giving \(\frac{3}{2} \le t \le \frac{7}{2}\) seconds.

qs.q: A manufacturer sells portable speakers at a price of \(p(x) = 150 - 0.5x\) dollars per unit, where \(x\) is the daily production (\(0 < x < 300\)). The daily cost in dollars is \(C(x) = 30x + 4000\). For what daily production levels \(x\) will the daily profit, \(P(x) = x \cdot p(x) - C(x)\), be at least $1400 dollars?
qs.s: The profit is \(P(x) = x(150 - 0.5x) - (30x + 4000) = -0.5x^2 + 120x - 4000\). Setting \(P(x) \ge 1400\) gives \(-0.5x^2 + 120x - 5400 \ge 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 240x + 10800 \le 0\) or \((x - 60)(x - 180) \le 0\), meaning \(60 \le x \le 180\) speakers.

qs.q: The temperature \(T\) in degrees Celsius of a chemical mixture is controlled by a coolant flow rate \(x\) in liters per minute (\(x > 0\)) according to \(T = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{19}{4}x + 22\). For what coolant flow rates is the temperature at most \(16^\circ\text{C}\)?
qs.s: Set \(\frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{19}{4}x + 22 \le 16\), which simplifies to \(\frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{19}{4}x + 6 \le 0\). Multiplying by 4 gives \(2x^2 - 19x + 24 \le 0\), which factors as \((2x - 3)(x - 8) \le 0\), so \(\frac{3}{2} \le x \le 8\) L/min.

qs.q: A company models its weekly profit \(P\) in thousands of dollars from producing \(x\) hundred units of a product by \(P(x) = -\frac{1}{3}x^2 + 14x - 75\), where \(0 < x < 40\). For what production levels will the weekly profit strictly exceed 45 thousand dollars?
qs.s: Set \(-\frac{1}{3}x^2 + 14x - 75 > 45\), which gives \(-\frac{1}{3}x^2 + 14x - 120 > 0\). Multiplying by \(-3\) reverses the inequality to \(x^2 - 42x + 360 < 0\), which factors as \((x - 12)(x - 30) < 0\), giving \(12 < x < 30\) hundred units.

qs.q: On a wet road, the stopping distance \(d\) in feet of a car traveling at speed \(v\) in mph (\(v > 0\)) is given by \(d = \frac{1}{12}v^2 + \frac{5}{3}v\). For what speeds will the stopping distance be at most 48 feet?
qs.s: Set \(\frac{1}{12}v^2 + \frac{5}{3}v \le 48\), which multiplies by 12 to become \(v^2 + 20v - 576 \le 0\), or \((v + 36)(v - 16) \le 0\). Since speed must be strictly positive (\(v > 0\)), the valid interval is \(0 < v \le 16\) mph.

exercises.name: Find projectile landing coordinates on a hillside

qs.q: An archer shoots an arrow up an incline along a path given by \(y = -0.005x^2 + 0.8x\), where \(x\) and \(y\) are measured in meters. The incline has a slope of \(\frac{1}{4}\). What are the landing coordinates of the arrow?
A golfer strikes a ball whose trajectory is modeled by \(y = -0.001x^2 + 0.45x\). The hillside rises with a slope of \(\frac{1}{20}\). What are the landing coordinates of the ball in yards?
A golfer hits a drive up a hillside, following a trajectory given by \(y = -0.002x^2 + 0.6x\). The hillside has a slope of \(\frac{1}{5}\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Equating the trajectory and hillside \(y = 0.2x\) yields \(-0.002x^2 + 0.4x = 0\), which gives \(x = 200\). Substituting into the slope equation gives \(y = 0.2(200) = 40\), so the landing coordinates are \((200, 40)\).

qs.q: A golf ball is driven up a slope in a path described by \(y = -0.0025x^2 + 0.7x\). The hillside has a slope of \(\frac{1}{4}\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Set \(-0.0025x^2 + 0.7x = 0.25x\), which simplifies to \(0.45x - 0.0025x^2 = 0\), yielding \(x = 180\). Calculating the height gives \(y = 0.25(180) = 45\), so the ball lands at \((180, 45)\).

qs.q: A golfer hits a drive up a hillside along the path \(y = -0.004x^2 + 0.9x\). The hillside has a slope of \(\frac{1}{10}\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Equating the path and the slope gives \(-0.004x^2 + 0.9x = 0.1x\), or \(0.8x - 0.004x^2 = 0\), which yields \(x = 200\). Substituting into the slope equation gives \(y = 0.1(200) = 20\), so the landing coordinates are \((200, 20)\).

qs.q: A golf ball is driven along a trajectory given by \(y = -0.002x^2 + 0.7x\). The ground is flat for the first 50 yards, after which a hillside rises with a slope of \(\frac{1}{4}\) (modeled by \(y = \frac{1}{4}(x - 50)\) for \(x \ge 50\)). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Set \(-0.002x^2 + 0.7x = 0.25(x - 50)\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 225x - 6250 = 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 250)(x + 25) = 0\), so \(x = 250\), and substituting into the hill equation gives \(y = 0.25(250 - 50) = 50\), producing \((250, 50)\).

qs.q: A projectile is launched such that its trajectory is described in vertex form by \(y = -0.0025(x - 120)^2 + 56\). It travels toward a hillside with a slope of \(\frac{1}{5}\) passing through the origin \((0,0)\). What are the landing coordinates \((x, y)\) of the projectile?
qs.s: Expanding the trajectory yields \(y = -0.0025x^2 + 0.6x + 20\). Setting this equal to \(y = 0.2x\) gives \(x^2 - 160x - 8000 = 0\), which factors as \((x - 200)(x + 40) = 0\), so \(x = 200\) and \(y = 0.2(200) = 40\), giving \((200, 40)\).

qs.q: A golfer hits a tee shot from an elevated tee box 12 yards above the ground. The trajectory of the ball is modeled by \(y = -0.005x^2 + 0.6x + 12\). The hillside rises from the origin \((0,0)\) with a slope of \(\frac{1}{10}\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Equate the trajectory to the hillside \(y = 0.1x\) to obtain \(-0.005x^2 + 0.5x + 12 = 0\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 100x - 2400 = 0\). Factoring as \((x - 120)(x + 20) = 0\) gives \(x = 120\), and evaluating \(y = 0.1(120)\) gives \(12\), so the coordinates are \((120, 12)\).

qs.q: A golfer hits a shot from an elevated tee 25 yards above the ground. The ball follows the trajectory \(y = -0.001x^2 + 0.375x + 25\). It lands on an elevated hillside whose profile is given by the line \(y = \frac{1}{8}x + 10\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Equate the equations to get \(-0.001x^2 + 0.375x + 25 = 0.125x + 10\), which simplifies to \(x^2 - 250x - 15000 = 0\). Factoring gives \((x - 300)(x + 50) = 0\), so \(x = 300\), and substituting into the line gives \(y = 0.125(300) + 10 = 47.5\), giving \((300, 47.5)\).

qs.q: A golfer hits a drive from a tee 16 yards above the valley floor downhill toward a slope. The trajectory of the ball is \(y = -0.0025x^2 + 0.5x + 16\), and the downward slope of the valley has a gradient of \(-\frac{1}{4}\) passing through \((0,0)\). What are the landing coordinates of the golf ball in yards?
qs.s: Set the trajectory equal to the downhill line \(y = -0.25x\), giving \(-0.0025x^2 + 0.75x + 16 = 0\), or \(x^2 - 300x - 6400 = 0\). Factoring yields \((x - 320)(x + 20) = 0\), so \(x = 320\), and evaluating \(y = -0.25(320)\) yields \(-80\), giving coordinates \((320, -80)\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of gourmet lunch boxes is given by \(p(x) = 18 - 0.1x, 0 \le x \le 180\), where \(x\) is the number of lunch boxes sold each day. The daily operating cost of the catering truck is $90, plus $5 per lunch box prepared. Find the daily revenue function, \(R(x)\).
qs.s: Daily revenue is calculated by multiplying the number of units sold by the price per unit: \(R(x) = x \cdot p(x) = x(18 - 0.1x) = 18x - 0.1x^2\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of ceramic mugs is given by \(p(n) = 30 - 0.25n, 0 \le n \le 120\), where \(n\) is the number of mugs sold each day. The studio has a fixed daily operating cost of $150, plus $6 in materials per mug. Find the daily revenue function, \(R(n)\).
qs.s: The daily revenue function is obtained by multiplying the number of units sold by the unit price: \(R(n) = n \cdot p(n) = n(30 - 0.25n) = 30n - 0.25n^2\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of scented candles is given by \(p(n) = 40 - 0.8n, 0 \le n \le 50\), where \(n\) is the number of candles sold each day. The boutique incurs an operating cost of $110 per day, plus $8 in supplies for each candle sold. Find the daily revenue function, \(R(n)\).
qs.s: Daily revenue equals the quantity sold times the selling price per item: \(R(n) = n \cdot p(n) = n(40 - 0.8n) = 40n - 0.8n^2\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of handcrafted leather wallets is given by \(p(n) = 48 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 96\), where \(n\) is the number of wallets sold each day. The operating cost of the shop is $120 per day, plus $14 to produce each wallet. Find the daily revenue function, \(R(n)\).
qs.s: Daily revenue is found by multiplying the number of items sold by the price per item: \(R(n) = n \cdot p(n) = n(48 - 0.5n) = 48n - 0.5n^2\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of custom T-shirts is given by \(p(x) = 25 - 0.2x, 0 \le x \le 125\), where \(x\) is the number of T-shirts sold each day. The business has a fixed overhead cost of $80 per day, plus $9 in materials for each shirt sold. Find the daily revenue function, \(R(x)\).
qs.s: Daily revenue is the product of the quantity sold and the price per item: \(R(x) = x \cdot p(x) = x(25 - 0.2x) = 25x - 0.2x^2\).

qs.q: A bicycle manufacturer produces commuter bikes. The daily fixed costs consist of $1200 for factory rent, $450 for administrative salaries, and $150 for equipment maintenance. The variable production cost per bicycle includes $65 for components, $40 for assembly labor, and $15 for packaging. Write the simplified daily cost function, \(C(x)\), where \(x\) is the number of bicycles produced each day.
qs.s: Total fixed cost is \(1200 + 450 + 150 = 1800\), and total variable cost per bicycle is \(65 + 40 + 15 = 120\). Combining these gives \(C(x) = 120x + 1800\).

qs.q: An appliance manufacturer sells portable air conditioners. The base selling price is given by \(p(x) = 280 - 0.05x\), where \(x\) is the number of units sold each day (\(0 \le x \le 4000\)). Each buyer pays a mandatory environmental disposal fee of $12 per unit, and the manufacturer applies an instant promotional rebate of $8 per unit. Daily operating costs are $5000 plus $45 per unit. Find the simplified daily revenue function, \(R(x)\).
qs.s: The effective price per unit after accounting for the disposal fee and rebate is \(p(x) = 280 - 0.05x + 12 - 8 = 284 - 0.05x\). Multiplying by \(x\) units gives \(R(x) = x(284 - 0.05x) = 284x - 0.05x^2\).

qs.q: A publishing company prints daily specialty journals. The fixed daily expenses include $320 for warehouse rent, $180 for machinery leasing, and $50 for licensing. The variable production costs per journal are $4.25 for paper and binding, $1.50 for ink, and $0.75 for distribution. Find the simplified daily cost function, \(C(n)\), where \(n\) is the number of journals printed each day.
qs.s: Sum the daily fixed costs (\(320 + 180 + 50 = 550\)) and the variable costs per journal (\(4.25 + 1.50 + 0.75 = 6.5\)). The daily cost function is \(C(n) = 6.5n + 550\).

qs.q: An electronics company sells tablet computers. The base price is $420, but the price drops by \(0.05n\) due to competition and by \(0.15n\) for bulk purchasing, where \(n\) is the number of tablets sold daily (\(0 \le n \le 2100\)). The company also charges a flat shipping and handling fee of $15 per tablet sold. Find the simplified daily revenue function, \(R(n)\).
qs.s: First combine like terms to find the net price per tablet: \(p(n) = 420 - 0.05n - 0.15n + 15 = 435 - 0.2n\). Multiplying by \(n\) units yields \(R(n) = n(435 - 0.2n) = 435n - 0.2n^2\).

qs.q: A specialty food distributor sells cases of olive oil. The selling price per case is given by \(p(x) = 60 - \frac{1}{4}x, 0 \le x \le 240\), where \(x\) is the number of cases sold each day. For every case sold, the distributor also collects a mandatory $5 bottle recycling deposit that contributes to daily revenue. Operating costs are $400 per day plus $12 per case. Find the simplified daily revenue function, \(R(x)\).
qs.s: The total revenue per case is \(\left(60 - \frac{1}{4}x\right) + 5 = 65 - \frac{1}{4}x\). Multiplying by \(x\) cases sold gives \(R(x) = x\left(65 - \frac{1}{4}x\right) = 65x - \frac{1}{4}x^2\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a handcrafted wallet is given by \(p(n) = 45 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 90\), where \(n\) is the number of wallets sold each day. The daily operating cost of the workshop is $150, plus $15 for materials and labor for each wallet sold. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: The total daily cost is the fixed cost of $150 plus the variable cost of $15 per wallet, so \(C(n) = 15n + 150\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a bag of artisanal coffee beans is given by \(p(n) = 28 - 0.2n, 0 \le n \le 140\), where \(n\) is the number of bags sold each day. The operating cost of the roastery is $120 per day, plus $8 for packaging and commission for each bag sold. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: The daily cost consists of the fixed operating cost of $120 plus $8 per bag sold, giving \(C(n) = 8n + 120\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a specialty cake is given by \(p(n) = 50 - 0.8n, 0 \le n \le 60\), where \(n\) is the number of cakes sold each day. The bakery has a fixed operating cost of $200 per day, plus $14 in ingredients and decorating supplies for each cake sold. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: The daily cost combines the fixed daily operating cost of $200 and the variable cost of $14 per cake, giving \(C(n) = 14n + 200\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a custom t-shirt is given by \(p(n) = 24 - 0.1n, 0 \le n \le 240\), where \(n\) is the number of shirts sold each day. The shop's daily overhead cost is $80, plus $6 in printing costs for each shirt sold. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: The daily cost is the sum of the fixed overhead of $80 and $6 per shirt printed, which yields \(C(n) = 6n + 80\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a scented candle is given by \(p(n) = 32 - 0.25n, 0 \le n \le 120\), where \(n\) is the number of candles sold each day. The daily operating cost of the studio is $95, plus $7 in materials and sales commission for each candle sold. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: The daily cost function is the sum of the fixed cost of $95 and the variable cost of $7 per candle, which gives \(C(n) = 7n + 95\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a bicycle helmet is given by \(p(n) = 85 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 150\), where \(n\) is the number of helmets sold each day. Daily fixed expenses include $450 for rent and $180 for equipment maintenance. For each helmet produced, costs include $16.50 in raw materials, $9.75 in assembly labor, and $1.75 in packaging. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: Combine the daily fixed costs ($450 + $180 = $630) and the variable costs per helmet ($16.50 + $9.75 + $1.75 = $28) to get \(C(n) = 28n + 630\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a high-end audio speaker is given by \(p(n) = 350 - 0.75n, 0 \le n \le 400\), where \(n\) is the number of speakers sold daily. The company incurs daily fixed costs of $3250 in facility lease and $1150 in equipment amortization. Variable costs are $64.25 for electronics, $42.50 for cabinetry, and $8.25 for packaging per speaker. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: Add the daily fixed expenses ($3250 + $1150 = $4400) and the variable expenses per speaker ($64.25 + $42.50 + $8.25 = $115) to find \(C(n) = 115n + 4400\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of an electric scooter is given by \(p(n) = 650 - 2.5n, 0 \le n \le 200\), where \(n\) is the number of scooters sold daily. Daily fixed operating expenses consist of $6400 in plant operations, $2100 in administration, and $1300 in fixed marketing. Each scooter costs $135 for the battery, $92.50 for the chassis and motor, and $22.50 for warranty and packaging. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: Add the total daily fixed costs ($6400 + $2100 + $1300 = $9800) and the total variable costs per scooter ($135 + $92.50 + $22.50 = $250) to get \(C(n) = 250n + 9800\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of an ergonomic chair is given by \(p(n) = 480 - 1.2n, 0 \le n \le 350\), where \(n\) is the number of chairs produced and sold each day. Daily overhead includes $5200 for factory rent, $1650 for machinery leasing, and $950 for storage. Variable costs per chair include $112.50 for frame materials, $48.75 for upholstery labor, and $18.75 for handling. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: Sum the fixed costs ($5200 + $1650 + $950 = $7800) and the per-unit variable costs ($112.50 + $48.75 + $18.75 = $180) to produce \(C(n) = 180n + 7800\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a commercial drone is given by \(p(n) = 1200 - 4n, 0 \le n \le 250\), where \(n\) is the number of drones sold each day. Fixed daily expenses consist of $4800 for facility leasing, $2700 for administrative salaries, and $1500 for insurance and utilities. Each drone requires $340 for components, $185 for technician labor, and $35 for quality testing. Find the daily cost function, \(C(n)\).
qs.s: Sum the total fixed expenses ($4800 + $2700 + $1500 = $9000) and the total variable costs per drone ($340 + $185 + $35 = $560) to obtain \(C(n) = 560n + 9000\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a ceramic mug is given by \(p(n) = 40 - 0.4n, 0 \le n \le 100\), where \(n\) is the number of mugs sold each day. The operating cost of the shop is $270 per day, plus $16 in materials for each mug sold. If the profit function is given by \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the profit be greater than or equal to zero?
qs.s: Profit is \(P(n) = n(40 - 0.4n) - (270 + 16n) = -0.4n^2 + 24n - 270 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-0.4\) yields \(n^2 - 60n + 675 \le 0\), which factors as \((n - 15)(n - 45) \le 0\), giving \(15 \le n \le 45\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a handcrafted wallet is given by \(p(n) = 40 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 80\), where \(n\) is the number of wallets sold each day. The operating cost of the business is $250 per day, plus $10 in materials for each wallet sold. If the profit function is given by \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the profit be greater than or equal to zero?
qs.s: The revenue is \(R(n) = n(40 - 0.5n) = 40n - 0.5n^2\) and the cost is \(C(n) = 250 + 10n\), so \(P(n) = -0.5n^2 + 30n - 250 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-0.5\) yields \(n^2 - 60n + 500 \le 0\), which factors as \((n - 10)(n - 50) \le 0\), giving \(10 \le n \le 50\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a travel tumbler is given by \(p(n) = 28 - 0.1n, 0 \le n \le 280\), where \(n\) is the number of tumblers sold each day. The operating cost of the company is $210 per day, plus $18 in commission and packaging for each item sold. If the profit function is given by \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the profit be greater than or equal to zero?

The price, \(p\), in dollars of a custom phone case is given by \(p(n) = 35 - 0.2n, 0 \le n \le 175\), where \(n\) is the number of cases sold each day. The operating cost of the business is $320 per day, plus $15 in production costs for each phone case sold. If the profit function is given by \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the profit be greater than or equal to zero?

The price, \(p\), in dollars of a scented candle is given by \(p(n) = 65 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 130\), where \(n\) is the number of candles sold each day. The daily operating cost is $600, plus $25 in materials and commission for each candle sold. If the profit function is given by \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the profit be greater than or equal to zero?
qs.s: Profit is \(P(n) = n(65 - 0.5n) - (600 + 25n) = -0.5n^2 + 40n - 600 \ge 0\). Dividing by \(-0.5\) gives \(n^2 - 80n + 1200 \le 0\), which factors into \((n - 20)(n - 60) \le 0\), yielding \(20 \le n \le 60\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of a smartwatch is given by \(p(n) = 85 - 0.05n, 0 \le n \le 1700\), where \(n\) is the number of watches sold each week. Fixed weekly costs are $5,500 for rent and $3,000 for licensing. Variable costs per watch are $15 for components and $10 for assembly. If \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the weekly profit be at least $5,000?

The price, \(p\), in dollars of a designer jacket is given by \(p(n) = 240 - 0.8n, 0 \le n \le 300\), where \(n\) is the number of jackets sold each month. Fixed overhead costs are $3,500 for shop rental and $1,000 for administration. Variable costs per jacket are $50 for fabric and $30 for tailoring. If \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the monthly profit be at least $1,500?

The price, \(p\), in dollars of a mountain bike is given by \(p(n) = 160 - 0.25n, 0 \le n \le 640\), where \(n\) is the number of bikes sold each month. Fixed monthly costs are $3,400 for facility lease and $1,000 for insurance. Variable costs per bike are $40 for materials, $15 for sales commission, and $5 for packaging. If \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the monthly profit be at least $4,000?
qs.s: Total cost is \(C(n) = 4,400 + 60n\), and revenue is \(R(n) = 160n - 0.25n^2\). Requiring \(P(n) \ge 4,000\) gives \(-0.25n^2 + 100n - 4,400 \ge 4,000 \implies n^2 - 400n + 33,600 \le 0\), which factors as \((n - 120)(n - 280) \le 0\), so \(120 \le n \le 280\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of an electric skateboard is given by \(p(n) = 200 - 0.2n, 0 \le n \le 1000\), where \(n\) is the number of boards sold each month. Monthly fixed costs are $4,500 for warehouse rent and $3,000 for equipment leasing. Production costs per skateboard are $45 for materials, $25 for labor, and $10 for shipping. If \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the monthly profit be at least $6,000?
qs.s: Total cost is \(C(n) = 7,500 + 80n\), so \(P(n) = -0.2n^2 + 120n - 7,500\). Setting \(P(n) \ge 6,000\) yields \(-0.2n^2 + 120n - 13,500 \ge 0 \implies n^2 - 600n + 67,500 \le 0\), which factors into \((n - 150)(n - 450) \le 0\), resulting in \(150 \le n \le 450\).

qs.q: The price, \(p\), in dollars of an electronic tablet is given by \(p(n) = 450 - 0.5n, 0 \le n \le 900\), where \(n\) is the number of tablets sold each week. Fixed weekly operating costs are $12,000 for rent and $6,000 for maintenance. Each tablet also requires $120 in parts and $30 in labor to assemble. If \(P(n) = R(n) - C(n)\), for what values of \(n\) will the weekly profit be at least $22,000?

exercises.name: Find maximum vertical distance between parabola and line

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -x^2 + x + 6\) and the line \(y = -2x\) for the shaded region shown in the figure.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + x + 6) - (-2x) = -x^2 + 3x + 6\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{3}{2(-1)} = 1.5\), giving \(d(1.5) = -(1.5)^2 + 3(1.5) + 6 = 8.25\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -x^2 + 4\) and the line \(y = x - 2\) in the shaded region shown in the graph.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + 4) - (x - 2) = -x^2 - x + 6\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{-1}{2(-1)} = -0.5\), which gives \(d(-0.5) = -(-0.5)^2 - (-0.5) + 6 = 6.25\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -2x^2 + 6x + 1\) and the line \(y = 2x - 3\) for the shaded region shown in the figure.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (-2x^2 + 6x + 1) - (2x - 3) = -2x^2 + 4x + 4\). The vertex occurs at \(x = -\frac{4}{2(-2)} = 1\), giving the maximum vertical distance \(d(1) = -2(1)^2 + 4(1) + 4 = 6\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -x^2 + 3x + 4\) and the line \(y = -x - 1\) for the shaded region shown in the figure.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + 3x + 4) - (-x - 1) = -x^2 + 4x + 5\). The vertex occurs at \(x = -\frac{4}{2(-1)} = 2\), yielding a maximum distance of \(d(2) = -(2)^2 + 4(2) + 5 = 9\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -x^2 + 4x + 1\) and the line \(y = 2x - 2\) in the shaded region.
qs.s: The vertical distance between the curves is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + 4x + 1) - (2x - 2) = -x^2 + 2x + 3\). The vertex of this quadratic function is at \(x = -\frac{2}{2(-1)} = 1\), giving a maximum distance of \(d(1) = -(1)^2 + 2(1) + 3 = 4\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 2x + 4\) and the line \(y = \frac{1}{2}x - 1\) over the shaded region bounded by their intersection points.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = \left(-\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 2x + 4\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2}x - 1\right) = -\frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{3}{2}x + 5\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{3/2}{2(-1/2)} = \frac{3}{2}\), giving \(d\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) + 5 = \frac{49}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -\frac{3}{4}x^2 + 3x + 2\) and the line \(y = -\frac{1}{2}x - 1\) for the shaded region shown in the figure.
qs.s: The distance function is \(d(x) = \left(-\frac{3}{4}x^2 + 3x + 2\right) - \left(-\frac{1}{2}x - 1\right) = -\frac{3}{4}x^2 + \frac{7}{2}x + 3\). The vertex occurs at \(x = -\frac{7/2}{2(-3/4)} = \frac{7}{3}\), so the maximum distance is \(d\left(\frac{7}{3}\right) = -\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)^2 + \frac{7}{2}\left(\frac{7}{3}\right) + 3 = \frac{85}{12}\).

qs.q: Use the graph to set up the distance function and determine the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -2x^2 + 3x + 4\) and the line \(y = -2x - 1\) for the shaded region.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (-2x^2 + 3x + 4) - (-2x - 1) = -2x^2 + 5x + 5\). The maximum occurs at \(x = -\frac{5}{2(-2)} = \frac{5}{4}\), giving \(d\left(\frac{5}{4}\right) = -2\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^2 + 5\left(\frac{5}{4}\right) + 5 = \frac{65}{8}\).

qs.q: Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the parabola \(y = -3x^2 + x + 7\) and the line \(y = 2x - 1\) over the shaded region.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-3x^2 + x + 7) - (2x - 1) = -3x^2 - x + 8\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{-1}{2(-3)} = -\frac{1}{6}\), giving \(d\left(-\frac{1}{6}\right) = -3\left(-\frac{1}{6}\right)^2 - \left(-\frac{1}{6}\right) + 8 = \frac{97}{12}\).

qs.q: In the given figure, the line \(y = -x + 7\) lies above the parabola \(y = \frac{1}{3}x^2 - 2x + 1\) between their points of intersection. Find the maximum vertical distance, \(d\), between the line and the parabola in this region.
qs.s: The distance is \(d(x) = (-x + 7) - \left(\frac{1}{3}x^2 - 2x + 1\right) = -\frac{1}{3}x^2 + x + 6\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{1}{2(-1/3)} = \frac{3}{2}\), yielding \(d\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = -\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3}{2} + 6 = \frac{27}{4}\).

exercises.name: Find maximum vertical distance between parabola and line

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded above by the parabola \(y = -x^2 + 4\) and below by the line \(y = x - 2\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the parabola and the line in this region.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + 4) - (x - 2) = -x^2 - x + 6\). The maximum occurs at the vertex \(x = -\frac{-1}{2(-1)} = -0.5\), which yields \(d(-0.5) = -(-0.5)^2 - (-0.5) + 6 = 6.25\).

qs.q: The figure shows the region bounded above by the line \(y = x + 4\) and below by the parabola \(y = x^2 - x - 4\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola in this region.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (x + 4) - (x^2 - x - 4) = -x^2 + 2x + 8\). In vertex form, \(d(x) = -(x - 1)^2 + 9\), so the maximum vertical distance is 9 at \(x = 1\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded above by the line \(y = -x + 3\) and below by the parabola \(y = x^2 - 3x\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola in this region.
qs.s: The vertical distance function is \(d(x) = (-x + 3) - (x^2 - 3x) = -x^2 + 2x + 3\). Completing the square gives \(d(x) = -(x - 1)^2 + 4\), so the maximum vertical distance is 4 at \(x = 1\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded by the line \(y = x + 1\) and the parabola \(y = x^2 - 1\). Determine the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola over this region.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (x + 1) - (x^2 - 1) = -x^2 + x + 2\). The maximum is at the vertex \(x = -\frac{1}{2(-1)} = 0.5\), giving \(d(0.5) = -(0.5)^2 + 0.5 + 2 = 2.25\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded by the line \(y = x + 3\) and the parabola \(y = x^2 - 3x + 1\). What is the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola within this region?
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (x + 3) - (x^2 - 3x + 1) = -x^2 + 4x + 2\). Completing the square gives \(-(x - 2)^2 + 6\), so the maximum vertical distance is 6 at \(x = 2\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded above by the parabola \(y = -x^2 + 4x + 1\) and below by the line passing through \((0, -3)\) and \((4, 1)\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the parabola and the line in this region.
qs.s: The line has slope \(m = \frac{1 - (-3)}{4 - 0} = 1\) and equation \(y = x - 3\). The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-x^2 + 4x + 1) - (x - 3) = -x^2 + 3x + 4\), which reaches its maximum of 6.25 at \(x = 1.5\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded above by the parabola \(y = -2x^2 + 4x + 3\) and below by the line \(y = -2x - 1\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the parabola and the line in this region.
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-2x^2 + 4x + 3) - (-2x - 1) = -2x^2 + 6x + 4\). Writing this in vertex form gives \(d(x) = -2(x - 1.5)^2 + 8.5\), so the maximum vertical distance is 8.5.

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded by the parabola \(y = -2x^2 + 2x + 5\) and the line \(2x + y = -1\). At what value of \(x\) does the maximum vertical distance occur, and what is this maximum distance \(d\)?
qs.s: The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (-2x^2 + 2x + 5) - (-2x - 1) = -2x^2 + 4x + 6 = -2(x - 1)^2 + 8\). The maximum distance is \(d = 8\), occurring at \(x = 1\).

qs.q: The shaded region is bounded above by the line \(x - 2y = -4\) and below by the parabola \(y = \frac{1}{4}x^2 - x - 2\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola in this region.
qs.s: Solving for \(y\) gives the line \(y = \frac{1}{2}x + 2\). The vertical distance is \(d(x) = (\frac{1}{2}x + 2) - (\frac{1}{4}x^2 - x - 2) = -\frac{1}{4}x^2 + \frac{3}{2}x + 4 = -\frac{1}{4}(x - 3)^2 + 6.25\), so the maximum distance is 6.25.

qs.q: The figure shows the region bounded above by the line \(x - y = -1\) and below by the parabola \(y = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - x - 3\). Find the maximum vertical distance between the line and the parabola in this region.
qs.s: Expressing the line as \(y = x + 1\), the vertical distance is \(d(x) = (x + 1) - (\frac{1}{2}x^2 - x - 3) = -\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 2x + 4\). In vertex form, \(-\frac{1}{2}(x - 2)^2 + 6\), so the maximum distance is 6.

exercises.name: True or false statements about nth roots

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^2 = 36\) and \(x = 6\) are equivalent.
qs.a: False, because \(x^2 = 36\) has two real solutions, \(x = 6\) and \(x = -6\).
d: False, because \(x = 6\) is not a solution to \(x^2 = 36\).
qs.s: False. Two equations are equivalent if and only if they have the exact same solution set; \(x^2 = 36\) has solutions \(x = 6\) and \(x = -6\), whereas \(x = 6\) has only \(x = 6\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^3 = -27\) and \(x = \pm 3\) are equivalent.
qs.a: False, because \(x^3 = -27\) has only one real solution, \(x = -3\).
d: False, because \(x^3 = -27\) has no real solutions.
True, because odd powers always yield two real solutions with opposite signs.
qs.s: False. An odd root of a real number is unique, so \(x^3 = -27\) has only the solution \(x = -3\), whereas \(x = \pm 3\) includes both \(3\) and \(-3\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^2 = 25\) and \(x = \pm 5\) are equivalent.
qs.a: True, because both equations have the exact same solution set, \(\{-5, 5\}\).
d: False, because \(x^2 = 25\) has only the positive solution \(x = 5\).
False, because \(x = \pm 5\) represents two equations, not one.
qs.s: True. The equation \(x^2 = 25\) has two real solutions, \(x = 5\) and \(x = -5\), which matches the solution set \(\{-5, 5\}\) of \(x = \pm 5\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^3 = 8\) and \(x = 2\) are equivalent.
qs.a: True, because \(x = 2\) is the only real solution to \(x^3 = 8\).
d: False, because \(x^3 = 8\) also has the real solution \(x = -2\).
False, because an equation of degree 3 cannot be equivalent to an equation of degree 1.
qs.s: True. Since 3 is an odd index, \(x^3 = 8\) has exactly one real solution, \(x = 2\), so its solution set is identical to that of \(x = 2\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(\sqrt{x} = -4\) and \(x = 16\) are equivalent.
qs.a: False, because \(\sqrt{x} = -4\) has no real solution, while \(x = 16\) has one solution.
d: True, because squaring both sides of \(\sqrt{x} = -4\) gives \(x = 16\).
False, because the solution to \(\sqrt{x} = -4\) is \(x = -16\).
qs.s: False. The principal square root \(\sqrt{x}\) is defined to be non-negative, so \(\sqrt{x} = -4\) has no real solution, whereas \(x = 16\) has the solution 16.

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(\sqrt{x^2} = 6\) and \(x = 6\) are equivalent.
qs.a: False, because \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\), so the first equation has two solutions, \(x = 6\) and \(x = -6\).
d: True, because the radical and the exponent cancel out to give \(x = 6\).
True, because \((-6)^2\) is negative under the radical.
False, because \(\sqrt{x^2} = 6\) has no real solutions.
qs.s: False. Since \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) for all real numbers, \(\sqrt{x^2} = 6\) simplifies to \(|x| = 6\), which has solutions \(x = 6\) and \(x = -6\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^4 = 81\) and \(x^2 = 9\) are equivalent in the set of real numbers.
qs.a: True, because both equations have the exact same real solution set, \(\{-3, 3\}\).
d: False, because an equation of degree 4 must have four real solutions, while degree 2 has two.
False, because \(x = -3\) satisfies \(x^2 = 9\) but does not satisfy \(x^4 = 81\).
True, because \(x = 3\) is the only real solution to both equations.
qs.s: True. In the real numbers, \(x^4 = 81\) has solutions \(x = \pm \sqrt[4]{81} = \pm 3\), and \(x^2 = 9\) has solutions \(x = \pm 3\). Since their solution sets are identical, they are equivalent.

qs.q: True or false: The equations \((x + 2)^3 = -27\) and \(x = -5\) are equivalent.
qs.a: True, because the only real solution to \((x + 2)^3 = -27\) is \(x = -5\).
d: False, because \((x + 2)^3 = -27\) also has the real solution \(x = 1\).
False, because negative numbers have no real cube roots.
qs.s: True. Taking the cube root gives \(x + 2 = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\), which leads to the unique real solution \(x = -5\), exactly matching the solution set of \(x = -5\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \(x^2 + 16 = 0\) and \(x = \pm 4\) are equivalent in the set of real numbers.
qs.a: False, because \(x^2 + 16 = 0\) has no real solutions.
d: True, because subtracting 16 and taking the square root gives \(x = \pm 4\).
False, because the only real solution to \(x^2 + 16 = 0\) is \(x = -4\).
qs.s: False. Rearranging gives \(x^2 = -16\), which has no real solutions because the square of a real number cannot be negative; thus, it is not equivalent to \(x = \pm 4\).

qs.q: True or false: The equations \((x - 3)^2 = 25\) and \(x - 3 = 5\) are equivalent.
qs.a: False, because \((x - 3)^2 = 25\) has two solutions, \(x = 8\) and \(x = -2\).
d: True, because solving both equations gives \(x = 8\).

Add 75 to both sides to get \(2x^4 = 1250\), then divide by 2 to get \(x^4 = 625\). Since the exponent 4 is even and \(625 > 0\), \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{625} = \pm 5\).
Subtract 28 from both sides to get \(3x^3 = 192\), then divide by 3 to obtain \(x^3 = 64\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\).
Subtract 850 from both sides to get \(3x^4 = -768\), then divide by 3 to obtain \(x^4 = -256\). Since the power 4 is even and \(-256 < 0\), there is no real solution.
Subtract \(4x^5\) and 43 from both sides to get \(3x^5 = -96\), then divide by 3 to obtain \(x^5 = -32\). Taking the fifth root gives \(x = \sqrt[5]{-32} = -2\).
Add 5000 to both sides to get \(3x^4 = 30000\), then divide by 3 to get \(x^4 = 10000\). Since the exponent is even, \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{10000} = \pm 10\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^6 = -64\)
qs.s: An even power of a real number cannot be negative, so \(x^6 = -64\) has no real solution.

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^4 = -1\)
qs.s: Raising any real number to an even power results in a non-negative value, so \(x^4 = -1\) has no real solution.
Subtracting \(2x^2\) and 800 from both sides gives \(5x^2 = -720\), which simplifies to \(x^2 = -144\). Since the square of any real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Subtracting 53 from both sides gives \(3x^4 = -48\), and dividing by 3 yields \(x^4 = -16\). Since an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Subtracting \(x^2\) and 18 from both sides gives \(4x^2 = -256\), which simplifies to \(x^2 = -64\). Because the square of a real number is always non-negative, there is no real solution.
Expanding and rearranging terms gives \(3x^4 = -768\), so \(x^4 = -256\). Since an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Multiplying both sides by 2 and adding 15 gives \(x^6 = -729\). Since an even power of a real number cannot equal a negative number, there is no real solution.

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^5 = 243\)
qs.s: Since the exponent 5 is odd, there is only one real root: \(x = \sqrt[5]{243} = 3\).
Isolating \(x^6\) gives \(2x^6 = 128\), so \(x^6 = 64\). Because the index 6 is even and \(64 > 0\), \(x = \pm\sqrt[6]{64} = \pm 2\).
Subtract \(2x^3\) and add \(14\) to both sides to get \(3x^3 = 81\), so \(x^3 = 27\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = 3\).
Subtracting \(2x^4\) and \(73\) from both sides gives \(3x^4 = -48\), which simplifies to \(x^4 = -16\). Since an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Subtract \(15\) from both sides to obtain \(\frac{x^5}{9} = -27\), then multiply by \(9\) to get \(x^5 = -243\). Taking the fifth root gives \(x = -3\).
Add \(7\) to both sides to get \(\frac{x^4}{5} = 125\), then multiply by \(5\) to find \(x^4 = 625\). Since the exponent is even, \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{625} = \pm 5\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^5 = -1\)
qs.s: Since the exponent 5 is odd, taking the fifth root gives \(x = \sqrt[5]{-1} = -1\) because \((-1)^5 = -1\).
Subtracting \(2x^4\) and 19 gives \(3x^4 = -48\), so \(x^4 = -16\). Since an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Multiplying by 5 gives \(x^3 + 16 = -200\), so \(x^3 = -216\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = \sqrt[3]{-216} = -6\).
Subtracting \(3x^3\) and adding 50 gives \(4x^3 = 32\), so \(x^3 = 8\). Taking the cube root yields \(x = 2\).
Expanding gives \(3x^3 + 30 = x^3 - 220\), which simplifies to \(2x^3 = -250\), or \(x^3 = -125\). Thus, \(x = \sqrt[3]{-125} = -5\).
Subtracting \(x^7\) and 84 gives \(2x^7 = -256\), so \(x^7 = -128\). Taking the seventh root yields \(x = \sqrt[7]{-128} = -2\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^4 = 256\)
qs.s: Since the exponent 4 is even and \(256 > 0\), there are two real solutions: \(x = \pm \sqrt[4]{256} = \pm 4\).
Subtract 15 to get \(-2x^3 = 128\), then divide by \(-2\) to get \(x^3 = -64\). Taking the cube root yields the single real solution \(x = \sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\).
Subtract 135 to get \(2x^6 = -128\), then divide by 2 to yield \(x^6 = -64\). Since an even power cannot produce a negative real number, there is no real solution.
Subtract \(2x^4\) and add 17 to obtain \(3x^4 = 48\), so \(x^4 = 16\). Since the exponent is even, the solutions are \(x = \pm \sqrt[4]{16} = \pm 2\).
Add 14 to both sides to get \(3x^5 = 96\), then divide by 3 to get \(x^5 = 32\). Since the exponent is odd, the unique real solution is \(x = \sqrt[5]{32} = 2\).
Add 18 to both sides to obtain \(\frac{x^4}{5} = 125\), then multiply by 5 to find \(x^4 = 625\). Taking the fourth root gives \(x = \pm \sqrt[4]{625} = \pm 5\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^6 = -1\)
qs.s: Since the exponent \(6\) is an even integer, \(x^6\) cannot be negative for any real number \(x\). Therefore, \(x^6 = -1\) has no real solution.
Multiplying both sides by \(3\) gives \(x^4 - 15 = -96\), so \(x^4 = -81\). Because an even power cannot equal a negative number in the real numbers, there is no real solution.
Rearranging the equation yields \(4x^2 = -64\), which simplifies to \(x^2 = -16\). Since the square of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Because the exponent \(4\) is even, \((x - 3)^4 \geq 0\) for all real numbers \(x\). Since \(-81 < 0\), there is no real solution.
Since the square of any real expression is non-negative, \((2x + 1)^2 \geq 0\) for all real numbers \(x\). Because \(-25 < 0\), there is no real solution.
Subtracting 50 and dividing by 3 gives \(x^4 = -16\). Since an even power cannot equal a negative number, there is no real solution.
Subtracting 17 from both sides gives \(3x^5 = -96\), so \(x^5 = -32\). Taking the fifth root yields \(x = -2\).
Multiplying both sides by 2 gives \((x + 5)^3 = -216\). Taking the cube root gives \(x + 5 = -6\), so \(x = -11\).
Dividing by 2 gives \((x - 1)^3 = 64\). Taking the cube root yields \(x - 1 = 4\), so \(x = 5\).
Subtracting \(2x^3\) and adding 18 gives \(3x^3 = 81\), so \(x^3 = 27\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = 3\).
Since the index 3 is odd, there is exactly one real root: \(x = \sqrt[3]{-216} = -6\) because \((-6)^3 = -216\).
Divide both sides by 2 to get \(x^3 - 7 = -71\), then add 7 to obtain \(x^3 = -64\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = -4\).
Rearranging terms gives \(3x^4 = -48\), which simplifies to \(x^4 = -16\). Because an even power of a real number cannot equal a negative number, there is no real solution.
Subtract 40 from both sides to get \(3x^5 = -96\), then divide by 3 to obtain \(x^5 = -32\). Taking the fifth root gives \(x = \sqrt[5]{-32} = -2\).
Subtract 8 from both sides to get \(\frac{x^3}{5} = -25\), then multiply by 5 to obtain \(x^3 = -125\). Taking the cube root yields \(x = -5\).
Subtract \(2x^3\) and add 14 to both sides to get \(3x^3 = -81\), then divide by 3 to get \(x^3 = -27\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = -3\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^7 = 0\)
qs.s: Taking the seventh root of both sides gives \(x = \sqrt[7]{0} = 0\), since \(0^7 = 0\).
Adding \(19\) gives \(4x^3 = 256\), and dividing by \(4\) gives \(x^3 = 64\), so \(x = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\).
Dividing both sides by \(3\) gives \(x^8 - 5 = -5\), so \(x^8 = 0\), which yields \(x = 0\).
Subtracting \(80\) and dividing by \(3\) gives \(x^4 = -16\); since an even power cannot equal a negative real number, there is no real solution.
Subtracting \(75\) gives \(2x^3 = -54\), and dividing by \(2\) yields \(x^3 = -27\), so \(x = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\).
Adding \(43\) gives \(5x^4 = 80\), so \(x^4 = 16\); taking the fourth root of both sides gives \(x = \pm 2\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^6 = 0\)
qs.s: Since zero raised to any positive power is zero, the only real solution to \(x^6 = 0\) is \(x = 0\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^3 = -8\)
qs.s: Taking the cube root of both sides gives \(x = \sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\).
Subtract \(2x^4\) and add 25 to both sides to get \(4x^4 = 64\), then divide by 4 to get \(x^4 = 16\). Because the exponent is even and 16 is positive, \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{16} = \pm 2\).
Subtract 14 from both sides to get \(3x^3 = -81\), then divide by 3 to obtain \(x^3 = -27\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\).
Divide both sides by 2 to get \(x^5 + 7 = -25\), then subtract 7 to obtain \(x^5 = -32\). Taking the fifth root gives \(x = \sqrt[5]{-32} = -2\).
Multiply both sides by 2 to get \(x^5 + 16 = 16\), then subtract 16 from both sides to obtain \(x^5 = 0\). Since 0 is the only real number whose fifth power is 0, \(x = 0\).
Subtract 45 from both sides to get \(2x^4 = -32\), then divide by 2 to get \(x^4 = -16\). Since the exponent is even and \(-16\) is negative, there is no real solution.

qs.q: Solve for x: \(x^2 = 5\)

qs.q: Solve for x: \(x^2 = -7\)

qs.s: Subtract 3 from both sides to get \(4x^2 = 7\), then divide by 4 to get \(x^2 = \frac{7}{4}\). Taking the square root gives \(x = \pm\sqrt{\frac{7}{4}} = \pm\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\).

qs.q: Solve for x: \(3x^2 + 25 = 10\)

qs.q: Solve for x: \(2x^6 + 35 = 7\)

Subtracting 17 gives \(-3x^4 = 24\), and dividing by \(-3\) gives \(x^4 = -8\). Because the exponent 4 is even, \(x^4 = -8\) has no real solution.

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(\frac{x^8}{3} + 9 = 2\)
qs.s: Subtracting 9 gives \(\frac{x^8}{3} = -7\), and multiplying both sides by 3 yields \(x^8 = -21\). Since 8 is even, no real number raised to the 8th power can be negative, so there is no real solution.

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^5 = 6\)
qs.s: Since the exponent \(5\) is odd, the equation has one real solution. Taking the fifth root of both sides gives \(x = \sqrt[5]{6}\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^8 = 11\)
qs.s: Since the exponent \(8\) is even and \(11 > 0\), taking the eighth root of both sides gives two real solutions, \(x = \pm\sqrt[8]{11}\).
Subtract \(5\) from both sides to get \(2x^4 = 36\), then divide by \(2\) to find \(x^4 = 18\). Since the exponent is even and \(18 > 0\), the solutions are \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{18}\).
Subtract \(4\) from both sides to get \(-3x^5 = 36\), then divide by \(-3\) to find \(x^5 = -12\). Since the exponent is odd, taking the fifth root gives \(x = -\sqrt[5]{12}\).
Add \(7\) to both sides to get \(3x^5 = 48\), then divide by \(3\) to obtain \(x^5 = 16\). Since the exponent is odd, the solution is \(x = \sqrt[5]{16}\).
Subtract \(2x^3\) and add \(19\) to both sides to obtain \(5x^3 = 25\), then divide by \(5\) to get \(x^3 = 5\). Taking the cube root gives the single real solution \(x = \sqrt[3]{5}\).
Subtract \(11\) from both sides to get \(2x^5 = -36\), then divide by \(2\) to obtain \(x^5 = -18\). Since the exponent is odd, the only real solution is \(x = -\sqrt[5]{18}\).
Subtract \(17\) from both sides to get \(-2x^5 = 28\), then divide by \(-2\) to get \(x^5 = -14\). Since the index \(5\) is odd, there is one real solution: \(x = -\sqrt[5]{14}\).
Combine like terms to get \(2x^6 = 26\), then divide by \(2\) to obtain \(x^6 = 13\). Since the exponent \(6\) is even and \(13 > 0\), there are two real solutions: \(x = \pm\sqrt[6]{13}\).
Expand the left side to get \(3x^3 - 12 = x^3 - 22\), then collect like terms to find \(2x^3 = -10\), so \(x^3 = -5\). Taking the cube root yields the single real solution \(x = -\sqrt[3]{5}\).
Subtract \(2x^4\) and \(23\) from both sides to obtain \(3x^4 = -18\), which simplifies to \(x^4 = -6\). Because an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.

exercises.name: Simplifying square roots with real variables

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{16x^2}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{16} = 4\) and \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) for any real number \(x\), the simplified form is \(4|x|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{25y^2}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of each factor gives \(\sqrt{25}\sqrt{y^2} = 5|y|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{100b^2}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{100} = 10\) and \(\sqrt{b^2} = |b|\), the expression simplifies to \(10|b|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{49a^2}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{49} = 7\) and \(\sqrt{a^2} = |a|\), the simplified expression is \(7|a|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{64m^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square root yields \(\sqrt{64}\sqrt{m^2} = 8|m|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{144x^6}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{144} = 12\) and \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\); the absolute value is required because the resulting power is odd, giving \(12|x^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{49x^6}{64}}\)
qs.s: Applying the quotient property gives \(\frac{\sqrt{49x^6}}{\sqrt{64}} = \frac{7|x^3|}{8} = \frac{7}{8}|x^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36x^2y^4}\)
qs.s: Taking the square roots gives \(\sqrt{36} = 6\), \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) (odd power requires absolute value), and \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\) (even power is always non-negative), which yields \(6|x|y^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{25x^3}\)
qs.s: Factoring gives \(\sqrt{25x^2 \cdot x} = 5x\sqrt{x}\); because the radicand has an odd exponent, the restriction \(x \ge 0\) is required for the root to be a real number.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{81a^4b^6}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each component gives \(\sqrt{81} = 9\), \(\sqrt{a^4} = a^2\) (no absolute value needed for an even power), and \(\sqrt{b^6} = |b^3|\) (absolute value needed for an odd power), resulting in \(9a^2|b^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^6}\)
qs.s: Because the exponent 6 is even, \(a\) can be any real number. Taking the square root yields \(\sqrt{(a^3)^2} = |a^3|\), which requires absolute value notation because the resulting exponent 3 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{y^7}\)
qs.s: Since the exponent 7 is odd, \(y\) must be non-negative (\(y \ge 0\)) for the square root to be a real number. Factoring the radicand gives \(\sqrt{y^6 \cdot y} = y^3\sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^3}\)
qs.s: Since the exponent 3 is odd, \(m\) must be non-negative (\(m \ge 0\)) for the expression to be defined in the real numbers. Factoring gives \(\sqrt{m^2 \cdot m} = m\sqrt{m}, m \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{b^9}\)
qs.s: Because the exponent 9 is odd, \(b\) must be non-negative (\(b \ge 0\)) for the expression to represent a real number. Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{b^8 \cdot b} = b^4\sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{w^{10}}\)
qs.s: Since the radicand exponent 10 is even, \(w\) can be any real number. Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{(w^5)^2} = |w^5|\), which requires absolute value bars because the simplified exponent 5 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25 u^8 v^3}\)
qs.s: Since \(u^8 \ge 0\) for all real \(u\), the radicand requires \(v^3 \ge 0\), giving the restriction \(v \ge 0\). Evaluating gives \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), \(\sqrt{u^8} = u^4\) (no absolute value needed since 4 is even), and \(\sqrt{v^3} = v\sqrt{v}\), so the simplified result is \(5u^4 v\sqrt{v}, v \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{p^2 q^4 r^7}\)
qs.s: Because \(p^2 \ge 0\) and \(q^4 \ge 0\) for all real numbers, the radicand requires \(r^7 \ge 0\), which means \(r \ge 0\). Simplifying each factor gives \(\sqrt{p^2} = |p|\), \(\sqrt{q^4} = q^2\), and \(\sqrt{r^7} = r^3\sqrt{r}\), yielding \(|p|q^2 r^3\sqrt{r}, r \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49 c^{10} d^8}\)
qs.s: Since both exponents are even, the expression is defined for all real numbers \(c\) and \(d\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), \(\sqrt{c^{10}} = |c^5|\) (absolute value needed because the resulting exponent 5 is odd), and \(\sqrt{d^8} = d^4\) (no absolute value needed because 4 is even), giving \(7|c^5|d^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 a^2 b^4}\)
qs.s: Both exponents are even, so the radicand is non-negative for all real numbers \(a\) and \(b\). Evaluating the square root gives \(\sqrt{36} = 6\), \(\sqrt{a^2} = |a|\) (absolute value needed because the resulting exponent is odd), and \(\sqrt{b^4} = b^2\) (no absolute value needed because \(b^2 \ge 0\)), yielding \(6|a|b^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^6 y^5}\)
qs.s: Since \(x^6 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), the expression requires \(y^5 \ge 0\), which restricts \(y \ge 0\). Evaluating gives \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) (absolute value needed because \(x\) can be negative and the exponent 3 is odd) and \(\sqrt{y^5} = y^2\sqrt{y}\), resulting in \(|x^3|y^2\sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^8 v^2}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponents by 2 yields \(u^4\) and \(v^1\). Since \(v\) has an odd power, it must be written with absolute value bars, giving \(u^4 |v|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^8 y^6}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponents by 2 gives \(x^4\) and \(y^3\). Because \(y^3\) has an odd exponent, absolute value notation is necessary, yielding \(x^4 |y^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^2 b^4}\)
qs.s: Dividing each exponent by 2 gives \(a^1\) and \(b^2\). Because the resulting exponent of \(a\) is odd, absolute value notation is required to guarantee a non-negative result, giving \(|a|b^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{c^{10} d^4}\)
qs.s: Dividing each exponent by 2 gives \(c^5\) and \(d^2\). Since 5 is an odd exponent, absolute value notation is required on \(c^5\), producing \(|c^5| d^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^4 n^6}\)
qs.s: Dividing each exponent by 2 yields \(m^2\) and \(n^3\). Since the exponent of \(n\) is odd, absolute value notation is required, resulting in \(m^2 |n^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 u^2 v^7}\)
qs.s: First, \(\sqrt{36} = 6\). The odd power on \(v\) requires \(v \geq 0\) and simplifies to \(\sqrt{v^7} = v^3\sqrt{v}\), while \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\) because \(u\) can be negative, giving \(6 |u| v^3 \sqrt{v}, v \geq 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^5 y^6}\)
qs.s: Because \(x\) has an odd power under the radical, the restriction \(x \geq 0\) is required, and \(\sqrt{x^5} = x^2\sqrt{x}\). For \(y^6\), dividing the exponent by 2 gives an odd power \(y^3\), which requires absolute value notation, giving \(x^2 |y^3| \sqrt{x}, x \geq 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{100 a^4 b^6 c^8}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of 100 gives 10, and dividing each exponent by 2 gives \(a^2\), \(b^3\), and \(c^4\). Because \(b^3\) has an odd exponent, it requires absolute value bars, yielding \(10 a^2 |b^3| c^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers, with \(y \neq 0\): \(\sqrt{\frac{25 x^6}{y^4}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient property of radicals, simplify the numerator as \(\sqrt{25 x^6} = 5|x^3|\) and the denominator as \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\). This yields \(\frac{5 |x^3|}{y^2}\), with no absolute value needed in the denominator because \(y^2 > 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{81 m^{10} n^4}\)
qs.s: Taking the principal square root of 81 gives 9, and dividing each exponent by 2 gives \(m^5\) and \(n^2\). Since \(m^5\) has an odd power, absolute value notation is required, resulting in \(9 |m^5| n^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{p^8 q}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{p^8} = p^4\) has an even exponent, it is always non-negative so no absolute value is required, while \(q\) remains under the square root, requiring \(q \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^4 b}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{a^4} = a^2\) is always non-negative, no absolute value is needed, and because \(b\) has an odd exponent under the radical, we must have \(b \ge 0\). Thus, \(\sqrt{a^4 b} = a^2\sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u v^6}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{v^6} = |v^3|\) because the simplified exponent is odd, and the odd power of \(u\) remaining under the radical requires \(u \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{c^2 d}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of \(c^2\) gives \(|c|\) because \(c\) can be negative and its resulting exponent is odd, while \(d\) remains under the radical requiring \(d \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^{10} y}\)
qs.s: The square root of \(x^{10}\) is \(|x^5|\) because 5 is an odd exponent, and the variable \(y\) remains under the radical, which requires \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^3 y^4}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(x^2 \cdot x \cdot y^4\). Taking the square root gives \(|x| y^2\sqrt{x}\), but because \(x\) must be non-negative under the radical (\(x \ge 0\)), \(|x|\) simplifies to \(x\), giving \(x y^2\sqrt{x}, x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^3 y^6}\)
qs.s: We simplify \(\sqrt{x^3} = x\sqrt{x}\) with restriction \(x \ge 0\) (so no absolute value is needed on \(x\)), while \(\sqrt{y^6} = |y^3|\) requires absolute value because \(y\) can be negative, resulting in \(x|y^3|\sqrt{x}, x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25 p^4 q^6 r}\)
qs.s: We compute \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), \(\sqrt{p^4} = p^2\), and \(\sqrt{q^6} = |q^3|\), while \(r\) remains under the root requiring \(r \ge 0\), giving \(5p^2|q^3|\sqrt{r}, r \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{16 a^5 b^4}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{16} = 4\), \(\sqrt{a^5} = a^2\sqrt{a}\) with \(a \ge 0\), and \(\sqrt{b^4} = b^2\), which simplifies to \(4a^2 b^2\sqrt{a}, a \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^2 v^4 w^3}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each factor gives \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\), \(\sqrt{v^4} = v^2\), and \(\sqrt{w^3} = w\sqrt{w}\) with \(w \ge 0\), yielding \(|u| v^2 w\sqrt{w}, w \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^2 b}\)
qs.s: Since \(a\) can be any real number, \(\sqrt{a^2} = |a|\). The odd exponent on \(b\) requires the restriction \(b \ge 0\), giving \(|a|\sqrt{b},\ b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{9m^2 n}\)
qs.s: Taking the square roots of the factors gives \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt{m^2} = |m|\). Since \(n\) remains under the radical, we must restrict \(n \ge 0\), yielding \(3|m|\sqrt{n},\ n \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{16u v^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square root yields \(\sqrt{16} = 4\) and \(\sqrt{v^2} = |v|\) for any real \(v\). The variable \(u\) stays inside the radical with the restriction \(u \ge 0\), giving \(4|v|\sqrt{u},\ u \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{4x y^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square roots gives \(\sqrt{4} = 2\) and \(\sqrt{y^2} = |y|\) because \(y\) can be negative. The linear variable \(x\) remains under the radical with the restriction \(x \ge 0\), resulting in \(2|y|\sqrt{x},\ x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25c^2 d}\)
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) and \(\sqrt{c^2} = |c|\). Because \(d\) has an odd power, it must remain in the radicand with the restriction \(d \ge 0\), giving \(5|c|\sqrt{d},\ d \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49 x^6 y}\)
qs.s: We evaluate \(\sqrt{49} = 7\) and \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\), where the absolute value is necessary because \(x^3\) can be negative. The factor \(y\) remains under the radical with the restriction \(y \ge 0\), yielding \(7|x^3|\sqrt{y},\ y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^3 b^2}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(a^2 \cdot a \cdot b^2\); the odd power of \(a\) requires \(a \ge 0\), so \(\sqrt{a^2} = a\) without absolute value. Since \(b\) can be negative, \(\sqrt{b^2} = |b|\), giving \(a|b|\sqrt{a},\ a \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^5 n^6}\)
qs.s: Factoring gives \(\sqrt{m^4 \cdot m \cdot n^6}\); since \(m\) appears under an odd power we require \(m \ge 0\), meaning \(\sqrt{m^4} = m^2\). Because \(n\) can be negative and \(n^3\) is odd, an absolute value is needed on \(n^3\), giving \(m^2|n^3|\sqrt{m},\ m \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 a^2 b^4 c^3}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(36 \cdot a^2 \cdot b^4 \cdot c^2 \cdot c\); the odd power on \(c\) requires \(c \ge 0\), so \(\sqrt{c^2} = c\). The even powers evaluate to \(\sqrt{a^2} = |a|\) (since \(a\) can be negative) and \(\sqrt{b^4} = b^2\), giving \(6|a|b^2 c\sqrt{c},\ c \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{9x^2 y^4}\)
qs.s: Evaluating gives \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) because \(x\) can be negative, and \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\) which is already non-negative, resulting in \(3|x|y^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^6 v^2}\)
qs.s: Dividing each exponent by 2 yields \(u^3\) and \(v\), both of which have odd exponents and can be negative, so an absolute value is needed around their product to give \(|u^3 v|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^4 y^2}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent of \(x^4\) by 2 gives \(x^2\), which is always non-negative and needs no absolute value, while \(\sqrt{y^2} = |y|\) requires absolute value because \(y\) can be negative, giving \(x^2 |y|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{4a^2 b^2}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of the coefficient gives \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), and since \(a\) and \(b\) can be any real numbers, \(\sqrt{a^2 b^2} = |ab|\), yielding \(2|ab|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{64x^4 y^8 z^2}\)
qs.s: We compute \(\sqrt{64} = 8\) and divide each exponent by 2. The powers \(x^2\) and \(y^4\) are non-negative for all real numbers, but \(z\) has an odd exponent and requires an absolute value, giving \(8x^2 y^4 |z|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25a^2 b^5}\)
qs.s: Because \(b\) has an odd exponent under the radical, the expression is defined only when \(b \ge 0\), which gives \(\sqrt{b^5} = b^2\sqrt{b}\). Since \(a\) can be any real number, \(\sqrt{a^2} = |a|\), giving \(5|a|b^2\sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{100a^6 b^4 c^{12}}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{100} = 10\), \(\sqrt{a^6} = |a^3|\), \(\sqrt{b^4} = b^2\), and \(\sqrt{c^{12}} = c^6\). Absolute value is required on \(a^3\) because its exponent is odd, while \(b^2\) and \(c^6\) are always non-negative, giving \(10|a^3|b^2 c^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49x^9 y^4}\)
qs.s: Since \(x\) has an odd power in the radicand, we must have \(x \ge 0\), which simplifies to \(\sqrt{x^9} = x^4\sqrt{x}\). Simplifying the remaining factors gives \(\sqrt{49} = 7\) and \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\), resulting in \(7x^4 y^2\sqrt{x}, x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36u^6 v^3 w^4}\)
qs.s: Because \(v\) has an odd exponent, the radical is defined only for \(v \ge 0\), simplifying to \(\sqrt{v^3} = v\sqrt{v}\). For the even powers, \(\sqrt{u^6} = |u^3|\) requires absolute value because the exponent 3 is odd, whereas \(w^2 \ge 0\) does not, yielding \(6|u^3|v w^2\sqrt{v}, v \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 u^2 v^5}\)
qs.s: We evaluate \(\sqrt{36} = 6\) and \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\). For the odd power \(v^5\), the radicand requires \(v \ge 0\) to be defined, simplifying to \(v^2\sqrt{v}\), which yields \(6 |u| v^2 \sqrt{v}, v \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49 a^6 b^4}\)
qs.s: We evaluate \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), \(\sqrt{a^6} = |a^3|\) (absolute value needed since the resulting exponent is odd), and \(\sqrt{b^4} = b^2\) (no absolute value needed since the exponent is even), resulting in \(7 |a^3| b^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^4 b^6}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of each factor gives \(\sqrt{a^4} = a^2\) (which is always non-negative for real \(a\)) and \(\sqrt{b^6} = |b^3|\) (which requires absolute value notation because the exponent 3 is odd), giving \(a^2 |b^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{p^8 q^6}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square roots gives \(\sqrt{p^8} = p^4\) (even exponent, no absolute value needed) and \(\sqrt{q^6} = |q^3|\) (odd exponent, absolute value needed), resulting in \(p^4 |q^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^6 v^4}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{v^4} = v^2\) is non-negative and \(\sqrt{u^6} = |u^3|\) requires an absolute value because \(u^3\) can be negative for real \(u\), the simplified form is \(v^2 |u^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^2 n^4}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{n^4} = n^2\), which is non-negative for all real \(n\), and \(\sqrt{m^2} = |m|\), which requires absolute value notation since the exponent is odd. Thus, the expression simplifies to \(n^2 |m|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{c^8 d^2}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{c^8} = c^4\), which is always non-negative, and \(\sqrt{d^2} = |d|\), which requires absolute value notation, giving \(c^4 |d|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^{12} n^4 p^6 q^8}\)
