qs.s: Dividing each exponent by 2 gives \(\sqrt{m^{12}} = m^6\), \(\sqrt{n^4} = n^2\), and \(\sqrt{q^8} = q^4\), all of which have even exponents and need no absolute values, while \(\sqrt{p^6} = |p^3|\) has an odd exponent and requires absolute value notation, giving \(m^6 n^2 q^4 |p^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25 u^4 v^6 w^7}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), \(\sqrt{u^4} = u^2\), and \(\sqrt{v^6} = |v^3|\) (requiring absolute value notation since 3 is odd). For \(\sqrt{w^7} = w^3 \sqrt{w}\), the restriction \(w \ge 0\) is required for real values, resulting in \(5 u^2 w^3 |v^3| \sqrt{w}, w \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^6 y^3}\)
qs.s: Since \(x^6\) has an even exponent, \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) requires absolute value notation because the resulting power 3 is odd. For \(\sqrt{y^3}\) to be real, we must have \(y \ge 0\), simplifying to \(y \sqrt{y}\), which gives \(|x^3| y \sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 x^4 y^2 z^8}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square root of the coefficient gives \(\sqrt{36} = 6\). For the variables, \(\sqrt{x^4} = x^2\) and \(\sqrt{z^8} = z^4\) have even powers, while \(\sqrt{y^2} = |y|\) requires absolute value notation, yielding \(6 x^2 z^4 |y|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49 a^4 b^5}\)
qs.s: Factor the perfect square part as \(\sqrt{49 a^4 b^4} = 7 a^2 b^2\). For the expression under the square root to be defined for real numbers, the odd exponent requires \(b \ge 0\), leaving \(7 a^2 b^2 \sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^6 n^{12}}\)
qs.s: Since \(m^3\) can be negative for real \(m\), \(\sqrt{m^6} = |m^3|\), whereas \(\sqrt{n^{12}} = n^6\) is always non-negative. Thus, the expression simplifies to \(|m^3| n^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^{10} v^4}\)
qs.s: Simplifying each power gives \(\sqrt{u^{10}} = |u^5|\) because \(u^5\) is an odd power and may be negative, while \(\sqrt{v^4} = v^2\) is always non-negative. Hence, the result is \(|u^5| v^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25 m^2 n^7}\)
qs.s: The radicand requires \(n \ge 0\) for the odd power, simplifying \(\sqrt{n^7}\) to \(n^3 \sqrt{n}\). With \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) and \(\sqrt{m^2} = |m|\), the result is \(5 |m| n^3 \sqrt{n}, n \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{64 x^{10} y^4 z^7}\)
qs.s: The factor \(\sqrt{z^7}\) simplifies to \(z^3 \sqrt{z}\) with the restriction \(z \ge 0\). Evaluating \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), \(\sqrt{x^{10}} = |x^5|\), and \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\) gives \(8 |x^5| y^2 z^3 \sqrt{z}, z \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36 a^8 b^6 c^4}\)
qs.s: We evaluate \(\sqrt{36} = 6\), \(\sqrt{a^8} = a^4\), \(\sqrt{b^6} = |b^3|\) (since \(b^3\) can be negative), and \(\sqrt{c^4} = c^2\). Combining these factors gives \(6 a^4 |b^3| c^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^4 v^6 w^3}\)
qs.s: The odd exponent requires \(w \ge 0\), so \(\sqrt{w^3} = w\sqrt{w}\). Simplifying the even powers gives \(\sqrt{u^4} = u^2\) and \(\sqrt{v^6} = |v^3|\), resulting in \(u^2 |v^3| w \sqrt{w}, w \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 y^7}\)
qs.s: Since \(x\) can be any real number, \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\), while the odd exponent on \(y\) requires the restriction \(y \ge 0\) with \(\sqrt{y^7} = y^3\sqrt{y}\). Combining these gives \(|x| y^3 \sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^7 n^2}\)
qs.s: The odd exponent on \(m\) requires the restriction \(m \ge 0\), which simplifies to \(\sqrt{m^7} = m^3\sqrt{m}\). For \(n\), taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{n^2} = |n|\), so the result is \(m^3 |n| \sqrt{m}, m \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{p^6 q^5}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of \(p^6\) gives an odd exponent, requiring absolute value: \(\sqrt{p^6} = |p^3|\). The odd power on \(q\) requires \(q \ge 0\) with \(\sqrt{q^5} = q^2\sqrt{q}\), giving \(|p^3| q^2 \sqrt{q}, q \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{u^3 v^6}\)
qs.s: The odd power on \(u\) requires \(u \ge 0\) and simplifies to \(\sqrt{u^3} = u\sqrt{u}\). For \(v^6\), the resulting power is odd, so \(\sqrt{v^6} = |v^3|\), giving \(u |v^3| \sqrt{u}, u \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{16 x^5 y^4 z^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluate \(\sqrt{16} = 4\), \(\sqrt{x^5} = x^2\sqrt{x}\) with \(x \ge 0\), \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\) (no absolute value needed because \(y^2 \ge 0\)), and \(\sqrt{z^2} = |z|\). Multiplying these together yields \(4 x^2 y^2 |z| \sqrt{x}, x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{81 c^2 d^{11} e^{12}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate \(\sqrt{81} = 9\), \(\sqrt{c^2} = |c|\), \(\sqrt{d^{11}} = d^5\sqrt{d}\) with \(d \ge 0\), and \(\sqrt{e^{12}} = e^6\). Putting all factors together yields \(9 |c| d^5 e^6 \sqrt{d}, d \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49 a^6 b^7 c^4}\)
qs.s: Evaluate \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), \(\sqrt{a^6} = |a^3|\) (since \(a^3\) is an odd power), \(\sqrt{b^7} = b^3\sqrt{b}\) with restriction \(b \ge 0\), and \(\sqrt{c^4} = c^2\). Combining all factors gives \(7 |a^3| b^3 c^2 \sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25 u^4 v^3 w^6 x^8}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each component gives \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), \(\sqrt{u^4} = u^2\), \(\sqrt{v^3} = v\sqrt{v}\) with \(v \ge 0\), \(\sqrt{w^6} = |w^3|\), and \(\sqrt{x^8} = x^4\). Combining these results yields \(5 u^2 v |w^3| x^4 \sqrt{v}, v \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{a^{18}}\)
qs.s: We evaluate \(\sqrt{a^{18}} = \sqrt{(a^9)^2} = |a^9|\). Absolute value bars are necessary because the exponent 9 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{y^{14}}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent by 2 gives \(14 / 2 = 7\). Since 7 is odd, absolute value notation is required to guarantee a non-negative result, giving \(|y^7|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{c^{26}}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{c^{26}} = \sqrt{(c^{13})^2}\) and 13 is an odd exponent, the result must be written with absolute value bars as \(|c^{13}|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{w^{30}}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent by 2 gives 15, which is odd. Therefore, the simplified form is \(|w^{15}|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{b^{22}}\)
qs.s: The exponent simplifies to \(22 / 2 = 11\). Because 11 is an odd number, we write \(|b^{11}|\) to ensure the expression is always non-negative for any real number \(b\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{m^{22}}{64}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property of radicals to get \(\frac{\sqrt{m^{22}}}{\sqrt{64}} = \frac{|m^{11}|}{8}\). Absolute value notation is required on \(m^{11}\) because the exponent 11 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{x^{15}}\)
qs.s: Write \(x^{15}\) as \(x^{14} \cdot x\), so \(\sqrt{x^{15}} = \sqrt{x^{14}}\sqrt{x} = x^7\sqrt{x}\). Because an odd power of a negative number is negative (making the square root undefined in the real numbers), the restriction \(x \ge 0\) is required.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36u^{12}v^{10}}\)
qs.s: We calculate \(\sqrt{36} = 6\), \(\sqrt{u^{12}} = u^6\) (no absolute value needed since 6 is even), and \(\sqrt{v^{10}} = |v^5|\) (absolute value needed since 5 is odd). The final simplified expression is \(6u^6|v^5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^8 b^{14}}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of each factor gives \(\sqrt{a^8} = a^4\) and \(\sqrt{b^{14}} = |b^7|\). Since 4 is even, \(a^4\) is always non-negative and needs no absolute value bars, while \(b^7\) has an odd exponent and requires absolute value notation.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variable be any real number: \(\sqrt{49x^{18}}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square root of the coefficient gives \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), and \(\sqrt{x^{18}} = |x^9|\) because \(18 / 2 = 9\) is odd. Combining them gives \(7|x^9|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36a^8 b^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each term gives \(\sqrt{36} = 6\), \(\sqrt{a^8} = a^4\) (no absolute value needed because the exponent 4 is even), and \(\sqrt{b^2} = |b|\) (absolute value needed because the exponent is odd). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(6a^4|b|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49x^6 y^4}\)
qs.s: Taking the square root of each factor gives \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) (absolute value is required because the resulting exponent 3 is odd and \(x\) can be negative), and \(\sqrt{y^4} = y^2\). Thus, the simplified expression is \(7|x^3|y^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{100u^6 v^{12}}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{100} = 10\), \(\sqrt{u^6} = |u^3|\) since the exponent becomes odd, and \(\sqrt{v^{12}} = v^6\) since the exponent is even. The final result is \(10|u^3|v^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{64p^{10} q^4}\)
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), \(\sqrt{p^{10}} = |p^5|\) (as the simplified exponent 5 is odd), and \(\sqrt{q^4} = q^2\) (as 2 is even), the expression simplifies to \(8|p^5|q^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers (\(w \ne 0\)): \(\sqrt{\frac{81u^8 v^6}{16w^4}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient property gives \(\frac{\sqrt{81u^8 v^6}}{\sqrt{16w^4}}\). Simplifying the numerator gives \(9u^4|v^3|\) (absolute value needed since the power 3 is odd) and the denominator gives \(4w^2\), yielding \(\frac{9u^4|v^3|}{4w^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36a^6 b^3 c^4}\)
qs.s: The odd exponent on \(b\) requires \(b \ge 0\), simplifying to \(\sqrt{b^3} = b\sqrt{b}\). For the even exponents, \(\sqrt{a^6} = |a^3|\) and \(\sqrt{c^4} = c^2\), which combined with \(\sqrt{36} = 6\) gives \(6|a^3|b c^2\sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{144x^4 y^6 z^8}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each component gives \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), \(\sqrt{x^4} = x^2\), \(\sqrt{y^6} = |y^3|\) (absolute value is required because \(y^3\) can be negative), and \(\sqrt{z^8} = z^4\). Thus, the simplified expression is \(12x^2|y^3|z^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25x^6 y^5}\)
qs.s: Because the exponent on \(y\) is odd, the radicand is only defined for real numbers when \(y \ge 0\), giving \(\sqrt{y^5} = y^2\sqrt{y}\). Since \(x\) can be any real number, \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\), resulting in \(5|x^3|y^2\sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{225m^{14} n^8 p^{12}}\)
qs.s: Evaluating each factor gives \(\sqrt{225} = 15\), \(\sqrt{m^{14}} = |m^7|\) (since the simplified exponent 7 is odd), \(\sqrt{n^8} = n^4\), and \(\sqrt{p^{12}} = p^6\). The simplified result is \(15|m^7|n^4 p^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{9x^5}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as \(9 \cdot x^4 \cdot x\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{9}=3\) and \(\sqrt{x^4}=x^2\), leaving \(\sqrt{x}\); because the original exponent of \(x\) is odd, the restriction \(x \ge 0\) is required, giving \(3x^2\sqrt{x}, x \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25y^7}\)
qs.s: Rewrite \(\sqrt{25y^7}\) as \(\sqrt{25 \cdot y^6 \cdot y} = 5y^3\sqrt{y}\). Since \(y\) has an odd power in the radicand, \(y\) cannot be negative, so the restriction is \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{16a^3}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as \(16 \cdot a^2 \cdot a\) to obtain \(\sqrt{16a^2 \cdot a} = 4a\sqrt{a}\). The odd exponent requires \(a \ge 0\) for the radicand to be defined in the real numbers.

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49b^{11}}\)
qs.s: Separate the radicand into perfect square factors: \(\sqrt{49 \cdot b^{10} \cdot b} = 7b^5\sqrt{b}\). Because the exponent 11 is odd, the expression requires the restriction \(b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{16x^2 y^5}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{16}=4\). Since \(x^2\) has an even exponent whose half is odd, \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\); the odd power on \(y\) requires \(y \ge 0\) and simplifies to \(\sqrt{y^5}=y^2\sqrt{y}\), giving \(4|x|y^2\sqrt{y}, y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{100m^{10} n^7}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{100}=10\), \(\sqrt{m^{10}}=|m^5|\) because 5 is odd, and \(\sqrt{n^7}=n^3\sqrt{n}\) with the restriction \(n \ge 0\), giving \(10|m^5|n^3\sqrt{n}, n \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{36u^6 v^3}\)
qs.s: We compute \(\sqrt{36}=6\), \(\sqrt{u^6}=|u^3|\) (absolute value needed since the simplified exponent 3 is odd), and \(\sqrt{v^3}=v\sqrt{v}\) with restriction \(v \ge 0\), yielding \(6|u^3|v\sqrt{v}, v \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{49a^4 b^7}\)
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\sqrt{49}=7\) and \(\sqrt{a^4}=a^2\) (no absolute value needed because \(a^2 \ge 0\)). For \(b^7\), \(\sqrt{b^7}=b^3\sqrt{b}\) with the restriction \(b \ge 0\), resulting in \(7a^2 b^3\sqrt{b}, b \ge 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Let the variables be any real numbers: \(\sqrt{25x^4 y^6 z^5}\)
qs.s: Evaluate each part: \(\sqrt{25}=5\), \(\sqrt{x^4}=x^2\) (even power outside, no absolute value), \(\sqrt{y^6}=|y^3|\) (odd power outside, absolute value required), and \(\sqrt{z^5}=z^2\sqrt{z}\) with restriction \(z \ge 0\), giving \(5x^2|y^3|z^2\sqrt{z}, z \ge 0\).

exercises.name: Simplifying higher-index radicals with positive variables

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{64}\)
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\), the cube root of \(64\) is \(4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16}\)
qs.s: Since \(2^4 = 16\) and the radical symbol denotes the principal root, \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{216}\)
qs.s: Since \(6^3 = 216\), the cube root of \(216\) is \(6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{125}\)
qs.s: Since \(5^3 = 125\), the cube root of \(125\) is \(5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81}\)
qs.s: Since \(3^4 = 81\) and the radical symbol denotes the principal root, \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^8y^{12}}\)
qs.s: Take the fourth root of each factor: \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\), \(\sqrt[4]{x^8} = x^{8/4} = x^2\), and \(\sqrt[4]{y^{12}} = y^{12/4} = y^3\), resulting in \(3x^2y^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{125x^6}{8}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to simplify numerator and denominator separately: \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{125x^6}}{\sqrt[3]{8}} = \frac{5x^2}{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{27a^3b^9}{64c^{12}}}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of each factor in the numerator and denominator: \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{27a^3b^9}}{\sqrt[3]{64c^{12}}} = \frac{3ab^3}{4c^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{256x^{12}y^{20}}\)
qs.s: Find the fourth root of each factor: \(\sqrt[4]{256} = 4\), \(\sqrt[4]{x^{12}} = x^3\), and \(\sqrt[4]{y^{20}} = y^5\), giving \(4x^3y^5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{64x^9}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of the coefficient and the variable term: \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\) and \(\sqrt[3]{x^9} = x^{9/3} = x^3\), giving \(4x^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-8}\)
qs.s: Since \((-2)^3 = -8\), the real cube root of \(-8\) is \(-2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-1}\)
qs.s: Since \((-1)^3 = -1\), the real cube root of \(-1\) is \(-1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-\frac{27x^3}{64y^9}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to take the cube root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{-27x^3} = -3x\) and \(\sqrt[3]{64y^9} = 4y^3\), which gives \(-\frac{3x}{4y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-64x^6}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of the coefficient and the variable part: \(\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\) and \(\sqrt[3]{x^6} = x^{6/3} = x^2\), giving \(-4x^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-64x^3} + \sqrt[3]{-8x^3}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(\sqrt[3]{-64x^3} = -4x\) and \(\sqrt[3]{-8x^3} = -2x\), then combine the like terms: \(-4x + (-2x) = -6x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-125a^9b^3}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of each factor: \(\sqrt[3]{-125} = -5\), \(\sqrt[3]{a^9} = a^{9/3} = a^3\), and \(\sqrt[3]{b^3} = b^{3/3} = b\), giving \(-5a^3b\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{b^8}\)
qs.s: Using the rule \(\sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{\frac{m}{n}}\), we find \(\sqrt[4]{b^8} = b^{\frac{8}{4}} = b^2\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{z^{12}}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent by the index gives \(\sqrt[4]{z^{12}} = z^{\frac{12}{4}} = z^3\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{y^4}\)
qs.s: Using the property \(\sqrt[n]{x^n} = x\) for positive variables, we have \(\sqrt[4]{y^4} = y\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{a^6}\)
qs.s: Using the fractional exponent rule \(\sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{\frac{m}{n}}\), we get \(\sqrt[3]{a^6} = a^{\frac{6}{3}} = a^2\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{m^9}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent by the index gives \(\sqrt[3]{m^9} = m^{\frac{9}{3}} = m^3\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{\frac{8x^9}{125y^6}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property of radicals to simplify the numerator and denominator separately: \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{8x^9}}{\sqrt[3]{125y^6}} = \frac{2x^3}{5y^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{81c^4d^{16}e^8}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of the coefficient and each variable: \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\), \(\sqrt[4]{c^4} = c\), \(\sqrt[4]{d^{16}} = d^4\), and \(\sqrt[4]{e^8} = e^2\), giving \(3cd^4e^2\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{27x^6y^9}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of the coefficient and each variable power: \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\), \(\sqrt[3]{x^6} = x^2\), and \(\sqrt[3]{y^9} = y^3\), yielding \(3x^2y^3\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{16a^8b^{12}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of each factor: \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\), \(\sqrt[4]{a^8} = a^2\), and \(\sqrt[4]{b^{12}} = b^3\), giving \(2a^2b^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^4}\)
qs.s: Since \(3^4 = 81\) and \((x)^4 = x^4\), evaluating the fourth root gives \(3x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-z^6}\)
qs.s: Writing the radicand as \((-z^2)^3\), the cube root simplifies to \(-z^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-8y^3}\)
qs.s: Since \((-2y)^3 = -8y^3\), the cube root simplifies to \(-2y\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16a^4}\)
qs.s: Since \(2^4 = 16\) and \(a > 0\), taking the fourth root of \(16a^4\) yields \(2a\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-27b^3}\)
qs.s: Since \((-3b)^3 = -27b^3\), the cube root simplifies to \(-3b\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-\frac{27x^3}{125y^6}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to take the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately: \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{-27x^3}}{\sqrt[3]{125y^6}} = -\frac{3x}{5y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81a^8b^{12}}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the fourth root of each factor gives \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\), \(a^{8/4} = a^2\), and \(b^{12/4} = b^3\), which results in \(3a^2b^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-216u^9v^{12}w^3}\)
qs.s: Divide each exponent by the index 3 and take \(\sqrt[3]{-216} = -6\) to obtain \(-6u^3v^4w\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-64x^6y^9}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of each factor: \(\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\), \(\sqrt[3]{x^6} = x^2\), and \(\sqrt[3]{y^9} = y^3\), giving \(-4x^2y^3\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[4]{a^8}\]
qs.s: Convert the radical expression to exponential form: \(\sqrt[4]{a^8} = a^{8/4} = a^2\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{m^{15}}\]
qs.s: Divide the exponent of the radicand by the index of the radical: \(\sqrt[3]{m^{15}} = m^{15/3} = m^5\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{y^9}\]
qs.s: Using the rational exponent rule, rewrite the radical as \(\sqrt[3]{y^9} = y^{9/3} = y^3\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{w^{21}}\]
qs.s: Applying the property \(a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m}\), we obtain \(\sqrt[3]{w^{21}} = w^{21/3} = w^7\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[4]{x^{16}}\]
qs.s: Write the radical using a fractional exponent: \(\sqrt[4]{x^{16}} = x^{16/4} = x^4\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[4]{256x^{12}y^{24}z^4}\]
qs.s: Evaluate \(\sqrt[4]{256} = 4\) and divide each exponent by the index 4 to obtain \(x^{12/4} = x^3\), \(y^{24/4} = y^6\), and \(z^{4/4} = z\), giving \(4x^3 y^6 z\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{27x^9 y^{12}}\]
qs.s: Take the cube root of the coefficient, \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\), and divide each variable's exponent by 3: \(x^{9/3} = x^3\) and \(y^{12/3} = y^4\), giving \(3x^3 y^4\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{\frac{125a^{18}}{27b^9}}\]
qs.s: Simplify the cube roots of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{125a^{18}} = 5a^6\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27b^9} = 3b^3\), resulting in \(\frac{5a^6}{3b^3}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[3]{\frac{64x^{15}}{y^6}}\]
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule to simplify the numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt[3]{64x^{15}} = 4x^5\) and \(\sqrt[3]{y^6} = y^2\), which simplifies to \(\frac{4x^5}{y^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers:

\[\sqrt[4]{16a^8 b^{20}}\]
qs.s: Determine the fourth root of the numerical coefficient, \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\), and divide each variable's exponent by 4 to get \(a^{8/4} = a^2\) and \(b^{20/4} = b^5\), yielding \(2a^2 b^5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-y^{12}}\)
qs.s: Since \((-1)^3 = -1\) and \((y^4)^3 = y^{12}\), taking the cube root gives \(-y^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-a^9}\)
qs.s: Dividing the exponent by the index 3 and keeping the negative sign gives \(\sqrt[3]{-a^9} = -a^{9/3} = -a^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16b^8}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the fourth root of each factor gives \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\) and \(\sqrt[4]{b^8} = b^{8/4} = b^2\), so the simplified form is \(2b^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-8x^3}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of each factor: \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x\), giving \(-2x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{16a^8b^{24}}{625c^{16}}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of each factor in the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[4]{16a^8b^{24}} = 2a^2b^6\) and \(\sqrt[4]{625c^{16}} = 5c^4\), producing \(\frac{2a^2b^6}{5c^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-64x^9y^{15}}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the coefficient and each variable term: \(\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\), \(\sqrt[3]{x^9} = x^3\), and \(\sqrt[3]{y^{15}} = y^5\), giving \(-4x^3y^5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(-\sqrt[3]{-125x^6y^3z^{12}}\)
qs.s: First evaluate the cube root \(\sqrt[3]{-125x^6y^3z^{12}} = -5x^2yz^4\), then multiply by the negative sign in front to get \(5x^2yz^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-\frac{27x^{18}}{64y^9}}\)
qs.s: Taking the cube root of the numerator yields \(\sqrt[3]{-27x^{18}} = -3x^6\), and of the denominator yields \(\sqrt[3]{64y^9} = 4y^3\), resulting in \(-\frac{3x^6}{4y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{81a^{12}}{b^{16}}}\)
qs.s: Apply the fourth root to the numerator and denominator separately to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt[4]{81a^{12}}}{\sqrt[4]{b^{16}}} = \frac{3a^3}{b^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{256}\)
qs.s: Since \(4^4 = 256\), the principal fourth root is \(\sqrt[4]{256} = 4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{27x^6}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the coefficient and divide the exponent of \(x\) by 3: \(\sqrt[3]{27x^6} = \sqrt[3]{27} \cdot x^{6/3} = 3x^2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{64a^3b^9}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of the coefficient and divide each variable's exponent by 3: \(\sqrt[3]{64a^3b^9} = \sqrt[3]{64} \cdot a^{3/3}b^{9/3} = 4ab^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{16x^8}{81y^4}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule and simplify the fourth root of the numerator and denominator: \(\frac{\sqrt[4]{16x^8}}{\sqrt[4]{81y^4}} = \frac{2x^{8/4}}{3y^{4/4}} = \frac{2x^2}{3y}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^8y^4}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of the coefficient and divide each exponent by 4: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^8y^4} = \sqrt[4]{81} \cdot x^{8/4}y^{4/4} = 3x^2y\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16y^{12}}\)
qs.s: Take the fourth root of the coefficient and divide the exponent of \(y\) by 4: \(\sqrt[4]{16y^{12}} = \sqrt[4]{16} \cdot y^{12/4} = 2y^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{-\frac{1}{16}}\)
qs.s: An even root of a negative fraction is undefined in the set of real numbers. Therefore, \(\sqrt[4]{-\frac{1}{16}}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{-1}\)
qs.s: Since the fourth power of any real number is non-negative, no real number raised to the fourth power equals \(-1\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[4]{-1}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{-625}\)
qs.s: Since no real number raised to the fourth power equals \(-625\), the fourth root of \(-625\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(-2)^4x^{12}}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the base first gives \((-2)^4 = 16\), which is positive, so the expression becomes \(\sqrt[4]{16x^{12}}\). Taking the fourth root yields \(2x^3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16x^4} - \sqrt[3]{-27x^3}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical individually: \(\sqrt[4]{16x^4} = 2x\) and \(\sqrt[3]{-27x^3} = -3x\). Subtracting gives \(2x - (-3x) = 2x + 3x = 5x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{16x^8}{81y^{12}}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to simplify numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt[4]{16x^8} = 2x^2\) and \(\sqrt[4]{81y^{12}} = 3y^3\), giving \(\frac{2x^2}{3y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{x^7 y^4}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(x^4 \cdot x^3 \cdot y^4\). Simplifying the fourth roots yields \(\sqrt[4]{x^4 y^4} \cdot \sqrt[4]{x^3} = x y \sqrt[4]{x^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{p^9 q^4}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \((p^2)^4 \cdot p \cdot q^4\). Taking the fourth root gives \(\sqrt[4]{(p^2)^4 q^4} \cdot \sqrt[4]{p} = p^2 q \sqrt[4]{p}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{u^4 v^6}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand into perfect cubes as \(u^3 \cdot u \cdot (v^2)^3\). Taking the cube root of the perfect cubes gives \(u v^2 \sqrt[3]{u}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{a^5 b^8}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(a^4 \cdot a \cdot (b^2)^4\). Taking the fourth root of the perfect fourth powers yields \(a b^2 \sqrt[4]{a}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{a^3 b^5}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand into perfect cubes as \(a^3 \cdot b^3 \cdot b^2\). Taking the cube root gives \(\sqrt[3]{a^3 b^3} \cdot \sqrt[3]{b^2} = a b \sqrt[3]{b^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{32 a^7 b^{11}}\)
qs.s: Factor \(32 = 2^4 \cdot 2\), \(a^7 = a^4 \cdot a^3\), and \(b^{11} = (b^2)^4 \cdot b^3\). Extracting the fourth root of the perfect powers gives \(2 a b^2 \sqrt[4]{2 a^3 b^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{54 x^4 y^8 z^6}\)
qs.s: Factor \(54 = 3^3 \cdot 2\), \(x^4 = x^3 \cdot x\), \(y^8 = (y^2)^3 \cdot y^2\), and \(z^6 = (z^2)^3\). Taking the cube root yields \(3 x y^2 z^2 \sqrt[3]{2 x y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{128 a^7 b^5 c^9}\)
qs.s: Factor \(128 = 4^3 \cdot 2\), \(a^7 = (a^2)^3 \cdot a\), \(b^5 = b^3 \cdot b^2\), and \(c^9 = (c^3)^3\). Extracting the cube root gives \(4 a^2 b c^3 \sqrt[3]{2 a b^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{24 x^5 y^7}\)
qs.s: Factor \(24 = 2^3 \cdot 3\), \(x^5 = x^3 \cdot x^2\), and \(y^7 = (y^2)^3 \cdot y\). Extracting the cube root of the perfect cubes gives \(2 x y^2 \sqrt[3]{3 x^2 y}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{m^7 n^{11}}\)
qs.s: Separate the largest fourth powers from the remaining factors: \(\sqrt[4]{m^7 n^{11}} = \sqrt[4]{(m^4 n^8)(m^3 n^3)}\). Evaluating the fourth root of the perfect powers yields \(mn^2\sqrt[4]{m^3n^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{162a^7 b^{15} c^5}\)
qs.s: Write the radicand as \((81a^4 b^{12} c^4)(2a^3b^3c)\). Since \(\sqrt[4]{81a^4 b^{12} c^4} = 3ab^3c\), the result is \(3ab^3c\sqrt[4]{2a^3b^3c}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume all variables represent positive numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{32x^{13} y^7 z^{10}}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as \((16x^{12} y^4 z^8)(2xy^3z^2)\). Evaluating \(\sqrt[4]{16x^{12} y^4 z^8} = 2x^3yz^2\) gives \(2x^3yz^2\sqrt[4]{2xy^3z^2}\).

exercises.name: Simplifying algebraic radicals with real variables

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(x + 5)^2}\)
qs.s: Since the principal square root of an expression squared is its absolute value, \(\sqrt{(x + 5)^2} = |x + 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(2x + 1)^2}\)
qs.s: Applying the rule \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\), we have \(\sqrt{(2x + 1)^2} = |2x + 1|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(y - 8)^2}\)
qs.s: For any real expression \(A\), \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\), which gives \(\sqrt{(y - 8)^2} = |y - 8|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(b - 11)^2}\)
qs.s: The square root simplifies to the absolute value of the base, so \(\sqrt{(b - 11)^2} = |b - 11|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(a + 3)^2}\)
qs.s: Using the property \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\) for real variables, \(\sqrt{(a + 3)^2} = |a + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(y + 4)^6}\)
qs.s: Using the exponent property of radicals, \(\sqrt{A^6} = |A^3|\) for any real number \(A\). Thus, \(\sqrt{(y + 4)^6} = |(y + 4)^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{x^2 - 10x + 25}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\). Then simplify to obtain \(\sqrt{(x - 5)^2} = |x - 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{4x^2 - 12x + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand into \((2x - 3)^2\). Taking the principal square root gives \(\sqrt{(2x - 3)^2} = |2x - 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{(2m - 1)^2}{36}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property of radicals: \(\frac{\sqrt{(2m - 1)^2}}{\sqrt{36}} = \frac{|2m - 1|}{6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + 6x + 9}{49}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((x + 3)^2\), then simplify the radical to get \(\frac{\sqrt{(x + 3)^2}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{|x + 3|}{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 5)^3}\)
qs.s: Since the index 3 is odd, \(\sqrt[3]{A^3} = A\) for any real number \(A\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 5)^3} = x + 5\) without requiring absolute value notation.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(m + 7)^4}\)
qs.s: Because the index 4 is even, simplifying \(\sqrt[4]{A^4}\) requires absolute value notation to ensure a non-negative result, giving \(|m + 7|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(1 - 4x)^3}\)
qs.s: Since the radical has an odd index of 3, \(\sqrt[3]{A^3} = A\) for any real number \(A\). Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{(1 - 4x)^3} = 1 - 4x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{(2a - 3)^5}\)
qs.s: For any odd index \(n\), \(\sqrt[n]{A^n} = A\) for all real numbers. Since the index 5 is odd, \(\sqrt[5]{(2a - 3)^5} = 2a - 3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(y - 4)^2}\)
qs.s: Since the index 2 is even, \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\) for any real number \(A\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{(y - 4)^2} = |y - 4|\) to ensure the principal square root is non-negative.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{9x^2 + 12x + 4}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand into \((3x + 2)^2\). For an even root of a real expression, \(\sqrt{(3x + 2)^2} = |3x + 2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{(2x + 1)^4}{16}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to get \(\frac{\sqrt[4]{(2x + 1)^4}}{\sqrt[4]{16}}\). Since 4 is an even index, \(\sqrt[4]{(2x + 1)^4} = |2x + 1|\), and \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\), yielding \(\frac{|2x + 1|}{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 - 14x + 49}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(x^2 - 14x + 49 = (x - 7)^2\). Since the index 2 is even, \(\sqrt{(x - 7)^2} = |x - 7|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{(4x - 1)^3}{125}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{(4x - 1)^3}}{\sqrt[3]{125}}\). Because the index is odd, \(\sqrt[3]{(4x - 1)^3} = 4x - 1\), and since \(\sqrt[3]{125} = 5\), the result is \(\frac{4x - 1}{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{4x^2 - 20x + 25}{81}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((2x - 5)^2\), then apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{\sqrt{(2x - 5)^2}}{\sqrt{81}} = \frac{|2x - 5|}{9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[6]{(a + 4)^6}\)
qs.s: For any even positive integer \(n\), \(\sqrt[n]{u^n} = |u|\). Thus, \(\sqrt[6]{(a + 4)^6} = |a + 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(3w + 1)^2}\)
qs.s: The principal square root of an expression squared is its absolute value, so \(\sqrt{(3w + 1)^2} = |3w + 1|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(2k - 3)^4}\)
qs.s: Since the root index 4 is an even integer, \(\sqrt[4]{(2k - 3)^4} = |2k - 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x + 5)^2}\)
qs.s: Since the index 2 is even and the exponent is 2, \(\sqrt{(x + 5)^2} = |x + 5|\). The absolute value is required because \(x\) can be any real number.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(y - 7)^4}\)
qs.s: Because the index 4 is even, taking the fourth root of \((y - 7)^4\) yields \(|y - 7|\). Absolute value notation ensures the simplified radical is nonnegative.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{(m + 6)^2}{49}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, \(\sqrt{\frac{(m + 6)^2}{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{(m + 6)^2}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{|m + 6|}{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 - 10x + 25}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\). Then \(\sqrt{(x - 5)^2} = |x - 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{9x^2 - 24x + 16}{25}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to get \(\sqrt{\frac{(3x - 4)^2}{25}}\). Applying the quotient property yields \(\frac{\sqrt{(3x - 4)^2}}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{|3x - 4|}{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{4a^2 + 12a + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as \((2a + 3)^2\). Simplifying the square root gives \(\sqrt{(2a + 3)^2} = |2a + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{16(y - 3)^4}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule: \(\sqrt[4]{16(y - 3)^4} = \sqrt[4]{16} \cdot \sqrt[4]{(y - 3)^4}\). Since \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\) and the index is even, this simplifies to \(2|y - 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[7]{(2a - 3)^7}\)
qs.s: Since the index 7 is odd, \(\sqrt[7]{A^7} = A\) for all real numbers \(A\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[7]{(2a - 3)^7} = 2a - 3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[5]{(3x + 2)^5}\)
qs.s: Because the index 5 is odd, the radical simplifies directly as \(\sqrt[5]{A^5} = A\). Hence, \(\sqrt[5]{(3x + 2)^5} = 3x + 2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[4]{(m + 5)^4}\)
qs.s: Since the index 4 is even, taking the fourth root of a fourth power requires an absolute value to guarantee a non-negative result. Thus, \(\sqrt[4]{(m + 5)^4} = |m + 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(y - 4)^2}\)
qs.s: Since the index 2 is even, the principal square root must be non-negative, so \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{(y - 4)^2} = |y - 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 6)^3}\)
qs.s: Since the index 3 is odd, \(\sqrt[3]{A^3} = A\) for any real number \(A\) without needing an absolute value. Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 6)^3} = x + 6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[4]{81(y - 3)^4}\)
qs.s: Apply the product property of radicals: \(\sqrt[4]{81(y - 3)^4} = \sqrt[4]{81} \cdot \sqrt[4]{(y - 3)^4}\). Since \(81 = 3^4\) and the index is even, this simplifies to \(3|y - 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{(x - 2)^6}\)
qs.s: Divide the exponent by the index: \(6 \div 2 = 3\). Because the index 2 is even and the resulting exponent 3 is odd, an absolute value is required, giving \(|(x - 2)^3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt[5]{-32(x + 3)^5}\)
qs.s: Because the index 5 is odd, absolute value is not used: \(\sqrt[5]{-32} = -2\) and \(\sqrt[5]{(x + 3)^5} = x + 3\). Multiplying these gives \(-2(x + 3)\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + 10x + 25}{36}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((x + 5)^2\) and apply the quotient property: \(\frac{\sqrt{(x + 5)^2}}{\sqrt{36}}\). Since the square root requires a non-negative value, the result is \(\frac{|x + 5|}{6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{9x^2 - 12x + 4}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(9x^2 - 12x + 4 = (3x - 2)^2\). Because the index 2 is even, \(\sqrt{(3x - 2)^2} = |3x - 2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(3a + 1)^2}\)
qs.s: Because \(a\) can be any real number, the expression inside the radical could be negative before squaring, so \(\sqrt{(3a + 1)^2} = |3a + 1|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(2m - 9)^2}\)
qs.s: Applying the property \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\) for real numbers yields \(\sqrt{(2m - 9)^2} = |2m - 9|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(7 - y)^2}\)
qs.s: Taking the principal square root of an even power requires absolute value notation for real variables, so \(\sqrt{(7 - y)^2} = |7 - y|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(4 - 3b)^2}\)
qs.s: For any real number \(b\), the principal square root simplifies to the absolute value of the base: \(\sqrt{(4 - 3b)^2} = |4 - 3b|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{4n^2 - 20n + 25}{49}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((2n - 5)^2\) to rewrite the expression as \(\frac{\sqrt{(2n - 5)^2}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{|2n - 5|}{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{25(4 - k)^2}\)
qs.s: Apply the product property of radicals to obtain \(\sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt{(4 - k)^2} = 5|4 - k|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{9p^2 - 12p + 4}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand by factoring the perfect square trinomial as \((3p - 2)^2\), which simplifies to \(\sqrt{(3p - 2)^2} = |3p - 2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{y^2 + 6y + 9}{16}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((y + 3)^2\) and apply the quotient property to get \(\frac{\sqrt{(y + 3)^2}}{\sqrt{16}} = \frac{|y + 3|}{4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(1 - 3x)^3}\)
qs.s: The index 3 is odd, so \(\sqrt[3]{a^3} = a\) for any real number \(a\). Hence, \(\sqrt[3]{(1 - 3x)^3} = 1 - 3x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(4 - y)^3}\)
qs.s: For any real number, the cube root of a cubed expression simplifies directly to the base. Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{(4 - y)^3} = 4 - y\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{(2x + 1)^5}\)
qs.s: Because the index 5 is an odd integer, the fifth root and fifth power cancel directly for any real number: \(\sqrt[5]{(2x + 1)^5} = 2x + 1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{(m - 8)^5}\)
qs.s: Since the radical has an odd index of 5, no absolute value notation is needed and the expression simplifies directly to \(m - 8\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(5x - 2)^3} - \sqrt[3]{(2x - 7)^3}\)
qs.s: Simplify both odd roots to obtain \((5x - 2) - (2x - 7)\). Distribute the negative sign and combine like terms: \(5x - 2 - 2x + 7 = 3x + 5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-27(x - 4)^3}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of each factor: \(\sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{(x - 4)^3} = x - 4\). Multiplying them yields \(-3(x - 4)\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 - 12x + 36}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial, \((x - 6)^2\). Since the square root has an even index of 2, \(\sqrt{(x - 6)^2} = |x - 6|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{(1 - 2x)^3}{64}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property to take the cube root of numerator and denominator separately: \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{(1 - 2x)^3}}{\sqrt[3]{64}} = \frac{1 - 2x}{4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(3m - 2)^2}\)
qs.s: Since the radical has an even index of 2, simplifying \(\sqrt{(3m - 2)^2}\) gives \(|3m - 2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(y + 3)^4}\)
qs.s: Because the index is an even number (4), taking the 4th root of \((y + 3)^4\) requires an absolute value, giving \(|y + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(5a + 1)^4}\)
qs.s: Because 4 is an even index, taking the 4th root of \((5a + 1)^4\) yields \(|5a + 1|\) to ensure a non-negative result.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[6]{(4 - t)^6}\)
qs.s: For an even index of 6, the 6th root of an expression raised to the 6th power is its absolute value, \(|4 - t|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{4y^2 + 12y + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(4y^2 + 12y + 9 = (2y + 3)^2\). Taking the principal square root gives \(|2y + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{(b + 2)^4}{16}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient property of radicals to get \(\frac{\sqrt[4]{(b + 2)^4}}{\sqrt[4]{16}}\). Evaluating each radical gives \(\frac{|b + 2|}{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{81(2 - x)^4}\)
qs.s: Apply the product property of radicals to separate the factors: \(\sqrt[4]{81} \cdot \sqrt[4]{(2 - x)^4}\). Since \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\) and the even index requires an absolute value, the result is \(3|2 - x|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{c^2 - 8c + 16}{49}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to write \(\sqrt{\frac{(c - 4)^2}{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{(c - 4)^2}}{\sqrt{49}}\). Evaluating each root yields \(\frac{|c - 4|}{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(x - 6)^3}\)
qs.s: Since the index 3 is odd, \(\sqrt[3]{a^3} = a\) for any real number \(a\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{(x - 6)^3} = x - 6\) without needing absolute value bars.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{(4x - 3)^5}\)
qs.s: The index 5 is odd, so \(\sqrt[5]{a^5} = a\) for any real number \(a\). Thus, \(\sqrt[5]{(4x - 3)^5} = 4x - 3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[7]{(5 - y)^7}\)
qs.s: Because 7 is an odd integer, the radical simplifies directly to the base without absolute value notation, giving \(5 - y\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{(3 - x)^5}\)
qs.s: Because the index 5 is odd, the fifth root of any real number raised to the fifth power is the number itself: \(\sqrt[5]{(3 - x)^5} = 3 - x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(2x + 1)^3}\)
qs.s: Because the index 3 is odd, \(\sqrt[3]{a^3} = a\) for all real numbers \(a\), which gives \(\sqrt[3]{(2x + 1)^3} = 2x + 1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[5]{\frac{(1 - 2x)^5}{32}}\)
qs.s: Applying the quotient property gives \(\frac{\sqrt[5]{(1 - 2x)^5}}{\sqrt[5]{32}}\). Because the index 5 is odd, the numerator is \(1 - 2x\) and \(\sqrt[5]{32} = 2\), resulting in \(\frac{1 - 2x}{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{4x^2 + 12x + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the perfect square trinomial inside the radical to get \(\sqrt{(2x + 3)^2}\). Since the index 2 is even and the variable represents a real number, the result is \(|2x + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 - 8x + 16}\)
qs.s: First, factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(x^2 - 8x + 16 = (x - 4)^2\). Because the index 2 is even and \(x\) can be any real number, \(\sqrt{(x - 4)^2} = |x - 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 - 6x + 9}{25}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to write \(\sqrt{\frac{(x - 3)^2}{25}} = \frac{\sqrt{(x - 3)^2}}{\sqrt{25}}\). For real \(x\), \(\sqrt{(x - 3)^2} = |x - 3|\) and \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), yielding \(\frac{|x - 3|}{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{(5 - x)^3}{64}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient property, write \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{(5 - x)^3}}{\sqrt[3]{64}}\). Since 3 is odd, the numerator simplifies to \(5 - x\) and the denominator is \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\), giving \(\frac{5 - x}{4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{x^2 + 6x + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square: \(x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2\). Because \(x\) represents any real number, the square root simplifies to \(\sqrt{(x + 3)^2} = |x + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{m^2 - 2m + 1}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(m^2 - 2m + 1 = (m - 1)^2\). The square root of \((m - 1)^2\) is \(|m - 1|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{y^2 - 10y + 25}\)
qs.s: Write the radicand as a squared binomial: \(y^2 - 10y + 25 = (y - 5)^2\). Since \(y\) is a real number, \(\sqrt{(y - 5)^2} = |y - 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{a^2 + 12a + 36}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as \((a + 6)^2\). The principal square root for any real number \(a\) is \(|a + 6|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{16a^2 + 24a + 9}{25}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to get \(\sqrt{\frac{(4a + 3)^2}{25}}\). Taking the square roots of numerator and denominator yields \(\frac{|4a + 3|}{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{9x^2 - 24x + 16}\)
qs.s: Factor the non-monic trinomial as \((3x - 4)^2\). For any real \(x\), \(\sqrt{(3x - 4)^2} = |3x - 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers with \(y \neq 0\): \(\sqrt{\frac{4x^2 - 12x + 9}{y^4}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to obtain \(\frac{\sqrt{(2x - 3)^2}}{\sqrt{y^4}}\). Since \(2x - 3\) can be negative, its square root requires absolute value bars, while \(y^2 \geq 0\) does not, giving \(\frac{|2x - 3|}{y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 - 14x + 49}{64}}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the expression as \(\frac{\sqrt{(x - 7)^2}}{\sqrt{64}}\). Simplifying the numerator and denominator gives \(\frac{|x - 7|}{8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{4x^2 + 20xy + 25y^2}\)
qs.s: Factor the two-variable trinomial into \((2x + 5y)^2\). Taking the square root gives \(|2x + 5y|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{c^2 - 12c + 36}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand to obtain \(\sqrt{(c - 6)^2}\). Since \(c\) represents any real number, the square root simplifies to \(|c - 6|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{m^2 + 14m + 49}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as a squared binomial: \(\sqrt{(m + 7)^2}\). Since \(m\) is a real number, the expression simplifies to \(|m + 7|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{a^2 - 8a + 16}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand into \(\sqrt{(a - 4)^2}\). For real numbers, simplifying the square root of an even power of a binomial requires absolute value bars, giving \(|a - 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{y^2 - 10y + 25}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand to get \(\sqrt{(y - 5)^2}\). Because \(y\) represents a real number, the principal square root is \(|y - 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{x^2 + 6x + 9}\)
qs.s: Factor the radicand as a perfect square trinomial: \(\sqrt{x^2 + 6x + 9} = \sqrt{(x + 3)^2}\). Since the index is even and the variable represents a real number, the result is \(|x + 3|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers and \(y \neq 0\): \(\sqrt{\frac{9x^2 - 30x + 25}{y^4}}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the expression as \(\frac{\sqrt{(3x - 5)^2}}{\sqrt{y^4}}\). This simplifies to \(\frac{|3x - 5|}{y^2}\), where no absolute value bars are needed on the denominator because \(y^2 > 0\) for all real \(y \neq 0\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{25x^2 - 70x + 49}\)
qs.s: Factor the trinomial as \(\sqrt{(5x - 7)^2}\). Since the index is even and \(x\) is a real number, the simplified radical is \(|5x - 7|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{\frac{16x^2 + 24x + 9}{25}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator to write \(\sqrt{\frac{(4x + 3)^2}{25}}\). Applying the quotient property of radicals yields \(\frac{\sqrt{(4x + 3)^2}}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{|4x + 3|}{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{25a^2 - 30ab + 9b^2}\)
qs.s: Factor the multivariable trinant as a perfect square: \(\sqrt{(5a - 3b)^2}\). Because \(a\) and \(b\) represent real numbers, the principal square root is \(|5a - 3b|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variable represents a real number: \(\sqrt{x^4 - 10x^2 + 25}\)
qs.s: Factor the expression as a quadratic in form: \(\sqrt{(x^2 - 5)^2}\). Since \(x^2 - 5\) can be negative for real values of \(x\), absolute value bars are required, giving \(|x^2 - 5|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 + 6x + 9)(x^2 - 6x + 9)}\)
qs.s: Factor each perfect square trinomial to obtain \(\sqrt{(x+3)^2(x-3)^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 - 9)^2}\). Taking the principal square root gives \(|x^2 - 9|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 - 10x + 25)(x^2 + 10x + 25)}\)
qs.s: Factor to obtain \(\sqrt{(x-5)^2(x+5)^2} = \sqrt{((x-5)(x+5))^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 - 25)^2}\). Since \(x^2 - 25\) can be negative for real values of \(x\), the result is \(|x^2 - 25|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(4x^2 + 4x + 1)(4x^2 - 4x + 1)}\)
qs.s: Factor each quadratic into \((2x+1)^2\) and \((2x-1)^2\), giving \(\sqrt{((2x+1)(2x-1))^2} = \sqrt{(4x^2 - 1)^2}\). Taking the square root yields \(|4x^2 - 1|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 + 4x + 4)(x^2 - 4x + 4)}\)
qs.s: Factor each quadratic to get \(\sqrt{(x+2)^2(x-2)^2} = \sqrt{((x+2)(x-2))^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 - 4)^2}\). Since \(x^2 - 4\) can be negative for real values of \(x\), taking the principal square root yields \(|x^2 - 4|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 + 2xy + y^2)(x^2 - 2xy + y^2)}\)
qs.s: Factor the trinomials to get \(\sqrt{(x+y)^2(x-y)^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 - y^2)^2}\). Since the variables represent real numbers, the principal square root is \(|x^2 - y^2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(9x^2 + 12xy + 4y^2)(9x^2 - 12xy + 4y^2)}\)
qs.s: Factor into perfect squares: \((3x+2y)^2(3x-2y)^2 = ((3x+2y)(3x-2y))^2 = (9x^2 - 4y^2)^2\). Taking the square root yields \(|9x^2 - 4y^2|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 + 6x + 9)^2(x^2 - 6x + 9)}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radicand as \(((x+3)^2)^2(x-3)^2 = (x+3)^4(x-3)^2\). Taking the square root gives \((x+3)^2|x-3|\), where no absolute value is needed on \((x+3)^2\) because it is non-negative for all real \(x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(x^2 + 10x + 25)(x^2 - 10x + 25)(x^2 - 25)^2}\)
qs.s: The first two factors simplify to \((x+5)^2(x-5)^2 = (x^2 - 25)^2\), making the radicand \((x^2 - 25)^4\). Since 4 is an even index, taking the 4th root yields \(\sqrt[4]{(x^2 - 25)^4} = |x^2 - 25|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{(x^2 + 4x + 4)(x^2 - 4x + 4)}{x^4 + 8x^2 + 16}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \(((x+2)(x-2))^2 = (x^2 - 4)^2\) and the denominator as \((x^2 + 4)^2\). Taking the square root gives \(\frac{|x^2 - 4|}{x^2 + 4}\), where absolute value is omitted in the denominator because \(x^2 + 4 > 0\) for all real \(x\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{(x^2 - 9)^2(x^2 + 6x + 9)(x^2 - 6x + 9)}\)
qs.s: Factor \((x^2+6x+9)(x^2-6x+9)\) as \((x+3)^2(x-3)^2 = (x^2-9)^2\), so the radicand is \((x^2-9)^2(x^2-9)^2 = (x^2-9)^4\). Taking the square root yields \((x^2 - 9)^2\), which requires no absolute value because an even power is always non-negative.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(y - 3)(y^2 - 6y + 9)}\)
qs.s: Factor \(y^2 - 6y + 9\) as \((y - 3)^2\) to rewrite the expression as \(\sqrt[3]{(y - 3)^3}\). Since the index 3 is odd, no absolute value is needed, yielding \(y - 3\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(m - 5)(m^2 - 10m + 25)}\)
qs.s: Factor \(m^2 - 10m + 25\) as \((m - 5)^2\), so the radicand becomes \((m - 5)^3\). Taking the cube root gives \(m - 5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 2)(x^2 + 4x + 4)}\)
qs.s: Factor \(x^2 + 4x + 4\) as \((x + 2)^2\) to write the radicand as \((x + 2)^3\). Taking the cube root gives \(\sqrt[3]{(x + 2)^3} = x + 2\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(a + 4)(a^2 + 8a + 16)}\)
qs.s: Recognize that \(a^2 + 8a + 16 = (a + 4)^2\), which gives \(\sqrt[3]{(a + 4)^3}\). Evaluating the cube root results in \(a + 4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(2x + 1)(4x^2 + 4x + 1)}\)
qs.s: Factor \(4x^2 + 4x + 1\) as \((2x + 1)^2\), rewriting the radicand as \((2x + 1)^3\). Taking the cube root yields \(2x + 1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{(x - 6)^2(x^2 - 12x + 36)}\)
qs.s: Factor the quadratic to obtain \((x - 6)^2(x - 6)^2 = (x - 6)^4\). Because the index 4 is even, taking the fourth root requires absolute value notation, giving \(|x - 6|\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{-8(a - 2b)(a^2 - 4ab + 4b^2)}\)
qs.s: Factor \(a^2 - 4ab + 4b^2\) as \((a - 2b)^2\), giving the radicand \(-8(a - 2b)^3\). Evaluating the cube root gives \(\sqrt[3]{-8}\sqrt[3]{(a - 2b)^3} = -2(a - 2b)\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{(x - 4)(x^2 - 8x + 16)}{(x + 2)(x^2 + 4x + 4)}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator and denominator into \((x - 4)^3\) and \((x + 2)^3\) respectively. Applying the quotient rule for radicals gives \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{(x - 4)^3}}{\sqrt[3]{(x + 2)^3}} = \frac{x - 4}{x + 2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{(x - 3)(x + 3)(x^2 - 9)^2}\)
qs.s: Multiply \((x - 3)(x + 3)\) to get \(x^2 - 9\), so the radicand simplifies to \((x^2 - 9)(x^2 - 9)^2 = (x^2 - 9)^3\). Taking the cube root yields \(x^2 - 9\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{(3x + 2)(9x^2 + 12x + 4)}{8y^6}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((3x + 2)^3\) and write the denominator as \((2y^2)^3\). Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator yields \(\frac{3x + 2}{2y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-11}{216m^6}}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the numerator, \(\sqrt[3]{-11} = -\sqrt[3]{11}\), and the denominator, \(\sqrt[3]{216m^6} = 6m^2\). This simplifies to \(-\frac{\sqrt[3]{11}}{6m^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-5}{64a^{12}}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator as \(\sqrt[3]{-5} = -\sqrt[3]{5}\) and the denominator as \(\sqrt[3]{64a^{12}} = 4a^4\). This yields \(-\frac{\sqrt[3]{5}}{4a^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-2}{125x^9}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt[3]{-2} = -\sqrt[3]{2}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{125x^9} = 5x^3\). Since the index is odd, no absolute value is needed, giving \(-\frac{\sqrt[3]{2}}{5x^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-10}{27w^{15}}}\)
qs.s: Compute the cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{-10} = -\sqrt[3]{10}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27w^{15}} = 3w^5\). With an odd index, no absolute value is required, resulting in \(-\frac{\sqrt[3]{10}}{3w^5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-7}{8y^6}}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{-7} = -\sqrt[3]{7}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{8y^6} = 2y^2\). Combining these gives \(-\frac{\sqrt[3]{7}}{2y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-16a^7}{54a^2 b^6}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the fraction inside the radical first to obtain \(\frac{-8a^5}{27b^6}\). Then evaluate the cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{-8a^5} = -2a\sqrt[3]{a^2}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27b^6} = 3b^2\), giving \(-\frac{2a\sqrt[3]{a^2}}{3b^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{-16x^7}{27y^9}}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the numerator as \(\sqrt[3]{-8x^6 \cdot 2x} = -2x^2\sqrt[3]{2x}\) and the denominator as \(\sqrt[3]{27y^9} = 3y^3\). Since the index is odd, no absolute value signs are needed, yielding \(-\frac{2x^2\sqrt[3]{2x}}{3y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{17}{36b^2}}\)
qs.s: Separate the radical into \(\frac{\sqrt{17}}{\sqrt{36b^2}}\). Since \(\sqrt{36} = 6\) and \(\sqrt{b^2} = |b|\), the expression simplifies to \(\frac{\sqrt{17}}{6|b|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{15}{4y^2}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, rewrite the expression as \(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{\sqrt{4y^2}}\). Evaluating the denominator gives \(\sqrt{4}\sqrt{y^2} = 2|y|\), resulting in \(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2|y|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{13}{25a^2}}\)
qs.s: Take the square root of the numerator and denominator separately to get \(\frac{\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{25a^2}}\). Since \(\sqrt{25a^2} = 5|a|\), the simplified form is \(\frac{\sqrt{13}}{5|a|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{7}{9x^2}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule for radicals: \(\sqrt{\frac{7}{9x^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{9x^2}}\). Since \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) for any real number \(x\), the simplified expression is \(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3|x|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{21}{16m^2}}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the radical expression as \(\frac{\sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{16m^2}}\). Simplifying the denominator yields \(\sqrt{16}\sqrt{m^2} = 4|m|\), giving \(\frac{\sqrt{21}}{4|m|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{18x^2}{25y^4}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator as \(\sqrt{18x^2} = 3|x|\sqrt{2}\) and the denominator as \(\sqrt{25y^4} = 5y^2\). No absolute value is needed on \(y^2\) because \(y^2 \ge 0\) for all real numbers, giving \(\frac{3|x|\sqrt{2}}{5y^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{20}{x^2 - 8x + 16}}\)
qs.s: Factor the denominator as \((x - 4)^2\) and simplify the numerator as \(\sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Taking the square root of the denominator gives \(\sqrt{(x - 4)^2} = |x - 4|\), resulting in \(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{|x - 4|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{12}{9x^2 + 12x + 4}}\)
qs.s: Factor the denominator to obtain \((3x + 2)^2\) and simplify the numerator to \(\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt{3}\). Since \(\sqrt{(3x + 2)^2} = |3x + 2|\) for any real number \(x\), the simplified form is \(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{|3x + 2|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{8a^4}{(2b - 1)^2}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator as \(\sqrt{8a^4} = 2a^2\sqrt{2}\) (no absolute value needed since \(a^2 \ge 0\)). In the denominator, \(\sqrt{(2b - 1)^2} = |2b - 1|\) requires absolute value because \(2b - 1\) can be negative, producing \(\frac{2a^2\sqrt{2}}{|2b - 1|}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{50}{9x^6}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\) and the denominator to \(\sqrt{9x^6} = 3|x^3|\). The absolute value is retained on \(x^3\) because the resulting exponent is odd, yielding \(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{3|x^3|}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{\frac{81}{256x^8}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[4]{256x^8} = 4x^2\). Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x \neq 0\), no absolute value is needed, giving \(\frac{3}{4x^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{125y^6}}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{125y^6} = 5y^2\). Because the index is odd, no absolute value is required, yielding \(\frac{2}{5y^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{\frac{64}{27w^9}}\)
qs.s: Compute the cube root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27w^9} = 3w^3\). Since the index is odd, no absolute value is needed, yielding \(\frac{4}{3w^3}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{49}{100a^4}}\)
qs.s: Take the square root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt{49} = 7\) and \(\sqrt{100a^4} = 10a^2\). Since \(a^2 \ge 0\), no absolute value is needed, giving \(\frac{7}{10a^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{\frac{81x^4}{16y^8}}\)
qs.s: Take the fourth root of each part: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^4} = 3|x|\) because the root index is even and the resulting exponent is odd, while \(\sqrt[4]{16y^8} = 2y^2\) because \(y^2 \ge 0\). This yields \(\frac{3|x|}{2y^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{\frac{125(x - 2)^6}{64(y + 1)^3}}\)
qs.s: Compute the cube root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[3]{125(x - 2)^6} = 5(x - 2)^2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{64(y + 1)^3} = 4(y + 1)\). Because the root index is odd, no absolute value notation is required, giving \(\frac{5(x - 2)^2}{4(y + 1)}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{18x^2 + 24x + 8}{50y^4}}\)
qs.s: Factor out 2 from the numerator and denominator to simplify the radicand to \(\frac{(3x + 2)^2}{25y^4}\). Taking the square root gives \(|3x + 2|\) in the numerator and \(5y^2\) in the denominator, resulting in \(\frac{|3x + 2|}{5y^2}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{\frac{256(a - 2)^8}{81b^4}}\)
qs.s: Extract the fourth roots: \(\sqrt[4]{256(a - 2)^8} = 4(a - 2)^2\), which needs no absolute value since \((a - 2)^2 \ge 0\), and \(\sqrt[4]{81b^4} = 3|b|\), which requires an absolute value because the index is even and the power is odd. This results in \(\frac{4(a - 2)^2}{3|b|}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers:

\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{\frac{-16x^7}{2x y^9}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radicand first: \(\frac{-16x^7}{2x y^9} = \frac{-8x^6}{y^9}\). Taking the cube root yields \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\), \(\sqrt[3]{x^6} = x^2\), and \(\sqrt[3]{y^9} = y^3\), which gives \(-\frac{2x^2}{y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{49x^6}}\)
qs.s: Take the square root of the numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) and \(\sqrt{49x^6} = 7|x^3|\). An absolute value is needed because the index 2 is even and the resulting exponent 3 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{64b^9}}\)
qs.s: Because the index is odd (\(n = 3\)), no absolute value is used: \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{64b^9} = 4b^3\), which gives \(\frac{3}{4b^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{1}{81y^4}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[4]{1} = 1\) and \(\sqrt[4]{81y^4} = 3|y|\). Since the root index is even and the resulting exponent is odd, the variable requires an absolute value.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{100a^2}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the square root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt{100a^2} = 10|a|\). The absolute value is needed because the index is even and the exponent of \(a\) simplifies to 1 (odd).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{16}{625c^{20}}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt[4]{16} = 2\) and \(\sqrt[4]{625c^{20}} = 5|c^5|\). An absolute value is required because the index 4 is even and the resulting exponent 5 is odd.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[4]{\frac{81x^8 y^{12}}{256z^{16}}}\)
qs.s: Evaluate the fourth root of each factor: \(\sqrt[4]{81x^8} = 3x^2\) and \(\sqrt[4]{256y^{12}z^{16}} = 4|y^3|z^4\). An absolute value is placed only on \(y^3\) because its resulting exponent is odd, whereas \(x^2\) and \(z^4\) have even exponents.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{4x^2 + 12x + 9}{81y^8}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as \((2x + 3)^2\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{(2x + 3)^2} = |2x + 3|\) and \(\sqrt{81y^8} = 9y^4\), yielding \(\frac{|2x + 3|}{9y^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 - 10x + 25}{49y^4}}\)
qs.s: Factor the numerator as a perfect square trinomial, \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\). Taking the square root of numerator and denominator yields \(\frac{|x - 5|}{7y^2}\), where an absolute value is needed on \(x - 5\) because its resulting exponent is 1.

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{8(x + 3)^3}{27y^9}}\)
qs.s: For an odd root (\(n = 3\)), every real number has a unique real root and absolute value notation is not used. Taking the cube root gives \(\sqrt[3]{8(x + 3)^3} = 2(x + 3)\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27y^9} = 3y^3\), resulting in \(\frac{2(x + 3)}{3y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Assume that the variables represent real numbers: \(\sqrt{\frac{36(x - 7)^2}{121y^4}}\)
qs.s: Take the square root of the numerator and denominator: \(\sqrt{36(x - 7)^2} = 6|x - 7|\) and \(\sqrt{121y^4} = 11y^2\). The binomial requires an absolute value because its exponent simplifies from 2 to 1 (odd) under an even root, while \(y^2\) is always non-negative.

exercises.name: Rewriting nested radicals as a single radical

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[7]{z}}\)
qs.s: Since the outer radical has an index of 2, multiply the indices: \(2 \times 7 = 14\). Thus, \(\sqrt{\sqrt[7]{z}} = \sqrt[14]{z}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{x}}\)
qs.s: The outer square root has an index of 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 3 = 6\), so \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{x}} = \sqrt[6]{x}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt[3]{y}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the radicals: \(5 \times 3 = 15\). Thus, \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt[3]{y}} = \sqrt[15]{y}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{a}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the two indices: \(4 \times 5 = 20\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{a}} = \sqrt[20]{a}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{m}}\)
qs.s: Multiplying the indices yields \(3 \times 3 = 9\), which gives \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{m}} = \sqrt[9]{m}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{m}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices across all three radicals: \(3 \times 4 \times 5 = 60\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{m}}} = \sqrt[60]{m}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[4]{x^5}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three indices: \(3 \times 2 \times 4 = 24\). Keeping the radicand \(x^5\), the result is \(\sqrt[24]{x^5}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[5]{x}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three indices together, noting that the outermost square root has an index of 2: \(2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30\). Thus, \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[5]{x}}} = \sqrt[30]{x}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[7]{\frac{a}{b}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the nested radicals: \(4 \times 7 = 28\). The single radical expression is \(\sqrt[28]{\frac{a}{b}}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[6]{\sqrt[8]{xy}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radical indices: \(6 \times 8 = 48\). The radicand remains \(xy\), giving \(\sqrt[48]{xy}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{a^5 b}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the outer and inner radicals: \(3 \times 2 = 6\). Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{a^5 b}} = \sqrt[6]{a^5 b}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{p^4 q}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of both cube roots: \(3 \times 3 = 9\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{p^4 q}} = \sqrt[9]{p^4 q}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{w^2 z^5}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radical indices: \(4 \times 3 = 12\). Hence, \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{w^2 z^5}} = \sqrt[12]{w^2 z^5}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{u^3 v^2}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the outer index (5) by the inner square root index (2): \(5 \times 2 = 10\). This gives \(\sqrt[10]{u^3 v^2}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[4]{m n^3}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the index of the outer square root (2) by the index of the inner root (4): \(2 \times 4 = 8\). Thus, \(\sqrt{\sqrt[4]{m n^3}} = \sqrt[8]{m n^3}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{2 a^5 b^7 c}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radical indices: \(2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24\). The expression rewritten as a single radical is \(\sqrt[24]{2 a^5 b^7 c}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{p^5 q^9}}}}\)
qs.s: Each square root has an index of 2. Multiplying all four indices gives \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16\), resulting in \(\sqrt[16]{p^5 q^9}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{\frac{3 m^7}{n^3}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the outer and inner radicals: \(4 \times 5 = 20\). The single radical is \(\sqrt[20]{\frac{3 m^7}{n^3}}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{5 x^7 y^3}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of all three nested radicals: \(2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\). Therefore, the expression simplifies to \(\sqrt[12]{5 x^7 y^3}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[5]{\frac{7 x^2 y}{z^4}}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the three radicals: \(3 \times 2 \times 5 = 30\). Thus, the expression becomes \(\sqrt[30]{\frac{7 x^2 y}{z^4}}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{k}}}\)
qs.s: Each of the three square roots has an index of 2. Multiplying their indices gives \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\), yielding \(\sqrt[8]{k}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{z}}}\)
qs.s: Each square root has an index of 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 2 \times 3 = 12\), resulting in \(\sqrt[12]{z}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{\sqrt{a}}}\)
qs.s: Each square root has an index of 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(5 \times 2 \times 2 = 20\), so the expression is \(\sqrt[20]{a}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[5]{x}}}\)
qs.s: The square root has an index of 2. Multiplying the indices of the nested radicals gives \(3 \times 2 \times 5 = 30\), resulting in \(\sqrt[30]{x}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[3]{m}}}\)
qs.s: The outermost square root has an index of 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 3 \times 3 = 18\), which simplifies to \(\sqrt[18]{m}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{\sqrt{x}}}}\)
qs.s: The innermost radical is a square root with index 2. Multiplying all four indices gives \(5 \times 3 \times 4 \times 2 = 120\), giving \(\sqrt[120]{x}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical in simplest form (assume \(x > 0\)): \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{x^8}}}\)
qs.s: Multiplying the indices gives \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\), yielding \(\sqrt[24]{x^8}\). Dividing the index and exponent by their greatest common factor, 8, simplifies the expression to \(\sqrt[3]{x}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt[4]{a}}}}\)
qs.s: Both middle radicals are square roots with index 2. Multiplying all four indices gives \(3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 4 = 48\), giving \(\sqrt[48]{a}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[5]{b}}}}\)
qs.s: The first and third radicals are square roots with index 2. Multiplying the four indices gives \(2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 5 = 60\), giving \(\sqrt[60]{b}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical in simplest form (assume \(y > 0\)): \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{y^6}}}\)
qs.s: Multiplying the indices gives \(5 \times 2 \times 3 = 30\), producing \(\sqrt[30]{y^6}\). Dividing both the index and exponent by 6 gives \(\sqrt[5]{y}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt{x^3 y z^5}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the outer index \(4\) by the inner index \(2\) to obtain \(4 \times 2 = 8\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(\sqrt[8]{x^3 y z^5}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{r^5 s^2 t}}\)
qs.s: The square root has an implied index of \(2\). Multiplying the indices gives \(3 \times 2 = 6\), which gives \(\sqrt[6]{r^5 s^2 t}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{u v^5 w^2}}\)
qs.s: Using the property \(\sqrt[m]{\sqrt[n]{A}} = \sqrt[mn]{A}\), multiply the indices \(3\) and \(4\) to get \(3 \times 4 = 12\), yielding \(\sqrt[12]{u v^5 w^2}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{a^2 b^5 c}}\)
qs.s: The outer radical has an index of \(2\) and the inner radical has an index of \(3\). Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 3 = 6\), so the expression is \(\sqrt[6]{a^2 b^5 c}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt[3]{m^2 n^4 p}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radical indices \(5\) and \(3\) to get a single index of \(5 \times 3 = 15\). The expression becomes \(\sqrt[15]{m^2 n^4 p}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[5]{a^4 b^2 c^7 d}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radical indices: \(3 \times 2 \times 5 = 30\). This gives the single radical \(\sqrt[30]{a^4 b^2 c^7 d}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{x^5 y z^7}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of all three nested radicals: \(2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\). The expression as a single radical is \(\sqrt[12]{x^5 y z^7}\).
