qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[6]{\sqrt[7]{2 p^{11} q^5 r^3}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the two indices: \(6 \times 7 = 42\). The expression rewritten as a single radical is \(\sqrt[42]{2 p^{11} q^5 r^3}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{\frac{3 x^7 y^2}{z^3}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the outer index \(4\) and inner index \(5\) to get \(4 \times 5 = 20\). The single radical expression is \(\sqrt[20]{\frac{3 x^7 y^2}{z^3}}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{\frac{u^5 v^7}{w^3}}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three indices together: \(2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24\). The result is \(\sqrt[24]{\frac{u^5 v^7}{w^3}}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{5 u^3 v w}}\)
qs.s: Each radical has an index of 2. Multiply the indices to get \(2 \times 2 = 4\), yielding \(\sqrt[4]{5 u^3 v w}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{2 x y^3 z^2}}\)
qs.s: The index of each square root is 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 2 = 4\), so the expression as a single radical is \(\sqrt[4]{2 x y^3 z^2}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{a^3 b c^2}}\)
qs.s: Each square root has an index of 2. Multiply the indices to express as a single radical: \(2 \times 2 = 4\), giving \(\sqrt[4]{a^3 b c^2}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{p q^2 r^3 s}}\)
qs.s: Since both nested radicals are square roots with index 2, multiply the indices: \(2 \times 2 = 4\). This gives \(\sqrt[4]{p q^2 r^3 s}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{m^2 n^3 p^3}}\)
qs.s: Both radicals are square roots with index 2. Multiplying the indices gives \(2 \times 2 = 4\), which results in \(\sqrt[4]{m^2 n^3 p^3}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{p^5 q^7 r}}}\)
qs.s: The three nested radicals have indices 2, 3, and 2. Multiplying them together gives \(2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\), so the expression is \(\sqrt[12]{p^5 q^7 r}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[5]{2 a^7 b^3 c^9}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the nested radicals: \(4 \times 5 = 20\). The single radical is \(\sqrt[20]{2 a^7 b^3 c^9}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{a^3 b^5 c}}}\)
qs.s: Each of the three nested square roots has an index of 2. Multiply the three indices together: \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\), yielding \(\sqrt[8]{a^3 b^5 c}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{x^5 y^7 z^2}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the outer and inner radicals: \(3 \times 4 = 12\). The expression as a single radical is \(\sqrt[12]{x^5 y^7 z^2}\).

qs.q: Re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\frac{u^4 v}{w^5}}}\)
qs.s: The outer radical has index 3 and the inner square root has index 2. Multiplying their indices gives \(3 \times 2 = 6\), resulting in \(\sqrt[6]{\frac{u^4 v}{w^5}}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt[5]{m^3 n^2 p}}}\)
qs.s: Each square root has an index of 2, so the single index is \(2 \times 2 \times 5 = 20\). This gives \(\sqrt[20]{m^3 n^2 p}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{5 x y^3 z^2}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radical indices: \(4 \times 2 \times 3 = 24\). The radicand remains \(5 x y^3 z^2\), giving \(\sqrt[24]{5 x y^3 z^2}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{a b^3 c^4}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices of the nested radicals: \(3 \times 5 \times 2 = 30\). Keeping the radicand unchanged gives \(\sqrt[30]{a b^3 c^4}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{x^3 y^2 z}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices together: \(5 \times 2 \times 3 = 30\). Written as a single radical, the expression is \(\sqrt[30]{x^3 y^2 z}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{u^2 v w^5}}}\)
qs.s: The outer radical is a square root with index 2, so the single combined index is \(2 \times 4 \times 3 = 24\). Thus, the expression becomes \(\sqrt[24]{u^2 v w^5}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[5]{2 x^3 y^7 z^{11}}}}}}\)
qs.s: There are three square roots (each index 2), a cube root (index 3), and a fifth root (index 5), giving a single index of \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\). The result is \(\sqrt[120]{2 x^3 y^7 z^{11}}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt[4]{\frac{11 u^5 v^{11}}{w^7}}}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the four radical indices: \(3 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4 = 72\). Keeping the radicand unchanged gives \(\sqrt[72]{\frac{11 u^5 v^{11}}{w^7}}\).

qs.q: Assuming all variables are positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[7]{\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{5 a^9 b^5 c^2}}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply all four indices: \(7 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 168\). Placing the radicand under this single index yields \(\sqrt[168]{5 a^9 b^5 c^2}\).

qs.q: Assuming \(x + y > 0\), re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[4]{\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{(x + y)^5}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radical indices: \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\). The binomial radicand \((x + y)^5\) remains intact, giving \(\sqrt[24]{(x + y)^5}\).

qs.q: Assuming \(a > b\) and \(x + y > 0\) with all variables positive, re-write as a single radical: \(\sqrt[5]{\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{\frac{(a - b)^2 c^7}{(x + y)^3}}}}\)
qs.s: Multiply the indices: \(5 \times 2 \times 3 = 30\). The rational expression remains unchanged inside the radical, yielding \(\sqrt[30]{\frac{(a - b)^2 c^7}{(x + y)^3}}\).

qs.q: Which statement explains why \(\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x\) does NOT require an absolute value symbol for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: Odd roots can have negative values and preserve the sign of \(x\)
d: The radicand of an odd root cannot be negative
The index 3 is an even integer
Odd roots always produce positive values only
qs.s: Because the index 3 is odd, the cube root of a negative number is defined and negative, so \(\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x\) for all real numbers without needing an absolute value.

qs.q: Which statement explains why \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) requires an absolute value symbol for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), but the principal square root must be non-negative
d: The square root of an even power is always undefined
\(x^3\) is non-negative for all real numbers \(x\)
qs.s: When \(x\) is negative, \(x^3\) is also negative; however, the radical sign denotes the principal (non-negative) square root, so \(|x^3|\) is required to ensure the result is non-negative.

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x y^2} = |y|\sqrt{x}\), which statement explains why the restriction \(x \ge 0\) is required?
qs.a: If \(x < 0\), then \(\sqrt{x}\) is not a real number
d: The variable under the radical must have an even exponent
The absolute value on \(y\) is only valid when \(x\) is negative
qs.s: For the square root \(\sqrt{x}\) to be defined in the real number system, the radicand \(x\) must be non-negative, so \(x \ge 0\) is required.

qs.q: Which statement explains why \(\sqrt{x^4} = x^2\) does NOT require an absolute value symbol for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real numbers \(x\), so it is already non-negative
d: The index of the square root is odd
Square roots can never result in an even power
qs.s: For any real number \(x\), \(x^2\) is never negative, meaning \(|x^2| = x^2\), so absolute value notation is not necessary.

qs.q: Which statement explains why the expression \(\sqrt{x^5}\) requires the restriction \(x \ge 0\) in the real number system?
qs.a: If \(x < 0\), then \(x^5 < 0\), and the square root of a negative number is not a real number
d: If \(x < 0\), the index of the radical becomes negative
Odd powers of negative numbers are always positive
An absolute value cannot be placed on an odd power
qs.s: When \(x < 0\), raising \(x\) to the odd power 5 produces a negative value, and square roots of negative numbers are undefined in the set of real numbers.

qs.q: For which of the following radical expressions does the simplified form require an absolute value on \(x\), NO absolute value on \(y\), and the restriction \(y \ge 0\) for all real values?
qs.s: For \(\sqrt{x^2 y^3}\), the odd power \(y^3\) requires the restriction \(y \ge 0\), which ensures \(y\) is non-negative so \(|y|\) is unnecessary; however, \(x\) can still be negative, so \(|x|\) is required, giving \(|x|y\sqrt{y}\).

qs.q: Which expression is the fully simplified form of \(\sqrt{16 x^6 y^4 z^7}\) for all real numbers, including all necessary absolute values and restrictions?
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt{16}=4\), \(\sqrt{x^6}=|x^3|\) (odd power of an unrestricted variable), and \(\sqrt{y^4}=y^2\) (always non-negative). The factor \(z^7\) requires \(z \ge 0\) to be real, which makes \(z^3 \ge 0\), simplifying to \(4|x^3|y^2 z^3\sqrt{z}, z \ge 0\).

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x^2 y^4 z^6}\) for all real values of \(x, y,\) and \(z\), which statement explains why \(y^2\) does NOT need absolute value bars while \(x\) and \(z^3\) do?
qs.a: \(y^2\) is always non-negative, whereas \(x\) and \(z^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\) or \(z < 0\)
d: \(y\) has an exponent of 4, which automatically restricts \(y \ge 0\)
\(x\) and \(z\) are in the radicand, but \(y\) is not
The product of three variables under a square root must always have exactly two absolute values
qs.s: Since \(y^2\) has an even exponent, \(y^2 \ge 0\) for any real \(y\); in contrast, \(x\) and \(z^3\) have odd exponents and can evaluate to negative values, requiring absolute value notation to keep the principal root non-negative.

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x^3 y^2}\) for real numbers, the result is \(x|y|\sqrt{x}\). Which statement explains why an absolute value is needed on \(y\), but NOT on \(x\)?
qs.a: \(x\) is already restricted to \(x \ge 0\) for \(\sqrt{x}\) to be real, but \(y\) can be negative
d: \(y\) is restricted to \(y \ge 0\), but \(x\) can be any real number
The exponent on \(y\) is even, which forces \(y\) to be negative
Absolute values are never placed on variables with odd exponents
qs.s: The presence of \(\sqrt{x^3}\) requires \(x \ge 0\) for the radicand to be non-negative, meaning \(|x| = x\); however, \(y\) can be any real number because \(y^2 \ge 0\), so \(|y|\) is needed to ensure the result is non-negative.

qs.q: Which statement explains why simplifying \(\sqrt[4]{x^4}\) for all real numbers requires an absolute value (\(|x|\)), while simplifying \(\sqrt[5]{x^5}\) does NOT require an absolute value (\(x\))?
qs.a: An even root must be non-negative, while an odd root can be negative and preserves the sign of \(x\)
d: A fifth root of a negative number is undefined in the real numbers
The exponent 4 is smaller than the exponent 5
Absolute value symbols are only permitted with square roots
qs.s: An even root (index 4) represents the principal, non-negative root and requires \(|x|\), whereas an odd root (index 5) is defined for negative numbers and preserves the sign of \(x\).

qs.q: Why does the simplification \(\sqrt{x^8 y} = x^4\sqrt{y}\) (\(y \ge 0\)) not require an absolute value symbol around \(x^4\)?
d: The index of the square root is an even number
\(x\) must be non-negative for \(x^8\) to be defined
qs.s: Because the exponent of \(x^4\) is even, \(x^4\) is non-negative for any real value of \(x\), so \(|x^4| = x^4\) and no absolute value is needed.

qs.q: Why does simplifying the cube root \(\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x\) never require an absolute value for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: The index is odd, so the nth root of a negative number is a real negative number
d: The variable \(x\) is restricted to \(x \ge 0\) for all real roots
Any root of \(x^3\) is automatically non-negative
Absolute values are only defined for square roots, not cube roots
qs.s: Odd roots of real numbers preserve sign (for example, \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\)), so the result can be negative and does not use absolute value.

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x^2 y} = |x|\sqrt{y}\) (\(y \ge 0\)), why is the absolute value symbol placed on \(x\)?
qs.a: \(x\) can be negative, and the principal square root must be non-negative
d: The exponent of \(x\) inside the radical is even, which makes the square root undefined if \(x < 0\)
Absolute value is required on any variable outside of a radical sign
qs.s: Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for any real number, \(x\) itself may be negative; the absolute value ensures the principal square root is non-negative.

qs.q: In the simplification \(\sqrt{x^7} = x^3\sqrt{x}\), why does the factor \(x^3\) outside the radical not require an absolute value?
qs.a: The radicand requires \(x \ge 0\) for the square root to be real, so \(x^3\) cannot be negative
d: \(x^3\) is always non-negative for all real numbers \(x\)
The exponent 3 is odd, which prevents the use of absolute value signs
The absolute value was already applied to the \(x\) inside the radical
qs.s: For \(\sqrt{x^7}\) to be defined in the real number system, the radicand requires \(x \ge 0\), which guarantees \(x^3 \ge 0\) without needing absolute value bars.

qs.q: Why does the simplification \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) require an absolute value symbol, whereas \(\sqrt{x^4} = x^2\) does not?
qs.a: \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), while \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\)
d: The radical \(\sqrt{x^6}\) is undefined for negative \(x\), but \(\sqrt{x^4}\) is defined
An absolute value is required whenever the exponent inside the radical is greater than 4
qs.s: The principal square root must be non-negative; since \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), an absolute value is required, but \(x^2\) is already non-negative for all real \(x\).

qs.q: In the simplification \(\sqrt[4]{a^4 b^8 c^{16}} = |a| b^2 c^4\) for all real numbers, why does only \(a\) require an absolute value?
qs.a: The simplified exponent of \(a\) is odd, while \(b^2\) and \(c^4\) are even powers that are always non-negative
d: \(a^4\) had the smallest exponent in the original radicand
\(b\) and \(c\) must be positive for the fourth root to be defined, but \(a\) can be negative
Fourth roots only place absolute values on the very first variable in the term
qs.s: An even root must be non-negative; since \(b^2 \ge 0\) and \(c^4 \ge 0\) for all real numbers, they need no absolute value, but \(a^1\) can be negative when \(a < 0\), so \(|a|\) is required.

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x^6 y^3 z^4} = |x^3| y z^2 \sqrt{y}\) for real numbers, why is an absolute value required on \(x^3\) but not on \(y\) or \(z^2\)?
qs.a: \(x^3\) can be negative, whereas \(z^2 \ge 0\) always and \(y \ge 0\) is required for the radical to be real
d: \(x\) is the only variable that had an even exponent in the original radicand
\(y\) and \(z\) are restricted to negative numbers, while \(x\) must be positive
\(x^3\) is outside the radical, while \(y\) and \(z^2\) remain partially under the radical sign
qs.s: \(x\) can be negative and its simplified power is odd, so \(|x^3|\) is required; \(z^2\) is an even power so \(z^2 \ge 0\), and the remaining \(\sqrt{y}\) already imposes the restriction \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: When simplifying \(\sqrt{x^{12} y^{10} z^6}\) for all real numbers \(x, y,\) and \(z\), which factors outside the radical must be enclosed in absolute value bars, and why?
qs.a: \(y^5\) and \(z^3\), because their simplified exponents are odd and can produce negative values
d: \(x^6, y^5,\) and \(z^3\), because all variables extracted from an even root require absolute values
Only \(x^6\), because it has the largest exponent outside the radical
None of them, because all exponents in the original radicand are even
qs.s: Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{x^{12} y^{10} z^6} = x^6 |y^5 z^3|\); \(x^6 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), but \(y^5\) and \(z^3\) have odd exponents and can be negative, requiring absolute value.

qs.q: In simplifying \(\sqrt{x y^2} = |y|\sqrt{x}\) for real numbers, why does \(y\) require an absolute value, but \(x\) does not?
qs.a: \(x\) is restricted to \(x \ge 0\) by the radical, while \(y\) can be negative
d: \(y\) had an even exponent inside the radical, which forces \(y < 0\)
\(x\) is inside the radical, so its value is automatically treated as zero
The square root of \(y^2\) is undefined for negative values of \(y\)
qs.s: Because \(x\) remains under the square root, the expression is only real if \(x \ge 0\), eliminating the need for \(|x|\); however, \(y\) can be any real number because \(y^2 \ge 0\), so \(|y|\) is needed to keep the principal root non-negative.

qs.q: Explain why \(\sqrt[6]{x^{12} y^6} = x^2 |y|\) requires an absolute value on \(y\), but \(\sqrt[3]{x^6 y^3} = x^2 y\) does not require an absolute value on \(y\).
qs.a: The 6th root has an even index so its output must be non-negative, while the 3rd root has an odd index and can have a negative output
d: The 6th root has larger radicand exponents, which forces \(y\) to be positive
The 3rd root simplifies to an expression with an even exponent on \(x\), eliminating the need for absolute value on \(y\)
Absolute values are only used when the index is a multiple of 6
qs.s: Even roots (like index 6) represent principal non-negative roots, requiring \(|y|\) when \(y\) can be negative; odd roots (like index 3) are defined for all real numbers and can be negative, so absolute values are never used.

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt{x^4} = x^2\) NOT require absolute value notation for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: Because \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real numbers \(x\), so the result is already guaranteed to be non-negative.
d: Because the exponent 4 is even, and even exponents never require absolute values.
Because the restriction \(x \ge 0\) is implicitly required for all powers of \(x\).
Because the square root of an even power is always an odd power.
qs.s: The principal square root must be non-negative. Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every real number \(x\), the expression is already non-negative without absolute value bars.

qs.q: Why is the simplified form of \(\sqrt{x^7}\) written as \(x^3\sqrt{x}\) with \(x \ge 0\), rather than using absolute value notation as \(|x^3|\sqrt{x}\)?
qs.a: Because the restriction \(x \ge 0\) ensures \(x^3 \ge 0\), making absolute value bars redundant.
d: Because absolute value bars are never permitted when a radical remains in the expression.
Because \(x^3\) is an odd power, and absolute values can only be applied to even powers.
Because the exponent 7 is odd, and odd powers inside a radical automatically remove absolute values.
qs.s: For \(\sqrt{x^7}\) to be real, the radicand requires \(x \ge 0\). Under this restriction, \(x^3\) is already non-negative, so \(|x^3| = x^3\) and absolute value bars are unnecessary.

qs.q: Why does the identity \(\sqrt{x^5} = x^2\sqrt{x}\) require the restriction \(x \ge 0\) in the real number system?
qs.a: If \(x < 0\), the radicand \(x^5\) is negative, and square roots of negative numbers are not defined in the real number system.
d: If \(x < 0\), the outside factor \(x^2\) would evaluate to a negative number.
Square roots of odd powers are undefined for all real numbers regardless of the sign of \(x\).
An odd exponent inside a radical is only defined when the index of the radical is also odd.
qs.s: Since 5 is an odd integer, any negative value of \(x\) makes \(x^5 < 0\). In the real number system, the square root of a negative number is undefined, so \(x \ge 0\) is required.

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt{x^6}\) for any real number \(x\) require absolute value notation, giving \(|x^3|\) instead of \(x^3\)?
qs.a: Because \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), but the principal square root must be non-negative.
d: Because the exponent 6 is an even number, so the radical cannot be simplified without absolute values.
Because any variable removed from any radical always requires absolute value notation.
qs.s: For any real number \(x\), the principal square root \(\sqrt{x^6}\) must be non-negative. Because \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), absolute value bars are necessary to ensure the result is non-negative.

qs.q: Why does the expression \(\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x\) require no restriction on the sign of \(x\) in the real number system?
qs.a: Because odd roots of negative numbers are defined in the real number system.
d: Because \(x^3\) is always non-negative for every real number \(x\).
Because the cube root of any negative number is always positive.
Because the exponent 3 cancels the negative sign before the root is taken.
qs.s: Unlike even roots, odd roots of negative numbers are well-defined in the real number system (for example, \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\)). Therefore, \(x\) can be any real number.

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt{x^2 y^5}\) to \(|x|y^2\sqrt{y}\) require an absolute value on \(x\), but a restriction \(y \ge 0\) on \(y\)?
qs.a: \(x\) can be negative because \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), but \(y\) must be non-negative so that the radicand \(y^5\) is not negative.
d: \(x\) is raised to an even power inside the radical, which forces \(x\) to be negative unless absolute values are used.
\(y\) is inside the remaining square root, so \(y\) must be strictly greater than \(x\).
The variable with the smaller exponent always receives the absolute value, while the other variable receives a restriction.
qs.s: Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), \(x\) can take negative values, so \(|x|\) is needed to ensure a non-negative principal root. In contrast, \(y^5 < 0\) when \(y < 0\), making the radicand negative, so \(y \ge 0\) is required.

qs.q: Why does the identity \(\sqrt{x^{14} y^{11}} = |x^7| y^5 \sqrt{y}\) require the restriction \(y \ge 0\), but no sign restriction on \(x\)?
qs.a: Because \(x^{14} \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), but \(y^{11} < 0\) when \(y < 0\), which would make the radicand negative.
d: Because \(x\) has an absolute value outside the radical, which forces \(x\) to be positive inside the radical.
Because the exponent 14 is greater than 11, so the sign of \(x\) dominates the sign of the radicand.
Because even powers under a square root are always positive, so \(x\) cannot be zero.
qs.s: The radicand \(x^{14}y^{11}\) must be non-negative. Since \(x^{14} \ge 0\) for any real \(x\), the sign of the radicand depends entirely on \(y^{11}\), which is non-negative if and only if \(y \ge 0\).

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt{\frac{x^6}{y^4}}\) for real numbers with \(y \ne 0\) require absolute value bars on the numerator (\(|x^3|\)) but not on the denominator (\(y^2\))?
qs.a: Because \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), while \(y^2\) is always positive for any real \(y \ne 0\).
d: Because absolute value bars are only mathematically defined for numerators of radical fractions.
Because \(x^6\) can be negative for negative \(x\), whereas \(y^4\) is always positive.
Because the denominator already has the restriction \(y \ne 0\), which prevents it from being negative.
qs.s: The principal square root must be non-negative. Since \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), \(|x^3|\) is required, but \(y^2 > 0\) for all real \(y \ne 0\), so no absolute value is needed on the denominator.

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt[6]{x^6 y^{12}} = |x| y^2\) for all real numbers require absolute value bars on \(x\), but not on \(y\)?
qs.a: The principal sixth root must be non-negative; \(x\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), but \(y^2\) is already non-negative for all real \(y\).
d: Because the exponent of \(x\) is equal to the index 6, which automatically requires absolute value bars.
Because \(x^6\) can be negative for negative values of \(x\), while \(y^{12}\) is always positive.
Because \(y^2\) has an even exponent, which makes it an imaginary number if enclosed in absolute values.
qs.s: The principal sixth root must be non-negative. Since \(\sqrt[6]{x^6} = |x|\) ensures the result is non-negative for negative \(x\), and \(y^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(y\), absolute value bars are only needed on \(x\).

qs.q: Why does simplifying \(\sqrt[4]{x^{12}}\) for any real number \(x\) equal \(|x^3|\), while simplifying \(\sqrt[4]{x^8}\) equals \(x^2\) without absolute value bars?
qs.a: The principal fourth root must be non-negative; \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), whereas \(x^2\) is always non-negative.
d: \(x^{12}\) can be negative for negative \(x\), whereas \(x^8\) is always non-negative.
The exponent 12 is a multiple of 3, which requires absolute value bars for all fourth roots.
Dividing 12 by 4 leaves an odd exponent, which is undefined for negative bases unless absolute values are used.
qs.s: For all real \(x\), \(x^{12} \ge 0\) and \(x^8 \ge 0\), and their fourth roots must be non-negative. Because \(x^3 < 0\) whenever \(x < 0\), it requires absolute value bars, whereas \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\) and does not.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt{-25}\) is not a real number, but \(\sqrt[3]{-125}\) is a real number?
qs.a: Even powers of real numbers cannot be negative, but odd powers of real numbers can be negative.
d: Even roots of negative numbers are always real, but odd roots of negative numbers are undefined.
The square root of \(-25\) is real because \(-5 \times 5 = -25\), but cube roots cannot be negative.
Neither expression is a real number because negative numbers cannot appear under any radical sign.
qs.s: No real number squared equals \(-25\) because \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), but \((-5)^3 = -125\), making \(\sqrt[3]{-125} = -5\) a real number.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt[5]{-32}\) is a real number, while \(\sqrt[6]{-64}\) is not a real number?
qs.a: Odd roots of negative numbers have one real solution, while even roots of negative numbers have no real solutions.
d: Even roots of negative numbers have one real solution, while odd roots have no real solutions.
The number \(-32\) is an odd number, while \(-64\) is an even number.
Both expressions are not real numbers because the radicands are negative.
qs.s: Because \((-2)^5 = -32\), the 5th root is \(-2\), which is real; however, an even power of a real number cannot equal \(-64\), so \(\sqrt[6]{-64}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt{-16}\) is not a real number?
d: Squaring any real number always results in a negative number.
The number \(-16\) is an even number, and even numbers cannot have square roots.
The square root of a negative number is always equal to zero.
qs.s: For every real number \(x\), \(x^2 \ge 0\), so no real number squared can equal \(-16\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{-16}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt[4]{-81}\) is not a real number?
qs.a: No real number raised to the 4th power equals \(-81\).
d: The number 81 is not divisible by 4.
Odd numbers cannot have even roots.
The 4th power of any real number is always negative.
qs.s: Because the index 4 is even, \(x^4 \ge 0\) for all real numbers \(x\). Since no real number raised to an even power can be negative, \(\sqrt[4]{-81}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt[3]{-27}\) is a real number?
qs.a: A negative real number raised to the third power is negative, so \((-3)^3 = -27\).
d: Squaring \(-3\) gives \(-27\), so the root is real.
Cube roots only exist for negative numbers.
The radicand \(-27\) is an odd number, which automatically makes any root real.
qs.s: Since \((-3)^3 = -27\), the cube root of \(-27\) is the real number \(-3\). Odd roots of negative numbers are always real numbers.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt{-x^2 - 9}\) is not a real number for any real value of \(x\)?
qs.a: Since \(x^2 \ge 0\) for all real \(x\), the radicand \(-x^2 - 9 \le -9 < 0\) is always negative under an even root.
d: Any radical expression that contains a variable \(x\) cannot be a real number.
Because \(x^2 \ge 0\), the expression \(-x^2 - 9\) is always positive, and positive radicands have no real roots.
The radicand is only negative when \(x\) is positive, so it is real for negative values of \(x\).
qs.s: For any real \(x\), \(x^2 \ge 0\), meaning \(-x^2 - 9 \le -9 < 0\). Because the radicand is strictly negative and the index is 2 (even), the expression is never a real number.

qs.q: Which of the following expressions does NOT represent a real number, and why?
qs.a: \(\sqrt[4]{-625}\), because an even root of a negative number has no real solution.
d: \(\sqrt[3]{-343}\), because an odd root of a negative number has no real solution.
\(\sqrt[5]{-243}\), because odd roots are only defined for positive radicands.
\(\sqrt[7]{-128}\), because the index 7 is an odd prime number.
qs.s: Odd roots of negative numbers are real (e.g., \(\sqrt[3]{-343} = -7\), \(\sqrt[5]{-243} = -3\), \(\sqrt[7]{-128} = -2\)), but an even root of a negative number like \(\sqrt[4]{-625}\) is not a real number.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt[4]{(-2)^4}\) is a real number, but \(\sqrt[4]{-2^4}\) is not a real number?
qs.a: The radicand \((-2)^4 = 16\) is positive, but \(-2^4 = -16\) is negative under an even root.
d: Both radicands equal \(-16\), but the parentheses in \((-2)^4\) cancel the negative sign.
The expression \((-2)^4 = -16\) has a real 4th root, but \(-2^4 = 16\) does not.
Neither expression is a real number because the base is 2 in both cases.
qs.s: By order of operations, \((-2)^4 = 16\), which has the real 4th root \(2\), whereas \(-2^4 = -16\), which is an even root of a negative number and therefore not real.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sqrt[3]{x - 5}\) is a real number for all real values of \(x\), but \(\sqrt{x - 5}\) is a real number only when \(x \ge 5\)?
qs.a: An odd root is defined for any real radicand, whereas an even root requires the radicand to be non-negative.
d: Cube roots require the radicand to be strictly positive, while square roots can take negative radicands.
The square root requires \(x \ge 5\) because square roots cannot be evaluated for numbers greater than 5.
Both expressions require \(x \ge 5\) because negative radicands are undefined for all roots.
qs.s: Odd roots can take any positive, negative, or zero radicand, but even roots are only real when the radicand is non-negative (\(x - 5 \ge 0 \implies x \ge 5\)).

qs.q: Why is \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\), while \(\sqrt{x^8} = x^4\) without absolute value bars, for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\), so \(|x^3|\) ensures a non-negative principal root, whereas \(x^4 \ge 0\) is already non-negative.
d: Absolute value bars are required whenever the exponent inside the radical is less than 8.
\(x^4\) can be negative for negative values of \(x\), so it does not need absolute value bars.
The exponent 6 is divisible by 3, which requires absolute value bars, but 8 is not divisible by 3.
qs.s: The principal square root must be non-negative; since an odd power like \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), absolute value bars are necessary, but an even power like \(x^4\) is always non-negative.

qs.q: A student claims that \(\sqrt[3]{-8}\) has no real solution because the radicand is negative. What is wrong with this claim?
qs.a: Odd roots of negative numbers are defined in the real numbers, and \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\).
d: The radicand is actually positive because \((-8)^1 = 8\).
The claim is correct; even and odd roots of negative numbers are always undefined in the real numbers.
The expression is defined, but it has two real solutions: \(2\) and \(-2\).
qs.s: Odd roots of negative numbers exist in the real numbers because \((-2)^3 = -8\), so \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{(-5)^2} = (\sqrt{-5})^2\)?
qs.a: \(\sqrt{-5}\) is not a real number, so the right side is undefined.
d: The left side evaluates to \(-5\), while the right side evaluates to \(5\).
Both sides are undefined because the radicand contains a negative number.
The left side simplifies to \(-25\), while the right side simplifies to \(25\).
qs.s: The left side simplifies to \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), but the right side contains \(\sqrt{-5}\), which is not a real number, making the right side undefined.

qs.q: What is wrong with concluding that \(x = 49\) is the solution to \(\sqrt{x} = -7\)?
qs.a: The principal square root \(\sqrt{x}\) cannot be negative, so the equation has no real solution.
d: Squaring \(-7\) gives \(-49\), so the correct solution is \(x = -49\).
The equation has two solutions: \(x = 49\) and \(x = -49\).
The radical cannot be eliminated by squaring both sides.
qs.s: The principal square root \(\sqrt{x}\) cannot be negative, so \(\sqrt{x} = -7\) has no real solution; substituting \(x = 49\) yields \(\sqrt{49} = 7 \neq -7\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{(-7)^2} = -7\)?
qs.a: The principal square root cannot be negative; \(\sqrt{(-7)^2} = 7\).
d: The radicand \((-7)^2\) is negative, so the expression is undefined.
The result must be written as \(\pm 7\), not just \(-7\).
The square root cancels the square only when the base is zero.
qs.s: Because \((-7)^2 = 49\), the principal square root is \(\sqrt{49} = 7\) (or \(|-7| = 7\)), which must be non-negative.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{-36} = -6\)?
qs.a: The square root of a negative number is undefined in the real numbers.
d: The negative sign should be placed outside the radical to get \(-(\sqrt{36}) = -6\).
qs.s: In the real number system, there is no real number whose square is negative, so \(\sqrt{-36}\) is undefined.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{\frac{-100}{-4}} = \frac{\sqrt{-100}}{\sqrt{-4}}\)?
qs.a: \(\sqrt{-100}\) and \(\sqrt{-4}\) are undefined in the real numbers, so the right side is undefined.
d: The left side simplifies to \(-5\), while the right side simplifies to \(5\).
The left side is undefined because the radicand is a fraction of negative numbers.
qs.s: The left side simplifies to \(\sqrt{25} = 5\), but on the right side, \(\sqrt{-100}\) and \(\sqrt{-4}\) are undefined in the real numbers, so the quotient property cannot be applied.

qs.q: A student simplifies the expression \(\sqrt{16x^6}\) for all real numbers \(x\) and writes \(\sqrt{16x^6} = 4x^3\). What is the error in this simplification?
qs.a: It should be \(4|x^3|\), because \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\), but the principal square root must be non-negative.
d: The coefficient should be \(|4| = -4\) when \(x\) is negative.
The exponent should be divided by 3 instead of 2, giving \(4x^2\).
The expression is undefined for all \(x < 0\) because \(x^6\) would be negative.
qs.s: For any real number \(x\), if \(x < 0\), then \(x^3 < 0\); absolute value notation is required to ensure the principal square root is non-negative: \(\sqrt{16x^6} = 4|x^3|\).

qs.q:
A student evaluates \(\sqrt[4]{(-2)^8}\) using the following steps:
Step 1: \(\sqrt[4]{(-2)^8} = (\sqrt[4]{-2})^8\)
Step 2: \((\sqrt[4]{-2})^8 = (-2)^{8/4} = (-2)^2 = 4\)
What is the error in the student's reasoning?
qs.a: In Step 1, \(\sqrt[4]{-2}\) is undefined in the real numbers, so the radical and exponent cannot be interchanged.
d: In Step 2, the exponent fraction \(8/4\) simplifies to \(1/2\), not \(2\).
The initial expression \(\sqrt[4]{(-2)^8}\) is undefined because the base \(-2\) is negative.
qs.s: The radicand evaluates to \((-2)^8 = 256\), so \(\sqrt[4]{256} = 4\); however, interchanging the radical and exponent in Step 1 produces \(\sqrt[4]{-2}\), which is undefined in the real numbers.

qs.q:
A student evaluates the expression \(\sqrt[3]{-125} - \sqrt{(-8)^2}\) in two steps:
Step 1: \(\sqrt[3]{-125} - \sqrt{(-8)^2} = -5 - (-8)\)
Step 2: \(-5 - (-8) = 3\)
What is the error in the student's work?
qs.a: In Step 1, \(\sqrt{(-8)^2}\) should simplify to \(8\), not \(-8\).
d: In Step 1, \(\sqrt[3]{-125}\) is undefined in the real numbers because the radicand is negative.
In Step 1, \(\sqrt[3]{-125}\) should evaluate to \(5\) instead of \(-5\).
qs.s: The principal square root must be non-negative, so \(\sqrt{(-8)^2} = |-8| = 8\); the correct expression in Step 1 is \(-5 - 8 = -13\).

qs.q:
A student attempts to solve the equation \(\sqrt{2x + 1} = -5\) using the following steps:
Step 1: \((\sqrt{2x + 1})^2 = (-5)^2\)
Step 2: \(2x + 1 = 25\)
Step 3: \(2x = 24\), so \(x = 12\)
What is the error in the student's work?
qs.a: The equation has no real solution because a principal square root cannot equal a negative number.
d: In Step 3, dividing 24 by 2 gives 14, not 12.
In Step 2, squaring the radical gives \(4x^2 + 1\), not \(2x + 1\).
qs.s: A principal square root cannot equal a negative number, so \(\sqrt{2x + 1} = -5\) has no real solution; substituting \(x = 12\) gives \(\sqrt{25} = 5 \neq -5\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x} = \sqrt{2x}\) for \(x > 0\)?
qs.a: Like radicals are combined by adding their coefficients, giving \(2\sqrt{x}\).
d: Radicals with the same radicand cannot be added together.
qs.s: Adding like radicals gives \((1 + 1)\sqrt{x} = 2\sqrt{x}\), whereas \(\sqrt{2x} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{x}\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{-25} = -5\) in the real number system?
qs.a: An even root of a negative number has no real solution.
d: The negative sign should be placed under a separate root.
qs.s: In the real number system, the square root of a negative number is undefined because no real number squared yields a negative result.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^2 + 64} = x + 8\) for \(x > 0\)?
qs.a: The square root of a sum is not equal to the sum of the square roots.
d: The square root of 64 was evaluated incorrectly.
The right-hand side must include a \(\pm\) sign.
qs.s: The square root operation does not distribute across addition, so \(\sqrt{x^2 + 64} \neq \sqrt{x^2} + \sqrt{64}\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{a^2 - b^2} = a - b\) for real numbers \(a > b > 0\)?
qs.a: The square root cannot be distributed over subtraction.
d: The correct simplified form is \(a + b\).
The expression under the radical is negative, so it is undefined.
The right-hand side must be written as \(|a| - |b|\).
qs.s: A radical cannot be applied to each term in a difference individually, because \(\sqrt{a^2 - b^2} \neq \sqrt{a^2} - \sqrt{b^2}\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{x^2} = x\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: It is false when \(x < 0\); the correct simplification is \(|x|\).
d: It is false when \(x > 0\); the correct simplification is \(-x\).
The expression \(\sqrt{x^2}\) is undefined whenever \(x\) is negative.
The value must always be written with a plus-or-minus sign: \(\pm x\).
qs.s: By definition, the principal square root is nonnegative; therefore, \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\), which does not equal \(x\) when \(x\) is negative.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^2 - 14x + 49} = x - 7\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: It is invalid when \(x < 7\); the correct simplification is \(|x - 7|\).
d: The expression under the radical does not factor into a perfect square.
The radical cannot be simplified because the radicand is negative for some values of \(x\).
The result must always be written with a plus-or-minus sign: \(\pm(x - 7)\).
qs.s: The radicand factors as \((x - 7)^2\), and \(\sqrt{(x - 7)^2} = |x - 7|\); when \(x < 7\), \(x - 7\) is negative, so absolute value notation is required.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\frac{\sqrt{4x^2 + 36y^2}}{2} = x + 3y\) for \(x, y > 0\)?
qs.a: The square root was incorrectly distributed over addition in the numerator.
d: The denominator 2 was divided into only one of the terms instead of both.
The square root of 36 was evaluated incorrectly as 6 instead of 18.
The expression is undefined because \(x\) and \(y\) are distinct variables.
qs.s: The radical in \(\sqrt{4x^2 + 36y^2}\) cannot distribute over addition; factoring gives \(2\sqrt{x^2 + 9y^2}\), which simplifies to \(\sqrt{x^2 + 9y^2}\) after dividing by 2.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{25x^6} = 5x^3\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: When \(x\) is negative, \(5x^3\) is negative; the correct result is \(5|x^3|\).
d: The exponent 6 was divided incorrectly; it should be \(5x^4\).
The coefficient 25 was simplified incorrectly; it should remain 25.
The expression \(\sqrt{25x^6}\) is undefined whenever \(x\) is negative.
qs.s: Because \(x^6 \geq 0\), \(\sqrt{25x^6}\) is defined and nonnegative for all real \(x\); when \(x < 0\), \(5x^3\) is negative, so an absolute value is required: \(5|x^3|\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(\sqrt{100x^2 - 64x^2}\) for \(x > 0\) as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt{100x^2 - 64x^2} = \sqrt{100x^2} - \sqrt{64x^2} = 10x - 8x = 2x\)
What error was made, and what is the correct value?
qs.a: The radical was distributed over subtraction; the correct value is \(6x\).
d: The coefficients were subtracted incorrectly; the correct value is \(4x\).
The square roots were evaluated incorrectly; \(\sqrt{100x^2} = 50x\), so the correct value is \(42x\).
The expression cannot be evaluated because the radicand contains subtraction.
qs.s: Like terms under the radical must be combined first: \(\sqrt{100x^2 - 64x^2} = \sqrt{36x^2} = 6x\). Distributing a square root across subtraction is invalid.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^4 + x^2} = x^2 + x\) for \(x > 0\)?
qs.a: The radical was distributed over addition; the correct simplified form is \(x\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\).
d: The square root of \(x^4\) should be \(x^3\), giving \(x^3 + x\).
The terms under the radical should be multiplied instead of added, giving \(x^3\).
The variable \(x\) cannot be factored out because the exponents are different.
qs.s: A square root cannot distribute over addition; instead, factor out \(x^2\) to obtain \(\sqrt{x^2(x^2 + 1)} = x\sqrt{x^2 + 1}\).

qs.q:
A student simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = \sqrt[5]{-32} = -2\)
What is the correct value of \(\sqrt[10]{(-32)^2}\)?
qs.s: Because the index 10 is even, the principal root of \((-32)^2 = 1024\) must be non-negative: \(\sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = \sqrt[10]{1024} = 2\).

qs.q:
A student simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-64)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\)
What is the correct value of \(\sqrt[6]{(-64)^2}\)?
qs.s: Evaluating the square first gives \((-64)^2 = 4096\), and the principal 6th root of 4096 is 4.

qs.q:
A student simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-\frac{1}{27}} = -\frac{1}{3}\)
What is the correct value of \(\sqrt[6]{\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)^2}\)?
qs.s: The base is squared first to obtain \(\frac{1}{729}\), and the principal even root is non-negative: \(\sqrt[6]{\frac{1}{729}} = \frac{1}{3}\).

qs.q:
A student simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\)
What is the correct value of \(\sqrt[6]{(-27)^2}\)?
qs.s: Since \((-27)^2 = 729\) and the 6th root is an even root, the principal root must be non-negative: \(\sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} = \sqrt[6]{729} = 3\).

qs.q:
A student simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-125)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-125} = -5\)
What is the correct value of \(\sqrt[6]{(-125)^2}\)?
qs.s: An even root of a real number is always non-negative; since \((-125)^2 = 5^6\), the correct value is \(\sqrt[6]{5^6} = 5\).

qs.q: A student simplified \(\sqrt{x^6} - \sqrt[4]{x^4}\) as \(x^3 - x\), and evaluated it at \(x = -3\) to get \((-3)^3 - (-3) = -24\). What is the correct value of \(\sqrt{x^6} - \sqrt[4]{x^4}\) when \(x = -3\)?
qs.s: Because even roots must yield non-negative values, \(\sqrt{x^6} = |x^3|\) and \(\sqrt[4]{x^4} = |x|\); for \(x = -3\), this gives \(|-27| - |-3| = 27 - 3 = 24\).

qs.q:
A student incorrectly evaluated an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-125)^2} + \sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} - \sqrt[12]{(-8)^4} = -5 + (-3) - (-2) = -6\)
What is the correct value of the expression?
qs.s: Each radical has an even index and evaluates to a positive value: \(\sqrt[6]{(-125)^2} = 5\), \(\sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} = 3\), and \(\sqrt[12]{(-8)^4} = 2\), so \(5 + 3 - 2 = 6\).

qs.q:
A student incorrectly evaluated an expression by reducing indices:
\(\displaystyle 5\sqrt[6]{(-64)^2} - 3\sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = 5(-4) - 3(-2) = -14\)
What is the correct value of the expression?
qs.s: Since both radicals represent principal even roots, \(\sqrt[6]{(-64)^2} = 4\) and \(\sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = 2\), so \(5(4) - 3(2) = 20 - 6 = 14\).

qs.q:
A student incorrectly simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} + \sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-27} + \sqrt[5]{-32} = -3 + (-2) = -5\)
What is the correct value of the expression?
qs.s: Both terms are principal even roots and must evaluate to positive values: \(\sqrt[6]{(-27)^2} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[10]{(-32)^2} = 2\), giving a sum of \(3 + 2 = 5\).

qs.q:
A student incorrectly simplified an expression as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[6]{(-729)^2} + \sqrt[10]{(-1024)^2} = \sqrt[3]{-729} + \sqrt[5]{-1024} = -9 + (-4) = -13\)
What is the correct value of the expression?
qs.s: Since both radicals have even indices, their outputs must be positive: \(\sqrt[6]{(-729)^2} = 9\) and \(\sqrt[10]{(-1024)^2} = 4\), yielding \(9 + 4 = 13\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{x^2 + 36} = x + 6\) for \(x > 0\)?
qs.a: The square root of a sum is not equal to the sum of the square roots.
d: The principal square root of 36 is \(\pm 6\), not 6.
The term \(x^2\) requires an absolute value sign, giving \(|x| + 6\).
The radical must first be factored into \((x + 6)(x - 6)\).
qs.s: Because \((x + 6)^2 = x^2 + 12x + 36 \neq x^2 + 36\), the square root cannot be taken term by term.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \((x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} = x + y\) for positive real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?
qs.a: A fractional exponent cannot be distributed across terms in an addition.
d: The correct result should be \(x^2 + y^2\).
The exponents should be multiplied by \(\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(x + y^{\frac{1}{2}}\).
The terms must be subtracted instead: \(x - y\).
qs.s: Squaring both sides shows that \((x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 \neq x^2 + y^2\), which means the exponent \(\frac{1}{2}\) cannot be distributed over addition.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{x^2} = x\) for any real number \(x\)?
qs.a: When \(x\) is negative, \(\sqrt{x^2} = -x\), so the result must be written as \(|x|\).
d: The radical is undefined whenever \(x\) is negative.
The correct result must always be \(\pm x\).
The exponent cancels the radical only if \(x = 0\).
qs.s: The principal square root of a real number is always non-negative, so \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\); for example, \(\sqrt{(-4)^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4 \neq -4\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt{x^2 - 25} = x - 5\) for \(x > 5\)?
qs.a: A radical cannot be distributed across subtraction.
d: The square root of \(-25\) is undefined, so the expression has no real value.
The result should be \(x + 5\) because principal roots must be positive.
qs.s: Expanding \((x - 5)^2 = x^2 - 10x + 25 \neq x^2 - 25\) shows that the square root cannot be applied separately to each term.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \(\sqrt[3]{-64} = \pm 4\)?
qs.a: An odd root of a real number has only one real value, so \(\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\).
d: Odd roots of negative numbers are undefined in the real number system.
The value must be \(+4\) because roots cannot equal a negative number.
An index of 3 requires three real solutions: \(4, -4,\) and \(0\).
qs.s: Since \((-4)^3 = -64\) but \((4)^3 = 64\), an odd index yields exactly one real root, which retains the sign of the radicand.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} = x + y + z\) for positive real numbers \(x, y,\) and \(z\)?
qs.a: The square root cannot be distributed over a sum; \((x + y + z)^2\) contains cross-terms like \(2xy, 2xz,\) and \(2yz\).
d: The expression cannot be simplified because it contains three different variables.
The terms must be grouped in pairs before taking the square root.
The result must have absolute value signs around each term: \(|x| + |y| + |z|\).
qs.s: Squaring the sum yields \((x + y + z)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2xy + 2xz + 2yz \neq x^2 + y^2 + z^2\), so the radical of a three-term sum is not the sum of the individual radicals.

qs.q: What is wrong with the statement \((64x^3 + 27y^3)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 4x + 3y\) for positive real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?
qs.a: The fractional exponent cannot be distributed across the sum, even though \(\sqrt[3]{64x^3} = 4x\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27y^3} = 3y\).
d: The coefficients should be added first to get \((91x^3y^3)^{\frac{1}{3}}\).
The cube root of 64 is 8 and the cube root of 27 is 9, so it should be \(8x + 9y\).
The correct simplified result should be \((4x + 3y)^3\).
qs.s: Expanding \((4x + 3y)^3 = 64x^3 + 144x^2y + 108xy^2 + 27y^3 \neq 64x^3 + 27y^3\) demonstrates that distributing the exponent \(\frac{1}{3}\) across the sum omits the cross terms.

qs.q:
What is wrong with the following simplification for \(x > 0\)?
\(\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt{16x^2 + 64}}{4} = \frac{4x + 8}{4} = x + 2\)
qs.a: The radical \(\sqrt{16x^2 + 64}\) was incorrectly distributed across the sum to obtain \(4x + 8\).
d: Dividing \(\frac{4x + 8}{4}\) to get \(x + 2\) is an invalid fraction cancellation.
The denominator 4 cannot divide terms that originated inside a radical.
The constant 64 inside the radical should have been divided by 4 before taking the square root.
qs.s: Factoring 16 gives \(\sqrt{16(x^2 + 4)} = 4\sqrt{x^2 + 4}\), so the correct simplification is \(\frac{4\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}{4} = \sqrt{x^2 + 4}\), which does not equal \(x + 2\).

qs.q:
What is wrong with the following simplification for \(x > 0\)?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt{9x^2 + 81} = \sqrt{9(x^2 + 9)} = 3\sqrt{x^2 + 9} = 3(x + 3) = 3x + 9\)
qs.a: In the step \(3\sqrt{x^2 + 9} = 3(x + 3)\), the square root was incorrectly distributed over the addition \(x^2 + 9\).
d: In the step \(\sqrt{9x^2 + 81} = \sqrt{9(x^2 + 9)}\), the number 9 was factored out incorrectly.
In the step \(\sqrt{9(x^2 + 9)} = 3\sqrt{x^2 + 9}\), the factor 9 cannot be pulled out of the radical.
In the step \(3(x + 3) = 3x + 9\), the 3 was not distributed to both terms.
qs.s: While factoring out 9 and simplifying \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) is correct, \(\sqrt{x^2 + 9} \neq x + 3\) because \((x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 6x + 9 \neq x^2 + 9\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{25x^6 y^4} = 5x^3 y^2\) for any real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?
qs.a: Because \(x^3\) can be negative while the principal root must be non-negative, the result must be \(5|x^3|y^2\).
d: Both variables have even radicand exponents, so both require absolute values: \(5|x^3||y^2|\).
The square root of 25 is \(\pm 5\), so the coefficient must be written as \(\pm 5\).
The expression is undefined whenever \(x\) or \(y\) is negative.
qs.s: Since \(x^6 = (x^3)^2\) and \(x^3\) can be negative, an absolute value is needed on \(x^3\), whereas \(y^2\) is already non-negative, giving \(\sqrt{25x^6 y^4} = 5|x^3|y^2\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt{(-6)^2} = -6\)
qs.a: The principal square root must be non-negative, so \(\sqrt{(-6)^2} = |-6| = 6\).
d: The square root of a negative number squared is undefined in the real numbers.
Squaring a negative number gives a negative result, so \(\sqrt{-36}\) has no solution.
The result must be written as \(\pm 6\).
qs.s: Squaring \(-6\) yields \(36\), and the principal square root \(\sqrt{36}\) is positive \(6\), meaning \(\sqrt{(-6)^2} = |-6| = 6\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt[3]{64}}{\sqrt{16}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{64}{16}} = \sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.a: The quotient property cannot be applied to radicals with different indices.
d: The cube root of 64 is not defined in the real number system.
The denominator \(\sqrt{16}\) must be simplified to \(\pm 4\).
qs.s: The quotient property \(\frac{\sqrt[n]{a}}{\sqrt[n]{b}} = \sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}}\) requires both radicals to have the same index \(n\). Since the indices are 3 and 2, each radical must be evaluated separately to give \(\frac{4}{4} = 1\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{125} = \pm 5\)
qs.a: An odd root of a real number has only one real value, so \(\sqrt[3]{125} = 5\).
d: The cube root of 125 is \(\pm 25\), not \(\pm 5\).
The cube root of a positive number must only be negative, so \(\sqrt[3]{125} = -5\).
The cube root of 125 has no real solutions.
qs.s: Odd roots have exactly one real root that preserves the sign of the radicand; since \(5^3 = 125\) and \((-5)^3 = -125\), the only value is \(5\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[3]{8} \cdot \sqrt{4} = \sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 4} = \sqrt[3]{32}\)
qs.a: The product property cannot be applied to radicals with different indices.
d: The cube root of 8 is not a real number.
The product must keep the square root index instead, giving \(\sqrt{32}\).
qs.s: Radicals can only be combined under a single radical sign through multiplication when they share the same index. Evaluating each radical individually gives \(2 \cdot 2 = 4\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt[4]{-81} = -3\)
qs.a: An even root of a negative number has no real solution.
d: The correct value is \(+3\) instead of \(-3\).
The answer must be written as \(\pm 3\).
The index 4 must be multiplied by \(-81\).
qs.s: When the index \(n\) is even, no real number raised to the \(n\)th power can be negative, so \(\sqrt[4]{-81}\) is undefined in the real number system.

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle (-64)^{-2/3} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{(-64)^2}} = -\frac{1}{16}\)
qs.a: The negative sign in the exponent denotes a reciprocal, not that the result is negative.
d: The expression \((-64)^2\) is negative, so its cube root does not exist.
The fraction \(-2/3\) means taking the square root and cubing, not the cube root and squaring.
A negative base cannot be raised to a rational exponent.
qs.s: A negative exponent indicates a reciprocal: \((-64)^{-2/3} = \frac{1}{(-64)^{2/3}} = \frac{1}{(\sqrt[3]{-64})^2} = \frac{1}{(-4)^2} = \frac{1}{16}\), which is positive.

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt[3]{-512} + \sqrt{256}}{\sqrt[4]{-16}} = \frac{-8 + 16}{-2} = \frac{8}{-2} = -4\)
qs.a: The radical \(\sqrt[4]{-16}\) is undefined in the real numbers because an even root cannot have a negative radicand.
d: The cube root \(\sqrt[3]{-512}\) is undefined because odd roots cannot have negative radicands.
The square root \(\sqrt{256}\) should simplify to \(\pm 16\).
The numerator addition \(-8 + 16\) was computed incorrectly.
qs.s: While odd roots of negative numbers are real (\(\sqrt[3]{-512} = -8\)), even roots of negative numbers have no real solutions, making the entire expression undefined in the real number system.

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \sqrt{x^6 y^8} = x^3 y^4 \text{ for all real numbers } x \text{ and } y\)
qs.a: An absolute value is required on \(x^3\) because \(x^3\) can be negative when \(x < 0\).
d: An absolute value is required on \(y^4\) because its exponent is even.
Both \(x^3\) and \(y^4\) require absolute values regardless of their exponents.
The expression cannot be simplified because the square root of variables with different powers is undefined.
qs.s: Because \(y^4 \ge 0\) for all real \(y\), no absolute value is needed on \(y^4\), but \(x^3\) is negative whenever \(x < 0\), requiring \(\sqrt{x^6 y^8} = |x^3|y^4\) to ensure a non-negative principal root.

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification (for \(x > 0\))?
\(\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt[3]{216x^6}}{\sqrt{36x^4}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{216x^6}{36x^4}} = \sqrt[3]{6x^2}\)
qs.a: The quotient property cannot be applied to radicals with different indices.
d: The cube root of 216 does not exist in the real number system.
The variable \(x\) cannot be simplified under a radical.
qs.s: The numerator has an index of 3 while the denominator has an index of 2, so the quotient rule cannot be applied; evaluating separately yields \(\frac{6x^2}{6x^2} = 1\).

qs.q:
Which statement explains the error in the following simplification?
\(\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt[3]{1000}}{\sqrt{100}} \cdot \sqrt[4]{16} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{1000}{100}} \cdot 2 = 2\sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.a: The quotient property was applied to \(\frac{\sqrt[3]{1000}}{\sqrt{100}}\) even though the radicals have different indices.
d: The fourth root \(\sqrt[4]{16}\) was evaluated incorrectly as 2.
The multiplication \(2 \cdot \sqrt[3]{10}\) should be written as \(\sqrt[3]{20}\).
The radicals \(\sqrt[3]{1000}\) and \(\sqrt{100}\) cannot be simplified individually.
qs.s: The radicals in the fraction have different indices (3 and 2) and cannot be combined under one radical; simplifying each part individually gives \(\frac{10}{10} \cdot 2 = 1 \cdot 2 = 2\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^6} = \sqrt{(x^3)^2} = x^3\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: The result should be \(|x^3|\) because \(x^3\) is negative when \(x < 0\).
d: The result should be \(\pm x^3\) because square roots always yield two values.
The exponent of the result should be 4 because \(6 - 2 = 4\).
The expression \(\sqrt{x^6}\) is undefined for all negative values of \(x\).
qs.s: Because \(x^3\) is negative whenever \(x < 0\), \(\sqrt{x^6} = \sqrt{(x^3)^2} = |x^3|\) is necessary to ensure the principal square root is non-negative.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{y^2 + 10y + 25} = \sqrt{(y + 5)^2} = y + 5\) for all real numbers \(y\)?
qs.a: The result should be \(|y + 5|\) because \(y + 5\) is negative when \(y < -5\).
d: The result should be \(\pm(y + 5)\) because the index of the radical is even.
The trinomial factors incorrectly; it should be \((y - 5)^2\).
The expression is undefined for all \(y \le -5\).
qs.s: Since \(y\) can be any real number, \(y + 5\) can be negative when \(y < -5\), so absolute value notation is required: \(\sqrt{(y + 5)^2} = |y + 5|\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{a^2 - 14a + 49} = \sqrt{(a - 7)^2} = a - 7\) for all real numbers \(a\)?
qs.a: An absolute value is needed, giving \(|a - 7|\), so the result is non-negative.
d: A plus-or-minus sign is needed, giving \(\pm(a - 7)\).
The expression has no real value when \(a < 7\).
qs.s: The principal square root of a squared real quantity satisfies \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\), which gives \(\sqrt{(a - 7)^2} = |a - 7|\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{w^2 + 2w + 1} = \sqrt{(w + 1)^2} = w + 1\) for all real numbers \(w\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(|w + 1|\) because the square root cannot evaluate to a negative number.
d: The result must be \(\pm(w + 1)\) because \(w^2\) indicates two solutions.
The expression inside the radical does not form a perfect square.
The radical is undefined for all values of \(w < 0\).
qs.s: For any real number \(w\), \(\sqrt{(w + 1)^2} = |w + 1|\), ensuring the simplified result is never negative when \(w < -1\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^2 - 6x + 9} = \sqrt{(x - 3)^2} = x - 3\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(|x - 3|\) because the principal square root cannot be negative.
d: The result must be \(\pm(x - 3)\) because every square root has two values.
The radicand factors incorrectly; it should be \((x + 3)^2\).
The expression is undefined for all real values of \(x < 3\).
qs.s: For any real number \(x\), \(\sqrt{A^2} = |A|\); since \(x - 3\) is negative when \(x < 3\), the principal square root must be written with absolute value bars as \(|x - 3|\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{\frac{x^2 + 12x + 36}{49}} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{x + 6}{7}\right)^2} = \frac{x + 6}{7}\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(\frac{|x + 6|}{7}\) because the numerator can be negative when \(x < -6\).
d: The result must be \(\pm\frac{x + 6}{7}\) because fractions under radicals have two roots.
The denominator should remain inside the radical as \(\sqrt{49}\).
The expression is undefined for all \(x < -6\).
qs.s: By the quotient property, \(\frac{\sqrt{(x + 6)^2}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{|x + 6|}{7}\), which requires absolute value bars on the numerator since \(x + 6\) can be negative.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^2 - 8xy + 16y^2} = \sqrt{(x - 4y)^2} = x - 4y\) for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(|x - 4y|\) because \(x - 4y\) is negative whenever \(x < 4y\).
d: The result must be \(\pm(x - 4y)\) because of the two variables.
Radicals containing two different variables cannot be simplified.
qs.s: For any real values of \(x\) and \(y\), the quantity \(x - 4y\) may be negative, so \(\sqrt{(x - 4y)^2} = |x - 4y|\) is required.

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{25x^2 - 70x + 49} = \sqrt{(5x - 7)^2} = 5x - 7\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(|5x - 7|\) because \(5x - 7\) is negative when \(x < \frac{7}{5}\).
d: The result must be \(\pm(5x - 7)\) because an even radical always produces two roots.
The expression is undefined for all \(x < \frac{7}{5}\).
qs.s: Because \(5x - 7 < 0\) whenever \(x < \frac{7}{5}\), absolute value bars are required: \(\sqrt{(5x - 7)^2} = |5x - 7|\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{x^4 - 6x^2 + 9} = \sqrt{(x^2 - 3)^2} = x^2 - 3\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: The result must be \(|x^2 - 3|\) because \(x^2 - 3\) is negative when \(x^2 < 3\).
d: The result must be \(\pm(x^2 - 3)\) because the radical has degree 4.
The trinomial factors incorrectly; it should be \((x - 3)^4\).
The expression is undefined for all real values of \(x\) where \(x^2 < 3\).
qs.s: Although \(x^2 \ge 0\), the expression \(x^2 - 3\) is negative for any \(x\) such that \(-\sqrt{3} < x < \sqrt{3}\), so the square root must be \(|x^2 - 3|\).

qs.q: What is wrong with the simplification \(\sqrt{9x^2 + 24x + 16} - 3x = \sqrt{(3x + 4)^2} - 3x = 3x + 4 - 3x = 4\) for all real numbers \(x\)?
qs.a: \(\sqrt{(3x + 4)^2} = |3x + 4|\), so the expression equals \(|3x + 4| - 3x\), which is not \(4\) when \(x < -\frac{4}{3}\).
d: The expression should simplify to \(-4\) for all real numbers \(x\).
The radical term should be written as \(\pm(3x + 4)\).
The radical and \(-3x\) cannot be combined because they are not like terms.
qs.s: Since \(\sqrt{(3x + 4)^2} = |3x + 4|\), for \(x < -\frac{4}{3}\) the expression becomes \(-(3x + 4) - 3x = -6x - 4\), rather than \(4\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^4 = 256\)
qs.s: Taking the fourth root of both sides gives \(x = \pm\sqrt[4]{256}\). Since \(4^4 = 256\), the real solutions are \(x = \pm 4\).
Subtract 40 to obtain \(3x^4 = -48\), then divide by 3 to get \(x^4 = -16\). Since an even power of a real number cannot be negative, there is no real solution.
Subtract 19 from both sides to get \(4x^3 = -108\), then divide by 4 to get \(x^3 = -27\). Taking the cube root gives \(x = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^5 = -1\)

Subtract 19 and divide by 2 to isolate the power: \((x - 1)^5 = -32\). Taking the fifth root gives \(x - 1 = -2\), so \(x = -1\).

qs.q: Solve for \(x\): \(x^6 = -1\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(-2\sqrt[3]{-250}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(2\sqrt{75}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(3\sqrt{28}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(6\sqrt{50}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(-5\sqrt{192}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(5\sqrt{288}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(14\sqrt{\frac{18}{49}}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{150}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{45}\)

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{112}\)
qs.s: Factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{112} = \sqrt{16 \cdot 7} = 4\sqrt{7}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{3}{2} \cdot 4\sqrt{7} = 6\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{48}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical by factoring out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{48} = \sqrt{16 \cdot 3} = 4\sqrt{3}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{5}{2} \cdot 4\sqrt{3} = 10\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{200}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical: \(\sqrt{200} = \sqrt{100 \cdot 2} = 10\sqrt{2}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{2}{5} \cdot 10\sqrt{2} = 4\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{7}{3}\sqrt{54}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical: \(\sqrt{54} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 6} = 3\sqrt{6}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{7}{3} \cdot 3\sqrt{6} = 7\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{8}\sqrt{1152}\)
qs.s: Prime factorize \(1152 = 576 \cdot 2\), so \(\sqrt{1152} = 24\sqrt{2}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{5}{8} \cdot 24\sqrt{2} = 15\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{7}{2}\sqrt{\frac{72}{49}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule: \(\sqrt{\frac{72}{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{72}}{\sqrt{49}} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{7}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{7}{2} \cdot \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{7} = 3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{3}\sqrt[4]{405}\)
qs.s: Factor out the largest perfect fourth power: \(\sqrt[4]{405} = \sqrt[4]{81 \cdot 5} = 3\sqrt[4]{5}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{5}{3} \cdot 3\sqrt[4]{5} = 5\sqrt[4]{5}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{675}\)
qs.s: Factor out the perfect cube from the radicand: \(\sqrt[3]{675} = \sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 25} = 3\sqrt[3]{25}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{2}{3} \cdot 3\sqrt[3]{25} = 2\sqrt[3]{25}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{-432}\)
qs.s: Extract the negative perfect cube: \(\sqrt[3]{-432} = \sqrt[3]{-216 \cdot 2} = -6\sqrt[3]{2}\). Multiply by the coefficient: \(\frac{3}{4} \cdot (-6\sqrt[3]{2}) = -\frac{9}{2}\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{24}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical by factoring out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{24} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 6} = 2\sqrt{6}\). Multiplying gives \(\frac{3}{2}(2\sqrt{6}) = 3\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical by factoring out the perfect square: \(\sqrt{75} = \sqrt{25 \cdot 3} = 5\sqrt{3}\). Multiplying gives \(\frac{2}{5}(5\sqrt{3}) = 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{4}\sqrt{48}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical: \(\sqrt{48} = \sqrt{16 \cdot 3} = 4\sqrt{3}\). Multiplying by the coefficient gives \(\frac{5}{4}(4\sqrt{3}) = 5\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{7}\sqrt{98}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical: \(\sqrt{98} = \sqrt{49 \cdot 2} = 7\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying gives \(\frac{3}{7}(7\sqrt{2}) = 3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{3}{2}\sqrt[3]{192}\)
qs.s: Factor the largest perfect cube from 192: \(\sqrt[3]{192} = \sqrt[3]{64 \cdot 3} = 4\sqrt[3]{3}\). Multiplying by the fraction gives \(\frac{3}{2}(4\sqrt[3]{3}) = 6\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[4]{405}\)
qs.s: Factor the largest perfect fourth power from 405: \(\sqrt[4]{405} = \sqrt[4]{81 \cdot 5} = 3\sqrt[4]{5}\). Multiplying gives \(\frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt[4]{5}) = 2\sqrt[4]{5}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{6}\sqrt{12}\cdot\sqrt{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicals first to get \(\sqrt{12 \cdot 18} = \sqrt{216} = \sqrt{36 \cdot 6} = 6\sqrt{6}\). Multiplying by the coefficient yields \(\frac{5}{6}(6\sqrt{6}) = 5\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{4}{5}\sqrt{\frac{75}{64}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radical quotient as \(\frac{\sqrt{75}}{\sqrt{64}} = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{8}\). Multiplying by the fraction gives \(\frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{8} = \frac{20\sqrt{3}}{40} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(\frac{5}{8}\sqrt{288}\)
qs.s: Factor the largest perfect square from 288: \(\sqrt{288} = \sqrt{144 \cdot 2} = 12\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying and simplifying gives \(\frac{5}{8}(12\sqrt{2}) = \frac{60\sqrt{2}}{8} = \frac{15\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

qs.q: Change to simplest radical form: \(-5\sqrt[3]{135}\)

Change to simplest radical form: \(4\sqrt[3]{54}\)
Change to simplest radical form: \(2\sqrt[3]{375}\)
