qs.s: Field A has altitude \(\sqrt{65^2 - 25^2} = \sqrt{3600} = 60\text{ m}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(50)(60) = 1500\text{ m}^2\). Field B has altitude \(\sqrt{65^2 - 39^2} = \sqrt{2704} = 52\text{ m}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(78)(52) = 2028\text{ m}^2\), so Field B has the greatest area.

qs.q: One isosceles triangle has sides 12 cm, 12 cm, and 16 cm. Another isosceles triangle has sides 12 cm, 12 cm, and 8 cm. Which triangle has the greatest area, and what is its exact area in simplest radical form?
qs.a: The triangle with base 16 cm, with an area of \(32\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}^2\)
d: The triangle with base 8 cm, with an area of \(32\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}^2\)
The triangle with base 16 cm, with an area of \(64\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}^2\)
Both triangles have the same area of \(32\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}^2\)
qs.s: The first triangle has height \(\sqrt{12^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(16)(4\sqrt{5}) = 32\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}^2\). The second triangle has height \(\sqrt{12^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{128} = 8\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(8)(8\sqrt{2}) = 32\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}^2\). Since \(32\sqrt{5} > 32\sqrt{2}\), the triangle with base 16 cm has the greatest area.

qs.q: Three isosceles triangles each have two equal sides of length 25 cm. Triangle A has a base of 30 cm, Triangle B has a base of 40 cm, and Triangle C has a base of 48 cm. Which triangle has the greatest area?
qs.a: Triangles A and B tie for the greatest area (\(300\text{ cm}^2\))
d: Triangle C, with an area of \(336\text{ cm}^2\)
Triangle C, with an area of \(168\text{ cm}^2\)
All three triangles have the same area of \(300\text{ cm}^2\)
qs.s: Triangles A and B have altitudes \(\sqrt{25^2 - 15^2} = 20\text{ cm}\) and \(\sqrt{25^2 - 20^2} = 15\text{ cm}\) respectively, giving each an area of \(300\text{ cm}^2\). Triangle C has altitude \(\sqrt{25^2 - 24^2} = 7\text{ cm}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(48)(7) = 168\text{ cm}^2\), so Triangles A and B tie for the greatest area.

qs.q: One isosceles triangular lot has boundary sides 29 m, 29 m, and 40 m. Another isosceles triangular lot has boundary sides 29 m, 29 m, and 42 m. Which lot has the greatest area?
qs.a: Both lots have the same area of 420 m\(^2\)
d: The lot with base 42 m, with an area of 840 m\(^2\)
The lot with base 40 m, with an area of 441 m\(^2\)
The lot with base 42 m, with an area of 462 m\(^2\)
qs.s: The first lot has altitude \(\sqrt{29^2 - 20^2} = \sqrt{441} = 21\text{ m}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(40)(21) = 420\text{ m}^2\). The second lot has altitude \(\sqrt{29^2 - 21^2} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ m}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(42)(20) = 420\text{ m}^2\), so both lots have identical areas.

qs.q: Triangle A is an isosceles triangle with sides 10 cm, 10 cm, and 8 cm. Triangle B is an isosceles triangle with sides 10 cm, 10 cm, and 14 cm. Which triangle has the greatest area, and what is its exact area in simplest radical form?
qs.a: Triangle B, with an area of \(7\sqrt{51}\text{ cm}^2\)
d: Triangle A, with an area of \(8\sqrt{21}\text{ cm}^2\)
Triangle B, with an area of \(14\sqrt{51}\text{ cm}^2\)
Both triangles have the same area of \(8\sqrt{21}\text{ cm}^2\)
qs.s: Triangle A has height \(\sqrt{10^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{84} = 2\sqrt{21}\text{ cm}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(8)(2\sqrt{21}) = 8\sqrt{21} = \sqrt{1344}\text{ cm}^2\). Triangle B has height \(\sqrt{10^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{51}\text{ cm}\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(14)(\sqrt{51}) = 7\sqrt{51} = \sqrt{2499}\text{ cm}^2\). Since \(\sqrt{2499} > \sqrt{1344}\), Triangle B has the greatest area.

qs.q: The diagonal of a square has length \(\sqrt{120}\text{ cm}\). Find the length of each side.
qs.s: By the Pythagorean theorem, \(s^2 + s^2 = (\sqrt{120})^2\), which simplifies to \(2s^2 = 120\) and \(s^2 = 60\). Thus, \(s = \sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The area of an equilateral triangle is \(24\sqrt{3}\text{ ft}^2\). Find the length of each side.
qs.s: Using \(A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\), set \(24\sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\), so \(s^2 = 96\). Simplifying the square root yields \(s = \sqrt{96} = 4\sqrt{6}\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: The volume of a cube is \(56\text{ cm}^3\). Find the length of each edge.
qs.s: The volume of a cube is \(V = s^3\), so \(s^3 = 56\). Taking the cube root gives \(s = \sqrt[3]{56} = \sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 7} = 2\sqrt[3]{7}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The total surface area of a cube is \(108\text{ cm}^2\). Find the length of each edge.
qs.s: The total surface area of a cube is \(6s^2 = 108\), so \(s^2 = 18\). Taking the square root gives \(s = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The area of an equilateral triangle is \(75\sqrt{3}\text{ m}^2\). Find the length of each side.
qs.s: Using the area formula \(A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\), set \(75\sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\), which gives \(s^2 = 300\). Taking the square root and simplifying gives \(s = \sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A right triangle has a base of \(3\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}\) and an area of \(27\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}^2\). Find the length of its hypotenuse.
qs.s: The height is \(h = \frac{2(27\sqrt{2})}{3\sqrt{6}} = \frac{18}{\sqrt{3}} = 6\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\). By the Pythagorean theorem, \(c = \sqrt{(3\sqrt{6})^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2} = \sqrt{54 + 108} = \sqrt{162} = 9\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The area of a square is \(150\text{ m}^2\). Find the length of its diagonal.
qs.s: Since \(s^2 = 150\), the diagonal length is \(d = \sqrt{s^2 + s^2} = \sqrt{300}\). Simplifying the radical gives \(d = 10\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The area of an equilateral triangle is \(\frac{75\sqrt{3}}{2}\text{ cm}^2\). Find the perimeter of the triangle.
qs.s: From \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2 = \frac{75\sqrt{3}}{2}\), we find \(s^2 = 150\), so \(s = 5\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}\). The perimeter is \(3s = 3(5\sqrt{6}) = 15\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangle has a width of \(2\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}\) and a diagonal of length \(4\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}\). Find the area of the rectangle.
qs.s: The length squared is \(l^2 = (4\sqrt{5})^2 - (2\sqrt{5})^2 = 80 - 20 = 60\), so \(l = 2\sqrt{15}\text{ cm}\). The area is \((2\sqrt{5})(2\sqrt{15}) = 4\sqrt{75} = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: The area of an equilateral triangle is \(72\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2\). Find the altitude of the triangle.
qs.s: Using \(A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2\), \(s^2 = 288\) so \(s = 12\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\). The altitude is \(h = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(12\sqrt{2}) = 6\sqrt{6}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When combining like radicals such as \(4\sqrt{5} + 7\sqrt{5}\), we add their _____ while keeping the radical factor the same.
qs.s: Like radicals are combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients: \((4 + 7)\sqrt{5} = 11\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

In the radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{x}\), the number or expression \(x\) under the radical symbol is called the _____.
qs.s: By definition, the value or expression under the radical symbol is called the radicand.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

Two radical expressions that have different radicands or different indices are called _____ radicals.
qs.s: Radicals that cannot be combined because they differ in index, radicand, or both are defined as unlike radicals.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

Terms with like radical factors can be combined in the same way as terms with like _____ factors.
qs.s: Just as terms with like variable factors combine by adding coefficients (\(5x + 3x = 8x\)), terms with like radical factors combine the same way (\(5\sqrt{3} + 3\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3}\)).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

In the radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{x}\), the number \(n\) that indicates which root is being taken is called the _____.
qs.s: The number \(n\) specifying the degree of the root is defined as the index of the radical.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When written in simplest radical form, the expressions \(\sqrt[3]{54x^4}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{16x^4}\) (where \(x \geq 0\)) are like radicals with a common radicand of _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each cube root yields \(\sqrt[3]{54x^4} = 3x\sqrt[3]{2x}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{16x^4} = 2x\sqrt[3]{2x}\). In simplest form, both expressions share the same radicand, \(2x\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When the expression \(\sqrt{32x} + \sqrt{75y} - \sqrt{18x} + \sqrt{12y}\) is fully simplified by combining like radicals, the coefficient of \(\sqrt{3y}\) is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying the terms containing \(y\) yields \(\sqrt{75y} = 5\sqrt{3y}\) and \(\sqrt{12y} = 2\sqrt{3y}\). Combining these like radicals gives \((5 + 2)\sqrt{3y} = 7\sqrt{3y}\), so the coefficient is 7.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When the expression \(-3\sqrt{28} + 5\sqrt{63}\) is simplified by combining like radicals, the resulting coefficient of \(\sqrt{7}\) is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(-3\sqrt{28} = -3(2\sqrt{7}) = -6\sqrt{7}\) and \(5\sqrt{63} = 5(3\sqrt{7}) = 15\sqrt{7}\). Combining these like terms gives \((-6 + 15)\sqrt{7} = 9\sqrt{7}\), so the coefficient is 9.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

Among the four radical expressions \(\sqrt{48}\), \(\sqrt{75}\), \(\sqrt{108}\), and \(\sqrt{128}\), exactly _____ can be combined with \(\sqrt{27}\) as like radicals.
qs.s: In simplest form, \(\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}\). Simplifying the four terms gives \(4\sqrt{3}\), \(5\sqrt{3}\), \(6\sqrt{3}\), and \(8\sqrt{2}\), meaning exactly 3 of them share the like radical factor \(\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

The radicals \(\sqrt{45}\) and \(\sqrt{80}\) are like radicals because each, when written in simplest radical form, has a radicand of _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each radical gives \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}\). Both have an index of 2 and a radicand of 5, which makes them like radicals.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
Like radicals must have the same index and the same _____.
qs.s: By definition, like radicals are radical expressions that have both the same index and the same radicand.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
To determine if radical terms can be combined, each radical should first be written in _____ radical form.
qs.s: Radicals must first be simplified into simplest radical form to identify whether they share the same radicand and index.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
In the radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{x}\), the number \(n\) is called the _____ of the radical.
qs.s: In the notation \(\sqrt[n]{x}\), the number \(n\) indicates the root to be taken and is called the index.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
Radical terms that have the same index and the same radicand are called _____ radicals.
qs.s: Radicals sharing the same index and radicand are defined as like radicals.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
To add or subtract like radicals, combine their _____ and keep the common radical factor unchanged.
qs.s: Just like combining algebraic like terms, like radicals are combined by adding or subtracting their numerical coefficients.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
When written in simplest radical form, the fourth-root expressions \(\sqrt[4]{32}\) and \(\sqrt[4]{162}\) are like radicals with index 4 and common radicand _____.
qs.s: In simplest form, \(\sqrt[4]{32} = 2\sqrt[4]{2}\) and \(\sqrt[4]{162} = 3\sqrt[4]{2}\), meaning both have index 4 and common radicand 2.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
In the expression \(4\sqrt{18} - 2\sqrt{50} + \sqrt{8}\), simplifying reveals like radicals of \(\sqrt{2}\) whose combined coefficient is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each term gives \(4(3\sqrt{2}) - 2(5\sqrt{2}) + 2\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2} - 10\sqrt{2} + 2\sqrt{2}\), and combining the coefficients gives \(12 - 10 + 2 = 4\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
For \(x > 0\), the expressions \(\sqrt{28x^3}\) and \(\sqrt{63x^3}\) are like radicals whose common simplified radicand is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each term yields \(\sqrt{28x^3} = 2x\sqrt{7x}\) and \(\sqrt{63x^3} = 3x\sqrt{7x}\), so both share the simplified radicand \(7x\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
The cube-root expressions \(\sqrt[3]{24}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{81}\) are like radicals because in simplest radical form, their common radicand is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each radical yields \(\sqrt[3]{24} = 2\sqrt[3]{3}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{81} = 3\sqrt[3]{3}\), which have a common radicand of 3.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:
The expressions \(\sqrt{45}\) and \(\sqrt{80}\) are like radicals because in simplest radical form, their common radicand is _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each radical gives \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}\), showing that both share a common radicand of 5.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

To combine like radicals by addition or subtraction, add or subtract their _____ and keep the common radical factor.
qs.s: When adding or subtracting like radicals, only the coefficients in front of the radical are combined, while the radical factor remains unchanged.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

Radicals that have the same index and the same radicand are called _____ radicals.
qs.s: By definition, radicals that share both the same index and the same radicand are called like radicals.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

The expressions \(4\sqrt{3}\) and \(4\sqrt{5}\) cannot be combined into a single radical term because they are _____ radicals.
qs.s: Although both terms have the same index and coefficient, their radicands (\(3\) and \(5\)) are different, which makes them unlike radicals that cannot be combined.

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When simplified, the radicals \(\sqrt{8}\) and \(\sqrt{32}\) are like radicals with a common radicand of _____.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\), which shows that both share the common radicand \(2\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

Two simplified radicals can only be like radicals if they have the same radicand and the same _____.
qs.s: Like radicals must share both the same radicand and the same index (for instance, \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{5}\) are not like radicals because their indices differ).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When simplifying the expression \(2\sqrt{20x} + \sqrt{45x} - \sqrt{80x}\) (where \(x \ge 0\)), the like radicals combine to give a coefficient of _____ in front of \(\sqrt{5x}\).
qs.s: Simplifying each term yields \(4\sqrt{5x} + 3\sqrt{5x} - 4\sqrt{5x}\), and combining the coefficients gives \(4 + 3 - 4 = 3\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When the expression \(5\sqrt[3]{16} - 2\sqrt[3]{54}\) is simplified, the two terms are like radicals that share the common radical factor _____.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(5\sqrt[3]{16} = 5(2\sqrt[3]{2}) = 10\sqrt[3]{2}\) and \(2\sqrt[3]{54} = 2(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = 6\sqrt[3]{2}\), so the shared radical factor is \(\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

When the expressions \(\sqrt{28x^3}\) and \(\sqrt{63x^3}\) (where \(x \ge 0\)) are expressed in simplest radical form, they share the common radical factor _____.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{28x^3} = 2x\sqrt{7x}\) and \(\sqrt{63x^3} = 3x\sqrt{7x}\), so both terms share the radical factor \(\sqrt{7x}\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

In the expression \(5\sqrt{48} - 2\sqrt{75} + \sqrt{108}\), the three terms can be combined because after simplifying, each term has the same radicand of _____.
qs.s: Simplifying each radical gives \(5(4\sqrt{3}) = 20\sqrt{3}\), \(2(5\sqrt{3}) = 10\sqrt{3}\), and \(6\sqrt{3}\), all of which share the common radicand \(3\).

qs.q:
Fill in the blank to make the statement true:

The expressions \(\sqrt{50x}\) and \(\sqrt{72y}\) (where \(x, y > 0\)) simplify to \(5\sqrt{2x}\) and \(6\sqrt{2y}\); they cannot be combined into a single term because they are _____ radicals.
qs.s: Because the radicands \(2x\) and \(2y\) contain different variables, the radicals have different radicands and are unlike radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(7\sqrt{2}\) and \(2\sqrt{7}\).
qs.a: No, because their radicands are different
d: Yes, because both expressions contain the numbers 2 and 7
Yes, because both radicals have an index of 2
No, because their coefficients are different
qs.s: Like radicals must have identical indices and identical radicands. Although both have an index of 2, their radicands are 2 and 7, so they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(4\sqrt{5}\) and \(-6\sqrt{5}\).
qs.a: Yes, because they have the same index and the same radicand
d: No, because their coefficients are different
No, because one coefficient is negative and the other is positive
Yes, because their coefficients are both even integers
qs.s: Both expressions have an index of 2 and a radicand of 5. Since their indices and radicands match, they are like radicals regardless of their coefficients.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(\sqrt{15}\) and \(6\sqrt{15}\).
qs.a: Yes, because they have the same index and the same radicand
d: No, because the first expression does not have a coefficient

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions \(\sqrt{50x}\) and \(\sqrt{72x}\) are like radicals.
qs.a: Yes, because both simplify to have an index of 2 and a radicand of \(2x\).
d: No, because their original radicands, \(50x\) and \(72x\), are different.
No, because they simplify to \(5\sqrt{2x}\) and \(6\sqrt{3x}\).
Yes, because both original radicands are divisible by 2.
qs.s: Simplifying both radicals gives \(\sqrt{50x} = 5\sqrt{2x}\) and \(\sqrt{72x} = 6\sqrt{2x}\). Since both simplified expressions have an index of 2 and a radicand of \(2x\), they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions \(\sqrt{45x}\) and \(\sqrt{75x}\) are like radicals.
qs.a: No, because they simplify to \(3\sqrt{5x}\) and \(5\sqrt{3x}\), which have different radicands.
d: Yes, because both simplify to have a radicand of \(5x\).
Yes, because both original radicands are multiples of \(5x\).
No, because neither 45 nor 75 is a perfect square.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{45x} = 3\sqrt{5x}\) and \(\sqrt{75x} = 5\sqrt{3x}\). Even though their indices are both 2, their simplified radicands (\(5x\) and \(3x\)) are different, so they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(-2\sqrt{11a}\) and \(9\sqrt{3a}\).
qs.a: No, because they have different radicands (\(11a\) and \(3a\)).
d: Yes, because both are square roots containing the variable \(a\).
No, because their indices are different.
No, only because their coefficients are different (\(-2\) and \(9\)).
qs.s: Both expressions have the same index of 2, but their radicands are \(11a\) and \(3a\), which are not equal. Therefore, they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(8\sqrt[3]{5x}\) and \(-3\sqrt[3]{5x}\).
qs.a: Yes, because both have index 3 and radicand \(5x\).
d: No, because their coefficients are different (\(8\) and \(-3\)).
No, because their radicands are different.
No, because their indices are different.
qs.s: Two radical expressions are like radicals if they have the same index and the same radicand. Both expressions have an index of 3 and a radicand of \(5x\), so they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(4\sqrt[4]{7y}\) and \(4\sqrt[3]{7y}\).
qs.a: No, because they have different indices (\(4\) and \(3\)).
d: Yes, because both have the same radicand \(7y\) and coefficient \(4\).
Yes, because both radicals contain the same variable \(y\).
No, because their radicands are different.
qs.s: Although both expressions share the same radicand \(7y\), their indices are different (\(4\) and \(3\)). Therefore, they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{10m}\) and \(\frac{5}{2}\sqrt[3]{10m}\).
qs.a: Yes, because both have index 3 and radicand \(10m\).
d: No, because their coefficients are different fractions.
No, because their radicands are different.
No, because their indices are different.
qs.s: The coefficients outside the radical do not affect whether expressions are like radicals. Both have index 3 and radicand \(10m\), so they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(7\sqrt[5]{2xy}\) and \(-6\sqrt[5]{2xy}\).
qs.a: Yes, because both have index 5 and radicand \(2xy\).
d: No, because their coefficients are different (\(7\) and \(-6\)).
No, because the radicand contains more than one variable.
No, because their indices are different.
qs.s: Like radicals must have identical indices and identical radicands; the coefficients do not need to be equal. Since both expressions have index 5 and radicand \(2xy\), they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(\sqrt{12x}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{24x}\).
qs.a: No, because their indices are different (\(2\) and \(3\)).
d: Yes, because in simplest form both have the same radicand \(3x\) and coefficient \(2\).
Yes, because both radicals simplify to multiples of \(3x\).
No, because their simplified radicands are different.
qs.s: Simplifying gives \(\sqrt{12x} = 2\sqrt{3x}\) (index 2) and \(\sqrt[3]{24x} = 2\sqrt[3]{3x}\) (index 3). Although both simplified expressions have radicand \(3x\), their indices are different, so they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(-2\sqrt[3]{16y}\) and \(5\sqrt[3]{54y}\).
qs.a: Yes, because in simplest form both have index 3 and radicand \(2y\).
d: No, because the original radicands \(16y\) and \(54y\) are not equal.
No, because their simplified forms are \(-4\sqrt[3]{4y}\) and \(15\sqrt[3]{2y}\).
No, because their simplified indices are different.
qs.s: Simplifying each radical yields \(-2\sqrt[3]{16y} = -2(2\sqrt[3]{2y}) = -4\sqrt[3]{2y}\) and \(5\sqrt[3]{54y} = 5(3\sqrt[3]{2y}) = 15\sqrt[3]{2y}\). Since both have index 3 and radicand \(2y\), they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(3\sqrt{20x}\) and \(-2\sqrt{45x}\).
qs.a: Yes, because in simplest form both have index 2 and radicand \(5x\).
d: No, because the original radicands \(20x\) and \(45x\) are different.
No, because their simplified forms are \(6\sqrt{5x}\) and \(-6\sqrt{3x}\).
No, because their simplified coefficients are different (\(6\) and \(-6\)).
qs.s: Simplifying each radical gives \(3\sqrt{20x} = 3(2\sqrt{5x}) = 6\sqrt{5x}\) and \(-2\sqrt{45x} = -2(3\sqrt{5x}) = -6\sqrt{5x}\). Since both simplified radicals have index 2 and radicand \(5x\), they are like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(4\sqrt{18a}\) and \(3\sqrt{24a}\).
qs.a: No, because in simplest form their radicands are different (\(2a\) and \(6a\)).
d: Yes, because both simplify to radical expressions with index 2.
Yes, because both simplify to integer multiples of \(\sqrt{3a}\).
No, because their indices are different.
qs.s: Simplifying each gives \(4\sqrt{18a} = 4(3\sqrt{2a}) = 12\sqrt{2a}\) and \(3\sqrt{24a} = 3(2\sqrt{6a}) = 6\sqrt{6a}\). Because the simplified radicands are \(2a\) and \(6a\), they are not like radicals.

qs.q: Indicate whether the expressions are like radicals: \(5\sqrt[4]{32x}\) and \(-2\sqrt[4]{162x}\).
qs.a: Yes, because in simplest form both have index 4 and radicand \(2x\).
d: No, because the original radicands \(32x\) and \(162x\) are different.
No, because their simplified forms are \(10\sqrt[4]{2x}\) and \(-6\sqrt[4]{3x}\).
No, because their simplified coefficients are different (\(10\) and \(-6\)).
qs.s: Simplifying each gives \(5\sqrt[4]{32x} = 5(2\sqrt[4]{2x}) = 10\sqrt[4]{2x}\) and \(-2\sqrt[4]{162x} = -2(3\sqrt[4]{2x}) = -6\sqrt[4]{2x}\). Both simplified expressions have index 4 and radicand \(2x\), so they are like radicals.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(9\sqrt{5} - 4\sqrt{3} = 5\sqrt{2}\).
qs.a: Unlike radicals cannot be combined by subtracting their radicands; the expression cannot be simplified.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of subtracted.
The radicands should have been divided to give \(5\sqrt{\frac{5}{3}}\).
The subtraction is correct, but \(\sqrt{2}\) can be simplified further.
qs.s: The radicals \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) are unlike radicals and cannot be combined by subtracting radicands. The expression \(9\sqrt{5} - 4\sqrt{3}\) is already in simplest form.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(4\sqrt{7} + 3\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{14}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added; like radicals are combined by adding only the coefficients to get \(7\sqrt{7}\).
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added to get \(12\sqrt{7}\).
The radicands should have been multiplied instead of added to get \(7\sqrt{49}\).
Radicals with the same radicand cannot be added together.
qs.s: Terms with like radical factors are combined by adding their coefficients while keeping the common radical factor: \((4 + 3)\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{7}\). Radicands are not added.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(7\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} = 7\).
qs.a: The coefficient of \(\sqrt{3}\) is 1, so subtracting gives \((7 - 1)\sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{3}\), not 7.
d: The radical \(\sqrt{3}\) cannot be subtracted from \(7\sqrt{3}\) because they are unlike radicals.
Subtracting \(\sqrt{3}\) from \(\sqrt{3}\) leaves \(\sqrt{0}\), so the entire expression equals 0.
The coefficients should have been divided to give \(\frac{7}{1}\sqrt{3} = 7\sqrt{3}\).
qs.s: The radical term \(-\sqrt{3}\) has an implicit coefficient of \(-1\). Combining like radicals gives \((7 - 1)\sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{3}\) rather than cancelling out the radical completely.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(2\sqrt{5} + 6\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{8}\).
qs.a: Unlike radicals cannot be combined by adding their radicands; \(2\sqrt{5} + 6\sqrt{3}\) cannot be simplified.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added to get \(12\sqrt{8}\).
The radicands should have been multiplied instead of added to get \(8\sqrt{15}\).
The radical \(\sqrt{8}\) should have been simplified to \(2\sqrt{2}\), giving a final answer of \(10\sqrt{2}\).
qs.s: Terms with unlike radicals cannot be combined by adding their radicands (\(2\sqrt{5} + 6\sqrt{3} \neq 8\sqrt{5 + 3}\)). Since \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) are unlike radicals in simplest form, the expression cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(3 + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\).
qs.a: A constant term and a radical term are not like terms and cannot be combined.
d: The number 3 should have been multiplied by 5 to get \(15\sqrt{2}\).
The number 3 should have been placed under the radical to get \(\sqrt{50}\).
The coefficient 5 should have been subtracted from 3 to get \(-2\sqrt{2}\).
qs.s: The constant 3 has no radical factor, so 3 and \(5\sqrt{2}\) are not like terms, just as \(3 + 5x \neq 8x\). The expression \(3 + 5\sqrt{2}\) cannot be simplified further.

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification for \(x \geq 0\):
\(5x\sqrt{8} - 2\sqrt{18x^2} = 5x(2\sqrt{2}) - 2(3x\sqrt{2}) = 10x\sqrt{2} - 6x\sqrt{2} = 4x\).
qs.a: The radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\) was dropped; subtracting like terms gives \(4x\sqrt{2}\), not \(4x\).
d: In the first step, \(\sqrt{18x^2}\) should simplify to \(9x\sqrt{2}\).
The coefficients should have been multiplied to get \(-60x^2\sqrt{2}\).
Terms containing both variables and radicals cannot be combined.
qs.s: Subtracting like radical terms gives \((10x - 6x)\sqrt{2} = 4x\sqrt{2}\). The radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\) must be retained and cannot simply be dropped.

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(2\sqrt[3]{16} + 5\sqrt[3]{54} = 2(2\sqrt[3]{2}) + 5(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = 4\sqrt[3]{2} + 15\sqrt[3]{2} = 19\sqrt[3]{4}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added in the final step; like cube roots combine to \(19\sqrt[3]{2}\).
d: The cube root \(\sqrt[3]{16}\) was simplified incorrectly in the first step.
The coefficients 4 and 15 should have been multiplied to get \(60\sqrt[3]{2}\).
Cube roots with the same radicand cannot be combined by addition.
qs.s: When adding like radicals, only the coefficients are added while the common radical factor is kept: \((4 + 15)\sqrt[3]{2} = 19\sqrt[3]{2}\). The radicands should not be added.

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(\sqrt{72} - \sqrt{32} = \sqrt{72 - 32} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\).
qs.a: The radicands were subtracted directly; radicals must each be simplified first to get \(6\sqrt{2} - 4\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\).
d: The radical \(\sqrt{40}\) was simplified incorrectly; it should be \(4\sqrt{10}\).
The radicands should have been divided instead of subtracted to get \(\sqrt{\frac{72}{32}} = \frac{3}{2}\).
Radicals with different radicands can never be simplified or combined under any method.
qs.s: Radicals cannot be subtracted by subtracting their radicands (\(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b} \neq \sqrt{a - b}\)). Each radical must be simplified first: \(\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\), giving \(6\sqrt{2} - 4\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(\sqrt{18} + \sqrt{50} - \sqrt{12} = 3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{3} = 6\).
qs.a: The unlike radicals \(8\sqrt{2}\) and \(2\sqrt{3}\) cannot be combined; the expression should remain \(8\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{3}\).
d: In the first step, \(\sqrt{18}\) was simplified incorrectly; it should be \(2\sqrt{3}\).
The coefficients 8 and 2 should have been added instead of subtracted to get 10.
qs.s: While \(3\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\) is correct, \(8\sqrt{2}\) and \(2\sqrt{3}\) have different radicands and are unlike radicals. They cannot be combined further, so the final answer is \(8\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(3\sqrt{20} - 2\sqrt{45} = 3(4\sqrt{5}) - 2(9\sqrt{5}) = 12\sqrt{5} - 18\sqrt{5} = -6\sqrt{5}\).
qs.a: The perfect square factors 4 and 9 were factored out without taking their square roots.
d: The coefficients 3 and 2 should have been added instead of multiplied by the factors.
Like radicals cannot have a negative coefficient, so \(-6\sqrt{5}\) is undefined.
The terms \(12\sqrt{5}\) and \(-18\sqrt{5}\) are unlike radicals and cannot be combined.
qs.s: When simplifying \(\sqrt{20} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 5}\) and \(\sqrt{45} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 5}\), the square roots of 4 and 9 are 2 and 3, not 4 and 9. The correct simplification is \(3(2\sqrt{5}) - 2(3\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5} - 6\sqrt{5} = 0\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(5 + 3\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2}\).
qs.a: A constant term was added to the coefficient of a radical term.
d: The number 5 should have been multiplied by 3 to get \(15\sqrt{2}\).
The radical \(\sqrt{2}\) should have been squared before adding.
The constant 5 should have been rewritten as \(\sqrt{5}\) and added to get \(\sqrt{7}\).
qs.s: The terms 5 and \(3\sqrt{2}\) are not like terms because 5 does not have a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\), so they cannot be combined into \(8\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(8\sqrt{7} - 3\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{5}\).
qs.a: Unlike radicals cannot be combined by subtracting their radicands.
d: The coefficients should have been added to get \(11\sqrt{5}\).
The radicands should have been divided to get \(5\sqrt{3.5}\).
The radicals should have been converted to entire radicals first.
qs.s: The terms \(8\sqrt{7}\) and \(3\sqrt{2}\) have different radicands in simplest form, so they cannot be combined.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(7\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{5} = 7\).
qs.a: The coefficient of \(-\sqrt{5}\) was treated as 0 instead of 1.
d: The radicands should have been subtracted to get \(7\sqrt{0} = 0\).
The terms cannot be subtracted because both contain \(\sqrt{5}\).
The coefficients should have been multiplied to get \(-7\sqrt{5}\).
qs.s: The term \(-\sqrt{5}\) has an understood coefficient of \(-1\), so the correct subtraction is \((7 - 1)\sqrt{5} = 6\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(4\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} = 9\sqrt{6}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added instead of keeping the common radical factor.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added.
The expression cannot be simplified because 3 is a prime number.
The radical factor \(\sqrt{3}\) should have been squared.
qs.s: When adding like radicals, only the coefficients are added while the radicand is kept unchanged: \(4\sqrt{3} + 5\sqrt{3} = (4+5)\sqrt{3} = 9\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{18} = \sqrt{26}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added directly instead of simplifying each radical first.
d: The radicands should have been multiplied to get \(\sqrt{144} = 12\).
The square root symbols should have been cancelled before adding.
The expression cannot be simplified because 8 and 18 are not like radicals.
qs.s: Radicands cannot be added across radicals (\(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} \ne \sqrt{a+b}\)); each term must be simplified first as \(2\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(4\sqrt{18x} - 2\sqrt{50x}\) (where \(x \ge 0\)) as follows:
Step 1: \(4(3\sqrt{2x}) - 2(5\sqrt{2x})\)
Step 2: \(12\sqrt{2x} - 10\sqrt{2x}\)
Step 3: \(2\sqrt{0} = 0\)
What error did the student make in Step 3?
qs.a: The radicands were subtracted instead of keeping the common radical factor.
d: The coefficients 12 and 10 were subtracted incorrectly.
The terms cannot be combined because they contain the variable \(x\).
The radical \(\sqrt{2x}\) should have been squared.
qs.s: When subtracting like radicals, only the coefficients are subtracted while the common radical factor is kept: \((12 - 10)\sqrt{2x} = 2\sqrt{2x}\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(7x\sqrt{28y} - 2\sqrt{63x^2y}\) (where \(x, y \ge 0\)) as follows:
Step 1: \(7x(2\sqrt{7y}) - 2(3x\sqrt{7y})\)
Step 2: \(14x\sqrt{7y} - 6x\sqrt{7y}\)
Step 3: \(8x\)
What error did the student make in Step 3?
qs.a: The common radical factor \(\sqrt{7y}\) was omitted instead of retained.
d: The coefficients \(14x\) and \(6x\) should have been added to get \(20x\).
The expression cannot be simplified because \(x\) is inside one radical and outside the other.
The radicands should have been subtracted to get \(8x\sqrt{0} = 0\).
qs.s: Subtracting like radicals applies to the coefficients while the radical factor is preserved: \((14x - 6x)\sqrt{7y} = 8x\sqrt{7y}\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(\sqrt[3]{54} + \sqrt[3]{16}\) as follows:
Step 1: \(\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 2} + \sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 2}\)
Step 2: \(3\sqrt{2} + 2\sqrt{2}\)
Step 3: \(5\sqrt{2}\)
What error did the student make in Step 2?
qs.a: The radical index 3 was dropped, incorrectly replacing cube roots with square roots.
d: The coefficients 3 and 2 should have been multiplied instead of added.
The radicand 2 should have been squared when simplifying.
qs.s: The cube root index 3 must be retained when simplifying \(\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 2} + \sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 2}\), which gives \(3\sqrt[3]{2} + 2\sqrt[3]{2} = 5\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(5\sqrt{48} - 2\sqrt{75}\) as follows:
Step 1: \(5\sqrt{16 \cdot 3} - 2\sqrt{25 \cdot 3}\)
Step 2: \(4\sqrt{3} - 5\sqrt{3}\)
Step 3: \(-\sqrt{3}\)
What error did the student make in Step 2?
qs.a: The square roots of the factors were not multiplied by the original coefficients.
d: 16 and 25 are not the correct perfect square factors.
The radical factor \(\sqrt{3}\) should have been eliminated.
The coefficients 4 and \(-5\) should have been added instead of subtracted in Step 3.
qs.s: In Step 2, the extracted square roots (4 and 5) must be multiplied by the existing coefficients to give \(5(4)\sqrt{3} - 2(5)\sqrt{3} = 20\sqrt{3} - 10\sqrt{3} = 10\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
A student simplifies \(2\sqrt{12} + 3\sqrt{20} - \sqrt{27} + 2\sqrt{45}\) as follows:
Step 1: \(4\sqrt{3} + 6\sqrt{5} - 3\sqrt{3} + 6\sqrt{5}\)
Step 2: \(\sqrt{3} + 12\sqrt{5}\)
Step 3: \(13\sqrt{8}\)
What error did the student make in Step 3?
qs.a: Unlike radicals \(\sqrt{3}\) and \(12\sqrt{5}\) were combined by adding coefficients and radicands.
d: The coefficient of \(\sqrt{3}\) in Step 2 should have been 0.
The radicands 3 and 5 should have been multiplied to get \(13\sqrt{15}\).
The like terms in Step 1 were combined incorrectly to produce Step 2.
qs.s: The terms \(\sqrt{3}\) and \(12\sqrt{5}\) have unlike radicands that cannot be simplified further, so the expression cannot be simplified beyond \(\sqrt{3} + 12\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the solution \(\sqrt{27} - \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{24}\)?
qs.a: Radicands cannot be subtracted directly; \(\sqrt{27}\) must be simplified first.
d: The radical \(\sqrt{24}\) cannot be simplified any further.
Radicals with different radicands can never be combined under any circumstances.
The subtraction should have been changed to division to give \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).
qs.s: Radicands cannot be subtracted directly; simplifying \(\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3}\) first gives \(3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{3} = 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the solution \(9 + 4\sqrt{5} = 13\sqrt{5}\)?
qs.a: An integer and a radical term are unlike terms and cannot be combined.
d: The radical \(\sqrt{5}\) should have been simplified before adding.
The terms should have been multiplied to give \(36\sqrt{5}\).
The sum should be \(13\sqrt{10}\) because the radicands must be added.
qs.s: The integer \(9\) and the radical term \(4\sqrt{5}\) are unlike terms because \(9\) has no radical factor of \(\sqrt{5}\), so they cannot be combined into \(13\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the solution \(3\sqrt{6} + 5\sqrt{6} = 8\sqrt{12}\)?
qs.a: The radicands were added, but the radicand of like radicals must remain unchanged.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added to get \(15\sqrt{6}\).
The expression cannot be simplified because like radicals cannot be added.
The radical \(\sqrt{6}\) should have been eliminated, leaving only the coefficient \(8\).
qs.s: When adding like radicals, only the coefficients are added while the common radical factor remains the same: \(3\sqrt{6} + 5\sqrt{6} = (3 + 5)\sqrt{6} = 8\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the solution \(6\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 6\)?
qs.a: The term \(\sqrt{2}\) has an implied coefficient of \(1\), so the result is \(5\sqrt{2}\).
d: The term \(\sqrt{2}\) has a coefficient of \(0\), so the result should be \(0\).
Subtracting like radicals always cancels the entire expression to \(0\).
The two terms are unlike radicals and cannot be subtracted.
qs.s: The term \(\sqrt{2}\) has an implied coefficient of \(1\), so subtracting gives \((6 - 1)\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\), not \(6\).

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the solution \(\sqrt{7} + \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{10}\)?
qs.a: Radicands cannot be added together when adding radical expressions.
d: The sum should be \(\sqrt{21}\) because radicands must be multiplied when adding.
Radicals can only be added if both radicands are perfect squares.
The answer \(\sqrt{10}\) must be simplified to \(2\sqrt{5}\).
qs.s: Radicals can only be combined if they have identical radicands and indices; since \(\sqrt{7}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) are unlike radicals, their radicands cannot be added.

qs.q:
A student simplified the expression \(\sqrt{75} + \sqrt{32} - \sqrt{12} - \sqrt{18}\) as follows:
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \sqrt{75} + \sqrt{32} - \sqrt{12} - \sqrt{18} &= 5\sqrt{3} + 4\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{2} \\ &= 3\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2} \\ &= 4\sqrt{5} \end{aligned}\)
Which statement correctly explains the student's error?
qs.a: In the final step, unlike radicals \(3\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{2}\) were incorrectly combined by adding coefficients and radicands.
d: In the first step, \(\sqrt{75}\) was incorrectly simplified because \(75 = 3 \times 25\).
In the second step, \(4\sqrt{2} - 3\sqrt{2}\) should have simplified to \(1\), not \(\sqrt{2}\).
The negative signs should have been distributed to make all terms positive.
qs.s: The expression \(3\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2}\) is already in simplest form because \(\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{2}\) have different radicands, so they cannot be combined into \(4\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
A student attempted to simplify \(3\sqrt{50} - 2\sqrt{18}\) and wrote:
\(\displaystyle 3\sqrt{50} - 2\sqrt{18} = (3 + 5)\sqrt{2} - (2 + 3)\sqrt{2} = 8\sqrt{2} - 5\sqrt{2} = 3\sqrt{2}\)
Which statement correctly explains the student's error?
qs.a: The extracted factors were added to the outer coefficients instead of multiplied by them.
d: The terms \(8\sqrt{2}\) and \(5\sqrt{2}\) are unlike radicals and cannot be subtracted.
The final difference should have been \(3\) because \(\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 0\).
qs.s: When simplifying \(3\sqrt{50} = 3\sqrt{25 \cdot 2}\), the extracted factor \(5\) must be multiplied by the coefficient \(3\) to yield \(15\sqrt{2}\), not added to it.

qs.q: Which statement explains what is wrong with the simplification \(3\sqrt[3]{5} + 2\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt[3]{5}\)?
qs.a: Radicals with different indices are unlike radicals and cannot be combined, even with the same radicand.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied to give \(6\sqrt[3]{5}\).
The radicands should have been added to yield \(5\sqrt[3]{10}\).
The radical index of the sum should be the average of the two indices, giving \(5\sqrt[2.5]{5}\).
qs.s: Terms can only be combined if both their indices and their radicands are identical; since \(\sqrt[3]{5}\) has index \(3\) and \(\sqrt{5}\) has index \(2\), they are unlike terms and cannot be combined.

qs.q:
A student simplified \(\sqrt{20x^2y} - 2\sqrt{45y^3}\) (where \(x, y \ge 0\)) as follows:
\(\displaystyle \sqrt{20x^2y} - 2\sqrt{45y^3} = 2x\sqrt{5y} - 6y\sqrt{5y} = -4xy\sqrt{5y}\)
Which statement correctly explains the student's error?
qs.a: The variable terms \(2x\) and \(6y\) are unlike terms and cannot be subtracted to get \(-4xy\).
d: The terms \(2x\sqrt{5y}\) and \(6y\sqrt{5y}\) are unlike radicals because their coefficients differ.
The radicand \(20x^2y\) should have simplified to \(4x\sqrt{5y}\) instead of \(2x\sqrt{5y}\).
The radical factor \(\sqrt{5y}\) should have been squared because both terms contain it.
qs.s: The radicals simplify correctly to \((2x - 6y)\sqrt{5y}\), but the coefficients \(2x\) and \(6y\) are unlike algebraic terms and cannot be combined into \(-4xy\).

qs.q:
A student simplified \(5\sqrt{72} - 2\sqrt{98}\) as follows:
\(\displaystyle 5\sqrt{72} - 2\sqrt{98} = 30\sqrt{2} - 14\sqrt{2} = 16\)
Which statement correctly explains the student's error?
qs.a: The radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\) was omitted from the final answer instead of kept with the coefficient.
d: The radical \(\sqrt{72}\) was incorrectly simplified because \(72\) has no square factor.
The coefficients \(30\) and \(14\) should have been added instead of subtracted.
The correct radical factor should be \(\sqrt{0}\) because \(\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{0}\).
qs.s: Combining like radicals gives \((30 - 14)\sqrt{2} = 16\sqrt{2}\); the student correctly subtracted the coefficients but improperly dropped the radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains what is wrong with the solution: \(\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{8}\)?
qs.a: The radicands were added, but radicals with different radicands are unlike terms.
d: The radicands should have been multiplied to give \(\sqrt{15}\).
The sum should include a coefficient of 2, giving \(2\sqrt{8}\).
The square roots should have been subtracted instead of added, giving \(\sqrt{2}\).
qs.s: Radicals cannot be combined by adding their radicands; since \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) have different radicands, they are unlike terms and cannot be combined.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains what is wrong with the solution: \(2\sqrt{7} + 5\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{14}\)?
qs.a: The radicands were added together instead of keeping the common radical factor \(\sqrt{7}\).
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added to give \(10\sqrt{7}\).
The radical factor \(\sqrt{7}\) should have cancelled out, leaving just the integer 7.
The terms cannot be combined because they have different coefficients.
qs.s: When adding like radicals, only the coefficients are added while the radicand remains unchanged: \((2 + 5)\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains what is wrong with the solution: \(6\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{5} = 6\)?
qs.a: The term \(-\sqrt{5}\) has a coefficient of 1, so the result should be \((6 - 1)\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{5}\).
d: Subtracting like radicals always cancels everything to 0.
The radicands should have been subtracted to give \(6\sqrt{0} = 0\).
The term \(-\sqrt{5}\) has a coefficient of 0, so the result should be \(6\sqrt{5}\).
qs.s: The radical \(-\sqrt{5}\) represents \(-1\sqrt{5}\); subtracting the coefficients gives \((6 - 1)\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{5}\), not 6.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains what is wrong with the solution: \(8 + 3\sqrt{5} = 11\sqrt{5}\)?
qs.a: A constant term and a radical term were added, but they are not like terms.
d: The coefficient 3 should have been multiplied by 8 instead of added.
The radicand 5 should have been added to 8 to give \(\sqrt{13}\).
The radical \(\sqrt{5}\) should have been simplified before adding.
qs.s: The constant 8 and the radical term \(3\sqrt{5}\) are unlike terms and cannot be combined; the expression \(8 + 3\sqrt{5}\) is already in simplest form.

qs.q: Which statement correctly explains what is wrong with the solution: \(9 - 4\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\)?
qs.a: A constant term was subtracted from the coefficient of an unlike radical term.
d: The subtraction should produce a negative coefficient: \(-5\sqrt{2}\).
The radicand 2 should have been subtracted from 9 to get \(\sqrt{7}\).
The coefficient 4 should have been divided by 9 rather than subtracted.
qs.s: The constant 9 and the radical term \(-4\sqrt{2}\) are not like terms, so the coefficient 4 cannot be subtracted from 9.

qs.q:
Which statement correctly explains the error in the solution below?

\(\displaystyle 4\sqrt[3]{16} + 3\sqrt[3]{54} = 8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.a: The radicands were added together, but the common radical factor \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) should not change.
d: The cube roots were simplified incorrectly; \(\sqrt[3]{16}\) should be \(4\sqrt[3]{2}\).
The coefficients 8 and 9 should have been multiplied instead of added to give \(72\sqrt[3]{2}\).
The terms cannot be combined because cube roots cannot be added together.
qs.s: The simplification to \(8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2}\) is correct, but adding like radicals only combines the coefficients: \((8 + 9)\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Which statement correctly explains the error in the solution below?

\(\displaystyle \sqrt{50} + \sqrt{18} = \sqrt{68} = 2\sqrt{17}\)
qs.a: The radicands were added directly instead of simplifying each radical first to combine like terms.
d: The radicand 68 was incorrectly factored and should have simplified to \(4\sqrt{17}\).
The square roots should have been multiplied instead of added, giving \(\sqrt{900} = 30\).
Radicals with different radicands can never be simplified or combined in any way.
qs.s: Each radical should first be written in simplest form: \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\). Since they share the radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\), they combine to \(8\sqrt{2}\), not \(\sqrt{68}\).

qs.q:
A student simplified \(\sqrt{32} + \sqrt{27} - \sqrt{18} + \sqrt{12}\) as shown:

Step 1: \(4\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{2} + 2\sqrt{3}\)
Step 2: \(6\sqrt{5}\)

Which statement correctly explains the error in Step 2?
qs.a: Terms with different radical factors (\(\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\)) were incorrectly combined by adding their radicands.
d: The coefficients 4, 3, \(-3\), and 2 were added incorrectly and should total 8.
In Step 1, \(\sqrt{32}\) was simplified incorrectly and should equal \(2\sqrt{8}\).
The radical factors \(\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) should have been multiplied to give \(6\sqrt{6}\).
qs.s: Only terms with like radical factors can be combined: \((4 - 3)\sqrt{2} + (3 + 2)\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{3}\), which cannot be simplified any further.

qs.q:
Which statement correctly explains the error in the solution below?

\(\displaystyle 3\sqrt{24} - 2\sqrt{54} = 3(4\sqrt{6}) - 2(9\sqrt{6}) = 12\sqrt{6} - 18\sqrt{6} = -6\sqrt{6}\)
qs.a: The square factors 4 and 9 were factored out of the radicals without taking their square roots.
d: The coefficients 12 and 18 should have been added instead of subtracted, giving \(30\sqrt{6}\).
The radicals cannot be subtracted because they have different original radicands 24 and 54.
In the final step, the like radical \(\sqrt{6}\) should have been dropped, leaving only \(-6\).
qs.s: When simplifying \(\sqrt{24} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 6}\) and \(\sqrt{54} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 6}\), the square root of each square factor must be taken, giving \(3(2\sqrt{6}) - 2(3\sqrt{6}) = 6\sqrt{6} - 6\sqrt{6} = 0\).

qs.q:
A student simplified \(7 + 3\sqrt{20} - 2\sqrt{5}\) using the steps below:

Step 1: \(7 + 6\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{5}\)
Step 2: \(13\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{5}\)
Step 3: \(11\sqrt{5}\)

Which statement correctly explains the error in the student's work?
qs.a: In Step 2, the constant 7 was added to the radical term \(6\sqrt{5}\), but they are unlike terms.
d: In Step 1, \(3\sqrt{20}\) was simplified incorrectly and should equal \(12\sqrt{5}\).
In Step 3, the radical terms were subtracted incorrectly and should equal \(11\sqrt{0} = 0\).
In Step 1, the constant 7 should have been multiplied by \(\sqrt{20}\).
qs.s: In Step 1, \(3\sqrt{20} = 3(2\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5}\) is correct, but in Step 2, the constant 7 cannot be combined with \(6\sqrt{5}\); the correct simplified answer is \(7 + 4\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(4\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{9} = 21\).
qs.a: Terms with unlike radicals cannot be combined by adding coefficients and radicands.
d: The square root of 9 was evaluated incorrectly as 3.
The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added.
The radicals should have been simplified before adding.
qs.s: Because \(\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{7}\) are unlike radicals and cannot be simplified further, they cannot be combined into a single term.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(9\sqrt{6} - 4\sqrt{6} = 5\).
qs.a: The common radical factor \(\sqrt{6}\) was omitted from the final answer.
d: The coefficients were subtracted instead of added.
The radicands should have been subtracted to get \(\sqrt{0}\).
The terms cannot be combined because 6 is not a prime number.
qs.s: Subtracting the coefficients gives \((9 - 4)\sqrt{6} = 5\sqrt{6}\), so the radical factor \(\sqrt{6}\) must be retained.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{a + b}\).
qs.a: Radicals cannot be combined by adding their radicands.
d: Radicands must be multiplied when adding radicals.
Radicals can only be added if both \(a\) and \(b\) are integers.
The sum of two square roots must include a factor of 2.
qs.s: Square roots do not distribute over addition; in general, \(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} \neq \sqrt{a + b}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(3\sqrt{5} + 2\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{10}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added instead of keeping the common radical.
d: The coefficients were added instead of multiplied.
The radicands should have been multiplied to get \(\sqrt{25}\).
The terms cannot be combined because they have different coefficients.
qs.s: When adding like radicals, only the coefficients are added: \(3\sqrt{5} + 2\sqrt{5} = (3 + 2)\sqrt{5} = 5\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(4\sqrt[3]{16} + 3\sqrt[3]{54} = 4(2\sqrt[3]{2}) + 3(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = 8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[3]{4}\).
qs.a: The radicands were added together instead of keeping the common radical \(\sqrt[3]{2}\).
d: The cube roots of 16 and 54 were simplified incorrectly.
The coefficients 8 and 9 should have been multiplied instead of added.
The index of the radical should have changed from 3 to 6.
qs.s: When adding like cube roots, add only the coefficients and leave the radical factor unchanged: \(8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(2\sqrt{45} - 3\sqrt{20} = 2(9)\sqrt{5} - 3(4)\sqrt{5} = 18\sqrt{5} - 12\sqrt{5} = 6\sqrt{5}\).
qs.a: The perfect square factors were not square-rooted when removed from the radicals.
d: The factors 9 and 4 are not perfect squares.
The coefficients were multiplied instead of added to the removed factors.
The final terms were subtracted incorrectly.
qs.s: When removing perfect square factors from radicals, their square roots must be taken, giving \(2(3)\sqrt{5} - 3(2)\sqrt{5} = 6\sqrt{5} - 6\sqrt{5} = 0\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(\sqrt{75} - \sqrt{27} = \sqrt{75 - 27} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\).
qs.a: The radicands were subtracted under a single radical instead of simplifying each term first.
d: The terms cannot be simplified because 75 and 27 are not multiples of each other.
qs.s: Radicals cannot be combined by subtracting their radicands; simplifying each radical first gives \(5\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{3} = 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the final step of the solution: \(\sqrt{32x} + \sqrt{48y} - \sqrt{50x} + \sqrt{27y} = 4\sqrt{2x} + 4\sqrt{3y} - 5\sqrt{2x} + 3\sqrt{3y} = -\sqrt{2x} + 7\sqrt{3y} = 6\sqrt{5xy}\).
qs.a: Terms with unlike radicals cannot be combined into a single radical.
d: The coefficients \(-1\) and \(7\) were added incorrectly to get 6.
The radicals \(\sqrt{32x}\) and \(\sqrt{50x}\) were simplified incorrectly in the first step.
The radicands \(2x\) and \(3y\) should have been multiplied to get \(6xy\) instead of \(5xy\).
qs.s: Because \(-\sqrt{2x}\) and \(7\sqrt{3y}\) have different radicands, they are unlike radicals and cannot be combined; the expression \(-\sqrt{2x} + 7\sqrt{3y}\) is already in simplest form.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(4\sqrt{18} - 2\sqrt{50} = (4 + 3)\sqrt{2} - (2 + 5)\sqrt{2} = 7\sqrt{2} - 7\sqrt{2} = 0\).
qs.a: The extracted factors were added to the outer coefficients instead of multiplied by them.
d: The radicals \(\sqrt{18}\) and \(\sqrt{50}\) do not share the common radical factor \(\sqrt{2}\).
The square roots of the perfect square factors 9 and 25 were calculated incorrectly.
qs.s: The square roots of the factored squares must multiply the outer coefficients: \(4(3)\sqrt{2} - 2(5)\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2} - 10\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(5a\sqrt{b} - 2b\sqrt{a} = 3ab\sqrt{ab}\).
qs.a: The terms are unlike terms because their radicands and variable coefficients differ, so they cannot be combined.
d: The coefficients should be subtracted to give \(3(a - b)\sqrt{ab}\).
The radicands should be subtracted instead of multiplied, giving \(3ab\sqrt{b - a}\).
The result should have a coefficient of \(10ab\) because the coefficients must be multiplied.
qs.s: Because the radicals \(\sqrt{b}\) and \(\sqrt{a}\) are different and the coefficients \(5a\) and \(2b\) are unlike, the terms cannot be combined and the expression is already in simplest form.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(3\sqrt{5} + 4\sqrt{2} = 7\sqrt{7}\).
qs.a: Terms with unlike radicands cannot be combined by adding their radicands.
d: The coefficients 3 and 4 should be multiplied, giving \(12\sqrt{7}\).
The radicands should be multiplied while adding coefficients, giving \(7\sqrt{10}\).
The radical terms cancel out, leaving only the sum of the coefficients, 7.
qs.s: Radicals can only be combined if they have the same radicand and index; since \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{2}\) are unlike radicals, the expression cannot be simplified further.

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(8 + 3\sqrt{2} = 11\sqrt{2}\).
qs.a: A constant term cannot be combined with a radical term by adding coefficients.
d: The constant 8 should be multiplied by 3, giving \(24\sqrt{2}\).
The constant 8 should be added directly to the radicand, giving \(3\sqrt{10}\).
The square root of 2 must be evaluated as an integer before adding to 8.
qs.s: The number 8 is a rational constant without a radical factor, so it cannot be combined with the radical term \(3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(5\sqrt{3} + 4\sqrt{3} = 9\sqrt{6}\).
qs.a: When adding like radicals, the radicand does not change; only the coefficients are added.
d: The coefficients 5 and 4 should be multiplied instead of added, giving \(20\sqrt{6}\).
Like radical terms cannot be combined into a single term.
The radicands should be multiplied instead of added, giving \(9\sqrt{9} = 27\).
qs.s: Since both terms have the like radical factor \(\sqrt{3}\), only the coefficients are added: \((5 + 4)\sqrt{3} = 9\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Explain what is wrong with the solution: \(7x\sqrt{3} - 4x\sqrt{3} = 3\).
qs.a: The common radical and variable factor \(x\sqrt{3}\) was omitted after subtracting the coefficients.
d: The coefficients 7 and 4 should be divided instead of subtracted, giving \(\frac{7}{4}\).
The radicands should be subtracted, resulting in \(3x\sqrt{0} = 0\).
The variable \(x\) must be squared when subtracting like terms, giving \(3x^2\sqrt{3}\).
qs.s: Subtracting like terms gives \((7 - 4)x\sqrt{3} = 3x\sqrt{3}\), so the common factor \(x\sqrt{3}\) must remain in the result.

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the last step of the solution:
\(3x\sqrt{28y} - \sqrt{63x^2y} = 6x\sqrt{7y} - 3x\sqrt{7y} = 3\sqrt{7y}\)
qs.a: Subtracting \(6x - 3x\) equals \(3x\), but the variable factor \(x\) was omitted from the result.
d: The terms \(6x\sqrt{7y}\) and \(3x\sqrt{7y}\) cannot be subtracted because they are unlike terms.
The radical factor \(\sqrt{7y}\) should be squared during subtraction, leaving \(3xy\).
qs.s: Subtracting like terms gives \((6x - 3x)\sqrt{7y} = 3x\sqrt{7y}\), so the variable factor \(x\) must remain in the final coefficient.

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the final step of the solution:
\(4\sqrt[3]{16} + 3\sqrt[3]{54} = 8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[6]{4}\)
qs.a: When adding like radical terms, the index and radicand must remain unchanged as \(\sqrt[3]{2}\).
d: The coefficients 8 and 9 should have been multiplied instead of added, giving \(72\sqrt[3]{2}\).
The indices should have been multiplied instead of added, resulting in an index of 9.
Cube root terms cannot be combined into a single term even if they share the same radicand.
qs.s: Like radical terms are combined by adding only their coefficients: \(8\sqrt[3]{2} + 9\sqrt[3]{2} = (8 + 9)\sqrt[3]{2} = 17\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the last step of the solution:
\(\sqrt{32x} + \sqrt{48y} - \sqrt{50x} + \sqrt{27y} = 4\sqrt{2x} + 4\sqrt{3y} - 5\sqrt{2x} + 3\sqrt{3y} = 6\sqrt{5xy}\)
qs.a: Terms with unlike radicals \(\sqrt{2x}\) and \(\sqrt{3y}\) cannot be combined together.
d: The coefficients should have been multiplied instead of added, giving \(-240\sqrt{5xy}\).
The radicals \(\sqrt{32x}\) and \(\sqrt{50x}\) were simplified incorrectly in the first step.
The radicands should have been multiplied to produce \(\sqrt{6xy}\) instead of \(\sqrt{5xy}\).
qs.s: Only terms with like radicals can be combined: \((4 - 5)\sqrt{2x} + (4 + 3)\sqrt{3y} = -\sqrt{2x} + 7\sqrt{3y}\).

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(4\sqrt{18} - 3\sqrt{50} = 4(3\sqrt{2}) - 3(5\sqrt{2}) = 7\sqrt{2} - 8\sqrt{2} = -\sqrt{2}\)
qs.a: The coefficients outside the parentheses were added to the numbers inside instead of multiplied.
d: The radicals \(\sqrt{18}\) and \(\sqrt{50}\) do not simplify to terms containing \(\sqrt{2}\).
The like radical \(\sqrt{2}\) should have been eliminated during subtraction, leaving only \(-1\).
qs.s: The numbers extracted from the radicals must be multiplied by the existing coefficients, giving \(4(3\sqrt{2}) = 12\sqrt{2}\) and \(3(5\sqrt{2}) = 15\sqrt{2}\), which subtract to \(-3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Explain what is wrong with the following simplification:
\(3\sqrt{20} + 2\sqrt{45} = 3(4\sqrt{5}) + 2(9\sqrt{5}) = 12\sqrt{5} + 18\sqrt{5} = 30\sqrt{5}\)
qs.a: The square roots of the perfect square factors 4 and 9 were not taken when simplifying the radicals.
d: The terms \(12\sqrt{5}\) and \(18\sqrt{5}\) cannot be added because their coefficients are different.
The radicals \(\sqrt{20}\) and \(\sqrt{45}\) should have been added directly to get \(5\sqrt{65}\).
The coefficients 3 and 2 should have been added first before simplifying the radicals.
qs.s: When factoring \(\sqrt{20} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 5}\), \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), not 4, so \(3\sqrt{20} = 3(2\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5}\). Similarly, \(2\sqrt{45} = 2(3\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5}\), giving a correct sum of \(12\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 4\sqrt{45} - 2\sqrt{20} &= 4\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 5} - 2\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 5} \\ &= 4 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{5} - 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{5} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{5} - \underline{\quad}\sqrt{5} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{5} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out the perfect squares yields \(4\sqrt{9 \cdot 5} - 2\sqrt{4 \cdot 5} = 4(3)\sqrt{5} - 2(2)\sqrt{5} = 12\sqrt{5} - 4\sqrt{5}\). Subtracting the coefficients gives \(8\sqrt{5}\), so the missing number is 8.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{50} + 4\sqrt{18} &= 3\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} + 4\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} \\ &= 3 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} + 4 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring gives \(3\sqrt{25 \cdot 2} + 4\sqrt{9 \cdot 2} = 3(5)\sqrt{2} + 4(3)\sqrt{2} = 15\sqrt{2} + 12\sqrt{2}\). Combining the like terms gives \(27\sqrt{2}\), so the missing number is 27.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 5\sqrt{24} + 3\sqrt{54} &= 5\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 6} + 3\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 6} \\ &= 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{6} + 3 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{6} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{6} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt{6} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{6} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(5\sqrt{4 \cdot 6} + 3\sqrt{9 \cdot 6} = 5(2)\sqrt{6} + 3(3)\sqrt{6} = 10\sqrt{6} + 9\sqrt{6}\). Adding the coefficients results in \(19\sqrt{6}\), so the missing number is 19.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{28} + 5\sqrt{63} &= 3\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 7} + 5\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 7} \\ &= 3 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{7} + 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{7} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{7} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt{7} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{7} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out the largest perfect square gives \(3\sqrt{4 \cdot 7} + 5\sqrt{9 \cdot 7} = 3(2)\sqrt{7} + 5(3)\sqrt{7} = 6\sqrt{7} + 15\sqrt{7}\). Combining like radicals gives \(21\sqrt{7}\), so the missing number is 21.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{27} + 5\sqrt{48} &= 2\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 3} + 5\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 3} \\ &= 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{3} + 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{3} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{3} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt{3} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Simplifying each radical gives \(2\sqrt{9 \cdot 3} + 5\sqrt{16 \cdot 3} = 2(3)\sqrt{3} + 5(4)\sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{3} + 20\sqrt{3}\). Adding the terms yields \(26\sqrt{3}\), so the missing number is 26.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 5\sqrt{98} - 2\sqrt{162} &= 5\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} - 2\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} \\ &= 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} - 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} - \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out the perfect squares gives \(5\sqrt{49 \cdot 2} - 2\sqrt{81 \cdot 2} = 5(7)\sqrt{2} - 2(9)\sqrt{2} = 35\sqrt{2} - 18\sqrt{2}\). Subtracting the coefficients yields \(17\sqrt{2}\), so the missing number is 17.

qs.q:
Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 5\sqrt[3]{24} + 2\sqrt[3]{81} &= 5\sqrt[3]{\underline{\quad} \cdot 3} + 2\sqrt[3]{\underline{\quad} \cdot 3} \\ &= 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{3} + 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{3} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{3} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{3} \\ &= [?]\sqrt[3]{3} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out the largest perfect cubes gives \(5\sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 3} + 2\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 3} = 5(2)\sqrt[3]{3} + 2(3)\sqrt[3]{3} = 10\sqrt[3]{3} + 6\sqrt[3]{3}\). Adding the coefficients gives \(16\sqrt[3]{3}\), so the missing number is 16.

Complete the solution. What number belongs in the blank marked with [?] in the final step?
\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 4\sqrt{18} - 2\sqrt{50} + 3\sqrt{32} &= 4\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} - 2\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} + 3\sqrt{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} \\ &= 4 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} - 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} + 3 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} - \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} + \underline{\quad}\sqrt{2} \\ &= [?]\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out perfect squares gives \(4(3)\sqrt{2} - 2(5)\sqrt{2} + 3(4)\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2} - 10\sqrt{2} + 12\sqrt{2}\). Combining the like terms gives \((12 - 10 + 12)\sqrt{2} = 14\sqrt{2}\), so the missing number is 14.

\(\displaystyle \begin{aligned} 5\sqrt[3]{54} - 2\sqrt[3]{128} &= 5\sqrt[3]{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} - 2\sqrt[3]{\underline{\quad} \cdot 2} \\ &= 5 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{2} - 2 \cdot \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{2} \\ &= \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{2} - \underline{\quad}\sqrt[3]{2} \\ &= [?]\sqrt[3]{2} \end{aligned}\)
qs.s: Factoring out the perfect cubes gives \(5\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 2} - 2\sqrt[3]{64 \cdot 2} = 5(3)\sqrt[3]{2} - 2(4)\sqrt[3]{2} = 15\sqrt[3]{2} - 8\sqrt[3]{2}\). Subtracting the coefficients gives \(7\sqrt[3]{2}\), so the missing number is 7.

qs.q: Simplify: \(9\sqrt{6} - 5\sqrt{6}\)
qs.s: Combine like terms by subtracting their coefficients: \((9 - 5)\sqrt{6} = 4\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{7} + 8\sqrt{7}\)
qs.s: Combine like terms by adding their coefficients: \((2 + 8)\sqrt{7} = 10\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\sqrt{45} + \sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(\sqrt{9 \cdot 5} + \sqrt{4 \cdot 5} = 3\sqrt{5} + 2\sqrt{5}\), then combine like terms to get \(5\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\sqrt{72} - \sqrt{32} + \sqrt{18}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(6\sqrt{2} - 4\sqrt{2} + 3\sqrt{2}\), then combine like terms: \((6 - 4 + 3)\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{12} - 2\sqrt{27}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(4(2\sqrt{3}) - 2(3\sqrt{3}) = 8\sqrt{3} - 6\sqrt{3}\), then subtract coefficients to get \(2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\sqrt[3]{40} + 2\sqrt[3]{135}\)
qs.s: Factor out perfect cubes to get \(\sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 5} + 2\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 5} = 2\sqrt[3]{5} + 6\sqrt[3]{5}\), then add like terms to get \(8\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\sqrt{28} + \sqrt{48} - \sqrt{63} + \sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to \(2\sqrt{7} + 4\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{7} + 5\sqrt{3}\), then combine like radical terms to get \(9\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{6} - 8\sqrt{6}\)
qs.s: Combine the like radical terms: \((2 - 8)\sqrt{6} = -6\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{5} - 11\sqrt{5}\)
qs.s: Subtract the coefficients of the like radicals: \((4 - 11)\sqrt{5} = -7\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(7\sqrt{11} - 12\sqrt{11}\)
qs.s: Subtract the coefficients: \((7 - 12)\sqrt{11} = -5\sqrt{11}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(6\sqrt{2} - 15\sqrt{2}\)
qs.s: Combine like terms by subtracting their coefficients: \((6 - 15)\sqrt{2} = -9\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt{7} - 10\sqrt{7}\)
qs.s: Subtract the coefficients of the like radicals: \((3 - 10)\sqrt{7} = -7\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{48} - \frac{4}{5}\sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radicals to get \(\frac{1}{2}(4\sqrt{3}) = 2\sqrt{3}\) and \(\frac{4}{5}(5\sqrt{3}) = 4\sqrt{3}\). Subtracting gives \((2 - 4)\sqrt{3} = -2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{50} - \sqrt{18} - 3\sqrt{32}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical: \(2\sqrt{50} = 10\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\), and \(3\sqrt{32} = 12\sqrt{2}\). Combining like terms yields \((10 - 3 - 12)\sqrt{2} = -5\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\sqrt{45} - 3\sqrt{20} + \sqrt{18}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical: \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\), \(3\sqrt{20} = 6\sqrt{5}\), and \(\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\). Combining the like terms gives \((3 - 6)\sqrt{5} + 3\sqrt{2} = -3\sqrt{5} + 3\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(5\sqrt[3]{24} - 4\sqrt[3]{81}\)
qs.s: Factor out perfect cubes: \(5\sqrt[3]{24} = 5(2\sqrt[3]{3}) = 10\sqrt[3]{3}\) and \(4\sqrt[3]{81} = 4(3\sqrt[3]{3}) = 12\sqrt[3]{3}\). Subtracting yields \((10 - 12)\sqrt[3]{3} = -2\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{45} - 4\sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Factor out perfect squares: \(2\sqrt{45} = 2(3\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5}\) and \(4\sqrt{20} = 4(2\sqrt{5}) = 8\sqrt{5}\). Subtracting gives \((6 - 8)\sqrt{5} = -2\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(3\sqrt{7} + 4\sqrt{28}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\sqrt{28}\) as \(2\sqrt{7}\), which gives \(3\sqrt{7} + 4(2\sqrt{7}) = 3\sqrt{7} + 8\sqrt{7}\). Combining the like terms gives \(11\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(5\sqrt{27} + 2\sqrt{3}\)
qs.s: Factor out the perfect square from \(\sqrt{27}\) to get \(5(3\sqrt{3}) + 2\sqrt{3} = 15\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(17\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(4\sqrt{45} + 7\sqrt{5}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\sqrt{45}\) as \(3\sqrt{5}\), giving \(4(3\sqrt{5}) + 7\sqrt{5} = 12\sqrt{5} + 7\sqrt{5}\). Combine the like terms to get \(19\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(6\sqrt{50} - 7\sqrt{2}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\sqrt{50}\) to \(5\sqrt{2}\), giving \(6(5\sqrt{2}) - 7\sqrt{2} = 30\sqrt{2} - 7\sqrt{2}\). Subtracting the coefficients yields \(23\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(8\sqrt{12} - 9\sqrt{3}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\sqrt{12}\) as \(2\sqrt{3}\) to obtain \(8(2\sqrt{3}) - 9\sqrt{3} = 16\sqrt{3} - 9\sqrt{3}\). Subtracting like terms yields \(7\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{72} - \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{162} + \sqrt{200}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to find like terms with \(\sqrt{2}\): \(\frac{5}{2}(6\sqrt{2}) - \frac{2}{3}(9\sqrt{2}) + 10\sqrt{2} = 15\sqrt{2} - 6\sqrt{2} + 10\sqrt{2}\). Combining coefficients gives \(19\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(3\sqrt{192} - 2\sqrt{243} + \sqrt{300}\)
qs.s: Factor the largest perfect square out of each radicand: \(3(8\sqrt{3}) - 2(9\sqrt{3}) + 10\sqrt{3} = 24\sqrt{3} - 18\sqrt{3} + 10\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(16\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(2\sqrt{72} - 3\sqrt{80} - \sqrt{50} + 2\sqrt{45}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical term to get \(12\sqrt{2} - 12\sqrt{5} - 5\sqrt{2} + 6\sqrt{5}\). Grouping and combining like radical terms yields \(7\sqrt{2} - 6\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(4\sqrt{75} - 2\sqrt{48} + 3\sqrt{108}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical by factoring out perfect squares: \(4(5\sqrt{3}) - 2(4\sqrt{3}) + 3(6\sqrt{3}) = 20\sqrt{3} - 8\sqrt{3} + 18\sqrt{3}\). Combining the coefficients yields \(30\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify the expression: \(5\sqrt[3]{54} + 2\sqrt[3]{128} - \sqrt[3]{250}\)
qs.s: Factor out perfect cubes from each radical: \(5(3\sqrt[3]{2}) + 2(4\sqrt[3]{2}) - 5\sqrt[3]{2} = 15\sqrt[3]{2} + 8\sqrt[3]{2} - 5\sqrt[3]{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(18\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt{75} - 5\sqrt{3}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(3\sqrt{75} = 3(5\sqrt{3}) = 15\sqrt{3}\). Then subtract like terms: \(15\sqrt{3} - 5\sqrt{3} = 10\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{32} + 5\sqrt{2}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(4\sqrt{32} = 4(4\sqrt{2}) = 16\sqrt{2}\). Then combine like terms: \(16\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2} = 21\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(5\sqrt{18} - 2\sqrt{2}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(5\sqrt{18} = 5(3\sqrt{2}) = 15\sqrt{2}\). Then subtract like terms: \(15\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{2} = 13\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(6\sqrt{20} + 3\sqrt{5}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(6\sqrt{20} = 6(2\sqrt{5}) = 12\sqrt{5}\). Then combine like terms: \(12\sqrt{5} + 3\sqrt{5} = 15\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(8\sqrt{2} - 3\sqrt{50}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(3\sqrt{50} = 3(5\sqrt{2}) = 15\sqrt{2}\). Then subtract like terms: \(8\sqrt{2} - 15\sqrt{2} = -7\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{27} - 3\sqrt{20} + 4\sqrt{12} + \sqrt{45}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(6\sqrt{3} - 6\sqrt{5} + 8\sqrt{3} + 3\sqrt{5}\). Combining like radicals gives \((6+8)\sqrt{3} + (-6+3)\sqrt{5} = 14\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt{72} - 2\sqrt{98} + \sqrt{50}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(3(6\sqrt{2}) - 2(7\sqrt{2}) + 5\sqrt{2} = 18\sqrt{2} - 14\sqrt{2} + 5\sqrt{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(9\sqrt{2}\).
Simplify each cube root to get \(4(3\sqrt[3]{2}) - 5\sqrt[3]{2} + 2(2\sqrt[3]{2}) = 12\sqrt[3]{2} - 5\sqrt[3]{2} + 4\sqrt[3]{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(11\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{45} - \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{20} + \sqrt{80}\)
qs.s: Simplify each term to get \(\frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt{5}) - \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{5}) + 4\sqrt{5} = 2\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{5} + 4\sqrt{5}\). Combining like terms gives \(5\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(5\sqrt{108} - 2\sqrt{147} - 3\sqrt{48}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(5(6\sqrt{3}) - 2(7\sqrt{3}) - 3(4\sqrt{3}) = 30\sqrt{3} - 14\sqrt{3} - 12\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt[3]{24} + 2\sqrt[3]{81}\)
qs.s: Factor each radicand using perfect cubes: \(4\sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 3} + 2\sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 3} = 4(2\sqrt[3]{3}) + 2(3\sqrt[3]{3}) = 8\sqrt[3]{3} + 6\sqrt[3]{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(14\sqrt[3]{3}\).
Simplify each radical: \(\frac{3}{4}(4\sqrt[3]{2}) - \frac{2}{5}(5\sqrt[3]{2}) + \frac{5}{3}(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = 3\sqrt[3]{2} - 2\sqrt[3]{2} + 5\sqrt[3]{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(6\sqrt[3]{2}\).
Extract negative perfect cubes: \(4(-3\sqrt[3]{2}) + 2(5\sqrt[3]{2}) + (-4\sqrt[3]{2}) = -12\sqrt[3]{2} + 10\sqrt[3]{2} - 4\sqrt[3]{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(-6\sqrt[3]{2}\).

Simplify each term by factoring out perfect cubes: \(3(5\sqrt[3]{4}) - 2(3\sqrt[3]{4}) - 4(2\sqrt[3]{4}) = 15\sqrt[3]{4} - 6\sqrt[3]{4} - 8\sqrt[3]{4}\). Combining the coefficients gives \((15 - 6 - 8)\sqrt[3]{4} = \sqrt[3]{4}\).

Factor perfect cubes from each radical: \(3(5\sqrt[3]{3}) - 2(4\sqrt[3]{3}) + 4(2\sqrt[3]{3}) - 3\sqrt[3]{3} = 15\sqrt[3]{3} - 8\sqrt[3]{3} + 8\sqrt[3]{3} - 3\sqrt[3]{3}\). Combining the coefficients gives \(12\sqrt[3]{3}\).
Factor out the fourth powers to get \(6(3\sqrt[4]{2}) - 7(2\sqrt[4]{2}) = 18\sqrt[4]{2} - 14\sqrt[4]{2} = 4\sqrt[4]{2}\).
Factor out the fourth powers to get \(4(3\sqrt[4]{7}) - 3(2\sqrt[4]{7}) = 12\sqrt[4]{7} - 6\sqrt[4]{7} = 6\sqrt[4]{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt[4]{80} - \sqrt[4]{405}\)
qs.s: Factor out the fourth powers to get \(3(2\sqrt[4]{5}) - 3\sqrt[4]{5} = 6\sqrt[4]{5} - 3\sqrt[4]{5} = 3\sqrt[4]{5}\).
Factor out the fourth powers to get \(2(2\sqrt[4]{6}) + 5(3\sqrt[4]{6}) = 4\sqrt[4]{6} + 15\sqrt[4]{6} = 19\sqrt[4]{6}\).
Factor out the fourth powers to get \(4(2\sqrt[4]{2}) + 3(3\sqrt[4]{2}) = 8\sqrt[4]{2} + 9\sqrt[4]{2} = 17\sqrt[4]{2}\).
Factor out the perfect fourth powers: \(3(2\sqrt[4]{2}) - 2(4\sqrt[4]{2}) + 5(3\sqrt[4]{2}) = 6\sqrt[4]{2} - 8\sqrt[4]{2} + 15\sqrt[4]{2} = 13\sqrt[4]{2}\).
Simplify each radical to \(4\sqrt[4]{3} + 6\sqrt[4]{5} - 3\sqrt[4]{3} + 3\sqrt[4]{5}\), then combine like terms to get \(\sqrt[4]{3} + 9\sqrt[4]{5}\).
Simplify each radical to get \(3(5\sqrt[4]{2}) - 2(4\sqrt[4]{2}) - 2(2\sqrt[4]{2}) = 15\sqrt[4]{2} - 8\sqrt[4]{2} - 4\sqrt[4]{2} = 3\sqrt[4]{2}\).
Simplify each radical to get \(\frac{5}{2}(2\sqrt[4]{3}) + \frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt[4]{3}) - 4\sqrt[4]{3} = 5\sqrt[4]{3} + 2\sqrt[4]{3} - 4\sqrt[4]{3} = 3\sqrt[4]{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(8\sqrt{12} - 3\sqrt{27}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(8(2\sqrt{3}) - 3(3\sqrt{3}) = 16\sqrt{3} - 9\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(7\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(5\sqrt{48} - 3\sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(5(4\sqrt{3}) - 3(5\sqrt{3}) = 20\sqrt{3} - 15\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms gives \(5\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{72} + 5\sqrt{32}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(2(6\sqrt{2}) + 5(4\sqrt{2}) = 12\sqrt{2} + 20\sqrt{2}\). Adding gives \(32\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{45} + 3\sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(4(3\sqrt{5}) + 3(2\sqrt{5}) = 12\sqrt{5} + 6\sqrt{5}\). Combining like terms gives \(18\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(6\sqrt{50} - 4\sqrt{18}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(6(5\sqrt{2}) - 4(3\sqrt{2}) = 30\sqrt{2} - 12\sqrt{2}\). Subtracting yields \(18\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{32} - \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{72} + \frac{3}{5}\sqrt{200}\)
qs.s: Simplify each term: \(\frac{3}{4}(4\sqrt{2}) - \frac{2}{3}(6\sqrt{2}) + \frac{3}{5}(10\sqrt{2}) = 3\sqrt{2} - 4\sqrt{2} + 6\sqrt{2}\). Combining gives \(5\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{150} - 3\sqrt{24} + \sqrt{96} - 2\sqrt{54}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical: \(2(5\sqrt{6}) - 3(2\sqrt{6}) + 4\sqrt{6} - 2(3\sqrt{6}) = 10\sqrt{6} - 6\sqrt{6} + 4\sqrt{6} - 6\sqrt{6}\). Combining like terms gives \(2\sqrt{6}\).
Simplify each cube root: \(5(3\sqrt[3]{2}) - 2(4\sqrt[3]{2}) + 5\sqrt[3]{2} = 15\sqrt[3]{2} - 8\sqrt[3]{2} + 5\sqrt[3]{2}\). Combining like terms gives \(12\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{28} + 3\sqrt{45} - \sqrt{63} - 2\sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical: \(2(2\sqrt{7}) + 3(3\sqrt{5}) - 3\sqrt{7} - 2(2\sqrt{5}) = 4\sqrt{7} + 9\sqrt{5} - 3\sqrt{7} - 4\sqrt{5}\). Grouping like terms yields \(\sqrt{7} + 5\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{48} - 2\sqrt{75} + 3\sqrt{108}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical: \(4(4\sqrt{3}) - 2(5\sqrt{3}) + 3(6\sqrt{3}) = 16\sqrt{3} - 10\sqrt{3} + 18\sqrt{3}\). Combining like terms yields \(24\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(4\sqrt{28} - 5\sqrt{63}\)
qs.s: Factor the perfect squares to get \(4(2\sqrt{7}) - 5(3\sqrt{7}) = 8\sqrt{7} - 15\sqrt{7}\). Combining like terms gives \(-7\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(5\sqrt{24} - 2\sqrt{54}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(5(2\sqrt{6}) - 2(3\sqrt{6}) = 10\sqrt{6} - 6\sqrt{6}\). Combining like terms gives \(4\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt{20} - 4\sqrt{45}\)
qs.s: Express in simplest radical form as \(3(2\sqrt{5}) - 4(3\sqrt{5}) = 6\sqrt{5} - 12\sqrt{5}\). Subtracting gives \(-6\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(7\sqrt{18} - 3\sqrt{50}\)
qs.s: Factor out perfect squares to obtain \(7(3\sqrt{2}) - 3(5\sqrt{2}) = 21\sqrt{2} - 15\sqrt{2}\). Subtracting yields \(6\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(2\sqrt{75} - 6\sqrt{12}\)
qs.s: Simplify each term to get \(2(5\sqrt{3}) - 6(2\sqrt{3}) = 10\sqrt{3} - 12\sqrt{3}\). Subtracting yields \(-2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Simplify: \(3\sqrt{108} - 2\sqrt{48} - 4\sqrt{27}\)
