qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 42^\circ\), \(\angle B = 53^\circ\), and \(a = 11.2\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(c\). Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, find \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 42^\circ - 53^\circ = 85^\circ\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(c = \frac{11.2 \sin 85^\circ}{\sin 42^\circ} \approx 16.7\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(a = 7.0\), and \(b = 9.0\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(c\)? Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using \(\sin B = \frac{9.0 \sin 35^\circ}{7.0} \approx 0.7375\), the angles are \(B_1 \approx 47.5^\circ\) and \(B_2 \approx 132.5^\circ\). The corresponding third sides are \(c_1 = \frac{7.0 \sin 97.5^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} \approx 12.1\) and \(c_2 = \frac{7.0 \sin 12.5^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} \approx 2.6\), so the difference is \(12.1 - 2.6 = 9.5\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 32^\circ\), \(a = 145\), and \(b = 210\). Two triangles exist. Find the measure of \(\angle C\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{210 \sin 32^\circ}{145} \approx 0.7675\), which gives the obtuse angle \(B = 180^\circ - 50.1^\circ = 129.9^\circ\). Thus, \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 129.9^\circ = 18.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 112^\circ\), \(b = 48.0\), and \(c = 26.0\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(a\). Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, \(\sin C = \frac{26.0 \sin 112^\circ}{48.0} \approx 0.5022\), so \(\angle C \approx 30.1^\circ\). Then \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 112^\circ - 30.1^\circ = 37.9^\circ\), and \(a = \frac{48.0 \sin 37.9^\circ}{\sin 112^\circ} \approx 31.8\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8.0\), and \(b = 12.0\). Two distinct triangles exist. Find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, \(\sin B = \frac{12.0 \sin 30^\circ}{8.0} = 0.75\), so the obtuse angle is \(B = 180^\circ - 48.6^\circ = 131.4^\circ\). Then \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 131.4^\circ = 18.6^\circ\), giving \(c = \frac{8.0 \sin 18.6^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 5.1\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 40^\circ\), \(a = 15.0\), and \(b = 20.0\). If \(\angle B\) is acute, find the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\). Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using \(\sin B = \frac{20.0 \sin 40^\circ}{15.0} \approx 0.8571\), the acute angle is \(B \approx 59.0^\circ\), giving \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 59.0^\circ = 81.0^\circ\). Then \(c = \frac{15.0 \sin 81.0^\circ}{\sin 40^\circ} \approx 23.0\), so the perimeter is \(15.0 + 20.0 + 23.0 = 58.0\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 140^\circ\), \(\angle C = 16^\circ\), and \(b = 75\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(c\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{c}{\sin 16^\circ} = \frac{75}{\sin 140^\circ}\). Solving gives \(c = \frac{75 \sin 16^\circ}{\sin 140^\circ} \approx 32.2\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 135^\circ\), \(\angle C = 15^\circ\), and \(a = 48\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(c\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{c}{\sin 15^\circ} = \frac{48}{\sin 135^\circ}\). Solving gives \(c = \frac{48 \sin 15^\circ}{\sin 135^\circ} \approx 17.6\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 20^\circ\), \(\angle B = 125^\circ\), and \(b = 50\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(a\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{a}{\sin 20^\circ} = \frac{50}{\sin 125^\circ}\). Solving gives \(a = \frac{50 \sin 20^\circ}{\sin 125^\circ} \approx 20.9\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 25^\circ\), \(\angle C = 110^\circ\), and \(c = 32\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(a\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, find \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 25^\circ - 110^\circ = 45^\circ\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(a = \frac{32 \sin 45^\circ}{\sin 110^\circ} \approx 24.1\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 32^\circ\), \(\angle B = 118^\circ\), and \(b = 64\). Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(c\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, find \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 118^\circ = 30^\circ\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(c = \frac{64 \sin 30^\circ}{\sin 118^\circ} \approx 36.2\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(\angle B = 115^\circ\), and \(c = 50\). Solve the triangle completely using the Law of Sines to find the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\). Round your answer to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 115^\circ = 30^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(a = \frac{50 \sin 35^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 57.36\) and \(b = \frac{50 \sin 115^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 90.63\), giving a perimeter of \(50 + 57.36 + 90.63 \approx 198.0\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(a = 12\), and \(b = 16\). Use the Law of Sines to find all possible measures of \(\angle B\). Round each value to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using \(\sin B = \frac{16 \sin 35^\circ}{12} \approx 0.7648\), the acute angle is \(\angle B \approx 49.9^\circ\). Because \(35^\circ + (180^\circ - 49.9^\circ) < 180^\circ\), the obtuse angle \(130.1^\circ\) is also valid, so \(\angle B = 49.9^\circ\) or \(130.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 22^\circ\), \(\angle B = 132^\circ\), and \(b = 180\). Solve the triangle using the Law of Sines to find the difference between the length of the longest side and the length of the shortest side. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 22^\circ - 132^\circ = 26^\circ\), so the longest side is \(b = 180\) and the shortest side is \(a = \frac{180 \sin 22^\circ}{\sin 132^\circ} \approx 90.7\). The difference is \(180 - 90.7 = 89.3\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 12\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Use the Law of Sines to find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: From \(\sin B = \frac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{8} = 0.75\), the obtuse angle is \(\angle B = 180^\circ - \arcsin(0.75) \approx 131.4^\circ\), which makes \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 131.4^\circ = 18.6^\circ\). Then \(c = \frac{8 \sin 18.6^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 5.1\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 10\), and \(b = 14\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Use the Law of Sines to find the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(c\). Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: From \(\sin B = \frac{14 \sin 30^\circ}{10} = 0.7\), the two values for \(\angle B\) are \(44.4^\circ\) and \(135.6^\circ\), giving \(\angle C = 105.6^\circ\) and \(14.4^\circ\). The two side lengths are \(c_1 = \frac{10 \sin 105.6^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 19.3\) and \(c_2 = \frac{10 \sin 14.4^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 5.0\), with a difference of \(19.3 - 5.0 = 14.3\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8.0\), and \(b = 12.0\). Find the larger possible measure of \(\angle B\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{12.0 \sin 30^\circ}{8.0} = 0.75\), giving an acute angle of \(\arcsin(0.75) \approx 48.6^\circ\). The larger possible obtuse measure is \(180^\circ - 48.6^\circ = 131.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 42^\circ\), \(b = 9.2\), and \(a = 12.5\). Find the larger possible measure of \(\angle A\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{12.5 \sin 42^\circ}{9.2} \approx 0.9091\), giving an acute angle of \(\arcsin(0.9091) \approx 65.4^\circ\). The larger possible measure is \(180^\circ - 65.4^\circ = 114.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 25^\circ\), \(a = 5.6\), and \(c = 9.8\). Find the smaller possible measure of \(\angle C\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{9.8 \sin 25^\circ}{5.6} \approx 0.7396\). The smaller possible angle is \(\arcsin(0.7396) \approx 47.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle C = 35^\circ\), \(c = 7.5\), and \(b = 11.0\). Find the smaller possible measure of \(\angle B\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{11.0 \sin 35^\circ}{7.5} \approx 0.8412\). The smaller possible measure is the acute angle \(\arcsin(0.8412) \approx 57.3^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 48^\circ\), \(b = 10.4\), and \(c = 13.0\). Find the larger possible measure of \(\angle C\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{13.0 \sin 48^\circ}{10.4} \approx 0.9289\), giving the acute angle \(\arcsin(0.9289) \approx 68.3^\circ\). The larger possible measure is \(180^\circ - 68.3^\circ = 111.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 32^\circ\), \(a = 9.0\), and \(b = 14.0\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse, rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: First, \(\sin B = \frac{14.0 \sin 32^\circ}{9.0} \approx 0.8243\), so the obtuse angle is \(B \approx 180^\circ - 55.5^\circ = 124.5^\circ\), making \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 124.5^\circ = 23.5^\circ\). Then \(c = \frac{9.0 \sin 23.5^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 6.8\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 34^\circ\), \(a = 8.5\), and \(b = 12.0\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the area of the triangle in which \(\angle B\) is obtuse, rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: The Law of Sines gives the obtuse angle \(B \approx 180^\circ - 52.1^\circ = 127.9^\circ\), which means \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 34^\circ - 127.9^\circ = 18.1^\circ\). The area is \(\frac{1}{2}ab \sin C = \frac{1}{2}(8.5)(12.0)\sin(18.1^\circ) \approx 15.9\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8.0\), and \(b = 11.0\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(c\), rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(B_1 \approx 43.4^\circ\) and \(B_2 \approx 136.6^\circ\), leading to \(C_1 \approx 106.6^\circ\) (\(c_1 \approx 15.3\)) and \(C_2 \approx 13.4^\circ\) (\(c_2 \approx 3.7\)). The difference between the two side lengths is \(15.3 - 3.7 = 11.6\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 36^\circ\), \(a = 9.5\), and \(b = 13.0\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the perimeter of the triangle in which \(\angle B\) is obtuse, rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Solving for the obtuse angle gives \(B \approx 180^\circ - 53.5^\circ = 126.5^\circ\), so \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 36^\circ - 126.5^\circ = 17.5^\circ\). Then side \(c = \frac{9.5 \sin 17.5^\circ}{\sin 36^\circ} \approx 4.9\), yielding a perimeter of \(9.5 + 13.0 + 4.9 = 27.4\).

qs.q: Two ranger stations, \(A\) and \(B\), are 15.0 km apart. From station \(A\), smoke is sighted at point \(C\) such that \(\angle BAC = 38^\circ\). The distance from station \(B\) to the smoke is 10.0 km. Since two locations for the smoke are possible, find the shorter possible distance from station \(A\) to the smoke, rounded to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{15.0 \sin 38^\circ}{10.0} \approx 0.9235\), so \(C \approx 112.6^\circ\) for the obtuse case. Then \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 38^\circ - 112.6^\circ = 29.4^\circ\), giving \(b = \frac{10.0 \sin 29.4^\circ}{\sin 38^\circ} \approx 8.0\) km.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle A = 115^\circ\), \(a = 11\), and \(b = 14\), find the measure of \(\angle B\).
qs.s: Because \(\angle A\) is obtuse, the opposite side \(a\) must be longer than adjacent side \(b\); since \(a = 11 \le 14\), \(\sin B = \frac{14 \sin 115^\circ}{11} \approx 1.15 > 1\), meaning no triangle exists.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 12\), find the acute measure of \(\angle B\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{8} = 0.75\). Taking the inverse sine gives the acute angle \(\angle B = \arcsin(0.75) \approx 48.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(a = 3\), and \(b = 7\), find the measure of \(\angle B\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 35^\circ}{3} \approx 1.34\). Since the sine of an angle cannot exceed 1, no triangle exists.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle B = 40^\circ\), \(b = 7\), and \(c = 9\), find the obtuse measure of \(\angle C\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{9 \sin 40^\circ}{7} \approx 0.8264\), which gives an acute angle of \(55.7^\circ\). The obtuse solution is \(180^\circ - 55.7^\circ = 124.3^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle C = 42^\circ\), \(c = 12\), and \(a = 10\), find the measure of \(\angle A\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{10 \sin 42^\circ}{12} \approx 0.5576\), yielding \(\angle A \approx 33.9^\circ\) (an obtuse angle of \(146.1^\circ\) is impossible because \(146.1^\circ + 42^\circ > 180^\circ\)).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using the Law of Sines. Given \(\angle B = 110^\circ\), \(b = 25\), and \(c = 18\), find the length of side \(a\), rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{18 \sin 110^\circ}{25} \approx 0.6766\), giving \(\angle C \approx 42.6^\circ\). Then \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 110^\circ - 42.6^\circ = 27.4^\circ\), so \(a = \frac{25 \sin 27.4^\circ}{\sin 110^\circ} \approx 12.3\).

qs.q: Two observation posts, \(A\) and \(B\), track a weather balloon \(C\). From post \(A\), the angle of elevation to the balloon is \(\angle A = 44^\circ\). The distance from post \(A\) to the balloon is \(b = 520\text{ m}\), and the distance from post \(B\) to the balloon is \(a = 380\text{ m}\). Find the larger possible distance between the two posts along the ground, rounded to the nearest meter.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{520 \sin 44^\circ}{380} \approx 0.9506\), so the acute angle is \(\angle B \approx 71.9^\circ\). The remaining angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 44^\circ - 71.9^\circ = 64.1^\circ\), which yields a ground distance of \(c = \frac{380 \sin 64.1^\circ}{\sin 44^\circ} \approx 492\text{ m}\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 10\), and \(b = 16\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(c\), rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: The Law of Sines gives \(\angle B_1 \approx 53.1^\circ\) and \(\angle B_2 \approx 126.9^\circ\), leading to third angles of \(96.9^\circ\) and \(23.1^\circ\). The two possible lengths for side \(c\) are \(\frac{10 \sin 96.9^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 19.9\) and \(\frac{10 \sin 23.1^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 7.9\), with a difference of \(12.0\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(b = 10\). If \(\angle B\) is obtuse, find the area of \(\Delta ABC\), rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{10 \sin 30^\circ}{7} = \frac{5}{7}\), giving obtuse angle \(\angle B \approx 134.4^\circ\). Thus \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 134.4^\circ = 15.6^\circ\), and the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(7)(10)\sin 15.6^\circ \approx 9.4\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 32^\circ\), \(a = 15\), and \(b = 22\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse, rounded to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{22 \sin 32^\circ}{15} \approx 0.7772\), so the obtuse angle is \(\angle B \approx 129.0^\circ\). Then \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 129.0^\circ = 19.0^\circ\), and \(c = \frac{15 \sin 19.0^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 9.2\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 26^\circ\), \(a = 5\), and \(b = 8\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the measure of the obtuse angle \(B\). Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{8 \sin 26^\circ}{5} \approx 0.7014\), which gives an acute angle of \(44.5^\circ\). The obtuse angle measure is \(180^\circ - 44.5^\circ = 135.5^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 28^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(b = 10\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the measure of the acute angle \(B\). Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{10 \sin 28^\circ}{7} \approx 0.6707\). Taking the inverse sine gives the acute angle \(B \approx 42.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 24^\circ\), \(b = 5\), and \(c = 8\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the measure of \(\angle A\) in the triangle where \(\angle C\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using \(\sin C = \frac{8 \sin 24^\circ}{5} \approx 0.6508\), the obtuse angle is \(C \approx 180^\circ - 40.6^\circ = 139.4^\circ\). Then \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 24^\circ - 139.4^\circ = 16.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 31^\circ\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 9\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the measure of the obtuse angle \(C\). Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{9 \sin 31^\circ}{6} \approx 0.7726\), which gives an acute angle of \(C \approx 50.6^\circ\). The obtuse angle measure is \(180^\circ - 50.6^\circ = 129.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle C = 33^\circ\), \(c = 6\), and \(a = 9\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the measure of \(\angle B\) in the triangle where \(\angle A\) is acute. Round to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using \(\sin A = \frac{9 \sin 33^\circ}{6} \approx 0.8170\), the acute angle is \(A \approx 54.8^\circ\). Then \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 33^\circ - 54.8^\circ = 92.2^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(a = 13\), and \(b = 18\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(c\)? Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Solving both triangles yields \(\angle C_1 \approx 92.4^\circ\) (\(c_1 \approx 22.6\)) and \(\angle C_2 \approx 17.6^\circ\) (\(c_2 \approx 6.8\)). The difference between the two possible lengths is \(22.64 - 6.84 \approx 15.8\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 29^\circ\), \(b = 11\), and \(c = 16\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the length of side \(a\) in the triangle where \(\angle C\) is acute. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using \(\sin C = \frac{16 \sin 29^\circ}{11} \approx 0.7052\), the acute angle is \(C \approx 44.8^\circ\), giving \(\angle A \approx 180^\circ - 29^\circ - 44.8^\circ = 106.2^\circ\). Then \(a = \frac{11 \sin 106.2^\circ}{\sin 29^\circ} \approx 21.8\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 34^\circ\), \(a = 15\), and \(b = 20\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using \(\sin B = \frac{20 \sin 34^\circ}{15} \approx 0.7456\), the obtuse angle is \(B \approx 131.8^\circ\), which gives \(\angle C \approx 180^\circ - 34^\circ - 131.8^\circ = 14.2^\circ\). Then \(c = \frac{15 \sin 14.2^\circ}{\sin 34^\circ} \approx 6.6\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 26^\circ\), \(b = 75\), and \(c = 110\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(a\)? Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Solving both triangles gives \(\angle A_1 \approx 114.0^\circ\) with \(a_1 \approx 156.3\), and \(\angle A_2 \approx 14.0^\circ\) with \(a_2 \approx 41.4\). The difference between the two lengths is \(156.31 - 41.43 \approx 114.9\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 38^\circ\), \(a = 125\), and \(b = 160\). Two triangles can be formed. Find the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse. Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using \(\sin B = \frac{160 \sin 38^\circ}{125} \approx 0.7880\), the obtuse angle is \(B \approx 128.0^\circ\), giving \(\angle C \approx 180^\circ - 38^\circ - 128.0^\circ = 14.0^\circ\). Then \(c = \frac{125 \sin 14.0^\circ}{\sin 38^\circ} \approx 49.1\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 45^\circ\), \(a = 2\sqrt{6}\), and \(b = 6\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the measure of \(\angle C\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{6 \sin 45^\circ}{2\sqrt{6}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so the obtuse angle is \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). Therefore, \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 120^\circ = 15^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 6\), and \(b = 6\sqrt{3}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the measure of \(\angle B\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b \sin A}{a} = \frac{6\sqrt{3} \sin 30^\circ}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Since \(\angle B\) is obtuse, \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: How many distinct triangles \(\Delta ABC\) can be formed if \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(b = 16\)?
qs.s: The altitude is \(h = b \sin A = 16 \sin 30^\circ = 8\). Since \(a = 7 < h\), \(\sin B = \frac{16 \sin 30^\circ}{7} = \frac{8}{7} > 1\), which is impossible, so no triangle can be formed.

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 30^\circ\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 8\sqrt{2}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the measure of the acute angle \(\angle C\)?
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{c \sin B}{b} = \frac{8\sqrt{2} \sin 30^\circ}{8} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). The acute angle with this sine value is \(\angle C = 45^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 10\), and \(b = 10\sqrt{3}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the length of side \(c\) in the triangle where \(\angle B\) is obtuse?
qs.s: Since \(\sin B = \frac{10\sqrt{3} \sin 30^\circ}{10} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\angle B\) is obtuse, \(\angle B = 120^\circ\), which leaves \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 120^\circ = 30^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(c = \frac{a \sin 30^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 10\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 6\), and \(b = 6\sqrt{3}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the perimeter of the triangle with the larger area?
qs.s: The larger triangle corresponds to \(\angle B = 60^\circ\) and \(\angle C = 90^\circ\), where \(c = \frac{6 \sin 90^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 12\). Its perimeter is \(a + b + c = 6 + 6\sqrt{3} + 12 = 18 + 6\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle B = 30^\circ\), \(b = 12\), and \(c = 12\sqrt{3}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side \(a\)?
qs.s: Since \(\sin C = \frac{12\sqrt{3} \sin 30^\circ}{12} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\angle C\) is either \(60^\circ\) (giving \(\angle A = 90^\circ\) and \(a = \frac{12 \sin 90^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 24\)) or \(120^\circ\) (giving \(\angle A = 30^\circ\) and \(a = 12\)). The positive difference is \(24 - 12 = 12\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\) and \(b = 18\). For what range of values of side \(a\) will exactly two distinct triangles exist?
qs.s: Two triangles exist in the ambiguous case when \(h < a < b\), where \(h = b \sin A = 18 \sin 30^\circ = 9\). Thus, exactly two triangles exist when \(9 < a < 18\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 8\sqrt{3}\). Two distinct triangles can be formed. What is the area of the triangle that contains an obtuse angle?
qs.s: Since \(\sin B = \frac{8\sqrt{3} \sin 30^\circ}{8} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), the obtuse angle is \(\angle B = 120^\circ\), which gives \(\angle C = 30^\circ\). The area is \(\frac{1}{2}ab \sin C = \frac{1}{2}(8)(8\sqrt{3})\sin 30^\circ = 16\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle A = 135^\circ\), \(a = 10\), and \(b = 10\sqrt{2}\). How many distinct triangles can be formed?
qs.s: Although \(\sin B = \frac{10\sqrt{2} \sin 135^\circ}{10} = 1\) suggests \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), the angle sum would be \(135^\circ + 90^\circ = 225^\circ > 180^\circ\). Since \(\angle A\) is obtuse and \(a \le b\), no triangle can exist.

qs.q: A lamp hangs at E from an arm WE attached to a wall at W. A brace BE, fixed to the wall at B, supports the arm. Use the figure to find the length \(l\) of the brace (exact value).
qs.s: \(\frac{l}{\sin120^\circ}=\frac{5}{\sin30^\circ}\), so \(l=5\cdot\frac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2}=5\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: A lamp hangs at E from an arm WE attached to a wall at W. A brace BE, fixed to the wall at B, supports the arm. Use the figure (find any missing angle first) to find the length \(l\) of the brace (exact value).
qs.s: \(\angle W=180^\circ-30^\circ-30^\circ=120^\circ\); \(\frac{l}{\sin120^\circ}=\frac{18}{\sin30^\circ}\), so \(l=18\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: A helicopter is hovering between two observers who are 800 meters apart on flat ground. Observer A measures the angle of elevation to the helicopter as \(53^\circ\), and Observer B measures it as \(67^\circ\). How high is the helicopter? (Round to the nearest meter.)
qs.s: The angle at the helicopter is \(180^\circ - (53^\circ + 67^\circ) = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance from Observer A to the helicopter is \(\frac{800 \sin 67^\circ}{\sin 60^\circ} \approx 850.33\text{ m}\), so the height is \(850.33 \sin 53^\circ \approx 679\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A police blimp is positioned between two officers who are 1200 meters apart on a flat highway. The angles of elevation from the two officers to the blimp are \(38^\circ\) and \(46^\circ\). How high is the blimp? (Round to the nearest meter.)
qs.s: The angle at the blimp is \(180^\circ - (38^\circ + 46^\circ) = 96^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance from the first officer to the blimp is \(\frac{1200 \sin 46^\circ}{\sin 96^\circ} \approx 867.96\text{ m}\), yielding a height of \(867.96 \sin 38^\circ \approx 534\text{ m}\).

qs.q: An airplane is flying between two observers who are 3 miles apart on flat terrain. The angle of elevation to the plane from the first observer is \(40^\circ\), and from the second observer it is \(72^\circ\). How high is the airplane? (Round to the nearest tenth of a mile.)
qs.s: The third angle of the triangle is \(180^\circ - (40^\circ + 72^\circ) = 68^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance from the first observer to the plane is \(\frac{3 \sin 72^\circ}{\sin 68^\circ} \approx 3.077\text{ miles}\), so the altitude is \(3.077 \sin 40^\circ \approx 2.0\text{ miles}\).

qs.q: A drone is hovering between two researchers standing 600 meters apart on level ground. The angles of elevation to the drone are \(58^\circ\) from the first researcher and \(65^\circ\) from the second researcher. How high is the drone? (Round to the nearest meter.)
qs.s: The angle at the drone is \(180^\circ - (58^\circ + 65^\circ) = 57^\circ\). Using the Law of Sines, the distance from the first researcher to the drone is \(\frac{600 \sin 65^\circ}{\sin 57^\circ} \approx 648.39\text{ m}\), which gives a height of \(648.39 \sin 58^\circ \approx 550\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A weather balloon is floating directly between two tracking stations that are 5 km apart on level ground. The angles of elevation from the two stations to the balloon are \(35^\circ\) and \(48^\circ\). How high is the weather balloon? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the balloon is \(180^\circ - (35^\circ + 48^\circ) = 97^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the slant range from the first station is \(\frac{5 \sin 48^\circ}{\sin 97^\circ} \approx 3.744\text{ km}\), giving a height of \(3.744 \sin 35^\circ \approx 2.1\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A surveyor measures the angle of elevation to a mountain peak as \(26^\circ\). After driving 2500 meters closer to the mountain along a straight, level road, the angle of elevation to the peak is \(41^\circ\). Find the height of the mountain peak above the road. (Round to the nearest meter.)
qs.s: In the triangle formed by the two observation points and the peak, the angles are \(26^\circ\), \(180^\circ - 41^\circ = 139^\circ\), and \(41^\circ - 26^\circ = 15^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance from the closer observation point to the peak is \(\frac{2500 \sin 26^\circ}{\sin 15^\circ} \approx 4234.34\text{ m}\), giving a vertical height of \(4234.34 \sin 41^\circ \approx 2778\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A lighthouse \(L\) and a port \(P\) are 15 km apart. A ship \(S\) is positioned such that \(\angle LPS = 32^\circ\), and the ship is known to be 10 km from lighthouse \(L\). Because this information allows two possible locations for the ship, find the difference between the two possible distances from the port to the ship. (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin S = \frac{15 \sin 32^\circ}{10} \approx 0.7949\), which gives \(\angle S_1 \approx 52.64^\circ\) or \(\angle S_2 \approx 127.36^\circ\). The third angles are \(95.36^\circ\) and \(20.64^\circ\), producing distances of \(\frac{10 \sin 95.36^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 18.79\text{ km}\) and \(\frac{10 \sin 20.64^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 6.65\text{ km}\), with a difference of \(18.79 - 6.65 = 12.1\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A vertical antenna stands on a hillside that slopes upward at an angle of \(18^\circ\) from the horizontal. From a point 65 meters down the slope from the base of the antenna, the angle of elevation to the top of the antenna is \(44^\circ\) above the horizontal. Find the height of the antenna. (Round to the nearest tenth of a meter.)
qs.s: In the triangle formed by the observer, the base, and the top of the antenna, the angle at the observer is \(44^\circ - 18^\circ = 26^\circ\), the angle at the base is \(90^\circ + 18^\circ = 108^\circ\), and the angle at the top is \(180^\circ - (26^\circ + 108^\circ) = 46^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the height is \(\frac{65 \sin 26^\circ}{\sin 46^\circ} \approx 39.6\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A research satellite is tracked simultaneously by two ground stations, A and B, that are 4200 km apart on opposite sides of the satellite. Station A measures an angle of elevation of \(54^\circ\), and Station B measures an angle of elevation of \(68^\circ\). Find the total length of the transmission path from Station A to the satellite and then to Station B. (Round to the nearest whole kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the satellite is \(180^\circ - (54^\circ + 68^\circ) = 58^\circ\). Using the Law of Sines, the distances from the stations to the satellite are \(a = \frac{4200 \sin 54^\circ}{\sin 58^\circ} \approx 4006.7\text{ km}\) and \(b = \frac{4200 \sin 68^\circ}{\sin 58^\circ} \approx 4591.9\text{ km}\), so the total path length is \(4006.7 + 4591.9 \approx 8599\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two observers on level ground are 4.5 km apart with an airplane flying in the vertical plane between them. The angle of elevation from Observer A is \(34^\circ\) and from Observer B is \(58^\circ\). How much closer is the airplane to Observer B than to Observer A? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the airplane is \(180^\circ - (34^\circ + 58^\circ) = 88^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distances to the plane are \(b = \frac{4.5 \sin 58^\circ}{\sin 88^\circ} \approx 3.82\text{ km}\) from Observer A and \(a = \frac{4.5 \sin 34^\circ}{\sin 88^\circ} \approx 2.52\text{ km}\) from Observer B, so the difference is \(3.82 - 2.52 = 1.3\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A traffic helicopter is hovering directly between two exits on a straight, level highway that are 5 km apart. The pilot spots one exit at an angle of depression of \(27^\circ\) and the other exit at an angle of depression of \(44^\circ\). How high above the highway is the helicopter? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the helicopter is \(180^\circ - (27^\circ + 44^\circ) = 109^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance to the first exit is \(\frac{5\sin 44^\circ}{\sin 109^\circ} \approx 3.67\text{ km}\), giving a height of \(3.67\sin 27^\circ \approx 1.7\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A search-and-rescue airplane is flying along a straight line directly between two emergency beacon stations located 10 km apart on flat terrain. The pilot notes the angles of depression to the two beacons are \(22^\circ\) and \(31^\circ\). How high above the ground is the airplane? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the airplane is \(180^\circ - (22^\circ + 31^\circ) = 127^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance to the first beacon is \(\frac{10\sin 31^\circ}{\sin 127^\circ} \approx 6.45\text{ km}\), so the altitude is \(6.45\sin 22^\circ \approx 2.4\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A weather balloon is floating directly between two tracking stations on level ground that are 8 km apart. The angle of elevation to the balloon from the first station is \(35^\circ\) and from the second station is \(52^\circ\). How high above the ground is the weather balloon? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The third angle of the triangle is \(180^\circ - (35^\circ + 52^\circ) = 93^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance from the first station to the balloon is \(\frac{8\sin 52^\circ}{\sin 93^\circ} \approx 6.31\text{ km}\), so the height is \(6.31\sin 35^\circ \approx 3.6\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A drone is hovering directly between two researchers who are standing on level ground 6 km apart. The drone operator observes the angle of depression to one researcher to be \(41^\circ\) and to the other researcher to be \(36^\circ\). How high above the ground is the drone? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the drone is \(180^\circ - (41^\circ + 36^\circ) = 103^\circ\). Using the Law of Sines, the distance to one researcher is \(\frac{6\sin 36^\circ}{\sin 103^\circ} \approx 3.62\text{ km}\), so the height is \(3.62\sin 41^\circ \approx 2.4\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A sightseeing blimp is flying directly between two coastal lighthouses that are 7 km apart. The navigator observes the angle of depression to the northern lighthouse to be \(25^\circ\) and to the southern lighthouse to be \(48^\circ\). How high above the water is the blimp? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The vertex angle at the blimp is \(180^\circ - (25^\circ + 48^\circ) = 107^\circ\). Using the Law of Sines, the line-of-sight distance to the northern lighthouse is \(\frac{7\sin 48^\circ}{\sin 107^\circ} \approx 5.44\text{ km}\), yielding a height of \(5.44\sin 25^\circ \approx 2.3\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A hot air balloon is flying directly between two tracking stations, \(A\) and \(B\), that are 6 km apart on level ground. The balloonist finds that the angle of depression to station \(A\) is \(32^\circ\) and to station \(B\) is \(41^\circ\). If the balloon must reach a target altitude of 3.5 km, how many more kilometers must it ascend vertically? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the balloon is \(180^\circ - (32^\circ + 41^\circ) = 107^\circ\), so the distance to station \(A\) is \(\frac{6\sin 41^\circ}{\sin 107^\circ} \approx 4.12\text{ km}\) and the current height is \(4.12\sin 32^\circ \approx 2.2\text{ km}\). The balloon must ascend \(3.5 - 2.2 = 1.3\text{ km}\) more.

qs.q: A helicopter is flying directly between Station West and Station East, two mountain rescue bases located 12.5 km apart on level ground. The pilot measures the angle of depression to Station West as \(34^\circ\) and to Station East as \(46^\circ\). The helicopter drops a supply crate that falls vertically to the ground directly beneath it. What is the ground distance from Station East to the crate? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the helicopter is \(180^\circ - (34^\circ + 46^\circ) = 100^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the slant distance to Station East is \(HE = \frac{12.5\sin 34^\circ}{\sin 100^\circ} \approx 7.10\text{ km}\), so the ground distance from Station East to the crate is \(7.10\cos 46^\circ \approx 4.9\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A fire-watch airplane is flying directly between two forest fires, Fire \(A\) and Fire \(B\), that are 15 km apart on level ground. The pilot measures the angle of depression to Fire \(A\) as \(24^\circ\) and to Fire \(B\) as \(37^\circ\). What is the difference between the straight-line distances from the airplane to the two fires? (Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.)
qs.s: The angle at the airplane is \(180^\circ - (24^\circ + 37^\circ) = 119^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the straight-line distances are \(d_A = \frac{15\sin 37^\circ}{\sin 119^\circ} \approx 10.32\text{ km}\) and \(d_B = \frac{15\sin 24^\circ}{\sin 119^\circ} \approx 6.98\text{ km}\), giving a difference of \(10.32 - 6.98 = 3.3\text{ km}\).

qs.q: An engineer measures the angle of elevation to the top of a communication tower from point \(A\) on level ground to be \(36^\circ\). Walking 75 m directly away from the tower to point \(B\), the angle of elevation to the top is \(23^\circ\). What is the height of the communication tower? (Round to the nearest meter.)
qs.s: In \(\triangle ABT\), the vertex angle at the top is \(36^\circ - 23^\circ = 13^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(AT = \frac{75\sin 23^\circ}{\sin 13^\circ} \approx 130.3\text{ m}\), so the tower's height is \(130.3\sin 36^\circ \approx 77\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two ships leave harbor \(A\) in different directions. One ship docks at port \(B\), \(180\text{ km}\) from harbor \(A\). The other ship docks at port \(C\). If \(\angle ABC = 45^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 30^\circ\), how far did the second ship travel from harbor \(A\) to port \(C\)?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{AC}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{180}{\sin 30^\circ}\). Solving for \(AC\) gives \(AC = 180 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1/2} = 180\sqrt{2}\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two surveying teams depart from base point \(A\). Team 1 sets up a marker at point \(B\), \(400\text{ m}\) from \(A\). Team 2 sets up a marker at point \(C\). If \(\angle ABC = 30^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 45^\circ\), what is the distance from base point \(A\) to marker \(C\)?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{AC}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{400}{\sin 45^\circ}\), which yields \(AC = 400 \cdot \frac{1/2}{\sqrt{2}/2} = \frac{400}{\sqrt{2}} = 200\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two rescue boats leave coast guard station \(A\). The first boat reaches buoy \(B\), located \(350\text{ m}\) from station \(A\). The second boat reaches buoy \(C\). If \(\angle ABC = 135^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 30^\circ\), find the distance from station \(A\) to buoy \(C\).
qs.s: Applying the Law of Sines gives \(\frac{AC}{\sin 135^\circ} = \frac{350}{\sin 30^\circ}\), which simplifies to \(AC = 350 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1/2} = 350\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two hiking groups set out from base camp \(A\). Group 1 hikes to shelter \(B\), located \(120\text{ m}\) from camp \(A\). Group 2 hikes to shelter \(C\). If \(\angle ABC = 60^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 45^\circ\), what is the distance from base camp \(A\) to shelter \(C\)?
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\frac{AC}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{120}{\sin 45^\circ}\), which gives \(AC = 120 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 60\sqrt{6}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two runners depart from park entrance \(A\). The first runner stops at water station \(B\), which is \(240\text{ m}\) from entrance \(A\). The second runner stops at water station \(C\). If \(\angle ABC = 120^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 30^\circ\), how far did the second runner travel from entrance \(A\) to station \(C\)?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{AC}{\sin 120^\circ} = \frac{240}{\sin 30^\circ}\). Since \(\sin 120^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\), we find \(AC = 240\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two expedition teams leave base camp \(A\). Team 1 treks to research station \(B\), which is \(1500\text{ m}\) from camp \(A\). Team 2 treks to research station \(C\). In \(\Delta ABC\), \(\angle ABC = 120^\circ\) and \(\angle ACB = 30^\circ\). How much farther did Team 2 trek than Team 1?
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, Team 2 treks \(AC = 1500 \cdot \frac{\sin 120^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 1500\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\). Subtracting Team 1's distance gives a difference of \((1500\sqrt{3} - 1500)\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two satellite tracking stations, \(A\) and \(B\), are located \(2400\text{ km}\) apart. Both stations track a satellite \(C\) in the same vertical plane. Station \(A\) detects the satellite at an angle of \(\angle CAB = 30^\circ\), while station \(B\) detects it at an angle of \(\angle CBA = 105^\circ\). What is the direct distance from station \(B\) to satellite \(C\)?
qs.s: The angle at the satellite is \(\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 105^\circ = 45^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{BC}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{2400}{\sin 45^\circ}\), which yields \(BC = 2400 \cdot \frac{1/2}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 1200\sqrt{2}\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two commercial jets depart from international airport \(A\). Jet 1 flies to city \(B\), which is \(1800\text{ km}\) from airport \(A\). Jet 2 flies to city \(C\). The angle between their flight paths at airport \(A\) is \(\angle BAC = 75^\circ\), and the angle at city \(B\) is \(\angle ABC = 60^\circ\). If Jet 2 completes its flight to city \(C\) in \(2\) hours, what was its average speed in kilometers per hour?
qs.s: First, \(\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 75^\circ - 60^\circ = 45^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, the distance flown by Jet 2 is \(AC = 1800 \cdot \frac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} = 900\sqrt{6}\text{ km}\), so its average speed is \(\frac{900\sqrt{6}\text{ km}}{2\text{ h}} = 450\sqrt{6}\text{ km/h}\).

qs.q: Two cargo ships leave port \(A\) at the same time. Ship 1 arrives at port \(B\), located \(420\text{ nautical miles}\) from port \(A\). Ship 2 arrives at port \(C\). The angle between their courses at port \(A\) is \(\angle BAC = 45^\circ\), and \(\angle ABC = 105^\circ\). What is the direct distance between port \(B\) and port \(C\)?
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 105^\circ = 30^\circ\). Applying the Law of Sines to find \(BC\) gives \(\frac{BC}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{420}{\sin 30^\circ}\), so \(BC = 420 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1/2} = 420\sqrt{2}\text{ nautical miles}\).

qs.q: Two drones are dispatched from control station \(A\). Drone 1 flies to sensor \(B\), a distance of \(1200\text{ m}\) from \(A\). Drone 2 flies to sensor \(C\). The angle between their flight paths is \(\angle BAC = 15^\circ\), and \(\angle ABC = 135^\circ\). What is the total combined distance flown by both drones from station \(A\)?
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 15^\circ - 135^\circ = 30^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, Drone 2 flies \(AC = 1200 \cdot \frac{\sin 135^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 1200\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\), giving a total combined distance of \((1200 + 1200\sqrt{2})\text{ m}\).

qs.q: From a control tower \(C\), two drones \(A\) and \(B\) are observed. The distance from \(C\) to drone \(A\) is \(90\text{ m}\) and to drone \(B\) is \(65\text{ m}\). An observer at drone \(A\) measures the angle between the tower and drone \(B\) as \(25^\circ\). What is the shorter possible distance between drone \(A\) and drone \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a meter.
qs.s: The Law of Sines gives \(\sin B = \frac{90 \sin 25^\circ}{65} \approx 0.5852\), yielding the obtuse angle \(B \approx 144.2^\circ\). Then \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 25^\circ - 144.2^\circ = 10.8^\circ\), so the shorter distance is \(AB = \frac{65 \sin 10.8^\circ}{\sin 25^\circ} \approx 28.9\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A surveyor at landmark \(S\) measures the distances to two boundary markers, \(A\) and \(B\), as \(50\text{ m}\) and \(35\text{ m}\) respectively. When \(\angle SAB = 32^\circ\), what is the shorter possible distance between marker \(A\) and marker \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a meter.
qs.s: Applying the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{50 \sin 32^\circ}{35} \approx 0.7570\), giving the obtuse angle \(B \approx 130.8^\circ\). The third angle is \(\angle S = 180^\circ - 32^\circ - 130.8^\circ = 17.2^\circ\), leading to \(AB = \frac{35 \sin 17.2^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 19.5\text{ m}\).

qs.q: In a planetary system, the distance from star \(S\) to planet \(A\) is \(75\text{ million km}\) and to planet \(B\) is \(50\text{ million km}\). When \(\angle SAB = 35^\circ\), what is the greater possible distance from planet \(A\) to planet \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a million kilometers.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{75 \sin 35^\circ}{50} \approx 0.8604\), giving acute angle \(B \approx 59.4^\circ\). The third angle is \(\angle S = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 59.4^\circ = 85.6^\circ\), which yields \(AB = \frac{50 \sin 85.6^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} \approx 86.9\text{ million km}\).

qs.q: In a planetary system, the distance from the central star \(S\) to planet \(A\) is \(80\text{ million miles}\) and to planet \(B\) is \(55\text{ million miles}\). When \(\angle SAB = 22^\circ\), what is the greater possible distance from planet \(A\) to planet \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a million miles.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{80 \sin 22^\circ}{55} \approx 0.5449\), so the acute angle is \(B \approx 33.0^\circ\). Then \(\angle S = 180^\circ - 22^\circ - 33.0^\circ = 125.0^\circ\), which gives \(AB = \frac{55 \sin 125.0^\circ}{\sin 22^\circ} \approx 120.3\text{ million miles}\).

qs.q: A radar station \(R\) tracks two boats, \(A\) and \(B\). The distance from \(R\) to boat \(A\) is \(40\text{ miles}\), and the distance from \(R\) to boat \(B\) is \(28\text{ miles}\). The angle formed at boat \(A\) between the station and boat \(B\) is \(30^\circ\). If the angle at boat \(B\) is obtuse, what is the distance from boat \(A\) to boat \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a mile.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{40 \sin 30^\circ}{28} = \frac{5}{7}\), so the obtuse angle is \(B \approx 134.4^\circ\). The remaining angle is \(\angle R = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 134.4^\circ = 15.6^\circ\), giving \(AB = \frac{28 \sin 15.6^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} \approx 15.0\text{ miles}\).

qs.q: A coast guard cutter \(C\) receives signals from two yachts, \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\), that are both \(40\text{ km}\) from a lighthouse \(L\). Cutter \(C\) is \(55\text{ km}\) from lighthouse \(L\), and an observer at \(C\) measures the angle between the lighthouse and both yachts along the same line of sight as \(\angle LCY = 35^\circ\). How far apart are the two yachts from each other? Round to the nearest tenth of a kilometer.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin Y = \frac{55 \sin 35^\circ}{40} \approx 0.7887\), producing angles of \(52.1^\circ\) and \(127.9^\circ\), with third angles \(92.9^\circ\) and \(17.1^\circ\). The distances from the cutter are \(69.6\text{ km}\) and \(20.5\text{ km}\), so the distance between the yachts is \(69.6 - 20.5 = 49.2\text{ km}\).

qs.q: In a solar system, star \(S\) is \(140\text{ million miles}\) from planet \(A\) and \(90\text{ million miles}\) from planet \(B\). When \(\angle SAB = 34^\circ\), planet \(B\) is at the position where \(\angle SBA\) is acute. A deep-space probe travels along the straight path from planet \(A\) toward planet \(B\). If the probe has traveled \(40\text{ million miles}\), how much farther must it travel to reach planet \(B\)? Round to the nearest tenth of a million miles.
qs.s: Applying the Law of Sines gives \(\sin B = \frac{140 \sin 34^\circ}{90} \approx 0.8699\), so the acute angle is \(B \approx 60.4^\circ\) and \(\angle S = 85.6^\circ\). The total distance is \(AB = \frac{90 \sin 85.6^\circ}{\sin 34^\circ} \approx 160.5\text{ million miles}\), leaving \(160.5 - 40 = 120.5\text{ million miles}\) remaining.

qs.q: In an exoplanetary system, star \(S\) has two planets \(A\) and \(B\). The distance from star \(S\) to planet \(A\) is \(95\text{ million miles}\) and to planet \(B\) is \(68\text{ million miles}\). An astronomer on planet \(A\) measures \(\angle SAB = 28^\circ\). Planet \(B\) can be in two possible positions, \(B\) and \(B'\). What is the perimeter of triangle \(SBB'\)? Round to the nearest million miles.
qs.s: The Law of Sines gives \(\sin B = \frac{95 \sin 28^\circ}{68} \approx 0.6559\), which yields the distances \(AB \approx 135.2\text{ million miles}\) and \(AB' \approx 32.6\text{ million miles}\), so \(BB' = 135.2 - 32.6 = 102.6\text{ million miles}\). The perimeter of isosceles triangle \(SBB'\) is \(68 + 68 + 102.6 \approx 239\text{ million miles}\).

qs.q: In a solar system, the distance from star \(S\) to planet \(A\) is \(1.5 \times 10^8\text{ km}\) and to planet \(B\) is \(9.0 \times 10^7\text{ km}\). When \(\angle SAB = 32^\circ\), planet \(B\) can be at two possible locations, \(B\) and \(B'\). What is the distance between these two possible locations? Round to the nearest million kilometers.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{1.5 \times 10^8 \sin 32^\circ}{9.0 \times 10^7} \approx 0.8832\), yielding \(B \approx 62.0^\circ\) and \(B' \approx 118.0^\circ\). The two distances from \(A\) are \(\frac{90 \sin 86.0^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 169.4\text{ million km}\) and \(\frac{90 \sin 30.0^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \approx 85.0\text{ million km}\), whose difference is \(169.4 - 85.0 = 84\text{ million km}\).

qs.q: A surveyor stands at point \(A\) and measures the distance to a tower \(T\) as \(60\text{ m}\). A second tower \(U\) is known to be \(42\text{ m}\) from tower \(T\). From point \(A\), the angle between the two towers is \(34^\circ\). Tower \(U\) has two possible locations, \(U_1\) (farther) and \(U_2\) (closer). What is the ratio of the greater distance \(AU_1\) to the shorter distance \(AU_2\)? Round to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: The Law of Sines gives \(\sin U = \frac{60 \sin 34^\circ}{42} \approx 0.7988\), yielding angles \(53.0^\circ\) and \(127.0^\circ\), with third angles \(93.0^\circ\) and \(19.0^\circ\). The two distances are \(AU_1 = \frac{42 \sin 93.0^\circ}{\sin 34^\circ} \approx 75.0\text{ m}\) and \(AU_2 = \frac{42 \sin 19.0^\circ}{\sin 34^\circ} \approx 24.5\text{ m}\), giving a ratio of \(\frac{75.0}{24.5} \approx 3.1\).

qs.q: A tree at B is seen across a river from points A and C on the bank, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the distance AB.
Two observers at A and B stand 20 m apart on level ground and both see a balloon at C. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the distance BC from observer B to the balloon.
A triangular plot ABC has BC = 10√2 m, angle A = 135° and angle B = 30°, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the length AC.
A support cable AB is attached to the tower top B as shown, and BC is 12 m long. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the length of the cable AB.
Points A and B are 30 m apart along a river bank, and a tree C is on the opposite bank. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the distance AC.
A triangular garden ABC has BC = 6√2 m, AC = 6 m and angle A = 45°, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find angle C (the angle at C, in degrees).
qs.s: sin B / 6 = sin 45° / 6√2 = 1/2, so B = 30° (AC is shorter than BC), and C = 180° − 45° − 30° = 105°.

qs.q: In triangle ABC, angle A = 45°, angle B = 75° and BC = 4√2 m, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find AB.
A ship C is seen from two lighthouses A and B that are 6√3 km apart, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the distance BC.

A tower CD stands on level ground. From A the angle of elevation of its top C is 30°, and from B, 60 m closer to the tower, it is 60°, as shown. Use the figure and the Law of Sines to find the height CD of the tower.
qs.s: Angle ACB = 60° − 30° = 30°, so BC = AB = 60 m by the Law of Sines; then CD = 60 sin 60° = 30√3 m.

exercises.name: Law of Cosines Concepts and Formulas

qs.q: Fill in the blank: When \(\angle A = 90^\circ\), \(\cos A = 0\), and the Law of Cosines \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A\) simplifies to the _____ theorem.
qs.s: Substituting \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\) eliminates the \(-2bc\cos A\) term, leaving \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2\), which is the Pythagorean theorem.

qs.q: Fill in the blank: Rearranging the Law of Cosines \(b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac\cos B\) to solve for the cosine of angle \(B\) yields \(\cos B = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\).
qs.s: Isolating \(2ac\cos B\) gives \(2ac\cos B = a^2 + c^2 - b^2\), so dividing by \(2ac\) yields \(\cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2ac}\).

qs.q: Fill in the blank: When using the Law of Cosines to solve a triangle given all three side lengths (SSS), one should always find the _____ angle first.
qs.s: Finding the largest angle first ensures the remaining two angles are strictly acute, avoiding any ambiguity when using the Law of Sines afterward.

qs.q: Fill in the blank: To begin solving an oblique triangle when given the lengths of all three sides (SSS), one must use the Law of _____.
qs.s: An SSS triangle has no known angle-side opposite pair, which means the Law of Sines cannot be used initially; the Law of Cosines must be used.

qs.q: Fill in the blank: In any triangle \(ABC\), the Law of Cosines states that \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\cos C\).
qs.s: The standard Law of Cosines formula for side \(c\) is \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C\), so the missing coefficient and side lengths are \(2ab\).

qs.q: Fill in the blank: For a triangle with side lengths \(a = 11\), \(b = 13\), and \(c = 20\), the Law of Cosines formula \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}\) gives the exact value of \(\cos C\) as _____.
qs.s: Substitute the given sides into the formula: \(\cos C = \frac{11^2 + 13^2 - 20^2}{2(11)(13)} = \frac{121 + 169 - 400}{286} = \frac{-110}{286} = -\frac{5}{13}\).

qs.q: Fill in the blank: In \(\Delta ABC\) with sides \(a = 15\), \(b = 24\), and \(c = 21\), following the SSS solving rule requires finding the largest angle first; the exact value of its cosine is _____.
qs.s: The longest side is \(b = 24\), so angle \(B\) is largest; using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos B = \frac{15^2 + 21^2 - 24^2}{2(15)(21)} = \frac{225 + 441 - 576}{630} = \frac{90}{630} = \frac{1}{7}\).

qs.q: Fill in the blank: If the sides of \(\Delta ABC\) satisfy the algebraic relationship \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + bc\), then according to the Law of Cosines, \(\cos A = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\).
qs.s: Comparing \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + bc\) to the Law of Cosines \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A\) gives \(-2bc\cos A = bc\), which simplifies to \(\cos A = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: Fill in the blank: In \(\Delta ABC\), if \(a = 8\), \(b = 5\), and \(\cos C = \frac{1}{2}\), then the exact length of side \(c\) is _____.

Fill in the blank: In the geometric derivation of the Law of Cosines using altitude \(h\) to side \(c\), equating \(h^2 = b^2 - x^2\) and \(h^2 = a^2 - (c - x)^2\) simplifies to \(a^2 = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\) before substituting \(x = b\cos A\).
qs.s: Expanding \(a^2 - (c - x)^2 = b^2 - x^2\) gives \(a^2 - (c^2 - 2cx + x^2) = b^2 - x^2\), which simplifies directly to \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2cx\).

qs.q: When solving a triangle with three known side lengths (SSS) using the Law of Cosines, which angle should be found first to ensure that the remaining two angles are acute?
qs.s: Finding the largest angle first guarantees that the remaining two angles are acute, preventing any ambiguity when using the Law of Sines for the remaining angles.

qs.q: If angle \(A\) of \(\triangle ABC\) is an acute angle (\(0^\circ < A < 90^\circ\)), what is the sign of the term \(-2bc \cos A\) in the Law of Cosines?
qs.s: For an acute angle, \(\cos A > 0\). Because triangle side lengths \(b\) and \(c\) are positive, multiplying by \(-2\) makes \(-2bc \cos A\) strictly negative.

qs.q: Which equation correctly shows the Law of Cosines solved for \(\cos A\) in terms of side lengths \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\)?
qs.s: Rearranging \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A\) to isolate the cosine term gives \(2bc \cos A = b^2 + c^2 - a^2\), which yields \(\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}\).

qs.q: For which set of given triangle information must the Law of Cosines be used rather than the Law of Sines as the initial solving step?
d: Two angles and the included side (ASA)
Two angles and a non-included side (AAS)
qs.s: With three known side lengths (SSS), no angle is known to set up an opposite angle-side ratio, so the Law of Sines cannot be used and the Law of Cosines is required.

qs.q: When the Law of Cosines \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cos C\) is applied to a right triangle with \(\angle C = 90^\circ\), what does the equation simplify to?
qs.s: Since \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), the term \(-2ab \cos C\) becomes 0, simplifying the expression directly to the Pythagorean theorem: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).

qs.q: For \(\triangle ABC\) with side lengths \(a = 7\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 9\), use the Law of Cosines formula \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}\) to find the exact value of \(\cos C\) in simplest form.
qs.s: Substituting the values gives \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 9^2}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{49 + 64 - 81}{112} = \frac{32}{112}\), which simplifies to \(\frac{2}{7}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths satisfy the relation \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + bc\). Comparing this with the Law of Cosines, what is the exact value of \(\cos A\)?
qs.s: Comparing \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + bc\) to \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A\) gives \(-2bc \cos A = bc\). Dividing both sides by \(-2bc\) yields \(\cos A = -\frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths satisfy the equation \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - \sqrt{3}bc\). Based on the Law of Cosines, what is the exact value of \(\cos A\)?
qs.s: Comparing \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - \sqrt{3}bc\) to \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A\), we set \(-2bc \cos A = -\sqrt{3}bc\), which simplifies to \(\cos A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 5\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 11\). Using the Law of Cosines formula for an angle, what is the exact value of \(\cos C\) in simplest form?
In \(\triangle ABC\) with side lengths \(a = 4\), \(b = 5\), and \(c = 6\), what is the numerical value of the expression \(2bc \cos A + 2ac \cos B\)?
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(2bc \cos A = b^2 + c^2 - a^2 = 45\) and \(2ac \cos B = a^2 + c^2 - b^2 = 27\). Adding these gives \(45 + 27 = 72\) (which equals \(2c^2\)).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve \(\Delta DEF\) for the unknown side, given \(\angle EDF = 39^\circ\), \(e = 14\), and \(f = 20\)?
qs.s: The given angle is \(\angle EDF\) (vertex \(D\)), and the two adjacent sides are \(e\) and \(f\). To solve for the opposite side \(d\), use the version \(d^2 = e^2 + f^2 - 2ef \cos D\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve \(\Delta RST\) for the unknown side, given \(\angle STR = 105^\circ\), \(r = 7\), and \(s = 11\)?
qs.s: The given angle is \(\angle STR\) (vertex \(T\)) between sides \(r\) and \(s\). To solve for the opposite side \(t\), use \(t^2 = r^2 + s^2 - 2rs \cos T\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve \(\Delta PQR\) for the unknown side, given \(\angle PQR = 62^\circ\), \(p = 9\), and \(r = 15\)?
qs.s: The given angle is \(\angle PQR\) (vertex \(Q\)), and the adjacent sides are \(p\) and \(r\). To find the missing opposite side \(q\), use \(q^2 = p^2 + r^2 - 2pr \cos Q\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve \(\Delta KLM\) for the unknown side, given \(\angle KLM = 28^\circ\), \(k = 17\), and \(m = 23\)?
qs.s: The given angle is \(\angle KLM\) (vertex \(L\)) with adjacent sides \(k\) and \(m\). To solve for side \(l\), use \(l^2 = k^2 + m^2 - 2km \cos L\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve \(\Delta ABC\) for the unknown side, given \(\angle BAC = 47^\circ\), \(b = 13\), and \(c = 18\)?
qs.s: The given angle is \(\angle BAC\) (vertex \(A\)) between sides \(b\) and \(c\). To solve for side \(a\), use \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve for \(\angle BAC\) in \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 65\), \(b = 48\), and \(c = 53\)?
qs.s: The angle to solve for is \(\angle BAC\) (vertex \(A\)), which lies opposite side \(a\). Rearranging \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A\) for \(\cos A\) gives \(\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve for the largest angle in \(\Delta PQR\), given \(p = 19\), \(q = 28\), and \(r = 35\)?
qs.s: The longest side is \(r = 35\), so the largest angle is \(\angle R\). Rearranging the Law of Cosines to solve for \(\angle R\) gives \(\cos R = \frac{p^2 + q^2 - r^2}{2pq}\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve for the smallest angle in \(\Delta KLM\), given \(k = 42\), \(l = 31\), and \(m = 56\)?
qs.s: The shortest side is \(l = 31\), so the smallest angle is \(\angle L\). Rearranging the Law of Cosines for \(\angle L\) yields \(\cos L = \frac{k^2 + m^2 - l^2}{2km}\).

qs.q: Which version of the Law of Cosines is needed to solve for \(\angle EDF\) in \(\Delta DEF\), given \(d = 37\), \(e = 52\), and \(f = 41\)?
qs.s: The angle \(\angle EDF\) has vertex \(D\) and lies opposite side \(d\). Solving the Law of Cosines for \(\cos D\) gives \(\cos D = \frac{e^2 + f^2 - d^2}{2ef}\).

qs.q: According to the Law of Cosines, which angle formula should be used first to begin solving \(\Delta TUV\), given \(t = 85\), \(u = 62\), and \(v = 74\)?
qs.s: In a triangle with three known sides (SSS), always find the largest angle first, which lies opposite the longest side \(t = 85\). Thus, the version to use first is \(\cos T = \frac{u^2 + v^2 - t^2}{2uv}\).

Solve the Law of Cosines equation for the unknown part (\(a > 0\)). Answer to 2 decimal places:
\(a^2 = 6^2 + 4^2 - 2 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cos 52^\circ\)
qs.s: Evaluate \(a^2 = 36 + 16 - 48 \cos 52^\circ \approx 52 - 29.55 = 22.45\). Taking the square root gives \(a \approx \sqrt{22.45} \approx 4.74\).

In \(\Delta DEF\), if \(\angle D = 41^\circ\), \(e = 7\), and \(f = 13\), which of the two angles \(\angle E\) or \(\angle F\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?
qs.a: \(\angle E\), because it is opposite the shorter side (\(e < f\))
d: \(\angle F\), because it is opposite the longer side (\(f > e\))

Neither angle, because side \(d\) is unknown
qs.s: Since \(e < f\), the angle opposite \(e\) must be smaller than the angle opposite \(f\) (\(\angle E < \angle F\)). Because a triangle can have at most one obtuse angle, \(\angle E\) cannot be obtuse and must be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta KLM\), if \(\angle M = 38^\circ\), \(k = 16\), and \(l = 21\), which of the two angles \(\angle K\) or \(\angle L\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

qs.s: Side \(k\) is shorter than side \(l\), which means \(\angle K < \angle L\). Since a triangle can contain at most one non-acute angle, \(\angle K\) must be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), if \(\angle A = 53^\circ\), \(b = 15\), and \(c = 8\), which of the two angles \(\angle B\) or \(\angle C\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

Both angles, because \(\angle A\) is acute
qs.s: In any triangle, there can be at most one obtuse angle, which must lie opposite the longest side. Since \(c < b\), \(\angle C < \angle B\), so \(\angle C\) cannot be the largest angle and is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta XYZ\), if \(\angle X = 72^\circ\), \(y = 26\), and \(z = 17\), which of the two angles \(\angle Y\) or \(\angle Z\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

Neither angle, because side \(x\) is not given
qs.s: Since \(z = 17 < 26 = y\), \(\angle Z\) is smaller than \(\angle Y\). Because a triangle cannot have more than one obtuse angle, \(\angle Z\) cannot be obtuse and is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta PQR\), if \(\angle Q = 64^\circ\), \(p = 19\), and \(r = 11\), which of the two angles \(\angle P\) or \(\angle R\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

qs.s: Because side \(r\) is shorter than side \(p\) (\(11 < 19\)), \(\angle R < \angle P\). At most one angle in a triangle can be obtuse, so the smaller angle \(\angle R\) is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), if \(\angle A = 47^\circ\), \(b = 4\sqrt{6}\), and \(c = 7\sqrt{2}\), which of the two angles \(\angle B\) or \(\angle C\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

qs.q: In \(\Delta DEF\), if \(\angle D = 56^\circ\), \(e = 3\sqrt{32} - \sqrt{50}\), and \(f = 2\sqrt{27} + \sqrt{12}\), which of the two angles \(\angle E\) or \(\angle F\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

qs.q: In \(\Delta KLM\), if \(\angle K = 44^\circ\), \(l = \sqrt{250} - \sqrt{40}\), and \(m = \sqrt{45} + \sqrt{20}\), which of the two angles \(\angle L\) or \(\angle M\) is guaranteed to be acute, and why?

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), if \(\angle A = 48^\circ\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 11\), which of the two angles \(\angle B\) or \(\angle C\) can be said for certain is acute?
qs.s: Since \(\angle A = 48^\circ\) is acute and \(b < c\), \(\angle B\) is smaller than \(\angle C\). A triangle can contain at most one obtuse angle, so the smaller angle \(\angle B\) is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta PQR\), if \(\angle P = 62^\circ\), \(q = 13\), and \(r = 7\), which of the two angles \(\angle Q\) or \(\angle R\) can be said for certain is acute?
qs.s: Since \(\angle P\) is acute and \(r < q\), \(\angle R\) is smaller than \(\angle Q\). Because a triangle can have at most one obtuse angle, the smaller non-given angle \(\angle R\) is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta KLM\), if \(\angle K = 37^\circ\), \(l = 9\), and \(m = 14\), which of the two angles \(\angle L\) or \(\angle M\) can be said for certain is acute?
qs.s: With \(\angle K\) acute and \(l < m\), \(\angle L\) is the smaller of the two remaining angles. A triangle can have at most one obtuse angle, so the smaller angle \(\angle L\) is guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta DEF\), if \(\angle D = 110^\circ\), \(e = 8\), and \(f = 5\), which of the two angles \(\angle E\) or \(\angle F\) can be said for certain is acute?
qs.s: Because \(\angle D = 110^\circ\) is obtuse, the sum of the remaining angles is \(180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ\). A triangle can have at most one obtuse angle, so both \(\angle E\) and \(\angle F\) must be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta XYZ\), if \(\angle X = 102^\circ\), \(y = 12\), and \(z = 15\), which of the two angles \(\angle Y\) or \(\angle Z\) can be said for certain is acute?
qs.s: Since \(\angle X = 102^\circ\) is obtuse, the remaining angles must sum to \(78^\circ\), which means neither angle can reach or exceed \(90^\circ\). Therefore, both \(\angle Y\) and \(\angle Z\) are guaranteed to be acute.

qs.q: In \(\Delta DEF\), if \(\angle D = 118^\circ\), \(e = 145\), and \(f = 208\), which of the two angles \(\angle E\) or \(\angle F\) can be said for certain is acute?

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), if \(\angle A = 54^\circ\), \(b = 3\sqrt{7}\), and \(c = 2\sqrt{15}\), which of the two angles \(\angle B\) or \(\angle C\) can be said for certain is acute?

qs.q: In \(\Delta XYZ\), if \(\angle X = 65^\circ\), \(y = 4k - 9\), and \(z = 3k + 5\) where \(k = 12\), which of the two angles \(\angle Y\) or \(\angle Z\) can be said for certain is acute?

qs.q: In \(\Delta PQR\), if \(\angle P = 44^\circ\), \(q = \frac{37}{4}\), and \(r = \frac{46}{5}\), which of the two angles \(\angle Q\) or \(\angle R\) can be said for certain is acute?

qs.q: In \(\Delta KLM\), if \(\angle K = 124^\circ\), \(l = 5\sqrt{6}\), and \(m = 7\sqrt{3}\), which of the two angles \(\angle L\) or \(\angle M\) can be said for certain is acute?

exercises.name: Solve Triangle Using Law of Cosines

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 70^\circ\), \(b = 12\), and \(c = 7\). Find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 54^\circ\), \(a = 6\), and \(c = 11\). Find the length of side \(b\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 6^2 + 11^2 - 2(6)(11)\cos 54^\circ \approx 157 - 77.59 = 79.41\), so \(b = \sqrt{79.41} \approx 8.9\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 48^\circ\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 13\). Find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 8^2 + 13^2 - 2(8)(13)\cos 48^\circ \approx 233 - 139.18 = 93.82\), so \(a = \sqrt{93.82} \approx 9.7\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C = 35^\circ\), \(a = 9\), and \(b = 16\). Find the length of side \(c\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Applying the Law of Cosines, \(c^2 = 9^2 + 16^2 - 2(9)(16)\cos 35^\circ \approx 337 - 235.92 = 101.08\), which yields \(c = \sqrt{101.08} \approx 10.1\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 62^\circ\), \(a = 11\), and \(c = 14\). Find the length of side \(b\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 11^2 + 14^2 - 2(11)(14)\cos 62^\circ \approx 317 - 144.60 = 172.40\), giving \(b = \sqrt{172.40} \approx 13.1\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 46^\circ\), \(b = 15\), and \(c = 8\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find side \(a = \sqrt{15^2 + 8^2 - 2(15)(8)\cos 46^\circ} \approx 11.06\), then use the Law of Sines \(\sin C = \frac{8\sin 46^\circ}{11.06} \approx 0.5204\), giving acute angle \(\angle C \approx 31.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 118^\circ\), \(b = 17\), and \(c = 25\). Find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 8\), \(b = 11\), and \(c = 14\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{8^2 + 11^2 - 14^2}{2(8)(11)} = \frac{-11}{176} = -0.0625\), giving \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.0625) \approx 93.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 15\), \(b = 21\), and \(c = 27\). Find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle A\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos A = \frac{21^2 + 27^2 - 15^2}{2(21)(27)} = \frac{945}{1134} = \frac{5}{6}\), which yields \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \approx 33.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 35^\circ\), \(b = 18\), and \(c = 10\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find \(a = \sqrt{18^2 + 10^2 - 2(18)(10)\cos 35^\circ} \approx 11.36\). Then find acute angle \(\angle C = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{10\sin 35^\circ}{11.36}\right) \approx 30.3^\circ\), so \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 30.3^\circ = 114.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C = 32^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(b = 11\). Find the length of side \(c\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 62^\circ\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 5\). Find the length of side \(a\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 8^2 + 5^2 - 2(8)(5)\cos 62^\circ \approx 89 - 37.558 = 51.442\), so \(a = \sqrt{51.442} \approx 7.2\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 25^\circ\), \(a = 5\), and \(c = 12\). Find the length of side \(b\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 40^\circ\), \(a = 5\), and \(c = 9\). Find the length of side \(b\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 5^2 + 9^2 - 2(5)(9)\cos 40^\circ \approx 106 - 68.944 = 37.056\), so \(b = \sqrt{37.056} \approx 6.1\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 55^\circ\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 10\). Find the length of side \(a\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 52^\circ\), \(b = 13\), and \(c = 6\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\), rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: First, find side \(a = \sqrt{13^2 + 6^2 - 2(13)(6)\cos 52^\circ} \approx 10.44\). Then use the Law of Sines: \(\sin C = \frac{6\sin 52^\circ}{10.44} \approx 0.4530\), yielding \(\angle C = \arcsin(0.4530) \approx 26.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 11\), \(b = 15\), and \(c = 21\). Find the measure of the largest angle, rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: The largest angle is opposite the longest side \(c = 21\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{11^2 + 15^2 - 21^2}{2(11)(15)} = \frac{-95}{330} \approx -0.2879\), so \(\angle C = \arccos(-0.2879) \approx 106.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C = 65^\circ\), \(a = 15\), and \(b = 22\). Find the perimeter of \(\triangle ABC\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Find side \(c = \sqrt{15^2 + 22^2 - 2(15)(22)\cos 65^\circ} \approx \sqrt{430.07} \approx 20.74\). The perimeter is \(P = 15 + 22 + 20.74 \approx 57.7\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 73^\circ\), \(b = 14.5\), and \(c = 18.2\). Find the length of side \(a\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle B = 118^\circ\), \(a = 14\), and \(c = 21\). Find the length of side \(b\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines with an obtuse angle, \(b^2 = 14^2 + 21^2 - 2(14)(21)\cos 118^\circ \approx 637 - 588(-0.4695) \approx 913.05\), which gives \(b = \sqrt{913.05} \approx 30.2\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle Q = 120^\circ\), \(p = 2\), and \(r = 3\). Find the length of side \(q\) in simplest radical form.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle C = 60^\circ\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 3\). Find the length of side \(c\).

In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 6\), \(b = 10\), and \(c = 14\). Find the measure of the largest angle.
qs.s: The largest angle is opposite the longest side \(c = 14\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{6^2 + 10^2 - 14^2}{2(6)(10)} = \frac{-60}{120} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle R = 45^\circ\), \(p = 4\sqrt{2}\), and \(q = 6\). Find the length of side \(r\) in simplest radical form.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(r^2 = (4\sqrt{2})^2 + 6^2 - 2(4\sqrt{2})(6)\cos 45^\circ = 68 - 48 = 20\), so \(r = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 6\), \(b = 3\sqrt{3}\), and \(\angle C = 30^\circ\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\).
In \(\triangle DEF\), \(d = 4\sqrt{2}\), \(e = 4\), and \(\angle F = 45^\circ\). Find the measure of \(\angle D\).
In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 3\), \(b = 5\), and \(c = 6\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{3^2 + 5^2 - 6^2}{2(3)(5)} = -\frac{2}{30} \approx -0.0667\). Thus, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.0667) \approx 93.8°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 5\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 7\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos B = \frac{5^2 + 7^2 - 6^2}{2(5)(7)} = \frac{38}{70} \approx 0.5429\). Taking the inverse cosine gives \(\angle B \approx 57.1°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 4\), \(b = 5\), and \(c = 7\). Find the measure of the largest angle. Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: The largest angle is opposite the longest side \(c = 7\), so \(\cos C = \frac{4^2 + 5^2 - 7^2}{2(4)(5)} = \frac{-8}{40} = -0.2\). Therefore, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.2) \approx 101.5°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 4\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 9\). Find the measure of the smallest angle. Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side \(a = 4\), so \(\cos A = \frac{6^2 + 9^2 - 4^2}{2(6)(9)} = \frac{101}{108} \approx 0.9352\). Thus, \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}(0.9352) \approx 20.7°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 3\), \(b = 7\), and \(c = 8\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{3^2 + 7^2 - 8^2}{2(3)(7)} = \frac{-6}{42} \approx -0.1429\). Therefore, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.1429) \approx 98.2°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 6.4\), \(b = 8.1\), and \(c = 11.5\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
In \(\Delta ABC\), \(a = 13\), \(b = 18\), and \(c = 24\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round your answer to one decimal place.

In \(\Delta ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 7\), \(b = 10\), and \(c = 12\). Find the difference between the measure of the largest angle and the measure of the smallest angle. Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{7^2 + 10^2 - 12^2}{2(7)(10)}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{140}\right) \approx 88.0°\), and the smallest is \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{10^2 + 12^2 - 7^2}{2(10)(12)}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{195}{240}\right) \approx 35.7°\). Their difference is \(88.0° - 35.7° = 52.3°\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(b = 14.2\), \(c = 9.5\), and \(\angle A = 65°\). Find the length of side \(a\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 14.2^2 + 9.5^2 - 2(14.2)(9.5)\cos 65° \approx 201.64 + 90.25 - 114.02 = 177.87\). Taking the square root gives \(a \approx 13.3\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), \(b = 8\), \(c = 11\), and \(\angle A = 42°\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\). Round your answer to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, find side \(a\) using \(a^2 = 8^2 + 11^2 - 2(8)(11)\cos 42° \approx 54.2065\), so \(a \approx 7.36\). Then, using \(\cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2ac} = \frac{54.2065 + 121 - 64}{2(7.3625)(11)} \approx 0.6866\), we find \(\angle B \approx 46.6°\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 5\), \(c = 8\), and \(\angle B = 60^\circ\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Applying the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 89 - 40 = 49\), so \(b = \sqrt{49} = 7\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 4\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 8\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{4^2 + 6^2 - 8^2}{2(4)(6)} = \frac{16 + 36 - 64}{48} = -0.25\). Therefore, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.25) \approx 104.5^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 6\), \(b = 10\), and \(c = 14\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{6^2 + 10^2 - 14^2}{2(6)(10)} = \frac{36 + 100 - 196}{120} = -\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(b = 8\), \(c = 11\), and \(\angle A = 37^\circ\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the length of side \(a\) to the nearest tenth.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 8^2 + 11^2 - 2(8)(11)\cos 37^\circ \approx 185 - 140.56 = 44.44\), which gives \(a = \sqrt{44.44} \approx 6.7\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 5\), \(b = 6\), and \(c = 7\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of \(\angle B\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos B = \frac{5^2 + 7^2 - 6^2}{2(5)(7)} = \frac{38}{70} \approx 0.5429\). Therefore, \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{38}{70}\right) \approx 57.1^\circ\).

qs.q: A parallelogram has adjacent sides of lengths \(18\text{ cm}\) and \(25\text{ cm}\), and the acute angle between them is \(58^\circ\). Find the length of the shorter diagonal to the nearest tenth of a centimeter.
qs.s: The shorter diagonal \(d\) lies opposite the \(58^\circ\) angle, so \(d^2 = 18^2 + 25^2 - 2(18)(25)\cos 58^\circ \approx 949 - 476.93 = 472.07\). Taking the square root gives \(d = \sqrt{472.07} \approx 21.7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 120\), \(b = 150\), and \(c = 200\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
