qs.s: Substitute into the Law of Cosines: \(\cos C = \frac{120^2 + 150^2 - 200^2}{2(120)(150)} = \frac{-3100}{36000} \approx -0.0861\). Thus, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{31}{360}\right) \approx 94.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), the side lengths are \(a = 13\), \(b = 14\), and \(c = 15\). Use the Law of Cosines to find the difference between the largest angle and the smallest angle, \(\angle C - \angle A\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: We find \(\cos C = \frac{13^2 + 14^2 - 15^2}{2(13)(14)} = \frac{5}{13} \implies \angle C \approx 67.38^\circ\) and \(\cos A = \frac{14^2 + 15^2 - 13^2}{2(14)(15)} = \frac{3}{5} \implies \angle A \approx 53.13^\circ\). The difference is \(67.38^\circ - 53.13^\circ \approx 14.3^\circ\).

qs.q: Two ships leave the same port simultaneously. One ship travels \(30\text{ km}\) and the other travels \(40\text{ km}\). If the angle between their travel paths is \(65^\circ\), how far apart are the two ships to the nearest tenth of a kilometer?
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, the distance \(d\) satisfies \(d^2 = 30^2 + 40^2 - 2(30)(40)\cos 65^\circ \approx 2500 - 1014.28 = 1485.72\). Taking the square root gives \(d = \sqrt{1485.72} \approx 38.5\text{ km}\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 9\), \(b = 14\), and \(\angle C = 44^\circ\). Use the Law of Cosines to find side \(c\), and then find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle A\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: First, \(c^2 = 9^2 + 14^2 - 2(9)(14)\cos 44^\circ \approx 95.73\), so \(c \approx 9.784\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{9\sin 44^\circ}{9.784} \approx 0.6390\), giving \(\angle A \approx 39.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 10\), \(b = 13\), and \(c = 17\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos B = \frac{10^2 + 17^2 - 13^2}{2(10)(17)} = \frac{220}{340} \approx 0.6471\). Thus, \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11}{17}\right) \approx 49.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 5\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 9\). Find the measure of \(\angle A\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos A = \frac{8^2 + 9^2 - 5^2}{2(8)(9)} = \frac{120}{144} \approx 0.8333\). Taking the inverse cosine gives \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \approx 33.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 8\), \(b = 12\), and \(c = 15\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos B = \frac{8^2 + 15^2 - 12^2}{2(8)(15)} = \frac{145}{240} \approx 0.6042\). Therefore, \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{29}{48}\right) \approx 52.8^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 7\), \(b = 11\), and \(c = 15\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 11^2 - 15^2}{2(7)(11)} = -\frac{55}{154} \approx -0.3571\). Taking the inverse cosine gives \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{5}{14}\right) \approx 110.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 6\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 11\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{6^2 + 8^2 - 11^2}{2(6)(8)} = -\frac{21}{96} = -0.21875\). Taking the inverse cosine gives \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.21875) \approx 102.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 11\), \(b = 16\), and \(c = 21\). Solve the triangle to find the positive difference between the measure of the largest angle and the measure of the smallest angle, rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{11^2 + 16^2 - 21^2}{2(11)(16)}\right) \approx 100.5^\circ\), and the smallest angle is \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{16^2 + 21^2 - 11^2}{2(16)(21)}\right) \approx 31.0^\circ\). The difference is \(100.48^\circ - 31.00^\circ \approx 69.5^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 21\), \(b = 15\), and \(\angle C = 75^\circ\). Solve the triangle completely to find the measure of \(\angle A\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, \(c = \sqrt{21^2 + 15^2 - 2(21)(15)\cos 75^\circ} \approx 22.43\). Next, find the smallest remaining angle \(\angle B\) using \(\sin B = \frac{15\sin 75^\circ}{22.43} \approx 0.6461\), giving \(\angle B \approx 40.2^\circ\), so \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 75^\circ - 40.2^\circ = 64.8^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(b = 26.5\), \(c = 38.2\), and \(\angle A = 64.5^\circ\). Find the length of side \(a\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 15.4\), \(b = 22.8\), and \(c = 34.6\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{15.4^2 + 22.8^2 - 34.6^2}{2(15.4)(22.8)} = \frac{-440.16}{702.24} \approx -0.6268\). Taking the inverse cosine yields \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.6268) \approx 128.8^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 14\), \(c = 9\), and \(\angle B = 112^\circ\). Solve the triangle completely to find the measure of \(\angle A\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, find side \(b\): \(b = \sqrt{14^2 + 9^2 - 2(14)(9)\cos 112^\circ} \approx 19.27\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{9\sin 112^\circ}{19.27} \approx 0.4330\), giving \(\angle C \approx 25.7^\circ\), so \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 112^\circ - 25.7^\circ = 42.3^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(b = 5\), \(c = 7\), and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\), find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 5^2 + 7^2 - 2(5)(7)\cos 60^\circ = 25 + 49 - 70(0.5) = 39\). Taking the square root gives \(a = \sqrt{39} \approx 6.2\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle DEF\), given \(d = 6\), \(e = 8\), and \(\angle F = 40^\circ\), find the length of side \(f\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(f^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 - 2(6)(8)\cos 40^\circ = 100 - 96(0.7660) \approx 26.46\). Taking the square root yields \(f \approx 5.1\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle PQR\), given \(q = 7\), \(r = 3\), and \(\angle P = 105^\circ\), find the length of side \(p\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(p^2 = 7^2 + 3^2 - 2(7)(3)\cos 105^\circ = 58 - 42(-0.2588) \approx 68.87\). Thus, \(p = \sqrt{68.87} \approx 8.3\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(a = 9\), \(c = 5\), and \(\angle B = 25^\circ\), find the length of side \(b\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 9^2 + 5^2 - 2(9)(5)\cos 25^\circ = 106 - 90(0.9063) \approx 24.43\). Taking the square root gives \(b \approx 4.9\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle XYZ\), given \(x = 4\), \(z = 6\), and \(\angle Y = 120^\circ\), find the length of side \(y\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(y^2 = 4^2 + 6^2 - 2(4)(6)\cos 120^\circ = 52 - 48(-0.5) = 76\). Taking the square root gives \(y = \sqrt{76} \approx 8.7\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle XYZ\), given \(x = 13\), \(y = 19\), and \(z = 24\), find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle X\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side: \(\cos X = \frac{19^2 + 24^2 - 13^2}{2(19)(24)} = \frac{768}{912} \approx 0.8421\). Therefore, \(\angle X = \cos^{-1}(0.8421) \approx 32.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(a = 8\), \(b = 11\), and \(\angle C = 35^\circ\), find the measure of \(\angle A\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find side \(c\): \(c^2 = 8^2 + 11^2 - 2(8)(11)\cos 35^\circ \approx 40.83\), so \(c \approx 6.39\). Then using the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{8\sin 35^\circ}{6.39} \approx 0.7181\), which yields \(\angle A \approx 45.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(a = 15\), \(b = 8\), and \(\angle C = 115^\circ\), find the measure of \(\angle A\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find side \(c\): \(c^2 = 15^2 + 8^2 - 2(15)(8)\cos 115^\circ = 289 - 240(-0.4226) \approx 390.43\), so \(c \approx 19.76\). Then \(\sin A = \frac{15\sin 115^\circ}{19.76} \approx 0.6880\), giving acute angle \(\angle A \approx 43.5^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(a = 7\), \(b = 9\), and \(c = 14\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), given \(a = 36\), \(b = 48\), and \(\angle C = 65^\circ\), find the length of side \(c\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(c^2 = 36^2 + 48^2 - 2(36)(48)\cos 65^\circ = 3600 - 3456(0.4226) \approx 2139.43\). Taking the square root gives \(c \approx 46.3\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta PQR\), given \(p = 7\), \(q = 8\), and \(r = 12\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle R\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos R = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 12^2}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{-31}{112} \approx -0.2768\). Therefore, \(\angle R = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{31}{112}\right) \approx 106.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(b = 6\), \(c = 9\), and \(\angle A = 52^\circ\), find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A = 6^2 + 9^2 - 2(6)(9)\cos 52^\circ \approx 117 - 66.491 = 50.509\). Taking the square root gives \(a \approx 7.1\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 5\), \(b = 7\), and \(c = 9\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \frac{5^2 + 7^2 - 9^2}{2(5)(7)} = \frac{-7}{70} = -0.1\). Taking the inverse cosine yields \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.1) \approx 95.7^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 4\), \(b = 5\), and \(c = 8\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines for the largest angle: \(\cos C = \frac{4^2 + 5^2 - 8^2}{2(4)(5)} = \frac{-23}{40} = -0.575\). Hence, \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(-0.575) \approx 125.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta XYZ\), given \(x = 6\), \(y = 8\), and \(z = 7\), find the measure of \(\angle X\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: Apply the Law of Cosines: \(\cos X = \frac{y^2 + z^2 - x^2}{2yz} = \frac{8^2 + 7^2 - 6^2}{2(8)(7)} = \frac{77}{112} = 0.6875\). Thus, \(\angle X = \cos^{-1}(0.6875) \approx 46.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 7\), \(b = 9\), and \(c = 13\), find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle A\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side \(a=7\). By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos A = \frac{9^2 + 13^2 - 7^2}{2(9)(13)} = \frac{201}{234} \approx 0.8590\), giving \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{67}{78}\right) \approx 30.8^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(b = 10\), \(c = 6\), and \(\angle A = 65^\circ\), find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find side \(a\): \(a^2 = 10^2 + 6^2 - 2(10)(6)\cos 65^\circ \approx 85.286 \implies a \approx 9.235\). Then use the Law of Sines: \(\sin C = \frac{c \sin A}{a} = \frac{6 \sin 65^\circ}{9.235} \approx 0.5888\), so \(\angle C = \sin^{-1}(0.5888) \approx 36.1^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 8\), \(b = 14\), and \(\angle C = 35^\circ\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle B\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find side \(c\): \(c^2 = 8^2 + 14^2 - 2(8)(14)\cos 35^\circ \approx 76.510 \implies c \approx 8.747\). Find the acute angle \(\angle A\) using the Law of Sines: \(\sin A = \frac{8 \sin 35^\circ}{8.747} \approx 0.5246 \implies \angle A \approx 31.6^\circ\). Then \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 31.6^\circ = 113.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 13.5\), \(b = 18.2\), and \(c = 24.6\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 15\), \(b = 20\), and \(\angle C = 118^\circ\), find the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 124.6^\circ\), \(b = 1350\), and \(c = 2140\). Find the length of side \(a\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle KLM\), \(\angle M = 106.5^\circ\), \(k = 1280\), and \(l = 1960\). Find the length of side \(m\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle DEF\), \(\angle D = 48.7^\circ\), \(e = 2150\), and \(f = 3420\). Find the length of side \(d\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(\angle Q = 138.2^\circ\), \(p = 1145\), and \(r = 1680\). Find the length of side \(q\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle XYZ\), \(\angle Y = 62.4^\circ\), \(x = 1820\), and \(z = 2450\). Find the length of side \(y\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle KLM\), \(\angle K = 115.8^\circ\), \(l = 1840\), and \(m = 2750\). Find the perimeter of \(\triangle KLM\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(p = 2450\), \(q = 3180\), and \(r = 4620\). Find the measure of the largest angle. Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle R\) opposite the longest side \(r\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos R = \frac{2450^2 + 3180^2 - 4620^2}{2(2450)(3180)} = \frac{-5229500}{15582000} \approx -0.3356\), so \(\angle R = \arccos(-0.3356) \approx 109.6^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle A = 52.0^\circ\), \(b = 1450\), and \(c = 850\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, find side \(a = \sqrt{1450^2 + 850^2 - 2(1450)(850)\cos(52^\circ)} \approx 1143.4\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{850\sin(52^\circ)}{1143.4} \approx 0.5858\), so \(\angle C = \arcsin(0.5858) \approx 35.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle STU\), \(\angle S = 132.4^\circ\), \(t = 12450\), and \(u = 18600\). Find the length of side \(s\). Round to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle DEF\), \(\angle D = 34.5^\circ\), \(e = 2400\), and \(f = 1500\). Find the measure of \(\angle E\). Round to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, find \(d = \sqrt{2400^2 + 1500^2 - 2(2400)(1500)\cos(34.5^\circ)} \approx 1440.9\). Using the Law of Cosines to avoid the ambiguous sine case, \(\cos E = \frac{1440.9^2 + 1500^2 - 2400^2}{2(1440.9)(1500)} \approx -0.3317\), giving \(\angle E = \arccos(-0.3317) \approx 109.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle XYZ\), \(x = 2460\), \(y = 1580\), and \(z = 1950\). Find the measure of \(\angle X\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 1420\), \(b = 1980\), and \(c = 2450\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle DEF\), \(d = 2150\), \(e = 1680\), and \(f = 2840\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle F\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(p = 1820\), \(q = 2540\), and \(r = 1360\). Find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle R\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle KLM\), \(k = 1150\), \(l = 1720\), and \(m = 2310\). Find the measure of \(\angle L\), rounded to one decimal place.

In \(\triangle PQR\), \(p = 14200\), \(q = 19500\), and \(r = 26800\). Find the difference between the measure of the largest angle and the measure of the smallest angle, rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, the largest angle is \(\angle R = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{14200^2 + 19500^2 - 26800^2}{2(14200)(19500)}\right) \approx 104.3^\circ\) and the smallest angle is \(\angle P = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{19500^2 + 26800^2 - 14200^2}{2(19500)(26800)}\right) \approx 30.9^\circ\), giving a difference of \(104.25^\circ - 30.90^\circ \approx 73.4^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 1600\), \(c = 850\), and \(\angle B = 32.0^\circ\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle A\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: First, find side \(b = \sqrt{1600^2 + 850^2 - 2(1600)(850)\cos 32^\circ} \approx 987.8\). Since \(a\) is the longest side, \(\angle A\) is obtuse and \(\cos A = \frac{987.8^2 + 850^2 - 1600^2}{2(987.8)(850)} \approx -0.51312\), so \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}(-0.51312) \approx 120.9^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(b = 1250\), \(c = 1840\), and \(\angle A = 58.0^\circ\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\), rounded to one decimal place.
qs.s: First find \(a = \sqrt{1250^2 + 1840^2 - 2(1250)(1840)\cos 58^\circ} \approx 1584.4\), then use the Law of Cosines: \(\cos C = \frac{1584.4^2 + 1250^2 - 1840^2}{2(1584.4)(1250)} \approx 0.17353\), so \(\angle C \approx 80.0^\circ\).

qs.q: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 15240\), \(b = 21350\), and \(c = 28600\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), rounded to one decimal place.
In \(\triangle ABC\), \(a = 3280\), \(b = 4520\), and \(\angle C = 118.4^\circ\). Find the length of side \(c\), rounded to one decimal place.

exercises.name: Solve Triangle Choosing Sines or Cosines

qs.q: Solve for the length of side \(b\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 120^\circ, a = 6, c = 10\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = 6^2 + 10^2 - 2(6)(10)\cos 120^\circ = 36 + 100 - 120(-0.5) = 196\). Taking the square root gives \(b = 14\).

qs.q: Solve for the length of side \(a\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 120^\circ, b = 7, c = 8\).
qs.s: Because two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), begin with the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A = 7^2 + 8^2 - 2(7)(8)\cos 120^\circ = 49 + 64 - 112(-0.5) = 169\). Taking the square root gives \(a = 13\).

qs.q: Solve for the length of side \(c\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle C = 60^\circ, a = 5, b = 8\).
qs.s: With SAS given, use the Law of Cosines to find side \(c\): \(c^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 25 + 64 - 80(0.5) = 49\). Taking the square root yields \(c = 7\).

qs.q: Solve for the length of side \(b\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 120^\circ, a = 5, c = 16\).
qs.s: Applying the Law of Cosines for the SAS configuration gives \(b^2 = 5^2 + 16^2 - 2(5)(16)\cos 120^\circ = 25 + 256 - 160(-0.5) = 361\). Thus, \(b = \sqrt{361} = 19\).

qs.q: Solve for the length of side \(a\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 60^\circ, b = 9, c = 24\).
qs.s: Substitute the given values into the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = 9^2 + 24^2 - 2(9)(24)\cos 60^\circ = 81 + 576 - 432(0.5) = 441\). Taking the square root yields \(a = 21\).

qs.q: Using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution, find the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\), given \(\angle A = 120^\circ, b = 11\), and \(c = 24\).
qs.s: First find side \(a\) using the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = 11^2 + 24^2 - 2(11)(24)\cos 120^\circ = 121 + 576 + 264 = 961\), so \(a = 31\). The perimeter is then \(P = a + b + c = 31 + 11 + 24 = 66\).

qs.q: Using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution, find the length of side \(a\) in \(\Delta ABC\), given \(\angle A = 30^\circ, \angle B = 105^\circ\), and \(c = 4\sqrt{2}\).
qs.s: Find the third angle first: \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (30^\circ + 105^\circ) = 45^\circ\). Using the Law of Sines, \(\frac{a}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{\sin 45^\circ}\), which simplifies to \(a = \frac{4\sqrt{2} \cdot (1/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 4\).

qs.q: Using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution, find the length of side \(c\) in \(\Delta ABC\), given \(\angle A = 45^\circ, \angle B = 75^\circ\), and \(a = 6\sqrt{2}\).
qs.s: Find the remaining angle: \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (45^\circ + 75^\circ) = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{c}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sin 45^\circ}\), so \(c = \frac{6\sqrt{2} \cdot (\sqrt{3}/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 6\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution, find the measure of the largest angle in \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 7, b = 8\), and \(c = 13\).
qs.s: Since three sides are given (SSS), the Law of Sines cannot be used to begin; apply the Law of Cosines for the largest angle opposite \(c = 13\): \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{-56}{112} = -\frac{1}{2}\), which gives \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution, find the measure of \(\angle A\) in \(\Delta ABC\), given \(a = 7, b = 3\), and \(c = 8\).
qs.s: Because all three sides are known, solve for \(\angle A\) using the Law of Cosines: \(\cos A = \frac{3^2 + 8^2 - 7^2}{2(3)(8)} = \frac{24}{48} = \frac{1}{2}\). Therefore, \(\angle A = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 36^\circ, \angle B = 48^\circ, c = 15.4\). Find the length of side \(a\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: First find \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 36^\circ - 48^\circ = 96^\circ\), then apply the Law of Sines: \(a = \frac{15.4 \sin 36^\circ}{\sin 96^\circ} \approx 9.1\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 115^\circ, b = 6.4, c = 9.1\). Find the length of side \(a\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines with \(\cos 115^\circ \approx -0.4226\), \(a = \sqrt{6.4^2 + 9.1^2 - 2(6.4)(9.1)\cos 115^\circ} = \sqrt{123.77 + 49.23} \approx 13.2\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 52^\circ, \angle C = 71^\circ, a = 8.6\). Find the length of side \(c\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines for the AAS case, \(c = \frac{8.6 \sin 71^\circ}{\sin 52^\circ} \approx 10.3\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle C = 44^\circ, a = 7.5, b = 11.2\). Find the length of side \(c\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for the SAS case, \(c = \sqrt{7.5^2 + 11.2^2 - 2(7.5)(11.2) \cos 44^\circ} = \sqrt{181.69 - 120.85} \approx 7.8\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 63^\circ, \angle C = 39^\circ, a = 12.8\). Find the length of side \(b\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: First find \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 63^\circ - 39^\circ = 78^\circ\), then apply the Law of Sines: \(b = \frac{12.8 \sin 63^\circ}{\sin 78^\circ} \approx 11.7\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 15.5, b = 22.4, c = 28.6\). Find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle A\) (round to the nearest tenth of a degree).
qs.s: The smallest angle is opposite side \(a\), so by the Law of Cosines, \(\cos A = \frac{22.4^2 + 28.6^2 - 15.5^2}{2(22.4)(28.6)} = \frac{1079.47}{1281.28} \approx 0.8425\), giving \(\angle A \approx 32.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 14.0, b = 19.0, c = 26.0\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\) (round to the nearest tenth of a degree).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for the largest angle in an SSS triangle, \(\cos C = \frac{14^2 + 19^2 - 26^2}{2(14)(19)} = -\frac{119}{532}\), so \(\angle C = \arccos\left(-\frac{119}{532}\right) \approx 102.9^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 124^\circ, a = 32.5, c = 44.0\). Find the measure of \(\angle A\) (round to the nearest tenth of a degree).
qs.s: First find \(b = \sqrt{32.5^2 + 44^2 - 2(32.5)(44)\cos 124^\circ} \approx 67.76\) by the Law of Cosines, then \(\angle A = \arcsin\left(\frac{32.5\sin 124^\circ}{67.76}\right) \approx 23.4^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 25^\circ, \angle B = 35^\circ, a = 125.0\). Find the length of the longest side of \(\Delta ABC\) (round to the nearest tenth).
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 25^\circ - 35^\circ = 120^\circ\), so the longest side is \(c = \frac{125.0 \sin 120^\circ}{\sin 25^\circ} \approx 256.1\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 48^\circ, b = 24.0, c = 15.0\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\) (round to the nearest tenth of a degree).
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines to find \(a = \sqrt{24^2 + 15^2 - 2(24)(15)\cos 48^\circ} \approx 17.87\), then find acute angle \(\angle C = \arcsin\left(\frac{15\sin 48^\circ}{17.87}\right) \approx 38.6^\circ\), giving \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 38.6^\circ = 93.4^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(a = 3, b = 5\), and \(c = 7\), find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\).
qs.s: With three sides given (SSS), apply the Law of Cosines for the largest angle: \(\cos C = \frac{3^2 + 5^2 - 7^2}{2(3)(5)} = \frac{9 + 25 - 49}{30} = -\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle A = 30^\circ, \angle B = 45^\circ\), and \(a = 6\), find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Since two angles and an opposite side are given (AAS), apply the Law of Sines: \(\frac{b}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{6}{\sin 30^\circ}\). Solving gives \(b = \frac{6(\sqrt{2}/2)}{1/2} = 6\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle B = 30^\circ, b = 6\), and \(c = 12\), find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\frac{\sin C}{12} = \frac{\sin 30^\circ}{6}\), so \(\sin C = \frac{12(1/2)}{6} = 1\). Therefore, \(\angle C = 90^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle A = 30^\circ, a = 4\), and \(b = 10\), determine the number of possible triangles that can be formed.
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines for the SSA case, the altitude from vertex \(C\) is \(h = b \sin A = 10\sin 30^\circ = 5\). Since side \(a = 4 < 5\), the side is too short to form a triangle, so \(0\) triangles can be formed.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle A = 60^\circ, b = 5\), and \(c = 8\), find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: Since two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), use the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 25 + 64 - 40 = 49\). Taking the square root gives \(a = 7\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle A = 60^\circ, b = 3\), and \(c = 8\), find the exact value of \(\sin B\).
qs.s: First, find side \(a\) using the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = 3^2 + 8^2 - 2(3)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 49\), so \(a = 7\). Then, use the Law of Sines to find \(\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{3\sin 60^\circ}{7} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle A = 30^\circ, a = 6\), and \(b = 6\sqrt{3}\), two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the measure of \(\angle C\) in the triangle that contains an obtuse angle.
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{6\sqrt{3}\sin 30^\circ}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), yielding the obtuse angle \(\angle B = 120^\circ\). Subtracting from \(180^\circ\) gives \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 120^\circ = 30^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle B = 60^\circ, a = 8\), and \(b = 7\), two distinct triangles can be formed. Find the longer of the two possible lengths of side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(7^2 = 8^2 + c^2 - 2(8)(c)\cos 60^\circ\), which simplifies to \(c^2 - 8c + 15 = 0\). Factoring yields \((c - 3)(c - 5) = 0\), so the longer possible length is \(c = 5\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(\angle C = 45^\circ, a = 4\sqrt{2}\), and \(b = 7\), find the exact value of \(\cos A\).
qs.s: First find side \(c\) using the Law of Cosines: \(c^2 = (4\sqrt{2})^2 + 7^2 - 2(4\sqrt{2})(7)\cos 45^\circ = 32 + 49 - 56 = 25\), so \(c = 5\). Then apply the Law of Cosines again to obtain \(\cos A = \frac{7^2 + 5^2 - (4\sqrt{2})^2}{2(7)(5)} = \frac{42}{70} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(a = 7, b = 8\), and \(c = 13\), find the exact value of \(\sin A\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines on the largest side gives \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 120^\circ\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{a\sin C}{c} = \frac{7\sin 120^\circ}{13} = \frac{7\sqrt{3}}{26}\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(b\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 60^\circ, a = 5, c = 8\).
qs.s: Since two sides and the included angle (SAS) are given, begin with the Law of Cosines: \(b^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 25 + 64 - 40 = 49\), which gives \(b = 7\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(c\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle C = 60^\circ, a = 7, b = 15\).
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Cosines for SAS: \(c^2 = 7^2 + 15^2 - 2(7)(15)\cos 60^\circ = 49 + 225 - 105 = 169\), which gives \(c = 13\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(b\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 60^\circ, a = 3, c = 5\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for the SAS configuration, \(b^2 = 3^2 + 5^2 - 2(3)(5)\cos 60^\circ = 9 + 25 - 15 = 19\), so \(b = \sqrt{19}\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(a\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 60^\circ, \angle B = 45^\circ, b = 6\).
qs.s: Apply the Law of Sines for AAS: \(\frac{a}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{6}{\sin 45^\circ}\), giving \(a = \frac{6(\sqrt{3}/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = \frac{6\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = 3\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(c\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 30^\circ, \angle C = 45^\circ, a = 8\).
qs.s: With two angles and a non-included side (AAS) given, begin with the Law of Sines: \(\frac{c}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{8}{\sin 30^\circ}\). Solving yields \(c = \frac{8(\sqrt{2}/2)}{1/2} = 8\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve for the measure of angle \(A\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 13, b = 7, c = 15\).
qs.s: Apply the Law of Cosines for SSS: \(\cos A = \frac{7^2 + 15^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(15)} = \frac{274 - 169}{210} = \frac{105}{210} = \frac{1}{2}\), which corresponds to \(\angle A = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve for the measure of the largest angle in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 7, b = 8, c = 13\).
qs.s: Since three sides (SSS) are given, begin with the Law of Cosines to find the angle opposite the longest side: \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{113 - 169}{112} = -\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 120^\circ, a = 7, c = 8\). What is the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\)?
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines to find side \(b\): \(b^2 = 7^2 + 8^2 - 2(7)(8)\cos 120^\circ = 113 - 112(-1/2) = 169\), so \(b = 13\). The perimeter is \(a + b + c = 7 + 13 + 8 = 28\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(a\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 45^\circ, \angle B = 75^\circ, c = 6\).
qs.s: First calculate the third angle \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (45^\circ + 75^\circ) = 60^\circ\), then apply the Law of Sines: \(\frac{a}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{6}{\sin 60^\circ}\) to obtain \(a = \frac{6(\sqrt{2}/2)}{\sqrt{3}/2} = 2\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Solve for side \(b\) in \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 45^\circ, a = 4\sqrt{2}, c = 7\).
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines for SAS: \(b^2 = (4\sqrt{2})^2 + 7^2 - 2(4\sqrt{2})(7)\cos 45^\circ = 32 + 49 - 56\sqrt{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) = 81 - 56 = 25\), yielding \(b = 5\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta PQR\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(p = 6.8\), \(q = 9.4\), and \(r = 11.2\). Find the measure of \(\angle Q\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines to begin, \(\cos Q = \frac{p^2 + r^2 - q^2}{2pr} = \frac{6.8^2 + 11.2^2 - 9.4^2}{2(6.8)(11.2)} = \frac{83.32}{152.32} \approx 0.5470\). Taking the inverse cosine gives \(\angle Q \approx 56.8^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta DEF\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(d = 7.4\), \(e = 11.6\), and \(f = 9.2\). Find the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle D\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for the angle opposite the shortest side, \(\cos D = \frac{e^2 + f^2 - d^2}{2ef} = \frac{11.6^2 + 9.2^2 - 7.4^2}{2(11.6)(9.2)} = \frac{164.44}{213.44} \approx 0.7704\). Thus, \(\angle D = \cos^{-1}(0.7704) \approx 39.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 11.4\), \(b = 13.7\), and \(c = 7.5\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for angle \(C\), \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \frac{11.4^2 + 13.7^2 - 7.5^2}{2(11.4)(13.7)} = \frac{261.40}{312.36} \approx 0.8369\), which yields \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}(0.8369) \approx 33.2^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 8.5\), \(b = 12.8\), and \(c = 10.4\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Beginning with the Law of Cosines for side \(b\), \(\cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2ac} = \frac{8.5^2 + 10.4^2 - 12.8^2}{2(8.5)(10.4)} = \frac{16.57}{176.8} \approx 0.0937\). Therefore, \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}(0.0937) \approx 84.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 13.8\), \(b = 9.5\), and \(c = 7.6\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle A\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Since all three sides are known (SSS), begin with the Law of Cosines to find the largest angle: \(\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc} = \frac{9.5^2 + 7.6^2 - 13.8^2}{2(9.5)(7.6)} = \frac{-42.43}{144.4} \approx -0.2938\), which gives \(\angle A = \cos^{-1}(-0.2938) \approx 107.1^\circ\).

qs.q: Three communication towers \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) form a triangle with distances \(a = 380\text{ km}\), \(b = 620\text{ km}\), and \(c = 450\text{ km}\). Determine the appropriate trigonometric law to begin solving the triangle, and find the measure of the angle at tower \(B\) (\(\,\angle B\)) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: Because all three distances are given (SSS), begin with the Law of Cosines: \(\cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2ac} = \frac{380^2 + 450^2 - 620^2}{2(380)(450)} = \frac{-37500}{342000} \approx -0.1096\). Thus, \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}(-0.1096) \approx 96.3^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 125\), \(b = 168\), and \(c = 94\). Find the difference between the measure of the largest angle and the measure of the smallest angle, rounded to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle B = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{125^2 + 94^2 - 168^2}{2(125)(94)}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-3763}{23500}\right) \approx 99.2^\circ\), and the smallest angle is \(\angle C = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{125^2 + 168^2 - 94^2}{2(125)(168)}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{35013}{42000}\right) \approx 33.5^\circ\). The difference is \(99.2^\circ - 33.5^\circ = 65.7^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 210\), \(b = 175\), and \(c = 295\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: The largest angle is \(\angle C\) opposite side \(c = 295\): \(\cos C = \frac{210^2 + 175^2 - 295^2}{2(210)(175)} = \frac{-12300}{73500} = -\frac{41}{245} \approx -0.1673\). Evaluating \(\cos^{-1}(-0.1673)\) gives \(\angle C \approx 99.6^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 15.2\), \(b = 24.5\), and \(c = 18.6\). Complete the solution of the triangle to find the measure of the remaining intermediate angle, \(\angle C\), to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: First, find the largest angle using the Law of Cosines: \(\cos B = \frac{15.2^2 + 18.6^2 - 24.5^2}{2(15.2)(18.6)} \approx -0.0411\), so \(\angle B \approx 92.4^\circ\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{15.2 \sin 92.4^\circ}{24.5} \approx 0.6199\), so \(\angle A \approx 38.3^\circ\); therefore, \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 92.4^\circ - 38.3^\circ = 49.3^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 16.4\), \(b = 21.8\), and \(c = 12.6\). Following the standard procedure of solving an SSS triangle completely by finding the largest angle first, find the measure of \(\angle A\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.
qs.s: First, find the largest angle using the Law of Cosines: \(\cos B = \frac{16.4^2 + 12.6^2 - 21.8^2}{2(16.4)(12.6)} \approx -0.1150\), so \(\angle B \approx 96.6^\circ\). Next, use the Law of Sines to find \(\angle A\): \(\sin A = \frac{16.4 \sin 96.6^\circ}{21.8} \approx 0.7473\), giving \(\angle A \approx 48.4^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle B = 45^\circ\), \(a = 6\), and \(b = 6\sqrt{2}\), find the measure of \(\angle A\).
qs.s: Since two sides and an opposite angle are given (SSA), begin with the Law of Sines: \(\sin A = \frac{a\sin B}{b} = \frac{6\sin 45^\circ}{6\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\). Because \(a < b\), \(\angle A < 45^\circ\), so \(\angle A = 30^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 45^\circ\), \(\angle B = 30^\circ\), and \(a = 6\sqrt{2}\), find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Since two angles and a non-included side are given (AAS), begin with the Law of Sines: \(b = \frac{a\sin B}{\sin A} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}\sin 30^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} = 6\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle B = 120^\circ\), \(a = 7\), and \(c = 8\), find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Since two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), begin with the Law of Cosines: \(b^2 = 7^2 + 8^2 - 2(7)(8)\cos 120^\circ = 113 - 112\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 169\), so \(b = 13\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(a = 7\), \(b = 15\), and \(c = 13\), find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for SSS, \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 15^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(15)} = \frac{105}{210} = \frac{1}{2}\), which corresponds to \(\angle C = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 60^\circ\), \(b = 16\), and \(c = 21\), find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: Beginning with the Law of Cosines for SAS, \(a^2 = 16^2 + 21^2 - 2(16)(21)\cos 60^\circ = 697 - 336 = 361\), which simplifies to \(a = 19\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 60^\circ\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 5\), find the exact value of \(\sin B\).
qs.s: First, use the Law of Cosines to find side \(a = \sqrt{8^2 + 5^2 - 2(8)(5)\cos 60^\circ} = 7\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{8\sin 60^\circ}{7} = \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{7}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 30^\circ\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 8\sqrt{3}\), find the larger of the two possible lengths for side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{8\sqrt{3}\sin 30^\circ}{8} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), giving \(\angle B = 60^\circ\) or \(120^\circ\). The acute case \(\angle B = 60^\circ\) yields \(\angle C = 90^\circ\), resulting in the larger length \(c = \frac{8}{\sin 30^\circ} = 16\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 45^\circ\), \(\angle B = 75^\circ\), and \(c = 6\sqrt{2}\), find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: First find the third angle \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (45^\circ + 75^\circ) = 60^\circ\). Then apply the Law of Sines: \(a = \frac{c\sin A}{\sin C} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{6}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = 4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 45^\circ, \angle B = 30^\circ,\) and \(a = 6\sqrt{2}\). Find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines for AAS, \(\frac{b}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sin 45^\circ}\), which simplifies to \(b = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 6\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(b = 5, c = 8,\) and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\). Find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for SAS, \(a^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 25 + 64 - 40 = 49\), so \(a = 7\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 3, b = 5,\) and \(c = 7\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for SSS, \(\cos C = \frac{3^2 + 5^2 - 7^2}{2(3)(5)} = -\frac{15}{30} = -\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 120^\circ, \angle B = 30^\circ,\) and \(b = 4\). Find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\frac{a}{\sin 120^\circ} = \frac{4}{\sin 30^\circ}\), which yields \(a = \frac{4(\sqrt{3}/2)}{1/2} = 4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 110^\circ, a = 8,\) and \(b = 11\). How many valid triangles can be formed?
qs.s: Because \(\angle A\) is obtuse, side \(a\) must be the longest side of the triangle; since \(a = 8 < 11 = b\), no valid triangle can be formed.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 45^\circ, \angle B = 105^\circ,\) and \(a = 4\). Find the length of side \(c\).
qs.s: First, find \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (45^\circ + 105^\circ) = 30^\circ\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\frac{c}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{4}{\sin 45^\circ}\), yielding \(c = \frac{4(1/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 2\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 8, b = 15,\) and \(c = 13\). Find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Cosines for SSS, \(\cos C = \frac{8^2 + 15^2 - 13^2}{2(8)(15)} = \frac{120}{240} = \frac{1}{2}\), which yields \(\angle C = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 7, b = 8,\) and \(\angle C = 120^\circ\). Find the length of side \(c\).

Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 30^\circ, a = 6,\) and \(b = 6\sqrt{3}\). If \(\angle B\) is obtuse, find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{6\sqrt{3}\sin 30^\circ}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Since \(\angle B\) is obtuse, \(\angle B = 120^\circ\), giving \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 120^\circ = 30^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 2\sqrt{3}, b = 2,\) and \(\angle C = 30^\circ\). Find the measure of \(\angle A\).
qs.s: First, find side \(c\) using the Law of Cosines: \(c^2 = (2\sqrt{3})^2 + 2^2 - 2(2\sqrt{3})(2)\cos 30^\circ = 4\), so \(c = 2\). Since \(b = c = 2\), \(\angle B = \angle C = 30^\circ\), which gives \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 30^\circ = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle B = 30^\circ, b = 3,\) and \(a = 6\), find the length of side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{a\sin B}{b} = \frac{6\sin 30^\circ}{3} = 1\), which gives \(\angle A = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle C = 60^\circ\). Then \(c = \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} = \sqrt{36 - 9} = 3\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle C = 60^\circ, a = 5,\) and \(b = 8\), find the length of side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 89 - 40 = 49\). Taking the positive square root gives \(c = 7\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 45^\circ, \angle B = 60^\circ,\) and \(a = 4\sqrt{2}\), find the length of side \(b\).
qs.s: Using the Law of Sines, \(\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}\), so \(b = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{3}/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 4\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 45^\circ, a = 4,\) and \(b = 4\sqrt{2}\), find the measure of \(\angle B\).
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\sin 45^\circ}{4} = 1\). Since \(\sin B = 1\), the only possible angle is \(\angle B = 90^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(a = 3, b = 5,\) and \(c = 7\), find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \frac{9 + 25 - 49}{2(3)(5)} = -\frac{15}{30} = -\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 120^\circ, \angle B = 30^\circ,\) and \(a = 18\), find the exact perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\).
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 30^\circ = 30^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(b = c = \frac{18\sin 30^\circ}{\sin 120^\circ} = \frac{9}{\sqrt{3}/2} = 6\sqrt{3}\), so the perimeter is \(18 + 6\sqrt{3} + 6\sqrt{3} = 18 + 12\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle B = 60^\circ, a = 1 + \sqrt{3},\) and \(c = 2\), find the measure of \(\angle C\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(b^2 = (1+\sqrt{3})^2 + 2^2 - 2(1+\sqrt{3})(2)\cos 60^\circ = 6\), so \(b = \sqrt{6}\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{c\sin B}{b} = \frac{2(\sqrt{3}/2)}{\sqrt{6}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), giving \(\angle C = 45^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 120^\circ, b = 12,\) and \(c = 20\), find the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 12^2 + 20^2 - 2(12)(20)\cos 120^\circ = 544 - 480\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 784\), so \(a = 28\). The perimeter is \(a + b + c = 28 + 12 + 20 = 60\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution. Given \(\angle A = 30^\circ, a = 6,\) and \(b = 6\sqrt{3}\), and that \(\angle B\) is obtuse, find the length of side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{6\sqrt{3}(1/2)}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\angle B = 120^\circ\) since it is obtuse. Then \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 120^\circ = 30^\circ\), and since \(\angle C = \angle A\), side \(c = a = 6\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 1.0\), \(b = 1.6\), and \(\angle C = 60^\circ\). Find the length of side \(c\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines for SAS, \(c^2 = 1.0^2 + 1.6^2 - 2(1.0)(1.6)\cos 60^\circ = 1.00 + 2.56 - 1.60 = 1.96\). Taking the square root yields \(c = 1.4\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 0.3\), \(b = 0.5\), and \(c = 0.7\). Find the measure of the largest angle, \(\angle C\).
qs.s: Since all three sides are known (SSS), begin with the Law of Cosines: \(\cos C = \frac{0.3^2 + 0.5^2 - 0.7^2}{2(0.3)(0.5)} = \frac{0.09 + 0.25 - 0.49}{0.30} = -\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, \(\angle C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(b = 0.5\), \(c = 0.8\), and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\). Find the length of side \(a\).
qs.s: Given two sides and the included angle (SAS), use the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = 0.5^2 + 0.8^2 - 2(0.5)(0.8)\cos 60^\circ = 0.25 + 0.64 - 0.40 = 0.49\). Taking the square root gives \(a = 0.7\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 0.5\), \(b = 0.7\), and \(c = 0.8\). Find the measure of \(\angle B\).
qs.s: With three sides given (SSS), apply the Law of Cosines: \(\cos B = \frac{0.5^2 + 0.8^2 - 0.7^2}{2(0.5)(0.8)} = \frac{0.25 + 0.64 - 0.49}{0.80} = \frac{1}{2}\). Therefore, \(\angle B = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(b = 0.7\), \(c = 0.8\), and \(\angle A = 120^\circ\). Find the length of side \(a\).

Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(b = 3\), \(c = 8\), and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\). Find the side length \(a\), and then determine the exact value of \(\sin B\).
qs.s: First, the Law of Cosines gives \(a^2 = 3^2 + 8^2 - 2(3)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 49\), so \(a = 7\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{3\sin 60^\circ}{7} = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{14}\).

qs.q: Two ships leave port at the same time along straight paths that form an angle of \(60^\circ\). After one hour, Ship A has traveled \(16\text{ km}\) and Ship B has traveled \(10\text{ km}\). Determine the appropriate trigonometric law and find the straight-line distance between the two ships.
qs.s: Model the scenario with SAS where \(b = 16\), \(c = 10\), and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(a^2 = 16^2 + 10^2 - 2(16)(10)\cos 60^\circ = 256 + 100 - 160 = 196\), so \(a = 14\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(a = 5\), \(b = 8\), and \(\angle C = 60^\circ\). Find the length of side \(c\), and then determine the exact value of \(\cos A\).
qs.s: First, the Law of Cosines gives \(c^2 = 5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 60^\circ = 89 - 40 = 49\), so \(c = 7\). Next, applying the Law of Cosines again for angle \(A\) yields \(\cos A = \frac{8^2 + 7^2 - 5^2}{2(8)(7)} = \frac{88}{112} = \frac{11}{14}\).

qs.q: Two lookout stations, \(A\) and \(B\), are separated by \(12\text{ km}\). Both stations spot a smoke plume at point \(C\). Station \(A\) measures \(\angle CAB = 30^\circ\) and station \(B\) measures \(\angle CBA = 105^\circ\). Determine the appropriate trigonometric law and calculate the distance from station \(B\) to the plume (side \(a\)).
qs.s: The third angle is \(\angle C = 180^\circ - (30^\circ + 105^\circ) = 45^\circ\). By the Law of Sines, \(\frac{a}{\sin 30^\circ} = \frac{12}{\sin 45^\circ}\), giving \(a = \frac{12(1/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 6\sqrt{2}\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: given \(a = 7\), \(b = 8\), and \(c = 13\). First find the largest angle, \(\angle C\), then use the Law of Sines to find the exact value of \(\sin A\).
qs.s: By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = -\frac{56}{112} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 120^\circ\). Then, by the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{7\sin 120^\circ}{13} = \frac{7(\sqrt{3}/2)}{13} = \frac{7\sqrt{3}}{26}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 45^\circ, b = 2, c = \sqrt{2}\). What is the exact length of side \(a\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Sines to find \(\sin C = \frac{c \sin 45^\circ}{b} = \frac{\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}/2)}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\), giving \(\angle C = 30^\circ\) since \(c < b\). Then \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 30^\circ = 105^\circ\), and \(a = \frac{b \sin 105^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{2((\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{2})/4)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = \sqrt{3} + 1\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 75^\circ, b = \sqrt{6}, c = 2\). What is the measure of \(\angle B\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Cosines to find \(a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos 75^\circ = 6 + 4 - 4\sqrt{6}\left(\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\right) = 4 + 2\sqrt{3} = (\sqrt{3}+1)^2\), so \(a = \sqrt{3}+1\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{2 \sin 75^\circ}{\sqrt{3}+1} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \implies \angle C = 45^\circ\), giving \(\angle B = 180^\circ - 75^\circ - 45^\circ = 60^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle C = 30^\circ, a = \sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}, b = 2\sqrt{2}\). What is the exact length of side \(c\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Cosines: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cos 30^\circ = (8 - 4\sqrt{3}) + 8 - 2(\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2})(2\sqrt{2})\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 16 - 4\sqrt{3} - (12 - 4\sqrt{3}) = 4\). Taking the positive square root gives \(c = 2\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = \sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}, b = 2\sqrt{2}, c = 2\sqrt{3}\). What is the measure of \(\angle B\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Cosines to find the largest angle: \(\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \frac{(8-4\sqrt{3}) + 8 - 12}{8\sqrt{3}-8} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 120^\circ\). Then use the Law of Sines to find \(\sin B = \frac{b \sin 120^\circ}{c} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{3}/2)}{2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), which yields \(\angle B = 45^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 45^\circ, a = 2, b = \sqrt{3} - 1\). What is the exact length of side \(c\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Sines to find \(\sin B = \frac{b \sin A}{a} = \frac{(\sqrt{3}-1)(\sqrt{2}/2)}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\), which gives \(\angle B = 15^\circ\) since \(b < a\). Then \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 15^\circ = 120^\circ\), so \(c = \frac{a \sin 120^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{2(\sqrt{3}/2)}{\sqrt{2}/2} = \sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 75^\circ, a = 2\sqrt{2}, c = 6 - 2\sqrt{3}\). What is the perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\)?
qs.s: Use the Law of Sines: \(\sin C = \frac{(6-2\sqrt{3})\sin 75^\circ}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 60^\circ\) since \(c < a\). Then \(\angle B = 45^\circ\), giving \(b = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\sin 45^\circ}{\sin 75^\circ} = 2\sqrt{6} - 2\sqrt{2}\), and the perimeter is \(a + b + c = 2\sqrt{2} + (2\sqrt{6}-2\sqrt{2}) + (6-2\sqrt{3}) = 6 + 2\sqrt{6} - 2\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle A = 105^\circ, b = 2\sqrt{6}, c = 2\sqrt{3}\). What is the exact length of side \(a\)?
qs.s: Begin with the Law of Cosines: \(a^2 = (2\sqrt{6})^2 + (2\sqrt{3})^2 - 2(2\sqrt{6})(2\sqrt{3})\cos 105^\circ = 36 - 24\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{6}}{4}\right) = 24 + 12\sqrt{3}\). Factoring yields \(a^2 = 6(4 + 2\sqrt{3}) = 6(\sqrt{3}+1)^2\), so \(a = \sqrt{6}(\sqrt{3}+1) = 3\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 135^\circ, a = 4, c = 2\sqrt{6} + 2\sqrt{2}\). What is the measure of \(\angle C\)?
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines: \(b^2 = 16 + (32+16\sqrt{3}) - 2(4)(2\sqrt{6}+2\sqrt{2})\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 64 + 32\sqrt{3} = (4\sqrt{3}+4)^2\), so \(b = 4\sqrt{3}+4\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin C = \frac{c \sin 135^\circ}{b} = \frac{(2\sqrt{6}+2\sqrt{2})(\sqrt{2}/2)}{4(\sqrt{3}+1)} = \frac{1}{2}\), giving \(\angle C = 30^\circ\) since \(\angle B\) is obtuse.

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(\angle B = 60^\circ, a = 2\sqrt{6}, c = 3\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}\). What is the measure of \(\angle C\)?
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines: \(b^2 = 24 + (24+12\sqrt{3}) - 2(2\sqrt{6})(3\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{6})\cos 60^\circ = 48 + 12\sqrt{3} - (12\sqrt{3}+12) = 36\), so \(b = 6\). By the Law of Sines, \(\sin A = \frac{2\sqrt{6}\sin 60^\circ}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \implies \angle A = 45^\circ\) (since \(a < b\)), giving \(\angle C = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 45^\circ = 75^\circ\).

qs.q: Solve \(\Delta ABC\) using either the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines to begin the solution: \(a = 2\sqrt{2}, b = 2\sqrt{6} + 2\sqrt{2}, c = 6 + 2\sqrt{3}\). What is the measure of the smallest angle, \(\angle A\)?
qs.s: Use the Law of Cosines on the largest side \(c\): \(\cos C = \frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab} = \frac{8 + (32+16\sqrt{3}) - (48+24\sqrt{3})}{16(1+\sqrt{3})} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\angle C = 120^\circ\). Then by the Law of Sines, \(\sin B = \frac{b \sin 120^\circ}{c} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \implies \angle B = 45^\circ\), leaving \(\angle A = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 45^\circ = 15^\circ\).

qs.q: A drone flies 30 km from a base station at a direction of \(50^\circ\) from due east, and then turns and flies 80 km at a direction of \(170^\circ\) from due east. How far is the drone from the base station?
qs.s: The interior angle between the two flight paths is \(180^\circ - (170^\circ - 50^\circ) = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the distance is \(\sqrt{30^2 + 80^2 - 2(30)(80)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{4900} = 70\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A cargo ship steams 70 km from port at a direction of \(20^\circ\) from due east and then changes course and steams 80 km at a direction of \(80^\circ\) from due east. How far is the ship from the port?
qs.s: The interior angle between the ship's legs is \(180^\circ - (80^\circ - 20^\circ) = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the distance from port is \(\sqrt{70^2 + 80^2 - 2(70)(80)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{16900} = 130\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A private plane flies 60 km from an airfield at a direction of \(45^\circ\) from due east and then flies 100 km at a direction of \(105^\circ\) from due east. How far is the plane from the airfield?
qs.s: The interior angle between the two flight legs is \(180^\circ - (105^\circ - 45^\circ) = 120^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, the distance is \(\sqrt{60^2 + 100^2 - 2(60)(100)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{19600} = 140\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A rescue helicopter flies 90 km from its station at a direction of \(130^\circ\) from due east and then travels 240 km at a direction of \(250^\circ\) from due east. How far is the helicopter from the station?
qs.s: The interior angle between the two flight paths is \(180^\circ - (250^\circ - 130^\circ) = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the distance is \(\sqrt{90^2 + 240^2 - 2(90)(240)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{44100} = 210\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A plane flies 150 km from point P at a direction of \(40^\circ\) from due east and then travels 250 km at a direction of \(100^\circ\) from due east. How far is the plane from point P?
qs.s: The interior angle between the two legs is \(180^\circ - (100^\circ - 40^\circ) = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the distance from point P is \(\sqrt{150^2 + 250^2 - 2(150)(250)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{122500} = 350\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A cargo plane flies 200 km from an airbase at a direction of \(40^\circ\) from due east, and then flies 320 km at a direction of \(160^\circ\) from due east to reach a delivery outpost. From the outpost, the plane flies directly back to the airbase. What is the total distance flown by the plane for the entire round trip?
qs.s: The interior angle between the first two legs is \(180^\circ - (160^\circ - 40^\circ) = 60^\circ\), giving a return leg distance of \(\sqrt{200^2 + 320^2 - 2(200)(320)\cos 60^\circ} = 280\text{ km}\). The total round-trip distance is \(200 + 320 + 280 = 800\text{ km}\).

qs.q: An airplane flies 450 km from city A at a direction of \(110^\circ\) from due east, and then flies 750 km at a direction of \(170^\circ\) from due east to reach city B. If the plane then flies directly back from city B to city A at an average speed of \(350\text{ km/h}\), how many hours will the return flight take?
qs.s: The interior angle of the flight path is \(180^\circ - (170^\circ - 110^\circ) = 120^\circ\), so the return distance is \(\sqrt{450^2 + 750^2 - 2(450)(750)\cos 120^\circ} = 1050\text{ km}\). The flight time back to city A is \(1050 / 350 = 3\text{ hours}\).

qs.q: Two airplanes depart from the same airport at the same time. The first plane flies at an average speed of \(360\text{ km/h}\) at a direction of \(15^\circ\) from due east, while the second plane flies at an average speed of \(600\text{ km/h}\) at a direction of \(135^\circ\) from due east. How far apart are the two planes after 30 minutes?
qs.s: After \(0.5\text{ h}\), the planes have traveled \(180\text{ km}\) and \(300\text{ km}\) respectively, with an included angle of \(135^\circ - 15^\circ = 120^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, the distance between them is \(\sqrt{180^2 + 300^2 - 2(180)(300)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{176400} = 420\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two ships, Alpha and Beta, leave the same harbor. Ship Alpha departs at 12:00 PM and sails at a constant speed of \(30\text{ km/h}\) at a direction of \(30^\circ\) from due east. Ship Beta departs at 1:00 PM and sails at a constant speed of \(75\text{ km/h}\) at a direction of \(150^\circ\) from due east. How far apart are the two ships at 3:00 PM?
qs.s: At 3:00 PM, Alpha has traveled \(30 \times 3 = 90\text{ km}\) and Beta has traveled \(75 \times 2 = 150\text{ km}\), separated by an angle of \(150^\circ - 30^\circ = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the separation distance is \(\sqrt{90^2 + 150^2 - 2(90)(150)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{44100} = 210\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A jet flies 560 km from point A at a direction of \(125^\circ\) from due east, and then flies 640 km at a direction of \(185^\circ\) from due east to reach point B. How many kilometers shorter is the direct flight from point A to point B than the two-leg route?
qs.s: The interior angle is \(180^\circ - (185^\circ - 125^\circ) = 120^\circ\), which yields a direct distance of \(\sqrt{560^2 + 640^2 - 2(560)(640)\cos 120^\circ} = 1040\text{ km}\). The difference in distance compared to the two-leg route (\(560 + 640 = 1200\text{ km}\)) is \(1200 - 1040 = 160\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two cargo ships leave a harbor at 1:00 pm. One ship travels due west at 25 km/h, while the other travels at 80 km/h in the direction \(\text{S } 30^\circ\text{ E}\). How far apart are the two ships at 3:00 pm?
qs.s: After 2 hours, the ships travel \(50\text{ km}\) and \(160\text{ km}\), and the angle between West and \(\text{S } 30^\circ\text{ E}\) is \(90^\circ + 30^\circ = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{50^2 + 160^2 - 2(50)(160)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{28100 + 8000} = 190\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two motorboats leave the same dock at 1:00 pm. One boat travels due west at 35 km/h, and the other travels at 40 km/h in the direction \(\text{N } 30^\circ\text{ E}\). How far apart are the two boats at 3:00 pm?
qs.s: After 2 hours, the boats have traveled \(70\text{ km}\) and \(80\text{ km}\), and the angle between due West and \(\text{N } 30^\circ\text{ E}\) is \(90^\circ + 30^\circ = 120^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{70^2 + 80^2 - 2(70)(80)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{11300 + 5600} = 130\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two airplanes leave an airport at 8:00 am. One flies due north at 300 km/h, while the other flies in the direction \(\text{N } 60^\circ\text{ E}\) at 480 km/h. How far apart are the planes at 8:30 am?
qs.s: In 0.5 hours, the planes cover \(150\text{ km}\) and \(240\text{ km}\) with an included angle of \(60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{150^2 + 240^2 - 2(150)(240)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{80100 - 36000} = 210\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two rescue helicopters leave a base at 7:00 am. Helicopter A flies due south at 30 km/h, and Helicopter B flies at 80 km/h in the direction \(\text{S } 60^\circ\text{ W}\). How far apart are the helicopters at 9:00 am?
qs.s: After 2 hours, the helicopters have traveled \(60\text{ km}\) and \(160\text{ km}\) with an angle of \(60^\circ\) between their paths. By the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{60^2 + 160^2 - 2(60)(160)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{29200 - 9600} = 140\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two ships leave port at 1:00 pm. Ship A sails due south at 30 km/h, while Ship B sails in the direction \(\text{N } 60^\circ\text{ W}\). At 3:00 pm, the two ships are 140 km apart. What is the speed of Ship B?
qs.s: In 2 hours, Ship A travels \(60\text{ km}\), Ship B travels \(2v\text{ km}\), and the angle between South and \(\text{N } 60^\circ\text{ W}\) is \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(140^2 = 60^2 + (2v)^2 - 2(60)(2v)\cos 120^\circ \implies 4v^2 + 120v - 16000 = 0\), which factors as \((v-50)(v+80) = 0\), giving \(v = 50\text{ km/h}\).

qs.q: An airplane leaves an airfield and flies 250 km on a bearing of \(040^\circ\). It then changes course and flies 400 km on a bearing of \(160^\circ\). How far is the airplane from its starting airfield?
qs.s: The aircraft turns by \(160^\circ - 40^\circ = 120^\circ\), so the interior angle of the triangle is \(180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the direct distance is \(d = \sqrt{250^2 + 400^2 - 2(250)(400)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{222500 - 100000} = 350\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two patrol ships leave a harbor at the same time. Ship Alpha travels in the direction \(\text{N } 35^\circ\text{ E}\) at 20 km/h, while Ship Beta travels in the direction \(\text{S } 85^\circ\text{ E}\) at 32 km/h. After 2.5 hours, Ship Alpha drops anchor, and Ship Beta immediately changes course to sail directly toward Ship Alpha at 35 km/h. How many hours will it take Ship Beta to reach Ship Alpha?
qs.s: After 2.5 hours, Alpha has sailed \(50\text{ km}\) and Beta has sailed \(80\text{ km}\) with an included angle of \(180^\circ - 35^\circ - 85^\circ = 60^\circ\), giving a separation of \(\sqrt{50^2 + 80^2 - 2(50)(80)\cos 60^\circ} = 70\text{ km}\). Traveling at \(35\text{ km/h}\), Ship Beta requires \(70 / 35 = 2\text{ hours}\) to reach Ship Alpha.

qs.q: Two planes leave an airport. Plane A leaves at 7:00 am traveling due east at 200 km/h. Plane B leaves the same airport at 8:00 am traveling at 500 km/h in the direction \(\text{N } 30^\circ\text{ E}\). How far apart are the two planes at 11:00 am?
qs.s: At 11:00 am, Plane A has traveled \(200 \times 4 = 800\text{ km}\) and Plane B has traveled \(500 \times 3 = 1500\text{ km}\), with an included angle of \(90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{800^2 + 1500^2 - 2(800)(1500)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{2890000 - 1200000} = 1300\text{ km}\).

qs.q: At 1:00 pm, two search planes leave a base. Plane A flies in the direction \(\text{N } 40^\circ\text{ W}\) at 300 km/h and lands at an outpost at 2:00 pm. Plane B flies in the direction \(\text{S } 80^\circ\text{ W}\) at 400 km/h and continues flying until 3:00 pm. How far apart are the two planes at 3:00 pm?
qs.s: Plane A traveled for 1 hour (\(300\text{ km}\)) and stopped, while Plane B traveled for 2 hours (\(800\text{ km}\)), with an included angle of \(180^\circ - 40^\circ - 80^\circ = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, \(d = \sqrt{300^2 + 800^2 - 2(300)(800)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{730000 - 240000} = 700\text{ km}\).

qs.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram meet at an angle of \(120^\circ\) and have lengths of 2 cm and 7 cm. What is the length of the smaller diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The smaller diagonal lies opposite the acute angle \(180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, its length is \(\sqrt{2^2 + 7^2 - 2(2)(7)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{4 + 49 - 14} = \sqrt{39}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram meet at an angle of \(60^\circ\) and have lengths of 5 m and 8 m. What is the length of the larger diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The larger diagonal lies opposite the supplementary angle \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). Applying the Law of Cosines gives \(\sqrt{5^2 + 8^2 - 2(5)(8)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{25 + 64 + 40} = \sqrt{129}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram meet at an angle of \(60^\circ\) and have lengths of 7 m and 8 m. What is the length of the larger diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The larger diagonal is opposite the obtuse angle \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). Using the Law of Cosines, the diagonal length is \(\sqrt{7^2 + 8^2 - 2(7)(8)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{49 + 64 + 56} = \sqrt{169} = 13\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram meet at an angle of \(60^\circ\) and have lengths of 4 cm and 6 cm. What is the length of the larger diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The angle opposite the larger diagonal is \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the length is \(\sqrt{4^2 + 6^2 - 2(4)(6)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{16 + 36 + 24} = \sqrt{76} = 2\sqrt{19}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram meet at an angle of \(60^\circ\) and have lengths of 3 cm and 5 cm. What is the length of the larger diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: Consecutive angles in a parallelogram are supplementary, so the larger diagonal lies opposite the angle \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the length of the larger diagonal is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 5^2 - 2(3)(5)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{9 + 25 + 15} = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram have lengths of 6 cm and 10 cm and intersect at an angle of \(60^\circ\). What is the length of the shorter side of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The diagonals bisect each other into segments of 3 cm and 5 cm, and the shorter side lies opposite the acute angle \(60^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the shorter side is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 5^2 - 2(3)(5)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{9 + 25 - 15} = \sqrt{19}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The perimeter of a parallelogram is 42 cm, and one of its sides has a length of 5 cm. If two adjacent sides meet at an angle of \(60^\circ\), what is the length of the larger diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: The adjacent side has length \(\frac{42}{2} - 5 = 16\text{ cm}\), and the larger diagonal lies opposite the supplementary angle \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\). By the Law of Cosines, the larger diagonal is \(\sqrt{5^2 + 16^2 - 2(5)(16)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{25 + 256 + 80} = \sqrt{361} = 19\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, adjacent sides have lengths \(AB = 8\text{ cm}\) and \(BC = 6\text{ cm}\), and \(\angle B = 60^\circ\). If \(M\) is the midpoint of side \(BC\), what is the length of segment \(AM\)?
qs.s: Since \(M\) is the midpoint of \(BC\), \(BM = 3\text{ cm}\) in triangle \(ABM\). By the Law of Cosines, \(AM = \sqrt{8^2 + 3^2 - 2(8)(3)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{64 + 9 - 24} = \sqrt{49} = 7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Two ships leave the same port at the same time. Ship A travels at \(6\text{ km/h}\) and Ship B travels at \(10\text{ km/h}\) along straight paths that diverge at an angle of \(120^\circ\). What is the straight-line distance between the two ships after 2 hours?
qs.s: After 2 hours, the ships have traveled 12 km and 20 km, respectively. Using the Law of Cosines, the distance between them is \(\sqrt{12^2 + 20^2 - 2(12)(20)\cos 120^\circ} = \sqrt{144 + 400 + 240} = \sqrt{784} = 28\text{ km}\).

qs.q: A parallelogram has adjacent sides of lengths 7 cm and 8 cm, and its larger diagonal has a length of 13 cm. What is the length of the smaller diagonal of the parallelogram?
qs.s: Applying the Law of Cosines gives \(\cos\theta = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so the obtuse angle is \(120^\circ\) and the adjacent acute angle is \(60^\circ\). The smaller diagonal is then \(\sqrt{7^2 + 8^2 - 2(7)(8)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{49 + 64 - 56} = \sqrt{57}\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Three circular gears with radii of \(1\text{ cm}\), \(5\text{ cm}\), and \(9\text{ cm}\) touch each other externally. Determine the measure of the largest angle in the triangle formed by joining their centres.
qs.s: The lengths of the sides joining the centres are \(6\text{ cm}\), \(10\text{ cm}\), and \(14\text{ cm}\). Using the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{6^2 + 10^2 - 14^2}{2(6)(10)} = \frac{-60}{120} = -\frac{1}{2}\), yielding \(C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Three circular pulleys of radius \(2\text{ cm}\), \(3\text{ cm}\), and \(10\text{ cm}\) are mounted so that they are mutually tangent to each other externally. What is the largest interior angle of the triangle formed by connecting their centres?
qs.s: The distances between the centres are \(2+3=5\text{ cm}\), \(2+10=12\text{ cm}\), and \(3+10=13\text{ cm}\). Applying the Law of Cosines for the largest angle yields \(\cos C = \frac{5^2 + 12^2 - 13^2}{2(5)(12)} = \frac{0}{120} = 0\), so the angle is \(90^\circ\).

qs.q: Three circular coins of radius \(1\text{ cm}\), \(2\text{ cm}\), and \(3\text{ cm}\) lie flat on a table such that each coin touches the other two externally. Find the largest angle of the triangle formed by joining their centres.
qs.s: The sides of the triangle connecting the centres are \(1+2=3\text{ cm}\), \(1+3=4\text{ cm}\), and \(2+3=5\text{ cm}\). By the Law of Cosines, the largest angle \(C\) satisfies \(\cos C = \frac{3^2 + 4^2 - 5^2}{2(3)(4)} = \frac{0}{24} = 0\), which gives \(C = 90^\circ\).

qs.q: Three cylindrical pipes with radii of \(1\text{ cm}\), \(6\text{ cm}\), and \(7\text{ cm}\) are bundled tightly together so that each touches the other two. Find the largest angle of the triangle formed by connecting the centres of their cross-sections.
qs.s: The side lengths connecting the centres are \(7\text{ cm}\), \(8\text{ cm}\), and \(13\text{ cm}\). By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2(7)(8)} = \frac{-56}{112} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so the largest angle is \(120^\circ\).

qs.q: Three circular friction rollers with radii of \(3\text{ cm}\), \(5\text{ cm}\), and \(12\text{ cm}\) are positioned so that they are externally tangent to one another. Find the largest angle of the triangle formed by joining their centres.
qs.s: The sides between the centres are \(3+5=8\text{ cm}\), \(3+12=15\text{ cm}\), and \(5+12=17\text{ cm}\). By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{8^2 + 15^2 - 17^2}{2(8)(15)} = \frac{0}{240} = 0\), which gives \(C = 90^\circ\).

qs.q: Three circular metal discs with radii of \(2\text{ cm}\), \(9\text{ cm}\), and \(22\text{ cm}\) are placed on a flat workbench so that each disc is externally tangent to the other two. Find the largest angle of the triangle formed by connecting their centres.
qs.s: The side lengths joining the centres are \(11\text{ cm}\), \(24\text{ cm}\), and \(31\text{ cm}\). By the Law of Cosines, \(\cos C = \frac{11^2 + 24^2 - 31^2}{2(11)(24)} = \frac{697 - 961}{528} = -\frac{264}{528} = -\frac{1}{2}\), which corresponds to \(C = 120^\circ\).

qs.q: Three mutually tangent circles have radii of \(x\text{ cm}\), \((x + 4)\text{ cm}\), and \((x + 8)\text{ cm}\). If the largest angle of the triangle formed by joining their centres is \(120^\circ\), find the perimeter of this triangle.
qs.s: The sides are \(2x+4\), \(2x+8\), and \(2x+12\). Using the Law of Cosines gives \((2x+12)^2 = (2x+4)^2 + (2x+8)^2 + (2x+4)(2x+8)\), which reduces to \(8x^2 + 24x - 32 = 0\), yielding \(x = 1\). The perimeter is \((2x+4) + (2x+8) + (2x+12) = 6(1) + 24 = 30\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Three circular storage tanks have radii of \(6\text{ m}\), \(14\text{ m}\), and \(15\text{ m}\). They are positioned on flat ground such that each is tangent to the other two. Find the largest angle of the triangle formed by connecting the centres of their bases.
qs.s: The side lengths between the tank centres are \(6+14=20\text{ m}\), \(6+15=21\text{ m}\), and \(14+15=29\text{ m}\). Applying the Law of Cosines gives \(\cos C = \frac{20^2 + 21^2 - 29^2}{2(20)(21)} = \frac{841 - 841}{840} = 0\), so the largest angle is \(90^\circ\).

qs.q: Three mutually tangent circles have radii of \(x\text{ cm}\), \((x + 5)\text{ cm}\), and \((x + 6)\text{ cm}\). If the largest angle of the triangle formed by joining their centres is \(120^\circ\), find the radius of the largest circle.
qs.s: The triangle's sides are \(2x+5\), \(2x+6\), and \(2x+11\); using the Law of Cosines with \(\cos 120^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}\) gives \((2x+11)^2 = (2x+5)^2 + (2x+6)^2 + (2x+5)(2x+6)\), which simplifies to \(8x^2 + 22x - 30 = 0\), so \(x = 1\). The largest radius is \(x + 6 = 1 + 6 = 7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Three externally tangent circles have radii of \(x\text{ cm}\), \((x + 1)\text{ cm}\), and \((x + 8)\text{ cm}\). If the largest angle of the triangle formed by joining their centres is \(90^\circ\), find the value of \(x\).
qs.s: The sides of the triangle are \(a = 2x+1\), \(b = 2x+8\), and \(c = 2x+9\). Using the Law of Cosines with \(C = 90^\circ\), \((2x+9)^2 = (2x+1)^2 + (2x+8)^2\), which simplifies to \(4x^2 = 16\), giving \(x = 2\).

qs.s: Convert the time to years, \(t = \frac{104}{52} = 2\text{ years}\), and substitute into \(A = P(1 + rt)\). This yields \(A = 8400(1 + 0.042 \times 2) = 8400(1.084) = \$9105.60\).

qs.q:
Find the future value of the loan using simple interest.
\(P = \$3600\), \(r = 6.5\%\), \(t = 156\text{ weeks}\)
qs.s: Convert the time to years, \(t = \frac{156}{52} = 3\text{ years}\), and compute the future value using \(A = P(1 + rt)\). This gives \(A = 3600(1 + 0.065 \times 3) = 3600(1.195) = \$4302\).
